Command line: sysreport-search latency (asks first; --yes starts at once). Results: a table (block size, time in ns, level) and a curve.

For the bandwidth of the RAM and the caches, see 9.11 Cache & Memory. The newer benchmarks - SRS Pi, Crypto, Prime Sieve, the Benchmark history, Cache & Memory, Storage, OS Latency, CPU Compute, Everyday Work, Network and the three GPU tests - are in 9.7 to 9.19.

9.5 Device ID Lookup

In plain words: every PCI and USB device has a number pair: vendor ID : device ID (for example 1002:7550 = AMD : Radeon RX 9070 series). This tool turns the numbers into names.

Open: Ctrl+L, Menu -> Device ID Lookup..., the Tools page -> Lookup..., or double-click an ID on any tab or panel. In the classic view also Menu -> Tools and the Lookup panel's ID Lookup button.

Controls:

  • ID - type the ID and press Enter or Lookup. Formats: VVVV, VVVV:DDDD, VVVV:DDDD:SSSS:ssss (with subsystem vendor and device), and an optional :RR revision at the end, e.g. 1002:7550:1EAE:7550:C0.
  • PCI / USB - which list to search.
  • Mode tick box - cycles through three modes, like SIV:
    • Tree - "bsearch() of a sorted table": loads the whole hwdata list once, then finds the ID instantly. Tries the most specific key first and falls back step by step.
    • Scan - reads the .ids file line by line. Slower, same answer; useful to check.
    • Info - asks the operating system's own device database (systemd-hwdb) instead of the file.

Output: each key tried (the matching one is marked <), then Vendor, Subsystem (if any), Stock (the plain device name) and Resolved (the best name found), and how long it took.

9.6 Find (search a full system report)

In plain words: search a saved full system report (made by SRS Full System Report, 13.3) for any text, like grep, with highlighting.

Open: Ctrl+Shift+F or Menu -> Find in System Report... in the main window, the Tools page -> Find..., or the menu entry's "Find in System Report" action. In the classic view: Ctrl+F or Menu -> Tools -> Find in Report....

Controls:

Control Meaning
Match What to search for. A regular expression (Python-style) unless Literal is ticked. Press Enter or Find.
Ignore case Upper and lower case count as the same.
Literal Search for the exact text; characters like . [ ( have no special meaning.
Highlight Matches Colour each match (also Ctrl+H or the Highlight button).
Max Show at most this many matches per report file (default 20).
Report The report folder to search. Filled with the newest one in ~/sysreports.
Browse... / Latest Pick another folder / go back to the newest.
Next / Prev (or F3 / Shift+F3) Jump between matches.
Colour Choose the highlight colour (saved).
Lookup Open Device ID Lookup.

If there is no report yet, Find tells you to run SRS Full System Report first.

9.7 SRS Pi

In plain words: SRS works out pi to many decimal places and checks every digit. The time shows how fast one core does heavy number work; a wrong digit means the PC made a mistake (often an unstable overclock or memory). Open: the Benchmarks & stress page -> SRS Pi..., or Menu -> Tools -> SRS Pi... in the classic view. On the command line: sysreport-search pi --digits 1m. Controls: Digits (128 thousand to 32 million; each choice shows the time it took on the author's PC), SuperPi sizes (tick for SuperPi's power-of-two digit counts: 16K = 16,384 ... 1M = 1,048,576 ... 32M = 33,554,432), Method (Chudnovsky = fast, can use threads; Gauss-Legendre / AGM = the method SuperPi uses, one thread), Threads (default 1, for a single-thread score), Run and Stop. Run asks first, with the expected time, the threads and the memory it needs; from 8 million digits, or with all threads, it warns about unstable overclocks and No is the default answer. On the command line it asks the same; --yes starts at once. While it runs the status line shows the time so far and the current step (series, division, square root). Closing the window also stops it.

Times are SRS Pi times, not SuperPi times. SuperPi's "1M" is 1,048,576 digits; SRS's 1 million is 1,000,000 - tick SuperPi sizes for the same digit counts as SuperPi. 32 million digits takes several minutes and 1-2 GB of memory.

9.8 Crypto

In plain words: how fast the CPU encrypts (AES-128) and fingerprints (SHA-256) data, with and without its built-in crypto instructions (AES-NI, SHA-NI). Open: the Benchmarks & stress page -> Crypto.... Command line: sysreport-search crypto. Controls: Threads (right-hand column; the left column is always one thread), Seconds per measurement (default 1; about 8 seconds in all), Run (asks first; with all threads - the default - every CPU thread is 100% busy, so No is the default answer). The official FIPS test vectors are checked before every run. On the command line it asks the same; --yes starts at once.

9.9 Prime Sieve

In plain words: counts the prime numbers up to 100 million, 1 billion, 10 billion or 100 billion and checks the count. Simple integer and cache work that scales with threads. Open: the Benchmarks & stress page -> Prime Sieve.... Command line: sysreport-search prime --limit 1e10. Controls: Count primes up to, Threads (default all), Run (asks first; from 10 billion or with all threads - the defaults - it warns about unstable overclocks and No is the default answer), Stop. On the command line it asks the same; --yes starts at once.

9.10 Benchmark history

Every SRS Pi, Crypto, Prime Sieve, Cache & Memory, Storage, OS Latency, CPU Compute, Everyday Work, Network, GPU Benchmark, GPU Burnin and GPU Compute comparison run adds a line to ~/.cache/srs/bench-history.tsv (time, test, settings, result, build). The Benchmark history tab on the Benchmarks & stress page shows it, newest first. Compare only lines with the same settings and the same Build: a package built for any x86-64 CPU (-march=x86-64 -O2) can score well below a build made for your own CPU (-march=native -O3) - for example SRS Pi 1 million digits 3.1 s vs 2.1 s on a 7800X3D.

9.11 Cache & Memory

In plain words: how fast the RAM and the L1, L2 and L3 caches read, write and copy, and how long they take to answer. Use it after a BIOS, EXPO/XMP or memory-timing change. Open: the Benchmarks & stress page -> Cache & Memory..., or Menu -> Tools -> Cache & Memory... in the classic view. Command line: sysreport-search cachemem. Controls: Threads (default all; the bandwidth results need all of them), Seconds per test (default 1), Run (asks first: every thread and the memory bus are busy for about 20 seconds), Stop. The status line names the value being measured. A stopped run shows the values it finished and says so.

Close other programs first and never run another benchmark at the same time (SRS lets only one run; it cannot stop other programs). The base clock is measured, so boards with a raised reference clock (for example 105 MHz) show the real value; the Infinity Fabric clock needs the ryzen_smu driver (Ryzen 7000 desktop); memory speed and type need root data (Tools > Collect root data). The engine is the one from Linux System Audit (LSA) 0.2.0, which is now part of SRS. x86-64 CPUs only.

9.12 Storage

In plain words: how fast the drive that holds a folder you choose reads and writes - big files, many small pieces at once, and one small piece at a time (how snappy it feels) - plus the response time of single reads and writes. It uses its own temporary test file only; your files are never touched, and nothing is left behind, even if SRS is stopped or crashes. Open: the Benchmarks & stress page -> Storage..., or Menu -> Tools -> Storage Benchmark... in the classic view. Command line: sysreport-search storage --dir FOLDER. Controls: Folder (the line below it names the drive, its connection, the file system and the free space - never the serial number), Test file (256 MB, 1 GB, 4 GB, 16 GB), Seconds per test (default 5), Standard / Light (Light uses at most 4 threads), Allow USB drives (off by default), Run (asks first), Stop.

Folders in RAM (/tmp on many systems is RAM, not a drive), on the network or on FUSE are refused, as is a drive with too little free space. Drive health (SMART) is on the Storage page.

9.13 OS Latency

In plain words: how quickly the operating system answers a program: how long a basic request to the kernel takes (a system call), how fast it switches between two programs (a context switch), how long it takes to start a thread or a program, how soon a sleeping program wakes up, how late a timer fires, and what a new page of memory or a small file costs. Lower is better. Steady numbers (95% and 99% close to the median) mean a smooth, responsive desktop. Open: the Benchmarks & stress page -> OS Latency..., or Menu -> Tools -> OS Latency... in the classic view. Command line: sysreport-search os-latency. Controls: Samples (1,000-200,000, default 20,000; the slower tests use a tenth or less), Tick test (s) (1-30, default 3: how long a 1 ms timer is watched), Run (asks first), Stop. It takes about 6 seconds at the defaults and keeps only one or two CPUs busy, never all of them.

What the numbers mean. Each row is one test, measured many times: Median is the typical time, 95% and 99% mean 19 in 20 and 99 in 100 tries were this fast or faster, Worst and Best are the extremes, and the sample count is shown. Times are in ns (billionths of a second), µs (millionths) and ms (thousandths). Below the table SRS names the CPU scheduler in use (for example scx_lavd under sched_ext, BORE or EEVDF), the preemption mode, the timer tick (CONFIG_HZ), the clock source, the timer slack, transparent huge pages, the CPUs used and the file system of the test folder. Typical values on a current desktop: a system call 35-70 ns, a switch between two programs 1-2 µs, starting a thread about 10 µs, starting a program about 150 µs, a wake-up about 2 µs. Sleeps and the 1 ms tick run about 50 µs late, which is Linux's default timer slack. Hundreds of µs or missed ticks point to deep power-saving states, heavy background work or a busy scheduler.

Safety: it only reads system settings - no root, and no scheduler, priority or timer change. The file test works in its own temporary folder in ~/.cache/srs, which is removed at the end, after Stop, and (if SRS was killed) on the next run. The result is saved to ~/.cache/srs/bench-os-latency.txt and added to the Benchmark history. Tested on one PC only - see the note at the start of this chapter.

9.14 CPU Compute

In plain words: how fast the processor does floating-point number crunching - the kind of maths in 3D, video, science and AI programs. Six kinds of work: matrix multiply (SGEMM in single and DGEMM in double precision), peak multiply-add (the most sums the CPU can do), FFT (splitting a signal into frequencies), N-body (gravity between 1,024 stars), Mandelbrot (a fractal picture) and a small ray tracer (a picture with shadows and reflections). Each runs on one thread and then on all threads at once. Higher is better. Every answer is checked against a known result: a wrong answer is shown as WRONG in red instead of a score, which points to an unstable overclock or undervolt. Open: the Benchmarks & stress page -> CPU Compute..., or Menu -> Tools -> CPU Compute... in the classic view. Command line: sysreport-search compute. Controls: Threads (default all), Seconds per test (default 0.5), Code (the best instruction set the CPU has - SSE2, AVX2 or AVX-512 - or a chosen one), 1 thread only (skips the all-threads column: light load, half the time), Run (asks first), Stop. It takes about 10 seconds at the defaults.

What the numbers mean. GFLOPS = billions of floating-point operations per second (matrix multiply, multiply-add, FFT, N-body); Mpixels/s = millions of picture points per second (Mandelbrot, ray tracer). The left column is one thread, the right column all the chosen threads; the Code column says which instruction set was used. FFT and the ray tracer are plain C. The numbers compare PCs and settings with each other; they are lower than a tuned maths library (BLAS) would reach.

Safety: with all threads, every CPU is 100% busy and gets hot, and AVX-512 draws a lot of power: an unstable overclock or undervolt can crash the PC under this load. Tick 1 thread only (command line --single) to keep it light. It will not start while CPU Burnin or Stress runs. The result is saved to ~/.cache/srs/bench-compute.txt and added to the Benchmark history. Tested on one PC only - see the note at the start of this chapter.

9.15 Everyday Work

In plain words: how fast the PC does the work it does all day: compressing and unpacking files (with the zlib, zstd, lz4 and xz libraries your system has), sorting numbers and words, checksums and hashes (CRC32, CRC32C, xxHash64, FNV-1a - the fingerprints used to spot damaged files), searching and checking text (finding words, checking JSON and UTF-8 text) and running a small program in an interpreter (like a script language does). Each test runs on one thread and on all threads. Higher is better. Every result is checked (unpacked data must equal the original, sorted lists must be in order and complete, checksums must match known values), so a wrong answer is reported instead of a fast number. Open: the Benchmarks & stress page -> Everyday Work..., or Menu -> Tools -> Everyday Work... in the classic view. Command line: sysreport-search work. Controls: Threads (default all), Seconds per test (default 0.5), 1 thread only, the test groups (Compression, Sorting, Checksums and hashes, Text processing, Bytecode interpreter) and the compression libraries (zlib, zstd, lz4, xz) as tick boxes, Run (asks first, with the expected time - about half a minute at the defaults), Stop.

What the numbers mean. MB/s for compression (million bytes of original data per second, 1 MB = 1,000,000 bytes) with the ratio (2.5 = the data became 2.5 times smaller) on text-like, record-like and random data; Mkeys/s for sorting (million items per second); GB/s for checksums and text (billion bytes per second); Mops/s for the interpreter (million instructions per second). A library that is not installed shows "not installed"; the rest still runs.

Safety: the test data is generated by SRS from fixed seeds (every run and every PC does the same work); none of your files are read or written, only the result is saved. With all threads every CPU is 100% busy, and xz -6 and zstd -19 use about 100 MB of memory per thread (fewer threads are used, with a note, when memory is short). The result is saved to ~/.cache/srs/bench-work.txt, and each test group adds a line to the Benchmark history. Tested on one PC only - see the note at the start of this chapter.

9.16 Network

In plain words: two separate tests. On this computer sends data between two programs on your own PC through the loopback connection (127.0.0.1): it shows how fast Linux and the CPU can move network data, and how long a message takes to go there and back. Nothing leaves the computer, and the network card is not involved. Internet speed test (optional) measures your real connection with Cloudflare's public speed test server (speed.cloudflare.com): how long a name lookup takes (DNS), how long it takes to connect, and your download and upload speed with one and with several connections at once. Open: the Benchmarks & stress page -> Network..., or Menu -> Tools -> Network Benchmark... in the classic view. Command line: sysreport-search net (loopback) and sysreport-search net --internet. Controls: On this computer (loopback) (ticked), Internet speed test (asks first) (not ticked), Streams (connections at once for the "N streams" tests, default 4), Seconds per test (default 5), IPv4 or IPv6 / IPv4 only / IPv6 only (internet test), Run, Stop. The line under the controls names the connection (wired, Wi-Fi, VPN ...), its link speed and whether libcurl is installed - never an address.

Asking first. Run asks before the loopback test (about 20 seconds, a few CPUs busy). The internet test asks separately, with No as the default answer, and says which server it contacts, what it measures, how long it takes and how much data it may use - up to about 1000 MB with the standard settings (each of the four speed tests stops after 5 seconds or 250 MB; about 250 MB on a 100 Mbit/s line). Do not run it on a metered or mobile connection. The server sees your public IP address, as with any web page; SRS does not show or save it. It never runs without that Yes. The speed rows need libcurl (installed on almost every Linux system); without it only the lookup and connect times are measured.

What the numbers mean. Mbit/s = million bits per second (internet speeds are sold in Mbit/s; divide by 8 for MB/s). Average counts from the first byte received; peak is the best half second. ms = thousandths of a second, µs = millionths. Median = the middle value, 99% under = all but the slowest 1%, jitter = how much the time changes from one try to the next, lost = UDP packets that never arrived. Internet results vary with the time of day, Wi-Fi, other traffic and the server.

Safety and privacy: no IP address, MAC address, Wi-Fi network name or host name is shown or saved; only the IP version used. The result is saved to ~/.cache/srs/bench-net.txt and added to the Benchmark history. Tested on one PC on a wired connection only - see the note at the start of this chapter.

9.17 GPU Benchmark

In plain words: how fast your graphics card (GPU) does sums and moves data. It runs short pieces of work on the GPU through Vulkan (the graphics and compute interface that every modern Linux GPU driver offers - the same one many games use) and checks every answer, so a wrong answer is reported instead of a fast number. Higher is better, except for the latency row, where lower is better. Open: the Benchmarks & stress page -> GPU Benchmark..., or Menu -> Tools -> GPU Benchmark... in the classic view. Command line: sysreport-search gpu. Controls: GPU (Default = the first discrete graphics card; open the list to pick another - SRS reads the list only when you open it), Seconds per test (default 1), Memory test size (0 = auto, 256 MiB on most cards), Run (asks first), Stop. The line under the controls says whether Vulkan is installed.

What it measures.

  • FP32, FP16, FP64 multiply-add - floating-point maths (numbers with a decimal point) at three precisions: FP32 (single precision) is what games and most GPU programs use, FP16 (half precision) is used by AI and some effects, FP64 (double precision) by science programs. In GFLOPS - billions of operations per second. Most gaming cards do FP64 at only a small fraction of their FP32 speed; that is normal. A card or driver without FP16 or FP64 says "not supported".
  • INT32 multiply-add - whole-number maths, in GIOPS (billions per second).
  • Video memory read, write and copy - how fast the GPU uses its own memory, in GB/s (1 GB = 1,000,000,000 bytes).
  • Upload and Download - how fast data moves between the system memory and the graphics card, over the PCIe slot, in GB/s.
  • Dispatch latency - how long the GPU takes to answer an empty piece of work, in µs (millionths of a second); lower is better.

On a GPU built into the processor (integrated graphics) the memory rows measure the system RAM it shares, and the page says so.

Reading the result. Compare runs on the same PC, with alike SRS builds and the same graphics driver version: a driver update alone can change the numbers, and the page says which driver ran. Much lower numbers than last time usually mean heat, a power-saving setting or another program using the GPU. Upload / download well below what the slot should give can mean the card sits in a slot with fewer lanes or its link has dropped to a slower speed. A WRONG RESULT means the GPU computed something wrong - usually too much overclock or undervolt, too much heat, or a faulty card; run GPU Burnin to check.

Safety: Run asks first, naming the GPU and the time (about 15 seconds at the defaults), and says that the GPU works at full load and that an unstable GPU overclock or undervolt can crash the PC or the display driver under that load. The work is cut into pieces of about 25 ms, one at a time, so the desktop stays usable; a GPU that stops answering ends the run cleanly with the results so far; Stop ends it at once. SRS never changes clocks, voltages or fans, and keeps Vulkan overlays such as MangoHud out of the run. Vulkan is loaded when needed: without it the window says "not available" and the rest of SRS works as before. The result is saved to ~/.cache/srs/bench-gpu.txt and added to the Benchmark history. Tested on a software GPU only - see the note at the start of this chapter.

9.18 GPU Burnin

In plain words: a stress test for the graphics card, like CPU Burnin is for the processor. It keeps the GPU as busy as it can be with large matrix multiplications (big blocks of sums) for as long as you choose, and checks every single result. A healthy card gets the same answer every time; a card that is pushed too far (overclocked, undervolted, too hot, short of power) sooner or later gets one wrong. 0 errors = PASS. While it runs you see the temperatures, power, clock and fan speed live. Open: the Benchmarks & stress page -> GPU Burnin..., or Menu -> Tools -> GPU Burnin... in the classic view. Command line: sysreport-search gpu-burn. Controls: Back end (see below; Auto = Vulkan), GPU (the first GPU, All GPUs, or one from the list), Precision (FP32, or FP64 for the double-precision units), Seconds (default 60; 600-1800 s, 10-30 minutes, checks an overclock or undervolt properly), Stop at °C (default 100), Run (asks first), Stop. The line under the controls says which back ends are installed.

The four back ends, in plain words. A program can talk to a GPU in several "languages". SRS can use four of them, and you choose which:

  • Vulkan - the modern graphics and compute interface that every current GPU driver on Linux speaks (AMD, Intel and NVIDIA). Nothing extra to install. The default, and the right choice for most people.
  • ROCm / HIP - AMD's own compute platform, used by AI and science programs on AMD cards. Only there if you installed ROCm.
  • CUDA - NVIDIA's compute platform, used by most AI programs. Needs the NVIDIA driver. If your "CUDA" is really ZLUDA (a translation layer that runs CUDA programs on an AMD card), SRS notices and calls it CUDA (ZLUDA).
  • OpenCL - the older compute interface that works across makers. Every OpenCL driver you have (ROCm, Mesa Rusticl, NVIDIA, PoCL on the CPU ...) shows as its own choice.

A back end that is not installed says "not installed" with a hint about what to install; the others still work. Testing through more than one back end tells you whether a problem is the card or one particular driver.

Reading the result. PASS = no wrong result in the whole run. FAIL = at least one wrong result: errors usually mean too much overclock or undervolt, too high a temperature, a weak power supply, or a faulty card or video memory - undo the overclock or undervolt and run it again. Ended early = a safety rule stopped it (see below); the page says which. Stopped = you pressed Stop (no errors so far). The page also shows the highest edge, hotspot / junction and memory temperatures, power, clock and fan speed, the average speed in GFLOPS, the number of multiplications, the matrix size, the back end and the driver version. "not available" means the card or driver does not report that sensor (for example NVIDIA's own driver gives Linux no temperature).

Safety - what stops it by itself. Run asks first, and No is the default answer. The question says that the GPU will draw a lot of power and get hot, that a bad overclock or undervolt can crash the PC or the display driver, and that a weak power supply or poor cooling can make the PC shut down. GPU Burnin then ends by itself when:

  • the GPU reaches the temperature limit (default 100 °C; the hotspot / junction temperature when the card reports one, else the edge temperature);
  • the driver reports any error, or the GPU stops answering (device lost);
  • one piece of work takes more than 2 seconds (each should take about 20 ms);
  • you press Stop.

SRS never changes clocks, voltages or fans - it only reads them. GPU Burnin does not start while CPU Burnin / Stress or another benchmark runs, and CPU Burnin waits until it has finished. The result is saved to ~/.cache/srs/bench-gpuburn.txt and added to the Benchmark history. The idea of comparing every result with the first one comes from gpu-burn by Ville Timonen; the code is SRS's own. Tested on a software GPU only - see the note at the start of this chapter.

9.19 GPU Compute: Vulkan vs HIP vs CUDA vs OpenCL

In plain words: the same GPU work, run through every way of programming your graphics card that you have installed (the four back ends explained in 9.18), on the same card, and shown side by side. It tells you which one is fastest on your PC, and how much faster the maker's own tuned library is than a plain program. Open: the Benchmarks & stress page -> GPU Compute: Vulkan vs HIP vs CUDA vs OpenCL..., or Menu -> Tools -> GPU Compute Comparison... in the classic view. Command line: sysreport-search gpu-compare. Controls: GPU (the card, picked by its Vulkan device; the other back ends find the same card by its PCI address), a tick box per back end (only installed ones can be ticked; the tooltip of a greyed one says what to install), Seconds per test (default 1), Run (asks first), Stop.

Reading the table. Each row is a test, each column a back end:

  • Own kernel rows: SRS's own plain matrix multiplication - the same work on every back end, so these rows compare the back ends fairly.
  • Vendor library rows: the maker's tuned library - hipBLAS for ROCm, cuBLAS for CUDA, CLBlast for OpenCL. Vulkan has none, so it says "not available". These rows show what real programs that use the libraries can get.
  • Multiply-add chain, video memory copy, upload / download and kernel launch round trip (lower is better) work as in the GPU Benchmark.
  • * marks the fastest in each row. (85%) after a number means that column reached 85% of Vulkan's speed in that row (above 100% = faster than Vulkan).
  • CUDA (ZLUDA): your CUDA library is really ZLUDA, which runs CUDA programs on an AMD card. It has no NVRTC compiler, so its own-kernel rows say "not available" and only the library rows run.
  • Every OpenCL driver is its own column, for example "OpenCL (ROCm)" and "OpenCL (Rusticl)" on the same card. Drivers that run on the CPU (PoCL) are marked CPU.
  • not installed means that back end is not on this PC; the line under the table says what to install. The other columns still run.

Compare results only between alike SRS builds and the same driver and runtime versions; the page lists each column's version.

Safety: Run asks first, naming the back ends, the GPU and the time (about 20 seconds per back end at the defaults) and that the GPU works at full load; an unstable GPU overclock or undervolt can crash the PC under that load. ROCm / HIP, CUDA and OpenCL start only after your Yes. The work is cut into short pieces, a GPU that fails ends its column cleanly, Stop ends the run at once, and SRS never changes clocks, voltages or fans. The result is saved to ~/.cache/srs/bench-gpucompare.txt and added to the Benchmark history. HIP, CUDA and OpenCL were not run on real hardware by the author - see the note at the start of this chapter.

GPU words used in 9.17-9.19.

  • GPU - graphics processing unit: the graphics card, or the graphics part of the processor.
  • Back end - the "language" a program uses to talk to the GPU: Vulkan, ROCm / HIP, CUDA or OpenCL.
  • Kernel - a small program that runs on the GPU, many copies at once.
  • Matrix multiplication (GEMM) - multiplying two big tables of numbers; the core of AI and many science programs, and a hard, steady load for a GPU.
  • FP32 / FP16 / FP64 - numbers with a decimal point stored in 32, 16 or 64 bits (single, half, double precision). INT32 - 32-bit whole numbers.
  • GFLOPS - billions of floating-point operations per second; a multiply-add counts as two.
  • Hotspot / junction temperature - the hottest point measured on the GPU chip, usually 10-20 °C above the edge temperature.
  • ZLUDA - a layer that lets CUDA programs run on AMD graphics cards.
  • Lavapipe - Mesa's software Vulkan driver that runs on the CPU; used to test SRS without a real GPU.
  • Device lost - the GPU stopped answering and the driver reset it.

10. Options

Menu -> Options (in the main window's menu, the classic Menu and the tray's SRS Menu). All are saved in ~/.config/srs/SRSDEF.ini and apply at once to every open window.

Option What it does Default
Theme -> Light (SIV classic) SIV's light look and colours. classic view
Theme -> Dark Dark panels, SIV's colours brightened so they stay readable, dark graphs.
Theme -> Follow desktop Uses your desktop's light/dark setting (via xdg-desktop-portal, set by KDE Plasma and GNOME) and switches live when you change it. Without a portal, it reads GTK_THEME or ~/.config/gtk-3.0/settings.ini. main window
Update interval How often live panels refresh: Default (each panel's own rate; the classic main window every 2 s; the Overview checks and the key-fact tiles always every 3 s), 0.5, 1, 2, 3, 5 or 10 seconds, or Paused (press F5 to refresh by hand). CPU Burnin / Stress always updates every second. Default
System tray icon Show the tray icon. on
Close button hides to tray Closing the main window hides it instead of exiting. off
Minimize hides to tray (X11 / XWayland) Minimising hides it to the tray. Native Wayland apps are not told when they are minimised, so this works only on X11 / XWayland. off
Start hidden in tray Start with no window, just the tray icon. off
Start with the desktop (autostart) Writes ~/.config/autostart/srs-gui.desktop, which runs srs-gui --gui-tray at login. Untick to remove it. off
Refresh root data at boot See 5.3. off
Redact identifiers in saved reports and copied text Save Report / Save All Items, the Copy button and right-click Copy / Ctrl+C mask serial numbers, UUIDs, MAC addresses (vendor half kept), boot / machine IDs and the host name - see 17. The panels still show everything. off
Start in classic view Start SRS in the SIV-style main window instead of the window with the sidebar (6.6). off
Sortable tables in the main window Click a column heading to sort a table (6.8). Off: tables are plain text as in 2.0. on
Tab bar One row that scrolls, Wrapped rows or Side list (6.7). Main window only, like the next five. One row
Lineup Basic, Enthusiast, Expert or your own; save, export, import (6.7). Expert
Tabs on each page... Per page: the standard tabs, the ticked ones, or every item. standard
Show every item as a tab (all pages) Every item that can show something here gets a tab on its page. off
Show hidden items List the items that cannot show anything on this PC (Windows-only, not present, empty), greyed, in All N items, and do not hide their tabs. off
Check daily which items have nothing to show On: once a day, in the background, SRS reads every item to find the ones with nothing to show on this PC and hides them. Off: only when you choose Check now. Windows-only items and hardware that is not present are hidden either way. The network items and Ping are never part of the check. off
Check now which items have nothing to show Does that check once, now, in the background.
Hide to Tray Hide all SRS windows now.

Until you pick a Theme, the main window follows the desktop and the classic view starts light.

The tray options are greyed out if the tray library is not installed (the menu then says "(tray needs libayatana-appindicator)").

11. System tray

Like SIV's Icon Tray, SRS can live in the system tray (needs libayatana-appindicator; works on KDE Plasma, XFCE, and GNOME with the AppIndicator extension).

  • Tooltip: CPU temperature and load, GPU temperature and load, updated every 2 seconds.
  • Middle-click: show / hide SRS.
  • Tray menu: Show SRS / Hide to Tray, Sensors, Processors, CPU Burnin..., CPU Stress..., Benchmark..., Find..., SRS Menu (the full menu), Exit. Sensors and Processors open their page in the main window (or their panel in the classic view).
  • srs-gui --gui-tray starts hidden in the tray.
  • Safety: SRS only hides its windows if a tray icon really exists, so it cannot get lost.

13. Reports and exports

13.1 Save Report and Save All Items (SIV-format text)

  • Menu -> Save Report... (or Ctrl+S) saves SIV's default set of items as text. Default file name: srs-<hostname>.txt (srs-report.txt when Options -> Redact identifiers in saved reports is on).
  • Menu -> Save All Items... saves every one of the 558 items. Default name: srs-<hostname>-all.txt. On the author's PC this is about 52,000 lines and takes about 12 seconds.

The same from the command line (CLI-REFERENCE.md):

sysreport-search -save                         # default items to the screen
sysreport-search -save=report.txt              # ... to a file
sysreport-search '-save=[cpuid][sensors]'      # chosen items
sysreport-search '-save=[all]=everything.txt'  # every item to a file
sysreport-search '-save=[all]=share.txt' --redact   # every item, identifiers masked

File layout: a header line with program, version, host, date and the item list, then each item starting with a line [id] [category]:

srs-gui - System Report Search V2.0.0 MYPC 2026-10-25 08:18:54  [[cache][sensors]]

[cache]  [hardware]

srs-gui - Cache Levels of CPU-0 on \\MYPC - CachyOS 7.3.0-273-tkg-bore-llvm

Cache                 Size      Ways      Line        Sets       Shared by      CPUs
L1 Data Cache         32K       8         64          64         2              0,8
...

Saving a report never starts the burner or a benchmark; benchmark items show their last stored result.

13.2 Copy

Copy on any window puts its whole text on the clipboard, ready to paste into a forum post or chat.

13.3 Full System Report (srs-sysreport)

In plain words: one click writes a folder with the output of many standard Linux tools, plus an index.html page that links them, and opens it in your browser. Good for sending to someone who helps you, and it is what Find searches.

Run: the menu entry SRS Full System Report, or srs-sysreport in a terminal.

  • Output folder: ~/sysreports/sysreport-YYYYMMDD-HHMMSS/.
  • Without root: inxi, lscpu, cpuid, sensors, lspci -vvnn, lsusb -tv, GPU (DRM) info, /proc/meminfo, lsblk -O, mounts, kernel and command line, and SRS's own devices.txt (every PCI/USB device resolved to a name).
  • With one pkexec password prompt: dmidecode, decode-dimms, hwinfo --all, lshw -html and smartctl -x for each NVMe and SATA disk. If you cancel the prompt, those are skipped and a note file says so.
  • Missing tools just leave a short error in that section's file.

13.4 Device list

sysreport-search devices prints every PCI and USB device in the PC with its ID and resolved name. See CLI-REFERENCE.md.

15. Reading results and comparing runs

  • Learn what normal looks like on your PC. Open the Sensors page at idle and note the temperatures, fan speeds and voltages. Then you can spot a change later. The Overview's Is my PC OK? gives a quick verdict; the Sensors page has the numbers.
  • Minimum / Maximum columns on the Sensor status tab (the Sensors panel in the classic view) record the extremes since SRS started (or since you pressed Zero). Press Zero, play a game or run a burn-in, then look at Maximum.
  • Compare two reports: save -save=[all] before and after a change and compare them with any diff tool, for example diff -u before.txt after.txt | less or meld before.txt after.txt. Expect live values (clocks, temperatures, up-time, counters) to differ every time; look for changes in settings, versions, link speeds, memory speed.
  • Burn-in and benchmarks: run them on an idle PC, the same way each time, and repeat 2-3 times. A difference smaller than the run-to-run spread is noise. Each burn-in is kept in ~/.cache/srs/burnin-YYYYMMDD-HHMMSS.txt, so you can put two runs side by side (meld old.txt new.txt). Benchmarks keep only the last run of each mode (~/.cache/srs/bench-<mode>.txt): copy that file somewhere before you run the mode again if you want to keep it.
  • Watch the PCIe link (the PCI bus tab of USB & PCI devices, or the classic PCI Bus panel): a graphics card should normally show its full width (x16) and speed under load; x4 or x8 can mean the wrong slot or a slot that shares lanes.
  • Watch memory speed (the Memory page's DIMMs tab, or Machine in the classic view): if it shows 4800 MT/s for a 6000 MT/s kit, the XMP / EXPO profile is not enabled in the BIOS.

The Section Reference has "Healthy / typical values" and "Unusual values" for every item: SECTIONS/README.md.

16. Known limits and differences from SIV

  • Two views, same data. The main window and the classic view show the same 558 items with the same text. The classic panels' extra buttons (for example Features, ARP, PnP Dev) are items in their own right: in the main window find them under All N items on the page, or with the search box. Open in window shows any tab as the classic panel with its button row.
  • "Is my PC OK?" limits. SRS knows the maximum temperature of Intel CPUs (they report it) and of AMD desktop Ryzen 5000, 7000 and 9000 models (from AMD's specifications). Other AMD CPUs (laptops, Threadripper, older models) and graphics cards that publish no limit are judged against a general limit; the tooltip says which. The checks are a quick guide, not a diagnosis.
  • Linux sources, not Windows ones. Values come from the Linux kernel and standard tools, so wording and some figures differ from SIV on Windows for the same PC.
  • Root data is a snapshot. Panels that use ~/.cache/srs/root show what was true when srs-root last ran.
  • No direct hardware access. SRS never touches SMBus / I2C, monitor DDC, raw HID, or the CPU's management firmware (SMU). Some SIV readings that need that are not available.
  • 136 "not present" items are for hardware most PCs do not have. 38 Windows-only items show a Linux equivalent or explain why there is none.
  • Benchmarks are SRS's own implementations of Dhrystone 2.1 and Whetstone. Scores are for comparing runs on the same PC, not for comparing with SIV's own numbers.
  • Minimize to tray works on X11 / XWayland only.
  • Hybrid (P-core / E-core) CPUs: E-cores are found from /sys/devices/cpu_atom/cpus, which Linux provides for Intel hybrid CPUs. AMD CPUs with mixed core types (Zen 5 / Zen 5c) are not told apart yet, so ec / ep report "No efficiency cores detected" there.
  • Latency tool level labels (L1 / L2 / L3 / DRAM) use your CPU's cache sizes from /sys/devices/system/cpu/cpu0/cache: a block is labelled with the smallest cache it fits in. Labels are indicative; the steps in the curve are the real boundaries.
  • Notes about fan control, RGB and Thunderbolt describe what SRS finds on your PC: which fan-control program is running (LACT, CoolerControl, CoreCtrl, fancontrol), whether the kernel exposes LED devices for the GPU, and which Thunderbolt / USB4 controllers and routers exist.
  • Super-I/O "not connected" inputs: an AUXTIN temperature far above the board's own SYSTIN / CPUTIN readings (more than 25 degrees C) is shown greyed as "probably not connected (floating high)". If you have a probe on that header, give the input a label in /etc/sensors.d/ and SRS treats it as connected.
  • DDR5 SPD: decode-dimms cannot read DDR5 SPD hubs; the SPD item then shows the SMBIOS memory-device summary instead (no timings or EXPO / XMP profiles).
  • The optional Windows images (SRS64X.exe, SRS32X.exe, source build only) have only the ID lookup and report search features.

17. Privacy: before you share a report

A full report describes your PC in detail. Some items include identifiers you may not want to post publicly:

  • Board and system serial numbers and the system UUID (the Motherboard & BIOS page: Machine and the SMBIOS items).
  • Disk serial numbers, volume serials and partition IDs (the Storage page).
  • MAC addresses, IP addresses, Wi-Fi network names (the Network page).
  • Monitor serial numbers and the GPU unique ID (the Graphics & audio page).
  • USB device serial numbers (Properties, on the USB & PCI devices page).
  • The kernel command line, which contains your root file system's UUID (General Info and Speculation Control; the classic Linux panel).
  • The boot ID, machine ID and your PC's host name.

Redact before you share. Save the report with identifiers masked:

sysreport-search '-save=[all]=for-forum.txt' --redact

or tick Menu -> Options -> Redact identifiers in saved reports and copied text and use Save Report / Save All Items. With the option on, the Copy button and right-click Copy (or Ctrl+C on a selection) mask the same things, so text you paste into a forum post is safe too. Serial numbers, UUIDs, WWNs, the GPU / Thunderbolt unique IDs, the boot and machine IDs and the host name become XXXX (same length, so columns stay aligned); MAC addresses keep their vendor half (04:7c:16:XX:XX:XX), which is useful for telling network chips apart. The report's first line ends with (identifiers redacted). Published constants such as GPT partition-type GUIDs are not masked.

The Power & cost history (~/.local/share/srs/power.db) is not part of any report; it says when the PC was in use, so think before sharing an export of it. Nothing on that page goes online.

Not masked: IP addresses and Wi-Fi network names. Look for them (or use Find) before you post. Or save only the items you need: sysreport-search '-save=[processors][sensors]=for-forum.txt'.

18. Troubleshooting

Problem What to do
The Overview says "Not checked yet" for drive health, or a tab shows Needs root data... Run Menu -> Run as root (srs-root)... once (or press Needs root data...). The drive health line turns green or red after that.
A line on the Overview is grey ("Unknown") SRS found nothing to check, for example no CPU or GPU temperature sensor. Look at the Sensors page; see "Sensors page is nearly empty" below.
DIMM lines, serials, SMART or SPD tabs are empty or say to run srs-root Run Menu -> Run as root once (needs polkit for the password prompt), or sudo srs-root. Install dmidecode, smartmontools, nvme-cli, i2c-tools for full data.
Run as root does nothing / "did not complete" You cancelled the password prompt, or no polkit agent is running (some minimal window managers). Use sudo srs-root in a terminal instead.
No tray icon Install libayatana-appindicator. On GNOME, install and enable the AppIndicator extension.
Closing the window does not exit SRS "Close button hides to tray" is on. Use Menu -> Quit (Ctrl+Q; Exit in the classic Menu) or the tray's Exit, or untick the option.
SRS opens the old SIV-style window Options -> Start in classic view is on. Untick it, or use Menu -> Open the new main window in the classic Menu, or start srs-gui --gui-new.
I want the old SIV-style window back Menu -> Classic View, the Classic view button under the sidebar, or srs-gui --gui-classic. Tick Options -> Start in classic view to always start there.
SRS starts hidden "Start hidden in tray" or "Start with the desktop" is on; click the tray icon.
Minimize to tray does nothing You are on native Wayland. The option works only on X11 / XWayland.
Colours look wrong or half-dark Pick Options -> Theme explicitly (Light or Dark).
Temperatures of 70-90 C or 0 C on some motherboard inputs Those inputs are not connected to a sensor. SRS greys them out ("not connected"). Ignore them. See sensors.md.
Sensors page (or panel) is nearly empty The kernel has no driver for your board's monitoring chip. Run sudo sensors-detect (from lm_sensors) and load the module it suggests.
CPU Burnin stops quickly with Fail The temperature limit was reached. Check cooling. Raise the limit only if you know your CPU's safe maximum.
"GPU load command not found" The program in GPU Load command is misspelled or not installed. Fix it, or untick GPU Load command. Its output is in ~/.cache/srs/gpu-load.log.
Find says there is no report Run SRS Full System Report first.
Device names show "Unknown Device" Your hwdata package is old. Update it (new hardware is added to pci.ids / usb.ids regularly).
Panels update too often / use CPU Options -> Update interval -> 2 or 5 seconds, or Paused. In the main window you can also turn off the Live switch of one tab.
I cannot find an item Type part of its name or its id into the search box (Ctrl+F), or look under All N items on the page.
-save=[...] gives "no matches found" in zsh Quote it: sysreport-search '-save=[cpuid]' (the brackets are a pattern in zsh).
Ping item hangs a moment It waits for your router to answer. Normal.

19. Uninstall

  • Arch: sudo pacman -R srs-sysinfo
  • AppImage: delete the .AppImage file.
  • Generic tarball: remove the files you copied (the tarball's file list), for example from /usr/local/bin and /usr/local/share, and any unit you placed in /etc/systemd/system.
  • Before uninstalling, if you enabled "Refresh root data at boot": sudo systemctl disable srs-root@$USER.service
  • Your data (optional): rm -r ~/.config/srs ~/.cache/srs ~/sysreports and rm -f ~/.config/autostart/srs-gui.desktop

20. FAQ

Is this SIV? No. It is an independent Linux program modelled on SIV's layout and items. It contains nothing from SIV and is not connected with RH Software.

Does it need root? No. It always runs as your user. Root is used only by the optional srs-root helper, once, to save root-only data for you.

Can it harm my PC? The viewer is read-only. The burn-in and benchmarks load the CPU like any stress tool; they ask first, stop at a temperature limit (default 90 C) and stop when you close the window. The Startup manager changes what starts with the PC only when you click it, asks before touching parts of the desktop, keeps every old file, and has Undo and Restore default.

Why are there items that say "not present"? They are SIV items for hardware most PCs do not have (Itanium, IPMI, RAID cards...). SRS keeps them so the item list matches SIV's.

Why "Linux" where SIV says "Windows"? SIV's "Windows" button opens its operating-system panel. On Linux that is Linux, so the classic view's button says Linux. The item itself is called General Info (id windows, as in SIV); in the main window it is the first tab of the Operating system page.

Where is the window from SRS 1.1? It is the classic view: Menu -> Classic View, the Classic view button under the sidebar, or srs-gui --gui-classic. Tick Options -> Start in classic view to make it the default. Nothing was removed: both views show the same items.

Can I use it over SSH or in a script? Yes. sysreport-search needs no desktop. See CLI-REFERENCE.md.

Where do device names come from? From the hwdata project's pci.ids, usb.ids and pnp.ids lists on your system, and the systemd hardware database. They are not part of SRS.

Does it run on ARM? The command line builds for aarch64 (make all), and the viewer is plain C. The release packages are x86-64.

21. Glossary

The full A-Z glossary is in GLOSSARY.md. The Section Reference explains each term the first time it uses it.

SRS Section Reference

Back to the User Guide - Glossary I wanted a Linux version of SIV (System Information Viewer) for myself, so I built one and set out to improve on it along the way. SRS is free and open source for the Linux and open-source community. (SRS is an independent project, not affiliated with SIV or its author.) SIV is the work of Ray Hinchliffe, RH Software (rh-software.com).

How to use this reference

This reference explains every item SRS can show - all 558 of them - one by one. For each item it says, in this order:

  1. In plain words - what it is, in one to three short sentences.
  2. What you see - every column and field, and why it matters.
  3. Healthy / typical values - what normal looks like, with real examples from the author's PC (AMD Ryzen 7 7800X3D, ASUS TUF GAMING X870-PRO WIFI7, 2 x 16 GB DDR5-6000, Radeon RX 9070 XT).
  4. Unusual values and what they suggest.
  5. Where Linux gets it - the file, table or tool the value comes from.
  6. Background - the idea behind it (what a cache is, what a P-state is, ...), where it helps.

Every technical word is explained the first time a page uses it, and again in the Glossary.

Badges under each title:

  • Linux data - shows real data from your Linux system.
  • Not present on most PCs - SIV items for hardware most PCs lack (Itanium, IPMI, RAID cards...). On a normal PC they say so.
  • Windows-only (Linux equivalent shown) - a Windows idea; SRS shows the nearest Linux equivalent.
  • Needs root data - some or all of the values come from the srs-root cache (~/.cache/srs/root, see the User Guide). Without it those values are empty.

How to open an item:

  • In the main window (SRS 2.0): pick the page in the sidebar (the table below names it). The most used items are tabs; All N items at the right end of the tab row lists every item of the page. Or type the item's name or id into the search box at the top (Ctrl+F). The Guide button (F1) on each tab opens the item's section here.
  • In the classic view: Menu -> the group -> the item (each menu entry shows the item id in brackets), or the panel buttons named in each group's introduction.
  • From the command line: sysreport-search '-save=[id]'.

Processors (SRS Section Reference)

Back to the section index - Glossary

Where to find these items (SRS 2.0). In the main window they are on the Processor page (Alt+2). Its tabs are CPU Summary, Processors, CPU Clocks, CPUID Features, Cache Levels, CPUID, Microcode and Speculation Control; All N items lists the rest, plus Each CPU and Cache levels of each CPU (SIV's CPU-n and Cache-n buttons). You can also type an item's name or id into the search box (Ctrl+F). The rest of this introduction describes the classic view (Menu -> Classic View), with its Menu and panel buttons.

This group covers everything about the processor (CPU): its name and family, how many cores and threads it has, its caches, the features it supports, its clock speeds, power and idle states, temperatures, voltages and the low-level registers behind them. Open any item from Menu -> Processors -> item. The quickest way in is the Processors button on the classic main panel. Its row of sub-buttons opens Features, Hypervisor, Groups, CPU-n (one processor in detail) and Cache-n (the cache table of CPU number n). Most items read normal Linux files and need nothing special. MSRs needs root data: run the srs-root helper once (Menu -> Run as root) and SRS shows the cached result. Several AMD items need the optional ryzen_smu, zenergy or k10temp drivers. Many pages start with a title line ("srs-gui - ... on \MYPC - CachyOS ...") and some end with the motherboard name and BIOS version.
