AMD Ryzen Power Management

amd-cpu - Linux data

In plain words. How the Linux amd_pstate driver controls the speed of each core on a modern AMD Ryzen CPU, and which cores the chip itself says are its best ones.

What you see.

  • Mode - the amd_pstate mode: active (the CPU picks its own speed inside limits the OS sets), guided, or passive (the OS picks the speed). Tells you who is really in charge of the clock.
  • A table, one row per logical CPU:
Column Meaning Why it matters
CPU Linux CPU number (CPU-0, CPU-1 ...) Which thread the row is about.
Highest perf The top CPPC performance level this core can reach (a unitless number) Higher means this core can boost higher.
Ranking The "preferred core" rank the CPU reports The scheduler puts busy work on the highest-ranked cores first.
Max freq Highest clock the driver will allow Your real boost ceiling.
Nonlinear Lowest non-linear frequency Below this speed, saving power gets much less efficient.
EPP Energy Performance Preference hint (performance, balance_performance, balance_power, power) Tells the CPU how much to favour speed over power saving.
HW prefcore Whether the hardware supports preferred-core ranking If disabled, all cores are treated as equal.

Healthy / typical values. On the author's Ryzen 7 7800X3D: Mode active, Highest perf 166 on every core, Max freq 5.05GHz, Nonlinear 2.98GHz, EPP performance, HW prefcore enabled. Rankings run from 166 to 196; CPU-1/CPU-9 and CPU-5/CPU-13 (the two threads of the same core) share the top rank 196.

Unusual values and what they suggest.

  • The page says "amd_pstate driver not active": the older acpi-cpufreq driver is in use, or the CPU is not an AMD Zen 2 or newer. Add amd_pstate=active (or guided) to the kernel command line.
  • Every Ranking is the same: preferred-core support is off in the BIOS or kernel.
  • Max freq well below the advertised boost: boost is off, or a power or temperature limit is set.

Where Linux gets it. /sys/devices/system/cpu/amd_pstate/status and /sys/devices/system/cpu/cpuN/cpufreq/amd_pstate_* plus energy_performance_preference.

Background. CPPC (Collaborative Processor Performance Control) is an ACPI standard. Instead of a few fixed speed steps, the CPU offers a smooth scale of "performance levels" and the OS gives it a target range. The CPU then picks the exact clock many times per second.

AMD Fuses

amd-fus - Linux data - Needs root data

In plain words. Fuses are one-time settings burned into the chip at the factory (which cores are on, limits, and so on). SRS does not read them.

What you see.

  • Status - always Not read.
  • Reason - reading fuses needs SMN (System Management Network) register access through the ryzen_smu driver, which means writing to the driver. SRS stays read-only, so it never does this.

Where Linux gets it. It would come from /sys/kernel/ryzen_smu_drv/smn (root, write-then-read).

AMD PM Table

amd-pmt - Linux data

In plain words. A raw dump of the power-management table that the CPU's own little control processor (the SMU) keeps up to date: powers, clocks, voltages, temperatures and limits, all as numbers.

What you see.

  • A summary line: table size in bytes, number of values, and a reminder that the meaning of each slot depends on the table version (shown in AMD SMU).
  • Then rows of four values each:
    • Offset (purple, hex) - the byte position in the table, e.g. 0000, 0010.
    • [n] - the slot number (0, 1, 2 ...).
    • value - that slot read as a 32-bit floating-point number. Values that are not real numbers or are huge are shown grey, because they are almost certainly not a float at all.

Healthy / typical values. On the author's 7800X3D: 1704 bytes, 426 values, table version 0x00540104. You can spot patterns: slots around 5.25 look like clock limits in GHz, slots near 1.1-1.5 look like voltages, slots in the 40s-50s change with load and look like temperatures or watts. The values change every time you open the page because the SMU updates them constantly.

Unusual values and what they suggest.

  • "ryzen_smu pm_table not available": the ryzen_smu kernel module is not installed or not loaded.
  • "pm_table not readable as this user": the file permissions on your system only let root read it.
  • All zeros: the driver loaded but the SMU has not filled the table yet, or the table version is not supported by the driver.

Where Linux gets it. /sys/kernel/ryzen_smu_drv/pm_table (from the out-of-tree ryzen_smu driver).

Background. The SMU (System Management Unit) is a small processor inside every Ryzen CPU. It runs its own firmware and makes the real decisions about boost clocks, voltages and power limits. Tools like Ryzen Master read this table to show live data. AMD does not publish the layout, so tools map it by version.

AMD PM Table 0

amd-pmt-0 - Linux data

In plain words. The same power-management table as AMD PM Table, for the first (and on most desktops the only) CPU package.

What you see. Exactly the same layout as AMD PM Table: summary line, then offset, slot number and float value, four per row. Because the table is live, two openings a moment apart show slightly different numbers (on the author's PC slot [3] read 42.69 in one capture and 55.19 in the next).

Where Linux gets it. /sys/kernel/ryzen_smu_drv/pm_table.

AMD PM table data @ second package/CCD

amd-pmt-1 - Not present on most PCs

In plain words. The power-management table of a second CPU package or die. Desktop Ryzen has one package and the driver gives one table, so there is nothing to show.

What you see. Status Not present on this system and Checked, the source SRS looked at (/sys/kernel/ryzen_smu_drv/pm_table (single CCD/package)). "Not present" is normal on single-socket PCs.

AMD SMU

amd-smu - Linux data - Needs root data

In plain words. Version information about the SMU (the CPU's built-in power-management processor) and the ryzen_smu driver that talks to it. SRS shows this part without root; the root flag is for the SMU mailbox commands, which SRS never sends.

What you see.

Field Meaning Why it matters
Driver version Version of the ryzen_smu driver (drv_version) Old drivers may not know new CPUs.
Codename The driver's number for your CPU generation (codename) Tells the driver which table layout to use.
SMU firmware version SMU firmware version (the driver's version file), e.g. 4.84.4.0 Changes with BIOS (AGESA) updates.
MP1 interface version Version of the MP1 mailbox interface (mp1_if_version) Driver/firmware compatibility.
PM table version Layout version of the PM table, in hex and decimal (pm_table_version, a binary 32-bit value) You need this to know what each PM table slot means.
PM table size Size of the PM table in bytes (pm_table_size, a binary 64-bit value) Should match the table dump.

A closing note says SRS is read-only and never sends SMU commands.

Healthy / typical values. On the author's 7800X3D: drv_version 0.1.7, codename 20, mp1_if_version 2, pm_table_version 0x00540104 (5505284), pm_table_size 1704. A field shows - when the driver does not provide it.

Unusual values and what they suggest. "ryzen_smu driver not loaded": install and load the ryzen_smu module (it is not part of the normal kernel).

Where Linux gets it. Files in /sys/kernel/ryzen_smu_drv/.

AMD Telemetry 0

amd-tel-0 - Linux data

In plain words. How much power each core and the whole CPU package is using right now, worked out from the CPU's energy counters.

What you see. A table with one row per energy counter:

  • Plane - the counter's label: Ecore000, Ecore001 ... (one per physical core) and Esocket0 (the whole package).
  • Power - watts, measured by reading the counter twice 200 ms apart.
  • Energy - total energy counted since the counter started, in kilojoules.

Healthy / typical values. On the author's 7800X3D at light load: cores 2.4-4.7 W each, socket 57.86 W. The socket figure is always larger than the cores added together, because it also counts the cache, memory controller, Infinity Fabric and I/O die.

Unusual values and what they suggest.

  • "No zenergy / amd_energy hwmon driver loaded": install the zenergy module (or the older amd_energy).
  • One core much higher than the rest at idle: a background task is pinned to it.
  • Socket power high while every core is low: often memory or fabric overclocking, or many devices keeping the I/O die busy.

Where Linux gets it. The zenergy or amd_energy hwmon driver, /sys/class/hwmon/hwmonN/energy*_input (these read AMD's RAPL energy counters).

Background. RAPL (Running Average Power Limit) counters add up energy used, in tiny steps. Power is energy divided by time, so reading the counter twice and dividing by the gap gives watts.

AMD SVI telemetry plane @ second die

amd-tel-1 - Not present on most PCs

In plain words. Power and voltage readings for a second die. Single-package PCs have no second plane.

What you see. Status Not present on this system and Checked (the source SRS looked at).

Background. SVI (Serial VID Interface) is the link the CPU uses to tell the motherboard's voltage regulator what voltage to give it, and to read back current and voltage.

AMD Thermal 0

amd-thm-0 - Linux data

In plain words. The CPU's own temperature sensors, read through the k10temp driver.

What you see. One line per sensor the driver offers, label and temperature in degrees Celsius:

  • Tctl - the control temperature that the CPU and fan curves use. On some models it includes a fixed offset, so it can read higher than the real die.
  • Tdie - the real die temperature (only on models where it differs from Tctl).
  • Tccd1, Tccd2 ... - one per CCD (core chiplet), the die that holds the cores.
  • Other labels the driver adds are shown as-is; unlabelled ones as temp1, temp2 ...

A note at the end explains Tctl and TccdN.

Healthy / typical values. On the author's 7800X3D (one CCD): Tctl 53.6°C, Tccd1 48.1°C. Idle on a desktop is usually 35-55°C. Under full load an X3D chip normally stays below about 89°C, the point where it starts holding clocks back.

Unusual values and what they suggest.

  • Tctl near 90-95°C under load: cooler not seated well, pump failing, or fans not ramping.
  • Tctl jumps quickly up and down by 10°C or more: normal for Ryzen at light load (single cores boosting).
  • "k10temp not loaded": the module is missing or blocked; some boards also hide it behind another driver.

Where Linux gets it. k10temp hwmon: /sys/class/hwmon/hwmonN/temp*_input and temp*_label.

AMD THM registers @ second die

amd-thm-1 - Not present on most PCs

In plain words. Thermal registers of a second CPU package. A single-socket PC has only one, so nothing is listed.

What you see. Status Not present on this system and Checked (/sys/bus/pci/drivers/k10temp (single package)).

AMD Temperatures

amd-tmp - Linux data

In plain words. The same CPU temperature list as AMD Thermal 0.

What you see. Identical to AMD Thermal 0: Tctl, Tdie (if present) and TccdN in °C, plus the explanatory note. The page refreshes every 2 seconds in the window.

Where Linux gets it. k10temp hwmon.

CPU Table

cpu - Linux data

In plain words. One line per logical CPU showing where it sits (node, package, core, thread), its IDs, and its current speed settings. The window refreshes it every 2 seconds.

What you see.

Column Meaning Why it matters
CPU Linux CPU number The name tools like taskset use.
Node NUMA node the CPU belongs to Matters on multi-node systems (see NUMA).
Pkg Physical package (socket) number 0 on single-socket PCs.
Die Die number inside the package Linux topology die ID.
Core Physical core number Two CPUs with the same Core are SMT siblings.
Thread 0 = first thread of the core, 1 = its SMT sibling Shows which CPU numbers share a core.
Affinity The CPU's bit in a 64-bit affinity mask, in hex Useful when setting masks by hand. Shown as zeros above CPU 63.
APIC The CPU's APIC ID in hex The hardware's own CPU number.
Current Current clock speed Changes all the time with load.
Minimum / Maximum The lowest / highest clock the OS currently allows Your active speed limits.
Governor cpufreq governor (performance, powersave, schedutil ...) The policy that picks speeds.
EPP Energy Performance Preference See AMD Ryzen Power Management.
Ranking amd_pstate preferred-core rank Higher = better core.
Highest amd_pstate highest perf level The core's boost potential.

Empty values show as -.

Healthy / typical values. On the author's 7800X3D: CPU-0 to CPU-7 are Thread 0 of cores 0-7 and CPU-8 to CPU-15 are their siblings (Thread 1). APIC IDs are even for first threads (0000, 0002 ...) and odd for siblings. Minimum and Maximum are both 5.05GHz because the owner pinned the minimum to the maximum; on a default setup Minimum is much lower (a few hundred MHz).

Unusual values and what they suggest.

  • Minimum = Maximum: someone set a fixed speed (gaming tweak, tuned profile). Higher idle power.
  • Maximum far below the CPU's boost speed: boost disabled or a power-saving profile is active.
  • Current shows -: no cpufreq driver loaded (common in virtual machines).

Where Linux gets it. /sys/devices/system/cpu/cpuN/topology/, cpufreq/, /proc/cpuinfo (apicid).

Background. SMT (Simultaneous Multi-Threading, Intel calls it Hyper-Threading) lets one physical core run two threads at once. Linux shows each thread as its own "CPU".

CPU Description

cpu-bits - Linux data

In plain words. SIV shows the CPU description Windows keeps in the registry. On Linux, SRS shows the same kind of facts straight from /proc/cpuinfo for one CPU (CPU-0 unless another number is given).

What you see. A label/value list of these /proc/cpuinfo fields:

  • model name - full CPU name. vendor_id - AuthenticAMD or GenuineIntel.
  • cpu family / model / stepping - the CPU's generation numbers, in decimal.
  • microcode - microcode revision loaded. cpu MHz - clock at the moment of reading.
  • cache size - the L2 cache per core, as the kernel reports it.
  • physical id / siblings / core id / cpu cores - package number, threads per package, this core's number, cores per package.
  • apicid / initial apicid - APIC IDs now and at power-on (normally equal).
  • fpu / fpu_exception / wp - basic x86 features (always yes on modern CPUs).
  • cpuid level - highest standard CPUID leaf.
  • bugs - known hardware weaknesses the kernel knows about (see Speculation Control).
  • bogomips - a rough "busy loop" speed number. It is not a benchmark.
  • TLB size - number of translation buffer entries (AMD only).
  • clflush size / cache_alignment - cache line size in bytes.
  • address sizes - physical and virtual address bits.
  • power management - power features (ts thermal sensor, hwpstate hardware P-states, cpb core boost, and so on; unknown bits appear as [13], [14]).
  • flags - every CPU feature the kernel found (long list).
  • vmx flags - Intel VT-x sub-features; empty on AMD.

Healthy / typical values. On the author's 7800X3D: family 25, model 97, stepping 2, microcode 0xa60120c, cache size 1024 KB, 16 siblings, 8 cpu cores, address sizes 48 bits physical / 48 bits virtual, TLB size 3584 4K pages, bogomips 8820.31.

Unusual values and what they suggest. siblings equal to cpu cores: SMT is off. A bugs list that grows after a kernel update is normal: newly found issues get added.

Where Linux gets it. /proc/cpuinfo.

CPU Clocks

cpu-clocks - Linux data

In plain words. The current, average and allowed clock speed of every CPU. Same page as CPU Speeds; it refreshes every second in the window.

What you see. The same layout as CPU Speeds: the driver/boost line and the per-CPU table (Current, Average, Minimum, Maximum, HW Min, HW Max, Governor, EPP). Below it, since 2.2, Stock and in effect now: each clock at stock next to what it is now.

Row Stock In effect now
Base clock 100 MHz, the standard reference clock Measured: the TSC rate x 100 / the CPU's nominal frequency from ACPI CPPC (once per run, 50 ms)
Core base The CPU's nominal frequency (CPPC) Nominal x base clock / 100
Core boost (max) cpufreq's maximum (the kernel works it out at 100 MHz) Maximum x base clock / 100
Core now (fastest) The same multiplier at 100 MHz cpufreq's current clock of the fastest core (already real)
FCLK, UCLK, MCLK What the SMU reports The same: these are shown, not measured

Difference gives MHz and percent where SRS measured. FCLK (Infinity Fabric), UCLK (memory controller) and MCLK (memory clock) come from the SMU's PM table through the ryzen_smu driver (read-only), for the Zen 4 desktop layout (Ryzen 7000, ryzen_smu codename 20) and only when the values make sense; elsewhere the row says why it is missing. Software cannot measure these clocks, so SRS does not claim a difference: on AM5 an eCLK drives the cores, and whether anything else follows it depends on the board's eCLK mode. The Memory line adds the DDR data rate (2 x MCLK), the UCLK:MCLK ratio (1:1 or 1:2) and FCLK.

Healthy / typical values. With the normal 100 MHz base clock every difference is about 0. The author's PC runs a 105 MHz eCLK: base clock 105.0 MHz (+5 %), core base 4201 -> 4410 MHz, boost 5053 -> 5305 MHz, FCLK 2133 MHz, UCLK 1500 MHz, MCLK 3000 MHz (DDR5-6000 at 1:2).

Where Linux gets it. cpufreq files in /sys/devices/system/cpu/cpuN/cpufreq/, the TSC (timed against the system clock), /sys/devices/system/cpu/cpu0/acpi_cppc/nominal_freq, and /sys/kernel/ryzen_smu_drv/pm_table (floats 70, 74 and 78 of the Zen 4 desktop table).

CPU Export

cpu-export - Linux data

In plain words. A tiny set of CPU values that other tools (LCD panels, on-screen displays, scripts) can read from a file SRS writes.

What you see.

  • CPU.Name - CPU model name.
  • CPU.Clock.Max - the highest current clock of any CPU at the moment of reading, in MHz.
  • CPU.Count - number of logical CPUs.
  • A note on how to write this to a file: srs-gui -save=[cpu-export]=FILE.

Healthy / typical values. On the author's PC: AMD Ryzen 7 7800X3D 8-Core Processor, 5115 MHz, 16.

Where Linux gets it. /proc/cpuinfo and scaling_cur_freq of every CPU.

CPUID

cpuid - Linux data

In plain words. A raw dump of every answer the CPU gives to the CPUID instruction. This is the source for most of the other pages in this group. It is for experts and for comparing two machines.

What you see. A title line (CPU number, CPU name, current speed), then one row per leaf and sub-leaf:

Column Meaning
Leaf The CPUID question number, in hex. 00000000-000000xx are standard leaves, 80000000-800000xx are extended leaves.
Sub Sub-leaf number, for leaves that have several pages (cache, topology, XSAVE ...). Empty extra sub-leaves are skipped.
EAX, EBX, ECX, EDX The four 32-bit registers of the answer, in hex.
ASCII The same 16 bytes as text, in register order EAX-EBX-ECX-EDX. Non-printable bytes show as ..

The ASCII column makes text answers readable: leaves 80000002-80000004 spell the brand name. In leaf 0 the vendor text looks scrambled ("AuthcAMDenti") because the CPU stores it in the order EBX-EDX-ECX.

Healthy / typical values. On the author's 7800X3D: highest standard leaf 00000010, highest extended leaf 80000028, leaf 1 EAX 00A60F12. Many leaves are all zero: that just means "not used by this CPU".

Unusual values and what they suggest. Leaf 1 ECX bit 31 set (hypervisor bit) means you are inside a virtual machine. Very few leaves: an old CPU or a hypervisor that hides features.

Where Linux gets it. The CPUID instruction itself, run with the thread pinned to the chosen CPU (argument = CPU number).

Background. CPUID is an x86 instruction. Software puts a number (the leaf) in a register and the CPU answers in four registers with facts about itself: vendor, family, features, caches, topology.

CPUID Leaf 0

cpuid-000 - Linux data

In plain words. The CPU's basic identity card from CPUID: who made it, its name and its exact generation.

What you see.

  • Maximum standard leaf - highest normal CPUID leaf (hex).
  • Vendor string - 12-letter maker code: AuthenticAMD, GenuineIntel, HygonGenuine ...
  • Maximum extended leaf - highest extended leaf (hex).
  • Brand string - the marketing name, built into the chip.
  • Signature (leaf 1 EAX) - the raw hex signature, then the decoded family, model and stepping (decimal).

Healthy / typical values. On the author's PC: 00000010, AuthenticAMD, 80000028, "AMD Ryzen 7 7800X3D 8-Core Processor", 00A60F12 = family 25 model 97 stepping 2.

Where Linux gets it. CPUID leaves 0, 1, 80000000 and 80000002-80000004.

Background. Family 25 (19h) is AMD Zen 3 and Zen 4; model 97 (61h) is the Zen 4 "Raphael" desktop chip. Stepping is the silicon revision.

CPU Idle Levels

cpu-levels - Linux data

In plain words. The sleep levels (C-states) each core can drop into when it has nothing to do, and how much each level has been used since boot.

What you see.

  • Driver - the cpuidle driver (acpi_idle, intel_idle, amd_idle ...) and its governor (the policy that picks a level: menu, teo, ladder, haltpoll).
  • A table with one block per CPU, one row per state:
Column Meaning Why it matters
CPU Shown on the first state of each CPU Group header.
State State name: POLL, C1, C2, C3 ... Deeper = more power saved, slower to wake.
Description What the state does (e.g. ACPI HLT, ACPI IOPORT 0x414) Shows how the state is entered.
Latency Time to wake from it, microseconds Deep states add this delay to the first work after idle.
Residency Minimum time worth staying in it, microseconds The governor skips a state if the idle gap is shorter.
Usage How many times it was entered Shows which states really get used.
Time Total time spent in it, seconds Where the core spends its idle time.

Healthy / typical values. On the author's 7800X3D: driver acpi_idle, governor teo; states POLL (0us), C1 HLT (0us), C2 (18us latency, 36us residency) and C3 (350us, 700us). Most idle time is in C2 and C3, which is what you want for low idle power.

Unusual values and what they suggest.

  • Only POLL and C1: deep C-states are off in the BIOS ("Global C-state Control"), or the kernel was booted with processor.max_cstate=1 / idle=poll. Idle power and temperature go up.
  • C3 Usage stays 0: the state is disabled (see CPU power states) or wake-ups are too frequent for it.

Where Linux gets it. /sys/devices/system/cpu/cpuidle/ and /sys/devices/system/cpu/cpuN/cpuidle/stateM/.

Background. A C-state is an idle power level. C0 is "running". C1 stops the clock to the core, deeper ones also cut voltage and flush caches. Waking from a deep state takes longer, which is why latency-sensitive setups sometimes limit them.

CPU OC Data

cpu-oc-data - Not present on most PCs - Needs root data

In plain words. Intel CPUs have an "overclocking mailbox" register that reports and sets overclocking limits. AMD CPUs do not have it.

What you see. Status Not present on this system and Reason: IA32_OC_MAILBOX is an Intel interface; on AMD look at AMD Ryzen Power Management and Turbo Boost instead.

CPU Summary

cpus - Linux data

In plain words. A short overview of the processor: name, maker, generation, how many cores and threads, and which speed driver Linux uses.

What you see.

  • Processor - full model name. Vendor - maker code.
  • Family - family, model and stepping in decimal with hex in brackets.
  • Topology - packages, cores, logical processors, and threads per core.
  • Microcode - loaded microcode revision. Address sizes - physical/virtual address bits.
  • BogoMIPS - rough loop speed (not a benchmark). TLB size - AMD translation buffer size.
  • Power management - power feature list from /proc/cpuinfo.
  • Frequency driver - the cpufreq driver: amd-pstate-epp, amd-pstate, acpi-cpufreq, intel_pstate ...
  • Board name and BIOS line at the bottom.

Healthy / typical values. On the author's PC: AMD Ryzen 7 7800X3D, Family 25 (0x19) Model 97 (0x61) Stepping 2, "1 package, 8 cores, 16 logical processors (2 per core)", Microcode 0xa60120c, Frequency driver amd-pstate-epp.

Unusual values and what they suggest. "1 per core" on a CPU that has SMT: SMT is off in the BIOS or with nosmt. Frequency driver acpi-cpufreq on a Zen 2+ Ryzen: amd_pstate is not enabled.

Where Linux gets it. /proc/cpuinfo, /sys/devices/system/cpu/cpuN/topology/, scaling_driver.

CPU SMU

cpu-smu - Linux data - Needs root data

In plain words. The same SMU version page as AMD SMU. SIV uses this item for SMU mailbox results; SRS shows the read-only version data and never sends mailbox commands.

What you see. Identical to AMD SMU: driver version, codename, SMU firmware version, MP1 interface version, PM table version and size, and the read-only note.

Where Linux gets it. /sys/kernel/ryzen_smu_drv/.

CPU Speeds

cpu-speeds - Linux data

In plain words. The clock speed of every CPU right now, plus the limits that control it. The window refreshes it every second.

What you see.

  • Driver - the cpufreq driver and whether boost is on, off, or - (unknown).
  • A per-CPU table:
Column Meaning Why it matters
CPU Linux CPU number
Current Clock the kernel last saw Jumps around with load.
Average Average clock over a short recent window (needs a recent kernel) Smoother than Current.
Minimum / Maximum Allowed range set by the OS (scaling limits) What policy currently allows.
HW Min / HW Max Range the hardware supports The absolute floor and ceiling.
Governor Speed policy performance = always aim high; powersave under amd-pstate-epp still boosts but follows EPP.
EPP Energy Performance Preference Speed vs power hint.

Healthy / typical values. On the author's 7800X3D: driver amd-pstate-epp, boost on; Current 4.2-5.1GHz under light load; HW Min 426MHz, HW Max 5.05GHz. Current can read a little above Maximum (5.11GHz vs 5.05GHz) because of rounding and a raised reference clock.

Unusual values and what they suggest.

  • Every core stuck at a low Current under load: a thermal or power limit, or the powersave governor with power EPP.
  • HW Max equal to the base clock: boost off in the BIOS.
  • All columns -: no cpufreq driver (virtual machine, or the driver failed to load).

Since 2.2 the same Stock and in effect now table as CPU Clocks follows the per-CPU table (both items share one page).

Where Linux gets it. /sys/devices/system/cpu/cpuN/cpufreq/ (scaling_*, cpuinfo_*, cpuinfo_avg_freq) and /sys/devices/system/cpu/cpufreq/boost.

Background. cpufreq is the Linux part that sets CPU speed. The driver talks to the hardware; the governor decides which speed to ask for.

CPU Timers

cpu-timer - Linux data

In plain words. Which hardware clock Linux uses to keep time, and how fast the CPU's own time counter (the TSC) runs.

What you see.

  • Clock source - the timer Linux uses now (tsc, hpet, acpi_pm).
  • Available - all usable timers.
  • TSC frequency - TSC rate measured by SRS over 50 ms, in MHz.
  • TSC properties - check boxes: constant (same rate at any CPU speed), nonstop (keeps counting in deep sleep), known freq (the kernel was told the exact rate), RDTSCP (the instruction that also returns the CPU number is available).
  • CLOCK_MONOTONIC res - resolution of the system's steady clock, in nanoseconds.
  • Kernel HZ (USER_HZ) - the tick unit the kernel uses when reporting times to programs.
  • Clock event - the device that fires timer interrupts (lapic, hpet ...).

Healthy / typical values. On the author's PC: clock source tsc; available tsc hpet acpi_pm; TSC 4409.857 MHz; constant, nonstop and RDTSCP ticked; resolution 1 ns; USER_HZ 100; clock event lapic. The 7800X3D's TSC is normally 4.20 GHz; 4.41 GHz here comes from the board's reference clock being raised to 105 MHz (4.20 x 1.05 = 4.41).

Unusual values and what they suggest.

  • Clock source hpet or acpi_pm: the kernel decided the TSC is unstable (look in dmesg for "clocksource tsc unstable"). Timing calls get much slower; games can stutter.
  • TSC frequency very different from the base clock with no reference-clock change: a virtual machine, or firmware bug.

Where Linux gets it. /sys/devices/system/clocksource/clocksource0/, /sys/devices/system/clockevents/, /proc/cpuinfo flags, and SRS's own timing with the RDTSC instruction.

Background. The TSC (Time Stamp Counter) is a counter inside the CPU that goes up at a fixed rate. Reading it is very cheap, which makes it the best clock for an OS when it is stable.

CPU Tunables

cpu-tweak - Linux data - Needs root data

In plain words. A read-only view of the CPU settings you can change in Linux: speed policy, boost, SMT and CPU isolation. SRS only shows them; changing them needs root and a tool such as tuned or cpupower.

What you see. (each line appears only if the file exists)

  • Governor (cpu0) and Available governors.
  • EPP (cpu0) and Available EPP values.
  • Boost - on or off.
  • SMT control - on, off, forceoff or notsupported. SMT active - 1 if SMT is running.
  • Isolated CPUs - CPUs kept away from normal tasks (isolcpus=), or none.
  • nohz_full CPUs - CPUs that run without the regular timer tick, or none.
  • sched_autogroup - 1 if the scheduler groups tasks by session (better desktop feel under load).
  • A note: changes are left to tuned / cpupower / LACT.

Healthy / typical values. On the author's PC: governor performance (available: performance, powersave), EPP performance (the only option offered while the performance governor is active), boost on, SMT on and active, no isolated CPUs, sched_autogroup 1.

Unusual values and what they suggest. SMT control forceoff: the kernel was booted with nosmt=force, usually for security. Only performance in Available EPP: that is normal while the performance governor is selected; switch to powersave to see the full list.

Where Linux gets it. /sys/devices/system/cpu/cpu0/cpufreq/, /sys/devices/system/cpu/smt/, /sys/devices/system/cpu/isolated, nohz_full, /proc/sys/kernel/sched_autogroup_enabled.

CPU Voltages

cpu-volts - Linux data

In plain words. The CPU core voltage as measured by the motherboard's sensor chip.

What you see. One line per voltage input of a supported motherboard sensor chip (Nuvoton nct*, ITE it87*, ASUS asus*, or zenpower): chip name, input label, and volts with three decimals. in0 is shown as "Vcore sense" when it has no label; in1 is shown too; other unlabelled inputs are skipped. A note says per-core voltage (VID) is not available from Linux drivers, so the board reading is shown.

Healthy / typical values. On the author's PC: nct6799 in0 (Vcore sense) 1.096 V, in1 1.000 V. Ryzen 7000 Vcore usually sits between about 0.9 and 1.35 V and moves constantly with load and boost.

Unusual values and what they suggest.

  • Nothing listed: no matching sensor driver is loaded (for many boards you need nct6775 or it87).
  • Vcore above about 1.40 V at all-core load: a manual overvolt or aggressive BIOS setting; check heat.
  • A reading of 0 or a fixed, unchanging odd value: that input is not wired to Vcore on your board.

Where Linux gets it. Super-I/O hwmon drivers, /sys/class/hwmon/hwmonN/in*_input and in*_label.

Background. Vcore is the main supply voltage of the CPU cores. The CPU asks the board's voltage regulator for a voltage (VID); the board's sensor measures what actually arrives.

CPUID Features

features - Linux data

In plain words. A checklist of 177 well-known CPU features (instruction sets, security and virtualization features), each ticked if CPU-0 reports it.

What you see.

  • A count line: "N of 177 features present on CPU-0 (CPU name)".
  • Two columns of Feature (short name) and CPUID Feature Description with a tick box. Present features are in normal colour; missing ones are grey.

The list covers standard leaf 1 (e.g. SSE, SSE2, SSE4.2, AVX, AES, RDRAND), leaf 6 (thermal/turbo), leaf 7 (AVX2, AVX-512 family, BMI1/2, SHA, SMEP/SMAP, CET, speculation controls), and AMD extended leaves (SVM, SSE4A, LM 64-bit mode, NX, 1GB pages, Invariant TSC, CPB boost, NPT, AVIC, SME/SEV).

Healthy / typical values. On the author's 7800X3D: 120 of 177. AVX2 and most AVX-512 parts are present (Zen 4 has AVX-512). Intel-only items (VMX, SGX, HLE, RTM, EIST) and old AMD items (3DNow!, FMA4, XOP) are correctly absent. The leaf-7 IBRS/STIBP/SSBD lines are Intel's bits; AMD reports the same protections in the AMD_IBRS, AMD_STIBP, AMD_SSBD lines, which are ticked.

Unusual values and what they suggest.

  • AVX or AVX2 missing on a CPU that should have it: inside a VM with a basic CPU model, or the OS has disabled the AVX state (OSXSAVE unticked).
  • HVM ticked: you are running under a hypervisor.
  • SVM/VMX present but virtualization tools fail: it is turned off in the BIOS (CPUID still shows it).

Where Linux gets it. The CPUID instruction (leaves 1, 6, 7, 80000001, 80000007, 80000008, 8000000A, 8000001F).

Background. Programs check these bits before using special instructions. If a game says "your CPU does not support AVX2", this page tells you whether that is true.

Hypervisor

hypervisor - Linux data

In plain words. Can this CPU run virtual machines well, and is this system itself a virtual machine?

What you see. A list of tick boxes for CPU-0:

  • SLAT - Second Level Address Translation (Intel EPT or AMD RVI): fast memory handling for VMs.
  • HVM - ticked if this OS is running under a hypervisor.
  • VT-x and EPT - Intel's virtualization and its page tables.
  • AMD-V (SVM), RVI (nested paging), AVIC (virtual interrupt controller) and SEV (encrypted VMs).

Then:

  • /dev/kvm - present (KVM available) or absent.
  • IOMMU - number of IOMMU groups, or disabled / none.
  • kvm_amd nested - 1 if VMs inside VMs are allowed (AMD only).
  • Board/BIOS line.

Healthy / typical values. On the author's PC: SLAT, AMD-V, RVI and AVIC ticked; SEV and HVM not; /dev/kvm present; 36 IOMMU groups; nested 1. That is a fully working KVM host.

Unusual values and what they suggest.

  • AMD-V or VT-x unticked on a CPU that has it: virtualization (SVM Mode / Intel VT) is probably off in the BIOS. On some systems the flag stays ticked even when the BIOS has it off; then dmesg shows "disabled by BIOS" when KVM loads.
  • /dev/kvm absent while AMD-V is ticked: the kvm_amd / kvm_intel module is not loaded.
  • IOMMU disabled / none: IOMMU off in the BIOS or kernel; GPU passthrough to a VM will not work.
  • SEV unticked on a desktop Ryzen: normal; SEV is an EPYC server feature.

Where Linux gets it. /proc/cpuinfo flags, /dev/kvm, /sys/kernel/iommu_groups/, /sys/module/kvm_amd/parameters/nested.

Background. An IOMMU (Input-Output Memory Management Unit) controls which memory each device may reach. IOMMU groups are the smallest sets of devices that can be handed to a VM together.

Microcode

microcode - Linux data

In plain words. The microcode version loaded on each CPU. Microcode is a small firmware patch for the processor, loaded by the BIOS or by Linux at boot.

What you see. A two-column table: CPU and Version (hex). - if the kernel does not report it.

Healthy / typical values. All CPUs show the same version. On the author's PC: 0xa60120c on all 16.

Unusual values and what they suggest.

  • Different versions on different CPUs: a failed or partial late update; reboot.
  • A version older than your BIOS or distro offers: install your distro's amd-ucode / intel-ucode package, or update the BIOS. New microcode fixes bugs and security issues.

Where Linux gets it. /sys/devices/system/cpu/cpuN/microcode/version.

MSRs

msrs - Linux data - Needs root data

In plain words. The raw values of a set of the CPU's internal control registers, for every CPU. Only root can read them, so SRS shows what the srs-root helper saved.

What you see. Without root data: Status Needs root and Source (/dev/cpu/*/msr, read by srs-root via Menu > Run as root). With root data: a table with MSR (register address, hex), Name, and one column per CPU with the 64-bit value in hex (n/a if unreadable). The registers are:

Name What it holds
APIC_BASE Where the interrupt controller lives; bit 8 marks the boot CPU.
MPERF / APERF Two counters: fixed-rate and actual-rate cycles. Their ratio is the true average clock.
EFER Extended features in use (64-bit mode, NX, SVM enabled).
HWCR AMD hardware configuration (boost lock, TSC behaviour ...).
PSTATE_CURRENT_LIMIT / CONTROL / STATUS Legacy P-state limit, requested and current state.
PSTATE_DEF_0..2 Definitions of the classic P-states (clock multiplier and voltage ID).
HW_PSTATE_STATUS The hardware's current effective P-state.
CPPC_CAP1 / CPPC_ENABLE / CPPC_REQUEST CPPC capabilities (highest/nominal/lowest perf), on/off, and the OS request (min/max/EPP).
RAPL_PWR_UNIT Units for the energy counters.
CORE_ENERGY_STAT / PKG_ENERGY_STAT Raw energy counters for the core and the whole package.

Healthy / typical values. On the author's PC most registers are identical on every CPU (EFER 0000000000009d01, CPPC_ENABLE 1). APIC_BASE differs only on CPU-0 (the boot CPU). MPERF, APERF, energy counters and CPPC_CAP1 differ per CPU, which is expected.

Unusual values and what they suggest. All n/a: the msr kernel module is not loaded (see MSR Setup), or Secure Boot / kernel lockdown blocks MSR access.

Where Linux gets it. /dev/cpu/N/msr (the msr kernel module), read by srs-root and cached.

Background. An MSR (Model Specific Register) is a CPU control register reached with the RDMSR and WRMSR instructions. They hold settings and counters that normal programs never see. SRS only reads them.

MSR Setup

msr-setup - Linux data - Needs root data

In plain words. Whether Linux has the drivers loaded that let root read MSRs and run CPUID per CPU.

What you see.

  • msr module - loaded (/dev/cpu/N/msr present) or not loaded.
  • cpuid module - loaded or not loaded.
  • Access - a reminder that reading MSRs is root-only and that SRS reads them through srs-root and never writes them.

Healthy / typical values. On the author's PC both modules are loaded.

Unusual values and what they suggest. not loaded: run modprobe msr (srs-root does this itself). If it still fails, kernel lockdown (Secure Boot) may be blocking it.

Where Linux gets it. Presence of /dev/cpu/0/msr and /dev/cpu/0/cpuid.

IBM/Cyrix MSRs

msrs-ibm - Not present on most PCs - Needs root data

In plain words. SIV can show the special registers of old IBM and Cyrix x86 CPUs (1990s). Modern AMD and Intel CPUs do not have them.

What you see. Status Not present on this system and Checked n/a (non-AMD MSR set). "Not present" is the expected result on any modern PC.

NexGen NXOP

nexgen-nxop - Not present on most PCs

In plain words. NexGen made x86 CPUs in the mid-1990s (their design became the AMD K6). SIV can show their special NxOP data. No current PC has one.

What you see. Status Not present on this system and Checked n/a (NexGen CPU).

Nodes

nodes - Linux data

In plain words. The same NUMA node table as NUMA.

What you see. Identical to NUMA: Node, CPUs, Memory, Free, Distances.

Where Linux gets it. /sys/devices/system/node/.

NUMA

numa - Linux data

In plain words. How memory and CPUs are grouped into nodes. Almost every desktop has one node, so all CPUs reach all memory at the same speed.

What you see.

Column Meaning Why it matters
Node Node name (node0, node1 ...)
CPUs CPUs in this node Programs run fastest using memory from their own node.
Memory RAM attached to this node Should roughly match your installed RAM split across nodes.
Free RAM free on this node right now One full node can slow programs even if total free RAM is fine.
Distances Relative cost to reach each node (10 = local) 20+ means going through another chip.

Healthy / typical values. On the author's PC: one node, node0, CPUs 0-15, 30.45GB memory, 3.44GB free at that moment, distance 10. Low Free RAM is normal on Linux because spare memory is used as cache.

Unusual values and what they suggest. Several nodes on a desktop: the BIOS has a "NPS" or "memory interleave" option set to split memory (some Threadripper/EPYC settings). Memory 0 on a node that has CPUs: a memory channel is empty.

Where Linux gets it. /sys/devices/system/node/nodeN/cpulist, meminfo, distance.

Background. NUMA (Non-Uniform Memory Access) means memory is attached to particular CPUs. Reaching "far" memory takes longer. Multi-socket servers and some large CPUs are NUMA; normal desktops are not.

NUMA memory speed

numa-speeds - Linux data

In plain words. SIV measures memory speed per NUMA node. SRS shows the node count and the result of the last memory latency test you ran. It never runs the test by itself.

What you see.

  • NUMA nodes - count; with one node it adds "(uniform memory access - every CPU sees the same latency)".
  • Last Latency run - the saved result of Menu > Tools > Latency: a table of Block size, Latency in nanoseconds and the cache Level that block size fits in, plus a note that the levels are indicative.
  • If no test has been run yet: Memory latency "Not measured yet - Menu > Tools > Latency, then Run".

Healthy / typical values. On the author's 7800X3D: 1 node. Latency about 1-4 ns up to 32KB (L1), about 3 ns up to 1MB (L2), and about 8.6-11 ns from 2MB to 64MB (the 96MB L3).

Unusual values and what they suggest. Latency jumps much earlier than the L3 size: other programs were busy during the run, or the L3 is shared with a busy neighbour. Re-run with the PC idle.

Where Linux gets it. /sys/devices/system/node/ and the saved file ~/.cache/srs/bench-latency.txt.

CPU power states

power-states - Linux data

In plain words. All the CPU's power levels in one place: performance levels (P-states), idle levels (C-states), and the whole-system sleep modes.

What you see.

Performance states (CPPC) - each line only if the file exists:

  • Highest perf (cpu0) - top CPPC level (boost).
  • Nominal perf - the level of the guaranteed base clock.
  • Lowest non-linear perf - below this, power savings drop off.
  • Lowest perf - absolute minimum level.
  • Nominal frequency / Lowest frequency - the clocks for nominal and lowest levels.
  • Maximum (boost) frequency - top clock from cpufreq.
  • Transition latency - time to change speed, in ns (0 = the hardware does it itself).

Idle states (cpu0) - each C-state with its description and exit latency in microseconds. A disabled state is shown grey with "(disabled)".

System sleep states:

  • Supported - from /sys/power/state: freeze (suspend-to-idle), mem (suspend to RAM), disk (hibernate).
  • Suspend type - from /sys/power/mem_sleep; the one in [brackets] is used: s2idle or deep (S3).
  • Hibernate mode - from /sys/power/disk; [bracketed] is active.

Healthy / typical values. On the author's 7800X3D: Highest perf 166, Nominal 138, Lowest non-linear 98, Lowest 14, nominal 4.20GHz, lowest 545MHz, boost 5.05GHz, transition 0 ns. Idle states POLL, C1, C2 (18 us), C3 (350 us). Sleep: freeze mem disk, suspend type [deep], hibernate [platform].

Unusual values and what they suggest.

  • Suspend type only s2idle: the firmware offers no S3. Fine on most new laptops; on desktops it can mean the BIOS S3 option is off.
  • disk missing from Supported: no swap big enough, or Secure Boot lockdown blocks hibernation.
  • A C-state marked disabled: someone turned it off (tuning tools do this for lower latency).

Where Linux gets it. /sys/devices/system/cpu/cpu0/acpi_cppc/, cpufreq/, cpuidle/, /sys/power/.

Background. A P-state (performance state) is a speed/voltage level while running. A C-state is an idle level. ACPI S-states (S3 = sleep, S4 = hibernate) are for the whole machine.

Processor Features Present

present - Linux data

In plain words. Windows has a function that answers "does this CPU support feature X?" for a fixed list of features. SIV shows that list; SRS shows the same list using the Linux feature flags.

What you see. CPU-0's name, then a table:

  • PF - the Windows feature number.
  • Windows feature (SIV) - the Windows name (e.g. PF_AVX2_INSTRUCTIONS_AVAILABLE), with a tick if present.
  • Linux flag - the /proc/cpuinfo flag SRS checks for it (e.g. avx2). A flag shown with a minus sign (-fpu) means "ticked when this flag is missing".

Healthy / typical values. On the author's PC everything is ticked except PF_FLOATING_POINT_PRECISION_ERRATA (the 1994 Pentium FDIV bug), PF_FLOATING_POINT_EMULATED and PF_3DNOW_INSTRUCTIONS_AVAILABLE. That is normal for any modern CPU.

Unusual values and what they suggest. PF_NX_ENABLED unticked: NX (no-execute) is off in the BIOS, which is a security risk. PF_VIRT_FIRMWARE_ENABLED unticked: virtualization may be off in the BIOS (SRS checks the svm flag for this line).

Where Linux gets it. /proc/cpuinfo flags of CPU 0.

Processor

processor - Linux data

In plain words. A short card for each CPU: name, generation, where it sits, its speed, its caches and its main instruction sets. The CPU-n panel buttons open one CPU; the menu item shows all.

What you see. For each CPU:

  • CPU-n, model name, then "Family X Model X Stepping n" (family and model in hex, no 0x) and APIC p.c.t (package.core.thread) with (core) for a first thread or (logical) for an SMT sibling.
  • Current speed, e.g. "4.96GHz Processor".
  • For first threads only, one line per cache level: name (L1 Data, L1 Code, L2 Unified, L3 Unified), ways, line size, size, sets, and how many CPUs share it with their numbers. On CPU-0 the size is written as "count x size" (e.g. "8 x 32KB") to show the total number of such caches in the chip.
  • For first threads, a line with the vendor and key features in brackets: MMX or MMX+, SSE4.2, XD (no-execute), SVM or VMX (virtualization), AVX512 or AVX2.

Healthy / typical values. On the author's 7800X3D, CPU-0: Family 19 Model 61 Stepping 2 (hex for 25/97), APIC 0.0.0 (core); L1 Data and L1 Code 8 x 32KB, 8-way, 64 sets, shared by CPUs 0 and 8; L2 8 x 1MB, 2048 sets; L3 1 x 96MB, 16-way, shared by 16 CPUs (0-15); [MMX+ SSE4.2 XD SVM AVX512].

Unusual values and what they suggest. An L1/L2 cache "shared by 1 CPU": SMT is off. A smaller L3 than the spec sheet: on multi-CCD chips each CCD has its own L3, so you see one CCD's share.

Where Linux gets it. /proc/cpuinfo, /sys/devices/system/cpu/cpuN/cache/indexM/, topology, cpufreq.

Processors

processors - Linux data

In plain words. The main processor page (the Processors panel button). It shows what kind of CPU system you have and lists every logical CPU with its IDs.

What you see.

Capabilities - four tick-box lines with a count and a legend:

  • Multi-processor System - ticked if there is more than one physical package (|P|).
  • Hybrid-processor System - mixed big/little cores; SRS always shows this unticked with 1 logical package (|e|).
  • Multi-core Processor - number of cores (|C|) and cores per package.
  • Multi-threading Cores - number of logical processors (|L|) and threads per core.

Then a note naming the board, and a table:

Column Meaning
Processors CPU name with a marker: |P| the first CPU, |C| the first thread of a core, |L| an SMT sibling.
APIC (first) package.core.thread ID.
APIC (second) The hardware APIC ID in hex.
Node NUMA node (always 0 in SRS).
Pkg Physical package.
N Linux CPU number.
CPU Affinity Mask This CPU's bit as a 64-bit hex mask.
Speed Current clock.
ACPI The ACPI device name of the CPU (e.g. ACPI0007:00).
CPU Device The ACPI path of the CPU object in the firmware tables (e.g. \_SB_.PLTF.C000).

Board/BIOS line at the end.

Healthy / typical values. On the author's 7800X3D: 1 package (unticked multi-processor), 8 cores, 16 logical processors, 2 per core. CPU-0 to CPU-7 are |P|/|C| (thread 0), CPU-8 to CPU-15 are |L|.

Unusual values and what they suggest. Missing ACPI names (-): the firmware does not link CPUs to ACPI objects (common in VMs). Fewer CPUs than the spec: some disabled in the BIOS, or maxcpus= / nosmt on the kernel command line (compare with CPU Groups).

Where Linux gets it. /sys/devices/system/cpu/cpuN/topology/, firmware_node, /proc/cpuinfo, cpufreq.

Background. The APIC (Advanced Programmable Interrupt Controller) ID is the number the hardware uses for each thread. Linux CPU numbers are just the order Linux brought them up.

Speculation Control

speculation - Linux data

In plain words. SIV shows the Windows "speculation control" settings. On Linux, SRS shows the kernel's own list of CPU security weaknesses (Spectre, Meltdown and friends) and whether each one is fixed on your machine.

What you see.

  • One line per known issue, as the kernel names it (e.g. spectre_v1, spectre_v2, meltdown, retbleed, spec_rstack_overflow, tsa, vmscape ...), and the kernel's status text:
    • green Not affected - this CPU does not have the weakness.
    • orange Mitigation: ... - the weakness exists and the kernel is protecting against it.
    • red Vulnerable - the weakness exists and is not protected.
  • Kernel command line - the boot options, so you can see if mitigations were turned off.

Healthy / typical values. On a default system every line says "Not affected" or "Mitigation: ...". On the author's PC several lines say "Vulnerable" because the owner boots with mitigations=off for a little more speed. That is a deliberate choice, not a fault.

Unusual values and what they suggest. "Vulnerable" without mitigations=off in the command line: old microcode (see Microcode) or an old kernel. "Vulnerable" on a shared or internet-facing machine is a real risk; on a single-user gaming PC it is a trade-off some people accept.

Where Linux gets it. /sys/devices/system/cpu/vulnerabilities/* and /proc/cmdline.

Background. Speculative execution means the CPU guesses ahead to run faster. Researchers found ways to leak data through those guesses. Mitigations close the leaks at some cost in speed.

Turbo Boost

turbo-boost - Linux data

In plain words. Whether the CPU is allowed to boost above its base clock, and how high it can go.

What you see. (lines appear only when the file exists)

  • CPB (CPUID 80000007 EDX bit 9) - ticked if the CPU supports Core Performance Boost.
  • cpufreq boost - enabled (green) or disabled (red).
  • amd_pstate status - active, guided or passive.
  • amd_pstate prefcore - whether preferred-core scheduling is on.
  • Maximum boost frequency - amd_pstate's top clock.
  • Lowest non-linear frequency - see AMD Ryzen Power Management.
  • cpuinfo_max_freq - top clock as cpufreq reports it.

Healthy / typical values. On the author's 7800X3D: CPB ticked, boost enabled, amd_pstate active, prefcore enabled, maximum 5.05GHz, non-linear 2.98GHz, cpuinfo_max_freq 5.05GHz.

Unusual values and what they suggest. Boost disabled: off in the BIOS ("Core Performance Boost"), or turned off by a power profile. Maximum equal to the base clock (4.20GHz on this chip): boost off.

Where Linux gets it. CPUID leaf 80000007, /sys/devices/system/cpu/cpufreq/boost, /sys/devices/system/cpu/amd_pstate/, cpu0/cpufreq/.

Background. "Turbo Boost" is Intel's name and "Core Performance Boost" (CPB) is AMD's for the same idea: run above the base clock when power and temperature allow.

Xeon PIRs

xeon-pir - Not present on most PCs

In plain words. Some older Intel Xeon chips had a small Processor Information ROM (PIR) with factory data. Desktop and AMD CPUs do not.

What you see. Status Not present on this system and Checked n/a (Intel Xeon only).

Cache Levels

cache - Linux data

In plain words. A table of the CPU's caches: size, layout and which CPUs share each one. The Cache-n panel buttons show the table for CPU number n.

What you see. Title "Cache Levels of CPU-n", then:

Column Meaning Why it matters
Cache Level and type: L1 Data, L1 Code, L2 Unified, L3 Unified L1 is fastest and smallest, L3 slowest and biggest.
Size Size of one such cache (K = kilobytes) Bigger caches hold more of a program's working data.
Ways Associativity How many places a line can go; more = fewer collisions.
Line Line size in bytes The unit the cache moves data in (64 on modern CPUs).
Sets Number of sets Size / (ways x line).
Shared by How many CPUs share it 2 = shared by the two threads of one core; all = whole chip.
CPUs Which CPUs share it

A note points to Menu > Tools > Latency for measured speeds.

Healthy / typical values. On the author's Ryzen 7 7800X3D, CPU-0: L1 Data 32K and L1 Code 32K (8-way, shared by CPUs 0,8), L2 1024K (8-way), L3 98304K (96MB, 16-way, 98304 sets), shared by 16 CPUs (0-15). The huge L3 is the "3D V-Cache" that the X3D name refers to.

Unusual values and what they suggest. No rows: the kernel has no cache info (some VMs). L3 shared by fewer CPUs than you have on a multi-CCD chip: normal, each CCD has its own L3.

Where Linux gets it. /sys/devices/system/cpu/cpuN/cache/indexM/ (level, type, size, ways_of_associativity, coherency_line_size, number_of_sets, shared_cpu_list).

Background. A cache is a small fast memory on the CPU that keeps copies of recently used RAM. L1 is inside each core, L2 is per core, L3 is shared. A cache hit takes a few nanoseconds; going out to RAM takes 60-80 ns or more.

CPU Groups

group - Linux data

In plain words. Windows splits large systems into "processor groups" of up to 64 CPUs. Linux has no such groups; SRS shows the Linux CPU sets instead (the Groups panel button).

What you see.

  • online - CPUs running now. offline - CPUs switched off (none if all are on).
  • possible - CPUs the kernel could ever bring up. present - CPUs physically there.
  • isolated - CPUs kept away from normal tasks. nohz_full - CPUs without the regular timer tick.
  • kernel_max - the highest CPU number this kernel supports.
  • This process affinity - the CPUs SRS itself is allowed to run on.

Healthy / typical values. On the author's PC: online, possible and present all 0-15; offline, isolated and nohz_full none; kernel_max 15; affinity 0-15.

Unusual values and what they suggest.

  • Offline CPUs: turned off by hand (echo 0 > .../online), by nosmt, or by maxcpus=.
  • possible larger than present: normal on servers and many desktops (room for hot-plug).
  • Process affinity smaller than online: SRS was started under taskset or a restricted cgroup.

Where Linux gets it. /sys/devices/system/cpu/online, offline, possible, present, isolated, nohz_full, kernel_max, and the process's own sched_getaffinity.

Machine / BIOS / Memory (SRS Section Reference)

Back to the section index - Glossary

Where to find these items (SRS 2.0). In the main window they are on two pages: Memory (Alt+3: the memory sticks, SPD, timings, memory map, NUMA) and Motherboard & BIOS (Alt+4: everything else). Each page's All N items lists the rest. You can also type an item's name or id into the search box (Ctrl+F). The rest of this introduction describes the classic view (Menu -> Classic View), with its Menu and panel buttons.

This group describes the computer itself rather than any one add-in card: the motherboard and its firmware (BIOS / UEFI), the memory sticks and how memory is laid out, the ACPI tables and devices the firmware hands to the operating system, the TPM security chip and the CMOS clock. Open it in SRS with Menu -> Machine / BIOS / Memory -> item, or use the Machine panel button and its sub-buttons DIMMs and Status. Most items work as a normal user. Items marked "Needs root data" are only complete after you run Menu > Run as root (srs-root) once. That helper saves four read-only copies that SRS then reads: dmidecode.txt (full SMBIOS data: serials, UUID, CPU socket), spd.txt (memory-stick SPD decode), acpi-tables/ (copies of the ACPI tables) and iomem.txt (the I/O memory map). The item Machine options shows which of these sources are present on your PC.

All examples come from the author's PC: an ASUS TUF GAMING X870-PRO WIFI7 W NEO board with an AMD Ryzen 7 7800X3D, 2 x 16 GB DDR5 and BIOS 1805.

A few words first

Some ideas come up again and again in this group. Read these once and the rest is easier.

  • ACPI (Advanced Configuration and Power Interface) is how the firmware describes the board to the operating system: which devices exist, how to power them on and off, how interrupts are wired. It comes as a set of binary tables, each with a four-letter signature such as DSDT or APIC.
  • The ACPI namespace is a tree of named objects built from those tables. Paths look like \_SB_.PCI0.GPP0 ("System Bus, PCI root 0, general purpose port 0"). Each device has a HID (hardware ID) such as PNP0A08 (a PCI Express root bridge) or AMDI0030 (an AMD GPIO controller).
  • _STA is the ACPI "status" value of a device. SRS prints it as a hex number plus four letters: P present, E enabled, S shown in the user interface, F functioning. 0x0F PESF means all four are true. 0x00 ---- means the firmware hides the device (normal for unused controllers). A - means the device has no _STA method, which the operating system treats as "present and working".
  • SMBIOS (System Management BIOS), also called DMI (Desktop Management Interface), is a second firmware table set. It is a plain inventory: board name, BIOS version, memory slots, serial numbers. Linux shows most of it in /sys/class/dmi/id; the serial numbers and some detail are root-only.
  • UEFI (Unified Extensible Firmware Interface) is the modern replacement for the old PC BIOS. Most people still say "BIOS" for both.
  • srs-root cache: root-only data that the srs-root helper copied for SRS. SRS itself never runs as root and never writes to hardware.

ACPI PCI root buses

acpi-buses - Linux data

In plain words. Shows where the PCI Express "tree" of the PC starts, and how every PCI bus hangs off a bridge that the firmware has named in ACPI.

What you see. Two tables.

First table, one row per PCI root bridge (HID PNP0A08, PNP0A03 or ACPI0016):

Field Meaning Why it matters
Device ACPI device name, e.g. PNP0A08:00 PNP0A08 = PCI Express root bridge, PNP0A03 = older PCI root
Path ACPI namespace path, e.g. \_SB_.PCI0 The name the firmware's own code uses for it
UID Unique ID inside that HID Tells several root bridges apart (servers often have more than one)
Physical node The Linux device it became, e.g. pci0000:00 Links the ACPI view to the Linux PCI view
Status _STA value and letters 0x0F PESF = present and working

Second table, one row per PCI bus Linux knows (from /sys/class/pci_bus):

Field Meaning Why it matters
PCI Bus Domain and bus number, e.g. 0000:05 Bus numbers are what lspci addresses start with
Bridge The PCI bridge that creates this bus, or root Shows the parent of each bus
Bridge ACPI path ACPI name of that bridge, e.g. \_SB_.PCI0.GPP7 Ties a bus to a named slot or chipset port
Bus range Secondary-subordinate bus numbers behind the bridge, e.g. 05-0C Everything below that bridge lives in this range

Healthy / typical values. One root bridge PNP0A08:00 \_SB_.PCI0 ... 0x0F PESF on a desktop. On the author's board the chipset hangs off GPP7 (buses 05-0C), the USB4 controller off GPP8 (buses 0D-74, a big range reserved for hot-plugged Thunderbolt devices) and the graphics card off GPP0 through two extra switch levels (SWUS, SWDS).

Unusual values and what they suggest.

  • A bridge with an empty ACPI path: the firmware did not describe it. Usually harmless, but power management and hot-plug for that branch may then fall back to generic code.
  • A very wide bus range (like 0D-74) on a USB4 / Thunderbolt port is normal: the firmware reserves bus numbers for devices you might plug in later.
  • More than one root bridge on a desktop: rare; normal on multi-socket servers.

Where Linux gets it. /sys/bus/acpi/devices/PNP0A08:* (path, uid, status, physical_node) and /sys/class/pci_bus/* plus /sys/bus/pci/devices/*/firmware_node and secondary_bus_number / subordinate_bus_number.

Background. A PCI bridge (shown elsewhere as "PtP", PCI-to-PCI) creates a new bus number behind it. Every slot, M.2 socket and chipset port is really a bridge. The GPU's own switch chips (SWUS = switch upstream, SWDS = switch downstream) are why a graphics card often appears three bus numbers deep.

ACPI devices

acpi-dev - Linux data

In plain words. The full list of devices the firmware describes in ACPI, with their status and which Linux driver picked each one up.

What you see. One row per ACPI device, sorted by name:

Field Meaning Why it matters
Device Linux name, HID plus instance, e.g. AMDI0030:00 Unique key for the detail view
HID Hardware ID, e.g. PNP0C14 (WMI), MSFT0101 (TPM 2.0) Tells you what kind of device it is
_STA Status hex value + P/E/S/F letters, or - if no _STA method Whether the firmware says it is present and working
Path ACPI namespace path, e.g. \_SB_.PCI0.SBRG.EC0_ The firmware's name for it
Physical node / driver The Linux device and driver bound to it Empty driver = nothing in Linux claimed it

The footer gives the device count and repeats the meaning of the _STA letters.

Detail view (acpi-dev:<device>, e.g. acpi-dev:PNP0C09:00): every attribute Linux exposes for that device, when present: path, hid, modalias, uid, adr (bus address), status, description, power_state, real_power_state, resource_in_use, then physical_node, driver, and one child line per child device.

Healthy / typical values. On the author's PC: 258 ACPI devices. The 16 ACPI0007 rows are the CPU threads (\_SB_.PLTF.C000 to C00F, bound to processor). PNP0A08:00 is the PCI root, PNP0B00:00 the CMOS clock (rtc_cmos), PNP0C09:00 the embedded controller (acpi-ec), MSFT0101:00 the TPM (tpm_crb_acpi), AMDI0030:00 the GPIO controller (amd_gpio). Many rows show 0x00 ----: spare I2C, I3C and UART controllers the board does not use.

Unusual values and what they suggest.

  • 0x0B PE-F (present, enabled, not shown, functioning) is normal for interrupt link devices (PNP0C0F, LNKA..LNKH) and the power button.
  • A device you expect (for example a touchpad on a laptop) that shows 0x0F PESF but has no driver: Linux is missing a driver or a kernel option for it.
  • A device with 0x00 ---- that you expected to work: it may be switched off in the BIOS setup.

Where Linux gets it. /sys/bus/acpi/devices/* (hid, status, path, physical_node, physical_node/driver).

Background. HID prefixes tell you who defined the ID: PNP and ACPI are industry-standard, LNX are Linux-internal pseudo-devices (LNXSYSTM is the root, LNXPOWER a power resource), and vendor IDs such as AMDI (AMD), MSFT (Microsoft), RTK (Realtek) and ASMT (ASMedia) are listed on their own in ACPI extension (PDX).

ACPI embedded controller

acpi-ec - Linux data - Needs root data

In plain words. The embedded controller (EC) is a small helper microcontroller on the board. On laptops it runs the keyboard, battery and fans; on desktops it is usually much simpler. This item shows whether ACPI describes one and how Linux talks to it.

What you see.

Field Meaning Why it matters
PNP0C09:00 (first line) ACPI path of the EC Confirms an EC is described
_STA Status of the EC - = no _STA method, treated as present
UID Unique ID Usually - or 0
Driver Linux driver acpi-ec is the normal one
ec_storm_threshold How many EC events in a row before Linux switches to polling Protects against "GPE storms" from buggy firmware
ec_busy_polling Whether Linux busy-waits for EC replies (Y/N) Y is a workaround on some laptops
ec_max_queries How many EC queries may be outstanding Tuning value, default 16
ec_sys module Whether the ec_sys debug module is loaded Needed for an EC register dump
EC register dump Not read: root-only debugfs file, not in the srs-root cache SRS never reads EC registers

If there is no EC, the item says "No ACPI EC (PNP0C09)".

Healthy / typical values. On the author's desktop: \_SB_.PCI0.SBRG.EC0_, driver acpi-ec, storm threshold 8, busy polling N, max queries 16, ec_sys not loaded.

Unusual values and what they suggest. No EC on a laptop is very unusual and means battery and lid events will not work. Changed ec_* values usually come from a kernel command-line workaround (acpi.ec_*=); check your boot loader settings.

Where Linux gets it. /sys/bus/acpi/devices/PNP0C09:00 and /sys/module/acpi/parameters/ec_*. A register dump would need /sys/kernel/debug/ec/ec0/io (root, ec_sys module).

ACPI method evaluation

acpi-eval - Linux data - Needs root data

In plain words. In the Windows original this item could run ("evaluate") ACPI methods. SRS is strictly read-only, so on Linux it only reports whether the tool that could do this is loaded, and points you to the read-only alternatives.

What you see.

  • acpi_call - whether the third-party acpi_call kernel module is loaded (/proc/acpi/call present (root) or not loaded).
  • Evaluation - always "disabled": running an ACPI method means writing to the kernel, and SRS never writes.
  • Read-only alternative - ACPI methods for the list of methods, and ACPI devices for _STA, _HID, _UID and _ADR values.

Where Linux gets it. Checks for /proc/acpi/call.

Background. An ACPI method is a small program written in AML (ACPI Machine Language) inside the firmware tables. Running the wrong one can switch off a device or the whole PC, which is why SRS does not do it.

ACPI HAL

acpi-hal - Linux data

In plain words. A summary of the ACPI layer as Linux sees it: what kind of machine the firmware claims to be, how many tables and devices there are, and the ACPI driver's settings. (HAL, Hardware Abstraction Layer, is the Windows name for this layer.)

What you see.

Field Meaning Why it matters
Preferred PM Profile Machine type the firmware reports: Desktop, Mobile, Workstation, Server, Tablet... Linux and Windows pick power defaults from it
ACPICA Version Version of the ACPI interpreter built into the kernel Newer versions fix firmware quirks
ACPI Tables Number of tables (including dynamically loaded ones) See ACPI tables
ACPI Devices Number of ACPI namespace devices See ACPI devices
SCI Interrupts Total System Control Interrupts since boot ACPI's own interrupt line
GPE Events Total General Purpose Events since boot Wake and hot-plug signals
Hardware-reduced ACPI No (fixed hardware present) or Yes / unknown Hardware-reduced is used by ARM and some tablets
Firmware Performance (FPDT) Whether a boot-timing table exists Used by Firmware
Hotplug ... One line per ACPI hot-plug type (memory, pci_root, processor) Enabled = Linux will react to hot-add events
acpi.* Every ACPI driver parameter and its value Shows kernel command-line tweaks

Healthy / typical values. Author's PC: 1 (Desktop), ACPICA 20260408, 30 tables, 258 devices, 3512 SCI interrupts, "No (fixed hardware present)", FPDT present, all three hot-plug types enabled.

Unusual values and what they suggest.

  • PM profile 2 (Mobile) on a desktop board, or 0 (Unspecified): lazy firmware; power defaults may be odd.
  • SCI and GPE counts that rise by thousands per second: an "interrupt storm", often a buggy GPE. Look at ACPI interrupts and GPEs to find which one.

Where Linux gets it. /sys/firmware/acpi/pm_profile, /sys/firmware/acpi/interrupts/, /sys/firmware/acpi/hotplug/, /sys/module/acpi/parameters/.

ACPI interrupts and GPEs

acpi-int - Linux data

In plain words. Counts how often each ACPI event has fired since boot: the power button, the real-time clock alarm, and the General Purpose Events (GPEs) that devices use to wake the PC or signal hot-plug.

What you see.

Field Meaning Why it matters
Event Event name: ff_* fixed events, gpeXX numbered GPEs, sci, gpe_all, error, sci_not Which signal
Count How many times it fired since boot Shows busy or stuck events
State Kernel state words: EN enabled, STS status bit set, enabled/disabled, masked/unmasked, invalid Whether Linux is listening to it

Then: how many idle (count 0 and not enabled) GPEs were hidden, and a line SCI IRQ n: total interrupts (all CPUs) from /proc/interrupts.

Healthy / typical values. Author's PC: gpe04 3506, gpe1B 6, everything else 0; sci and gpe_all 3512; SCI IRQ 9. ff_pwr_btn enabled (the power button works), ff_rt_clk disabled (no RTC alarm set). 27 idle GPEs hidden.

Unusual values and what they suggest.

  • One GPE with a huge, fast-rising count: a GPE storm. It costs CPU time and battery. The usual fix is a BIOS update or the kernel option acpi_mask_gpe=0xNN.
  • error above 0: the ACPI interpreter hit errors handling events; check dmesg for ACPI messages.
  • sci_not above 0: SCIs arrived that no handler claimed.

Where Linux gets it. /sys/firmware/acpi/interrupts/* and the acpi line in /proc/interrupts.

Background. The SCI (System Control Interrupt) is ACPI's single shared interrupt line, usually IRQ 9. Each GPE is one bit in the chipset's event register; the firmware's _Lxx / _Exx methods say what each bit means.

ACPI IPF (Intel Platform Framework) methods

acpi-ipf - Not present on most PCs

In plain words. Looks for Intel Platform Framework devices, Intel's newer laptop power and thermal framework (the successor of DPTF, Dynamic Platform and Thermal Framework).

What it would show. One line per matching ACPI device with its path, then Device (description), Probed HIDs (INTC1040 INTC1041 INTC1042 INTC1043) and Status (present or Not present on this system).

What "not present" means. Normal on AMD PCs and on desktops. It only appears on recent Intel laptops.

Where Linux gets it. Name match in /sys/bus/acpi/devices.

ACPI ICD0001 methods

acpi-itm - Not present on most PCs

In plain words. Looks for an ACPI device with ID ICD0001, a thermal / management device found on a few OEM systems.

What it would show. Matching devices with their ACPI path, then Device, Probed HIDs (ICD0001) and Status.

What "not present" means. Normal for nearly every PC.

Where Linux gets it. Name match in /sys/bus/acpi/devices.

ACPI methods

acpi-methods - Linux data - Needs root data

In plain words. Lists every method (small firmware program) defined in the main ACPI code tables, the DSDT and the SSDTs.

What you see.

Field Meaning Why it matters
Table Which table holds the method: DSDT, SSDT1... Tells you which firmware module defines it
Method Method name, relative to its enclosing Scope, e.g. _PRT, _STA, _CRS, WMBC Names starting with _ are standard ACPI; others are vendor-private
Args Number of arguments (0-7) Part of the method's definition
Flags Serialized or NotSerialized, plus Sync if a sync level is set Serialized methods cannot run twice at once

The footer gives the total. acpi-methods:<SIG> (e.g. acpi-methods:SSDT6) shows one table only.

Healthy / typical values. Hundreds to a few thousand rows. On the author's PC the DSDT alone has many _PRT (PCI interrupt routing), _STA, _CRS (current resources), _PRS/_SRS/_DIS (interrupt link handling), and vendor methods such as WMBC (an ASUS WMI method), _PTS/_WAK (prepare to sleep / wake).

Unusual values and what they suggest. The list is made by scanning the table bytes for the AML "Method" opcode, so an odd row (for example a standard name with an unexpected argument count) can be a scan match inside data rather than a real method. For exact work use acpidump and iasl -d. If the item says it needs the cached tables, run srs-root.

Where Linux gets it. The srs-root copies of /sys/firmware/acpi/tables/DSDT and SSDT* (root-only on Linux).

Background. Common standard methods: _STA status, _CRS resources, _PRW wake capability, _PSx / _PRx power states, _OSC operating-system capability handshake, _PTS and _WAK sleep and wake hooks, _Lxx GPE handlers.

ACPI extension (PDX)

acpi-pdx - Linux data

In plain words. Lists the vendor-specific device IDs in the ACPI namespace, that is, every device whose HID is not a standard PNP, LNX or ACPI one. These are the parts that need vendor drivers.

What you see.

Field Meaning Why it matters
HID Vendor hardware ID, e.g. AMDI0010 First letters name the vendor
Count How many devices share that HID e.g. 4 I2C controllers
First path ACPI path of the first one Where it sits
Driver Linux driver of the first one, or - - = unclaimed (often disabled anyway)

A note explains the prefixes: AMDI = AMD, MSFT = Microsoft, RTK = Realtek, ASMT = ASMedia.

Healthy / typical values. Author's PC: AMDI0010 x4 (I2C, i2c_designware), AMDI0030 (GPIO, amd_gpio), AMDI0101 (amd_x3d_vcache, the X3D cache-preference driver), AMDIF031 (pt-gpio), MSFT0101 (TPM, tpm_crb_acpi), RTK5439 and RTK5452 (Realtek USB-C / USB4 power-delivery chips on the I2C bus).

Unusual values and what they suggest. A vendor HID with no driver may simply be disabled in firmware (check its _STA in ACPI devices). If it is 0x0F PESF and has no driver, a feature (sensor, button, power profile) may not work until a newer kernel adds support.

Where Linux gets it. /sys/bus/acpi/devices.

ACPI PCI buses and ports

acpi-ports - Linux data

In plain words. Every PCI device that the firmware also describes in ACPI, matched to its ACPI name. This tells you which physical port or slot a device is behind.

What you see.

Field Meaning Why it matters
PCI PCI address bus:device.function, e.g. 03:00.0 Same as lspci
Class PCI class code; 0604 PtP marks a PCI-to-PCI bridge (a port) 0300 = display, 0108 = NVMe, 0C03 = USB, 0200 = Ethernet
ID Vendor:device ID, e.g. 1002:7550 Identifies the chip
ACPI node Linux name of the ACPI companion, e.g. device:3e Links to ACPI devices
ACPI path The firmware's name, e.g. \_SB_.PCI0.GPP0.SWUS.SWDS.VGA_ Shows the chain of ports down to the device
Driver Linux driver bound to the PCI device pcieport for ports

Footer: number of PCI functions with an ACPI companion.

Healthy / typical values. Author's PC: 45 functions. The graphics card is \_SB_.PCI0.GPP0.SWUS.SWDS.VGA_ (amdgpu); NVMe drives sit at ...GPP7.UP00.DP00.NV00 and ...DP40.EP00; the 5 GbE network chip at ...DP30.EP00 (r8169); Wi-Fi at ...DP38.EP00.

Unusual values and what they suggest. A PCI device missing from this list has no ACPI companion. That is normal for some devices behind the chipset, but can mean ACPI power management (D3cold, wake) will not work for it. Devices behind a port marked GPP7.UP00 share the chipset link to the CPU; heavy traffic on several of them at once shares that bandwidth.

Where Linux gets it. /sys/bus/pci/devices/*/firmware_node plus class, vendor, device and driver.

ACPI power resource methods

acpi-pwr - Linux data

In plain words. Shows the ACPI "power resources" (switchable power rails the firmware can turn on and off) and the ACPI power state of each device that supports power management.

What you see. Two tables.

Field (power resources) Meaning
Resource LNXPOWER:nn
Path ACPI path of the power resource, e.g. \_SB_.PCI0.GPP8.PWRS
In use on if a device is currently using it, else off
Status _STA of the resource (0x01 P--- = on)
Field (devices) Meaning
Device ACPI device name
Path ACPI path
power_state State Linux believes: D0 (fully on) to D3hot / D3cold (off)
real_power_state State read back from the hardware, or -

Footer: number of devices with ACPI power management (_PSx / _PRx methods).

Healthy / typical values. Author's PC: 14 power resources; the USB4 branch (GPP8...) all on, the graphics-card branch resources (M237) off. The I2C controller sits in D3hot (idle, powered down), the USB4 ports in D0.

Unusual values and what they suggest.

  • A device stuck in D0 that should idle (for example an unused USB4 controller) costs power. Check runtime power management settings (power/control in sysfs, or powertop).
  • power_state and real_power_state disagreeing: the device did not reach the state Linux asked for; a common cause of failed suspend.

Where Linux gets it. /sys/bus/acpi/devices/LNXPOWER:* (path, resource_in_use, status) and /sys/bus/acpi/devices/*/power_state, real_power_state.

Background. D-states are device power states: D0 on, D1/D2 light sleep (rare), D3hot off but still powered, D3cold power fully removed.

ACPI SPB (serial peripheral bus) methods

acpi-spb - Linux data

In plain words. Lists the low-speed serial buses on the board (I2C, I3C, UART serial ports, SPI) and the small devices on them, such as USB-C controllers or memory temperature sensors.

What you see. First table, ACPI serial-bus controllers and serial devices:

Field Meaning
Device ACPI device (AMDI0010 I2C, AMDI0015 I3C, AMDI0020 UART, PNP0500/PNP0501 serial port, RTK* Realtek devices...)
Path ACPI path
Driver Linux driver or -
Physical node Linux device it became

Second table, every I2C adapter and client Linux knows:

Field Meaning
I2C Linux name: i2c-N for a bus, N-00AA for a device at address 0xAA on bus N
Adapter / client name e.g. SMBus PIIX4 adapter port 0, spd5118, AMDGPU DM i2c hw bus 0
ACPI path ACPI companion if any

Then one line per SPI device, and a note that SRS lists names only and never talks on these buses.

Healthy / typical values. Author's PC: one active I2C controller \_SB_.I2CA (i2c_designware) with two Realtek chips on it (U4PD, TYPC, the USB4 / USB-C power controllers); one active serial port PNP0501:00 (serial); the chipset SMBus (SMBus PIIX4, three ports) with two spd5118 clients at 1-0051 and 1-0053, which are the two DDR5 sticks' temperature sensors; and many AMDGPU buses that belong to the graphics card's display outputs.

Unusual values and what they suggest. On DDR5 systems, no spd5118 clients means the memory temperature sensors are not visible (the driver is not loaded, or the board blocks SMBus access). See DIMM status/temperatures.

Where Linux gets it. /sys/bus/acpi/devices, /sys/bus/i2c/devices/*/name, /sys/bus/spi/devices.

Background. I2C / SMBus (System Management Bus) is a two-wire bus for slow chips: sensors, memory SPD chips, RGB controllers. Each chip has a 7-bit address; DDR5 memory sticks answer at 0x50-0x57.

ACPI tables

acpi-tables - Linux data - Needs root data

In plain words. Lists every ACPI table the firmware provides, with its header: size, version and who built it.

What you see.

Field Meaning Why it matters
Table Signature, e.g. DSDT, SSDT3, APIC (Linux numbers repeated tables) What the table is
Length Size in bytes
Rev Table revision Newer revisions add fields
Check Checksum byte All bytes of a valid table add up to 0
OEM OEM ID, e.g. ALASKA (AMI's placeholder), AMD Who supplied the table
OEM Table OEM table ID, e.g. A M I, AmdTable, CPMCMN Often names the firmware module
OEM Rev OEM revision
Creator Tool that compiled it: AMI, INTL (Intel's iasl compiler), MSFT, AMD
Creator Rev Version of that tool

Footer: total tables. Without the srs-root cache only the name and file size are shown. acpi-tables:<SIG> (e.g. acpi-tables:HPET) shows the parsed header of one table plus a hex dump of up to 4 KB.

Healthy / typical values. Author's PC: 30 tables, among them APIC (CPU interrupt controllers), DSDT (88990 bytes, the main ACPI code), FACP, FACS, HPET (timer), IVRS (AMD IOMMU), MCFG (PCIe configuration space), 16 SSDTs from AMD modules, TPM2, VFCT (a copy of the graphics card's video BIOS), WPBT, WSMT.

Unusual values and what they suggest.

  • WPBT (Windows Platform Binary Table) lets firmware hand Windows a program to run at startup (on ASUS boards, the Armoury Crate installer). Linux ignores it. You can usually turn it off in the BIOS setup ("Download Armoury Crate app").
  • FACS has no standard header, so its OEM and revision columns are not meaningful.
  • A missing MCFG or HPET on a modern PC is rare and worth a BIOS update.

Where Linux gets it. /sys/firmware/acpi/tables/ (root-only to read; SRS uses the srs-root copies in acpi-tables/). Same data as acpidump.

Background. DSDT (Differentiated System Description Table) holds the main ACPI code; SSDTs (Secondary System Description Tables) add more, often one per firmware module (CPU, USB4, memory tools).

ACPI Toshiba test

acpi-test - Not present on most PCs

In plain words. Looks for any ACPI device whose ID starts with TOS, which Toshiba (now Dynabook) laptops use.

What it would show. Matching devices with their ACPI path, then Device ("Toshiba laptop ACPI devices"), Probed HIDs (TOS) and Status.

What "not present" means. You do not have a Toshiba laptop. Normal.

Where Linux gets it. Name match in /sys/bus/acpi/devices.

ACPI TFP INT3403 methods

acpi-tfp - Not present on most PCs

In plain words. Looks for Intel DPTF (Dynamic Platform and Thermal Framework) thermal "participants", the temperature sensors and cooling devices of Intel laptops.
