What it would show. Matching devices with their ACPI path, then Device ("Intel DPTF thermal participant"), Probed HIDs (INT3403 INTC1043) and Status.

What "not present" means. Normal on AMD PCs and desktops.

Where Linux gets it. Name match in /sys/bus/acpi/devices.

ACPI TMS INT340E methods

acpi-tms - Not present on most PCs

In plain words. Looks for the Intel DPTF INT340E device (part of Intel's laptop thermal management).

What it would show. Matching devices with their ACPI path, then Device, Probed HIDs (INT340E) and Status.

What "not present" means. Normal on AMD PCs and desktops.

Where Linux gets it. Name match in /sys/bus/acpi/devices.

ACPI TOS1900 methods

acpi-tos - Not present on most PCs

In plain words. Looks for the Toshiba laptop "extras" device that controls hotkeys, backlight and fan on Toshiba / Dynabook laptops.

What it would show. Matching devices with their ACPI path, then Device ("Toshiba laptop extras"), Probed HIDs (TOS1900 TOS6200 TOS6207 TOS6208) and Status.

What "not present" means. Not a Toshiba laptop. Normal.

Where Linux gets it. Name match in /sys/bus/acpi/devices.

ACPI TPM

acpi-tpm - Linux data

In plain words. Shows how the firmware describes the TPM (Trusted Platform Module, the security chip used for disk encryption keys and Secure Boot measurements).

What you see. For each TPM device in ACPI (MSFT0101 = TPM 2.0, PNP0C31 / IFX0102 = TPM 1.2):

  • Path, HID, UID, _STA, Driver - as in ACPI devices.

Then the decoded TPM2 table (when the srs-root cache has it):

Field Meaning
Signature ... Creator Revision The standard ACPI table header (see ACPI tables)
Platform Class 0 (Client) for PCs, 1 (Server)
Control Area Memory address where commands are exchanged with the TPM
Start Method How the OS tells the TPM to start a command: 2 ACPI Start, 6 TIS 1.3 / FIFO, 7 Command Response Buffer, 8 CRB with ACPI Start, and ARM / I2C variants

Without the cache only the table size is shown. Without a TPM: "No ACPI TPM device" and / or "No TPM2 ACPI table".

Healthy / typical values. Author's PC: MSFT0101:00, \_SB_.TPM_, 0x0F PESF, tpm_crb_acpi; TPM2 table 76 bytes, Platform Class 0 (Client), Start Method 2 ACPI Start. That is the usual pattern for AMD's firmware TPM.

Unusual values and what they suggest. No MSFT0101 device on a board that has a TPM: it is switched off in the BIOS setup (on AMD boards look for "fTPM" or "Firmware TPM"). Windows 11 requires it.

Where Linux gets it. /sys/bus/acpi/devices/MSFT0101:* and the srs-root copy of /sys/firmware/acpi/tables/TPM2.

ACPI WMI (PNP0C14) methods

acpi-wmi - Linux data

In plain words. WMI (Windows Management Instrumentation) is a way for firmware to offer vendor features (fan modes, RGB, sensor readings, keyboard lights) through ACPI. This item lists the WMI interfaces the firmware offers and which Linux drivers use them.

What you see.

Field Meaning Why it matters
GUID The 128-bit ID of the WMI interface Each feature has its own GUID
Obj ACPI object id (the WQxx/WMxx suffix) or notify id Which firmware object implements it
Inst Instance count
Exp "Expensive" flag (1 = slow to query)
Set Whether the data block can be written (- for method / event blocks)
Driver Linux driver bound to it, or - e.g. wmi-bmof, asus-wmi, dell-wmi
Description Name SRS knows for a few common GUIDs e.g. "Binary MOF (WMI class descriptions)", "ASUS management (ATK / asus-wmi)"

Then WMI mapper devices: every PNP0C14 ACPI device with its path. A note says SRS never invokes WMI methods.

Healthy / typical values. Author's PC: six WMI mapper devices (\AWW0, \ALCW, \RMTW, \AMZW, \WFDV, \AOD_), several Binary MOF blocks bound to wmi-bmof, and the ASUS management GUID with no driver bound (normal on ASUS desktops; asus-wmi is mainly for laptops).

Unusual values and what they suggest. A vendor GUID with no driver means that feature is not used by Linux. That is common. Projects such as asus-wmi-sensors or vendor-specific modules may add support for some of them.

Where Linux gets it. /sys/bus/wmi/devices/* (guid, object_id / notify_id, instance_count, expensive, setable, driver).

Background. Binary MOF is a compressed description of the vendor's WMI classes; tools can decode it to learn what methods exist.

APIC (MADT) summary

bios-apic - Linux data - Needs root data

In plain words. Decodes the MADT (Multiple APIC Description Table, signature APIC). It tells the operating system how many CPU threads exist and how interrupts are wired to them.

What you see. The standard ACPI header (Signature, Length, Revision, Checksum, OEM ID, OEM Table ID, OEM Revision, Creator ID, Creator Revision), then:

  • Local APIC Address - memory address of each CPU's local interrupt controller (normally 0xFEE00000).
  • Flags - PCAT_COMPAT (dual 8259) means the old PC interrupt controllers also exist.

Then one row per entry:

Entry ID UID/Addr GSI/Flags Detail
Local APIC APIC ID of a CPU thread ACPI processor UID flags Enabled, Online capable or Disabled
Local x2APIC x2APIC ID (for more than 255 threads) UID flags Enabled / Disabled
I/O APIC I/O APIC ID its address GSI n = first interrupt number it handles
Int Override IRQ n (legacy ISA number) bus 0 GSI n it is remapped to flags (polarity / trigger)
Local APIC NMI all or a CPU UID flags which LINTn pin carries the NMI
LAPIC Addr Override, NMI Source, x2APIC NMI rarely used entry types
Other unknown type type n len n

Footer: counts of Local APIC, x2APIC, I/O APIC, Overrides and LAPIC NMI entries. Without the srs-root cache the item shows only "present, N bytes".

Healthy / typical values. Author's PC (8 cores, 16 threads): 32 Local APIC entries, 16 Enabled (IDs 0-15) and 16 Disabled placeholders; 2 I/O APICs at FEC00000 (GSI 0) and FEC01000 (GSI 24); overrides IRQ 0 -> GSI 2 (the timer) and IRQ 9 -> GSI 9 (the ACPI SCI).

Unusual values and what they suggest.

  • Fewer enabled entries than CPU threads you expect: SMT or some cores are disabled in the BIOS.
  • Disabled placeholders are normal. One firmware image supports several CPU models, so it lists slots for the biggest one (here 16 cores / 32 threads).

Where Linux gets it. The srs-root copy of /sys/firmware/acpi/tables/APIC.

Background. An APIC (Advanced Programmable Interrupt Controller) delivers interrupts to CPUs. Each thread has a local APIC; the I/O APIC collects device interrupts and maps them to GSIs (Global System Interrupts).

ASPT table summary

bios-aspt - Not present on most PCs - Needs root data

In plain words. Looks for the ASPT (AMD Secure Processor Table), which tells the OS where the AMD security processor's mailbox is.

What it would show. If present: the ACPI header and a hex dump (up to 1 KB) from the srs-root cache. If absent: ASPT not present in /sys/firmware/acpi/tables, its Purpose, and Tables present (count and list of all tables).

What "not present" means. Normal on most desktop boards, including the author's. The AMD security processor is still there; see HECI (Intel ME) status.

Where Linux gets it. /sys/firmware/acpi/tables.

DMAR table summary

bios-dmar - Not present on most PCs - Needs root data

In plain words. The DMAR (DMA Remapping) table describes Intel's IOMMU, called VT-d. AMD systems use a different table, IVRS, so on AMD this item decodes IVRS instead.

What you see. If DMAR is absent: DMAR not present, its Purpose ("Intel VT-d DMA remapping; AMD platforms use IVRS instead") and the Tables present line. If DMAR is present: its header and a hex dump.

If an IVRS table exists, a second block follows:

  • The ACPI header of IVRS.
  • IVinfo - capability word: virtual address bits (VA), physical address bits (PA), guest virtual address bits (GVA), and "EFR supported" (extended feature register).
  • One row per entry: Type (IVHD 10h/11h/40h = IOMMU hardware definition, IVMD = memory definition), Flags, DevID (PCI ID of the IOMMU), Segment, Base (register address).

Healthy / typical values. Author's PC: no DMAR (AMD). IVRS present: VA 64 bits, PA 48 bits, GVA 2 bits, EFR supported, two IVHD entries (types 10h and 11h) for one IOMMU at 00000000F7600000.

Unusual values and what they suggest. No IVRS (on AMD) or no DMAR (on Intel): the IOMMU is switched off in the BIOS setup ("IOMMU" / "SVM" / "VT-d"). You need it for passing a GPU through to a virtual machine and for DMA protection of Thunderbolt / USB4 ports.

Where Linux gets it. /sys/firmware/acpi/tables and the srs-root copy of IVRS.

Background. An IOMMU (Input-Output Memory Management Unit) controls which memory each device may read and write with DMA (direct memory access). It isolates devices from each other and from the OS.

FACP (FADT) summary

bios-facp - Linux data - Needs root data

In plain words. Decodes the FADT (Fixed ACPI Description Table, signature FACP). It is the "master" table: it points to the other key tables and lists the fixed power-management hardware.

What you see. The ACPI header, then:

Field Meaning
FIRMWARE_CTRL (FACS) Address of the FACS table (used for sleep / wake)
DSDT / X_DSDT 32-bit and 64-bit address of the DSDT
Preferred PM Profile Desktop, Mobile, Server...
SCI Interrupt IRQ used by ACPI (usually 9)
SMI Command Port I/O port used to switch between firmware and OS control, with the enable / disable values
PM1a Event / Control I/O ports of the main power-management registers
PM Timer Block ACPI timer port, length, and whether the timer is 24-bit or 32-bit
GPE0 Block / GPE1 Block I/O ports of the GPE registers (see ACPI interrupts and GPEs)
C2 / C3 Latency Advertised wake-up time of legacy CPU idle states, in microseconds (values above 100 / 1000 mean "not supported")
RTC Day/Month Alarm, Century CMOS register indexes for these RTC fields
FADT Minor Version Sub-version of the table
Reset Register How the OS can reset the PC: address space, address and value
Hypervisor Vendor Set only when running inside a virtual machine

Then Flags (hex) and a tick list of the 24 FADT feature flags (WBINVD, PROC_C1, SLP_BUTTON, RTC_S4, TMR_VAL_EXT, RESET_REG_SUP, PCI_EXP_WAK, USE_PLATFORM_CLOCK, HW_REDUCED_ACPI, LOW_POWER_S0_IDLE_CAPABLE and others). [=] = set, [_] = clear.

Then IA-PC Boot Architecture (hex) and its six flags: LEGACY_DEVICES, 8042 (PS/2 keyboard controller), VGA Not Present, MSI Not Supported, PCIe ASPM Controls, CMOS RTC Not Present.

Without the cache, only the PM profile from sysfs is shown.

Healthy / typical values. Author's PC: profile 1 (Desktop), SCI 9, SMI port 0xB2, PM timer 32-bit, C2/C3 latency 101 / 1001 us (that is, "not used": modern CPUs use their own idle states), reset by writing 0xBE to port 0xB2. Flags 0x0003C5A5 include RESET_REG_SUP, PCI_EXP_WAK and REMOTE_POWER_ON_CAPABLE. Boot architecture 0x0011: LEGACY_DEVICES and PCIe ASPM Controls set, 8042 clear (no PS/2 controller is advertised).

Unusual values and what they suggest.

  • LOW_POWER_S0_IDLE_CAPABLE set: the board prefers "Modern Standby" (s2idle) over classic S3 sleep. Common on laptops; if suspend misbehaves, check /sys/power/mem_sleep.
  • HW_REDUCED_ACPI set on a normal PC: unusual; fixed hardware (power button, PM timer) is then missing.
  • PCIe ASPM Controls set means the firmware asks the OS not to change PCIe link power saving (ASPM). Linux respects that unless told otherwise (pcie_aspm=force).

Where Linux gets it. The srs-root copy of /sys/firmware/acpi/tables/FACP; fallback /sys/firmware/acpi/pm_profile.

PCI IRQ routing ($PIR)

bios-irq - Not present on most PCs - Needs root data

In plain words. Old PCs had a BIOS table called $PIR that said which interrupt each PCI slot used. UEFI boards no longer have it; ACPI _PRT methods and the MADT do the job.

What you see.

  • Status - "Not present on this system".
  • Structure - "$PIR PCI IRQ routing table".
  • Reason - UEFI routes PCI interrupts through ACPI _PRT; scanning for $PIR would need /dev/mem, which SRS never opens.
  • Firmware - "UEFI x86-64 (ACPI MADT/_PRT replace the legacy tables)" or "Legacy BIOS".
  • Linux routing - how Linux actually routes interrupts: number of IO-APIC lines and PCI-MSI / MSI-X vectors in /proc/interrupts.

Healthy / typical values. Author's PC: 5 IO-APIC lines and 79 MSI / MSI-X vectors. On modern systems almost every device uses MSI (message-signalled interrupts).

Unusual values and what they suggest. Many devices on IO-APIC lines and few MSI vectors can mean MSI is disabled (pci=nomsi) or a driver does not support it. Shared IO-APIC lines are slower than MSI.

Where Linux gets it. /proc/interrupts.

BIOS maker

bios-make - Linux data

In plain words. Who made the firmware, which version and date it is, and what features it says it supports.

What you see.

Field Meaning
BIOS Vendor Firmware maker, e.g. American Megatrends Inc.
Family Product family SRS recognises: AMI (Aptio V UEFI), Phoenix, Insyde H2O
BIOS Version The version you compare with the board maker's download page
BIOS Date Release date
BIOS Release Major.minor release number from SMBIOS
Board Maker / Board Motherboard maker and model
Firmware Type UEFI or Legacy BIOS (how this boot started)
Address, Runtime Size, ROM Size, BIOS Revision, Firmware Revision From the srs-root cache, when listed by SMBIOS
Characteristics Tick list of the BIOS feature flags from SMBIOS type 0

Without the cache: "ROM Size / Address (needs root)".

Healthy / typical values. Author's PC: American Megatrends Inc., AMI (Aptio V UEFI), version 1805, 09/18/2026, release 18.5, UEFI, ROM 64 MiB, runtime 64 KiB at 0xF0000. Characteristics include "UEFI is supported", "ACPI is supported", "Firmware is upgradeable".

Unusual values and what they suggest. The characteristics list still shows ancient features (5.25" floppy, NEC 9800 floppy, CGA video): firmware makers keep these flags for compatibility. They do not mean the hardware exists. A BIOS date years older than the board's latest download means a BIOS update is available; updates often fix memory stability, CPU support and security issues.

Where Linux gets it. /sys/class/dmi/id/bios_*, board_*; /sys/firmware/efi; SMBIOS type 0 from the srs-root dmidecode.txt.

MPS table summary

bios-mps - Not present on most PCs - Needs root data

In plain words. The Intel MultiProcessor Specification (MPS) table was how 1990s PCs listed their CPUs. ACPI's MADT replaced it.

What you see. Status ("Not present on this system"), Structure ("Intel MultiProcessor Specification (MP floating pointer)"), Reason (superseded by the ACPI MADT; scanning needs /dev/mem, which SRS never opens), Firmware type.

What "not present" means. Normal on every UEFI PC. See APIC (MADT) summary for the modern equivalent.

MSDM table summary

bios-msdm - Not present on most PCs - Needs root data

In plain words. The MSDM (Microsoft Data Management) table holds an embedded Windows product key on PCs sold with Windows pre-installed.

What it would show. If present: ACPI header and hex dump from the srs-root cache. If absent: MSDM not present, its Purpose, and the Tables present list.

What "not present" means. The PC (or motherboard) was sold without an OEM Windows licence. Normal for self-built PCs.

Where Linux gets it. /sys/firmware/acpi/tables.

OEMB table summary

bios-oemb - Not present on most PCs - Needs root data

In plain words. OEMB is an AMI OEM-specific table found on some older AMI BIOS boards.

What it would show. If present: header and hex dump. If absent: OEMB not present, Purpose, Tables present.

What "not present" means. Normal on current boards.

Where Linux gets it. /sys/firmware/acpi/tables.

BIOS option ROMs

bios-option - Linux data - Needs root data

In plain words. Lists the PCI devices that carry their own firmware ROM (an "option ROM"), such as a graphics card's video BIOS or a storage controller's boot code.

What you see.

Field Meaning
PCI PCI address
Class PCI class code (030000 = VGA, 010601 = AHCI SATA...)
ID Vendor:device ID
ROM size Size of the expansion ROM window
Driver Linux driver

Footer: number of devices with an expansion ROM, and a note that the ROM images themselves (header, code type, EFI or legacy) are root-only and not read.

Healthy / typical values. Author's PC: the graphics card 03:00.0 (128 KB, amdgpu) and the SATA controller 0c:00.0 (512 KB, ahci).

Unusual values and what they suggest. If you turn off CSM (legacy boot support), the firmware uses only the EFI part of each option ROM. An old card without an EFI option ROM then shows no picture before Linux starts, or cannot boot.

Where Linux gets it. /sys/bus/pci/devices/*/rom (the file size only).

SDEV table summary

bios-sdev - Not present on most PCs - Needs root data

In plain words. The SDEV (Secure Devices) table lists devices that must only be used by the secure (virtualisation-protected) part of Windows, such as some fingerprint readers.

What it would show. If present: header and hex dump. If absent: SDEV not present, Purpose, Tables present.

What "not present" means. Normal on desktops.

Where Linux gets it. /sys/firmware/acpi/tables.

SFI summary

bios-sfi - Not present on most PCs

In plain words. SFI (Simple Firmware Interface) was a cut-down ACPI replacement for Intel's Moorestown / Medfield phone and tablet chips. Linux removed support in version 5.12.

What you see. Status ("Not present on this system"), Structure, Reason ("Intel MID only; removed from Linux 5.12"), Firmware type.

What "not present" means. Always the case on normal PCs.

SLIC table summary

bios-slic - Not present on most PCs - Needs root data

In plain words. The SLIC (Software Licensing) table was used for OEM activation of Windows Vista and 7 on brand-name PCs.

What it would show. If present: header and hex dump. If absent: SLIC not present, Purpose, Tables present.

What "not present" means. Normal on self-built and most current PCs.

Where Linux gets it. /sys/firmware/acpi/tables.

SLIT table summary

bios-slit - Not present on most PCs - Needs root data

In plain words. The SLIT (System Locality Information Table) gives the relative "distance" between NUMA nodes, that is, how much slower memory on another CPU socket is.

What it would show. If present: header and hex dump. If absent: SLIT not present, Purpose, Tables present.

What "not present" means. The PC has a single NUMA node (one CPU socket, one memory pool). Normal for desktops. Multi-socket servers and some workstation CPUs have it.

Where Linux gets it. /sys/firmware/acpi/tables. numactl --hardware shows the distances Linux uses.

Background. NUMA (Non-Uniform Memory Access): on big systems each CPU has "near" memory and "far" memory. The OS tries to keep a program's memory near the CPU running it.

SRAT table summary

bios-srat - Not present on most PCs - Needs root data

In plain words. The SRAT (System Resource Affinity Table) says which CPUs and which memory ranges belong to which NUMA node.

What it would show. If present: header and hex dump. If absent: SRAT not present, Purpose, Tables present.

What "not present" means. Single-node system. Normal for desktops. Some boards add it only when a "NUMA nodes per socket" BIOS option is enabled.

Where Linux gets it. /sys/firmware/acpi/tables.

BIOS / SMBIOS tables

bios-tables - Linux data - Needs root data

In plain words. An overview of the SMBIOS inventory tables: version, size, and how many records of each type the firmware provides.

What you see. Header row:

Field Meaning
BIOS SMBIOS version, e.g. SMBios V3.6.0 (only V3.x / V2.x without root)
Anchor Entry-point signature: "_SM3_" (64-bit, SMBIOS 3) or "_SM_" + "_DMI_" (32-bit, SMBIOS 2)
EP Size Size of the entry point: 24 bytes (SMBIOS 3) or 31 (SMBIOS 2)
Table Total size of the structure table in bytes
Structures Number of records (needs root)

Then Table address (memory address of the table), and a list: Type, Name, Count, one row per SMBIOS record type present (types 128 and up are shown as "OEM-specific"; unknown standard types as -).

Healthy / typical values. Author's PC: SMBIOS 3.6.0, _SM3_, 24-byte entry point, 3448-byte table, 80 structures. Types include 0 BIOS Information, 1 System, 2 Base Board, 4 Processor, 7 Cache (3), 8 Port Connector (36), 9 System Slots (7), 17 Memory Device (4, one per slot), 43 TPM Device, 45 Firmware Inventory.

Unusual values and what they suggest. Type 17 count lower than your number of slots: the firmware hides empty slots, so slot positions in DIMMs may not match the board printing. SMBIOS 2.x on a new board is very unusual.

Where Linux gets it. /sys/firmware/dmi/tables/smbios_entry_point and DMI (sizes); type counts from the srs-root dmidecode.txt.

Background. SMBIOS record types: each describes one kind of thing (type 4 a CPU socket, type 17 a memory slot, type 9 an expansion slot). dmidecode -t <type> prints one type.

CMOS / RTC status

cmos-status - Linux data

In plain words. The real-time clock (RTC) keeps the time while the PC is off, powered by the coin battery on the board. This item shows the clock, its alarm, its settings and the battery check.

What you see. First, every line the kernel's RTC driver reports:

Field Meaning
rtc_time / rtc_date Time and date stored in the clock chip
alrm_time / alrm_date Wake-up alarm setting
alarm_IRQ, alrm_pending Whether the alarm is armed / has fired
update IRQ enabled, periodic IRQ enabled, periodic IRQ frequency, max user IRQ frequency Timer interrupt settings of the chip
24hr, BCD Clock format (24-hour, binary-coded decimal)
periodic_IRQ, update_IRQ, HPET_emulated, DST_enable, periodic_freq More chip flags
batt_status Coin-battery check: okay (green) or a warning (red)

Then the /sys/class/rtc/rtc0 block: name (driver and ACPI device), date, time, since_epoch (seconds since 1970), hctosys (1 = Linux set its clock from this RTC at boot), max_user_freq, wakealarm and offset when set, then:

  • RTC - system clock - difference between the RTC and Linux's clock in seconds (orange if more than 2 s).
  • RTC time scale - whether the RTC holds UTC or local time (from /etc/adjtime).

Healthy / typical values. Author's PC: rtc_cmos PNP0B00:00, 24-hour BCD, batt_status okay, hctosys 1, difference -1 s, time scale UTC.

Unusual values and what they suggest.

  • batt_status not okay, or a clock that is wrong after every power cut: the CR2032 coin cell is flat. A flat cell can also reset BIOS settings.
  • A difference of many seconds or hours: time sync (NTP) is off, or Windows and Linux disagree on UTC versus local time on a dual-boot PC. Linux expects UTC.
  • hctosys 0: Linux did not read its clock from this RTC.

Where Linux gets it. /proc/driver/rtc, /sys/class/rtc/rtc0/*, /etc/adjtime.

Background. CMOS (originally the chip technology) is the old name for the RTC chip and its small battery-backed memory, which once held all BIOS settings.

Dell BIOS

dell-bios - Not present on most PCs

In plain words. Dell PCs have extra BIOS interfaces (for fans, sensors, settings). This item checks for them.

What you see. System Vendor. On a Dell: dell-smbios and dell_smm_hwmon, each loaded or not loaded. Otherwise Status: "Not a Dell system: Dell BIOS SMI data does not apply".

What "not present" means. Not a Dell. On a Dell where both show not loaded, load the dell_smm_hwmon module to get fan and temperature readings.

Where Linux gets it. /sys/class/dmi/id/sys_vendor, /sys/bus/platform/devices/dell-smbios.0, /sys/module/dell_smm_hwmon.

DIMMs

dimms - Linux data - Needs root data

In plain words. One line per memory slot: what is in it, how big, how fast it is rated, how fast it is actually running, who made it, and its temperature. Open it with the DIMMs panel button.

What you see.

Field Meaning Why it matters
Slot Slot name from the firmware, e.g. DIMM 1 Match it to the board printing
Bank Channel name, e.g. P0 CHANNEL A Which memory channel the slot is on
Size Capacity of the stick, or Empty
Type DDR4, DDR5...
Form DIMM (desktop) or SODIMM (laptop)
Rated Base speed the stick reports (JEDEC) The "safe default" speed
Configured Speed the memory is running at now Shows whether EXPO / XMP is active
Rank Number of ranks (1 or 2) Dual-rank is a little faster, harder to overclock
Manufacturer Module maker
Part Number Model code of the stick Use it to look up the kit's spec
Serial Module serial number Tells identical sticks apart
SPD The spd5118 sensor device paired with this slot, e.g. 1-0051
Temp Current stick temperature from that sensor

Footer: "N of M slots populated, X installed", the data source, and a note that the SPD pairing is inferred (slot index i is matched to the sensor at SMBus address 0x50 + i).

Detail view (dimms:<slot index>, e.g. dimms:1): every SMBIOS field the system has for that slot (from udev: locator, bank, size, type, type detail, form factor, speeds, manufacturer, module manufacturer ID, part number, serial, rank, configured voltage, memory technology...; or, from the srs-root cache: Locator, Bank Locator, Size, Type, Type Detail, Form Factor, Speed, Configured Memory Speed, Manufacturer, Part Number, Serial Number, Rank, Minimum / Maximum / Configured Voltage, Total Width, Data Width), plus a line for the paired SPD5118 sensor and its temperature.

Healthy / typical values. Author's PC: 2 of 4 slots used, 32 GB. Both sticks in the recommended slots (DIMM 1 of channel A and channel B, the "A2 / B2" slots on most boards): 16 GB DDR5 DIMM, rank 1, rated 4800 MT/s, configured 6000 MT/s (EXPO profile active), G.Skill, temperatures 30-31 °C.

Unusual values and what they suggest.

  • Configured equals Rated (for example 4800 on a 6000 kit): EXPO / XMP is off in the BIOS.
  • Two sticks in the same channel (both "CHANNEL A"): the memory runs single-channel, roughly half the bandwidth. Move one stick to the other channel.
  • Different part numbers on the sticks: a mixed pair. It can work, but mixed kits are a common cause of instability at EXPO / XMP speeds. Matched kits are safer.
  • Serial all zeros on a stick: some modules simply do not program a serial. Harmless by itself.
  • Size shown smaller than expected or a stick missing: poor seating, a dead stick, or a slot disabled by the board.

Where Linux gets it. SMBIOS type 17 as imported by systemd-udevd into /run/udev/data/+dmi:id (readable without root), else the srs-root dmidecode.txt; temperatures from the spd5118 hwmon driver. It is marked "needs root" because the fallback path and full detail come from the cache; on most systemd distributions the table is complete without it.

Background. MT/s (mega-transfers per second) is the data rate. DDR memory moves data twice per clock, so 6000 MT/s is a 3000 MHz clock. Marketing often writes "6000 MHz", which is not strictly right.

DIMM status/temperatures

dimm-status - Linux data

In plain words. Live temperatures and limits of the thermal sensors on DDR5 memory sticks. This is what the Status panel sub-button shows. It refreshes every 2 seconds.

What you see.

Field Meaning
Sensor Linux hwmon name, e.g. hwmon7
Device I2C device of the sensor, e.g. 1-0051 (bus 1, address 0x51)
Slot Compact slot label, e.g. A1 = channel A, DIMM 1 (inferred from the address)
Temp Current temperature
Min / Max / Crit / LCrit Limits programmed into the sensor: low warning, high warning, critical high, critical low
Alarms Which limit alarms are active (min, max, crit, lcrit), or none (green)
Enabled Whether the sensor is enabled

A note says only the hwmon values are read, never the SPD memory chip itself. If there are no sensors: "No spd5118 hwmon sensors" with a hint that the spd5118 driver must bind to SMBus addresses 0x50-0x57.

Healthy / typical values. Author's PC at idle: 31.0 °C and 30.5 °C; limits 0 / 55 / 85 / 0 °C; alarms none. Under heavy load DDR5 typically runs 40-55 °C.

Unusual values and what they suggest.

  • Above about 55 °C: the stick reaches its warning limit. DDR5 then refreshes more often (a little slower), and errors become more likely when overclocked. Add airflow over the memory.
  • One stick much hotter than the other: it may be under a CPU cooler's exhaust, or have no heat spreader contact.
  • No sensors on DDR5: the spd5118 module is not loaded, or the board's SMBus is locked. DDR4 sticks usually have no sensor.

Where Linux gets it. /sys/class/hwmon/hwmon*/ where name is spd5118: temp1_input, temp1_min, temp1_max, temp1_crit, temp1_lcrit, temp1_*_alarm, temp1_enable.

Background. Every DDR5 stick has an SPD hub chip (spd5118) that holds the stick's description (the SPD data) and contains a temperature sensor.

Firmware

firmware - Linux data

In plain words. How the PC's firmware started Linux: UEFI or legacy BIOS, Secure Boot state, firmware update records, and how long the firmware took to boot.

What you see.

Field Meaning
Firmware Type UEFI, or "Legacy BIOS (no /sys/firmware/efi)"
Platform Size 64-bit or 32-bit UEFI
Firmware Vendor Pointer, Runtime Services, Configuration Table Memory addresses of UEFI structures (for debugging)
System Table Address of the UEFI system table (root only)
Secure Boot Enabled / Disabled / Unknown
ESRT Entries Number of firmware-update resources (EFI System Resource Table); per-entry fw_version lines when readable
UEFI Variables Number of variables stored in firmware
BIOS Vendor / BIOS Version From SMBIOS

Firmware Boot Performance (ACPI FPDT), when the board provides it:

Field Meaning
Firmware start When firmware timing started
Boot loader load When the firmware started loading the boot loader
ExitBootServices When the OS took over from the firmware (start -> end)
Time in firmware + loader Total time from power-on timing start to OS hand-over

Healthy / typical values. Author's PC: UEFI, 64-bit, Secure Boot Disabled, 1 ESRT entry, 159 variables. Typical firmware time is 5-20 s; boards with DDR5 that re-train memory at every boot (or right after a BIOS settings change) can take much longer. The boot-loader-to-hand-over part also includes any time spent in the boot menu.

Unusual values and what they suggest.

  • A very long "Boot loader load" time: memory training. On AMD AM5 boards enable "Memory Context Restore" in the BIOS so training is skipped on normal boots (if your memory is stable with it).
  • Large gap between Boot loader load and ExitBootServices: time spent in the boot loader menu or its timeout.
  • ESRT 0: the firmware does not offer capsule updates, so fwupd cannot update it.

Where Linux gets it. /sys/firmware/efi/ (fw_platform_size, fw_vendor, runtime, config_table, systab, esrt/, efivars/), /sys/firmware/acpi/fpdt/boot/*_ns.

Firmware interface table

f-w-table - Not present on most PCs

In plain words. The Firmware Interface Table described firmware components on Intel Itanium (IA-64) servers.

What you see. Status ("Not present on this system"), Structure ("IA-64 (Itanium) firmware interface table"), Reason ("IA-64 only"), Firmware type.

What "not present" means. Always the case on x86 PCs.

Hardware summary

hardware - Linux data

In plain words. A one-page summary of the main parts of the PC.

What you see.

Field Meaning
Processor CPU model name
Logical CPUs Number of CPU threads
System System maker and product name (NA if the firmware left a placeholder)
Motherboard Board maker and model
BIOS Vendor, version, date, and (UEFI) or (Legacy)
Memory Total, type, speed, slots used, and the first stick's maker and part number
TPM TPM 2.0, TPM 1.2 or none
Secure Boot Enabled / Disabled / "n/a (legacy BIOS)"

Then a device list from lspci: Class, Address, Device for graphics, audio, network, NVMe, SATA, RAID, USB and Thunderbolt controllers.

Healthy / typical values. Author's PC: AMD Ryzen 7 7800X3D, 16 logical CPUs, ASUS TUF GAMING X870-PRO WIFI7 W NEO, BIOS 1805 (UEFI), 32GB DDR5 6000 MT/s in 2 of 4 DIMMs, TPM 2.0, Secure Boot Disabled; Radeon RX 9070 series graphics, three NVMe controllers, RTL8126 5GbE, RTL8922AE Wi-Fi 7, ASM4242 USB4.

Unusual values and what they suggest. "System ASUS NA": self-built boards often leave the system product name as a placeholder. That is normal. A missing controller (for example no network) usually means it is disabled in the BIOS setup.

Where Linux gets it. /sys/class/dmi/id, /sys/class/tpm/tpm0, efivars, lspci -mm.

HECI (Intel ME) status

heci-status - Not present on most PCs

In plain words. HECI (Host Embedded Controller Interface) is how the OS talks to the Intel Management Engine, a separate processor inside Intel chipsets. AMD has its own equivalent, the PSP (Platform Security Processor). This item reports either.

What you see.

  • Intel MEI / HECI - present (/sys/class/mei) or "Not present on this system".
  • AMD PSP / CCP - the PCI address of the AMD security processor bound to the ccp driver, or "no ccp-bound device".

Healthy / typical values. Author's PC (AMD): no Intel MEI; AMD PSP at 0000:75:00.2 (ccp).

What "not present" means. On an AMD PC, Intel MEI is never present. On an Intel PC with no MEI, the mei_me driver is not loaded or the ME interface is hidden in the BIOS.

Where Linux gets it. /sys/class/mei, /sys/bus/pci/drivers/ccp.

Background. The PSP runs the firmware TPM (fTPM) and memory encryption on AMD systems. It starts before the main CPU.

Machine

machine - Linux data

In plain words. The main page of this group, modelled on SIV's Machine panel: the SMBIOS identity of the PC in a compact grid, from BIOS to CPU socket to memory slots. The Machine panel button opens it.

What you see. Rows of four columns:

Row Contents
SMBios Version, record count ("Count (needs root)" without the cache), table size in decimal and hex
BIOS Version, date, release, vendor, plus ROM base address and ROM size (cache)
System Product name, version, vendor and UUID (needs root if not readable)
(second line) Family, SKU, system serial number
Chassis Version and chassis type (Desktop, Tower, Laptop, Mini PC...), vendor, serial, asset tag
Board Revision, model, board serial, maker
CPU-0 Socket #0 CPU vendor ID (AuthenticAMD / GenuineIntel), socket name (AM5, LGA1700...), model, max speed, external clock, cores, threads, voltage
System Boot SMBIOS boot status ("No errors detected"), and UEFI Secure Boot on/off or Legacy BIOS
Memory Array Location, maximum capacity, ECC type, DIMMs used of total, total installed
One row per slot Slot, bank, then size / type / configured speed and maker / part, or Empty

Placeholder strings the firmware leaves ("To be filled by O.E.M.", "Default string", "System Product Name"...) are shown as NA. If the record count, serials or socket are missing, the page ends with the "Needs root" hint.

Healthy / typical values. Author's PC: SMBios V3.6.0, Count 80, size 3448 (0D78); BIOS 1805 release 18.5, ROM 64 MiB; System NA NA ASUS (placeholders); Chassis Desktop; Board Rev 1.xx TUF GAMING X870-PRO WIFI7 W NEO, serial XXXX; socket AM5, Max 5050 MHz, Ext 100 MHz, 8 cores, 16 threads, 1.3 V; System Boot "No errors detected", UEFI Secure Boot off; Memory Array maximum 256GB, ECC None, 2 of 4 DIMMs, 32GB.

Unusual values and what they suggest.

  • Ext (external clock) not 100 MHz: base clock (BCLK) overclocking is active.
  • ECC other than None on a desktop with normal memory is unusual; with ECC sticks installed, "None" means ECC is not enabled.
  • System Boot status other than "No errors detected": the firmware logged a problem at the last boot (for example a memory training failure or a watchdog reset).

Where Linux gets it. /sys/class/dmi/id/*, /run/udev/data/+dmi:id, /proc/cpuinfo, efivars, plus SMBIOS types 0, 1, 4, 16, 32 from the srs-root dmidecode.txt.

Machine options

machine-opt - Linux data

In plain words. A checklist of the data sources this group can use on your PC, so you can see at a glance why an item is empty.

What you see. One tick line per source, [=] available, [_] not available, with its path:

  • DMI identification (unprivileged) - /sys/class/dmi/id/
  • SMBIOS memory devices via udev - /run/udev/data/+dmi:id
  • dmidecode cache (serials, UUID, socket) - ~/.cache/srs/root/dmidecode.txt
  • SPD decode cache - ~/.cache/srs/root/spd.txt
  • ACPI table copies - ~/.cache/srs/root/acpi-tables/
  • I/O memory map cache - ~/.cache/srs/root/iomem.txt
  • spd5118 DIMM thermal sensors - hwmon devices named spd5118
  • EDAC memory controllers - /sys/devices/system/edac/mc
  • UEFI variables (read-only) - /sys/firmware/efi/efivars
  • TPM - /sys/class/tpm/tpm0
  • CMOS RTC - /proc/driver/rtc
  • ACPI WMI bus - /sys/bus/wmi/devices
  • Three lines that are always off by design: direct SMBus / SPD EEPROM reads, ACPI method evaluation / EC writes, and /dev/mem, /dev/nvram, /dev/port.

Healthy / typical values. Author's PC: everything on except EDAC (non-ECC memory) and the three always-off lines.

Unusual values and what they suggest. Cache lines off: run Menu > Run as root (srs-root). EDAC off with ECC memory installed: load the amd64_edac (AMD) or ie31200_edac / igen6_edac (Intel) module, or ECC is disabled in the BIOS.

Where Linux gets it. Checks that each path exists.

Memory

memory - Linux data

In plain words. How much memory is in use, how much is free, and the detailed counters Linux keeps. Refreshes every second.

What you see. First a usage table:

Row Used Available Total Load
System Physical Memory RAM in use (total minus "available") RAM available to programs Usable RAM Percent used
System Paging File (swap) Swap in use Free swap Swap size Percent used
Commit Charge Memory programs have asked for (Committed_AS) Commit limit minus that Commit limit Percent of the limit

Then the /proc/meminfo counters: MemFree, Buffers, Cached, SwapCached, Active, Inactive, Dirty, AnonPages, Mapped, Shmem, Slab, SReclaimable, KernelStack, PageTables, VmallocUsed, Percpu, HardwareCorrupted (red if not 0), AnonHugePages, HugePages_Total, Hugepagesize, Zswap, Zswapped, DirectMap4k / 2M / 1G.

Then:

  • Installed (SMBIOS) - capacity and slots used, from the firmware.
  • Memory Speed - type, configured speed and rated speed.
  • Memory Blocks - online and total memory blocks, block size, online total.
  • Auto Online Blocks - policy for hot-added memory.
  • EDAC - number of memory controllers with error reporting and, for the first one, its name and counts of corrected (CE) and uncorrected (UE) errors; or "no memory controllers registered".

Healthy / typical values. Author's PC, desktop in use: 10.60 GB used of 30.45 GB (35%), swap 6.39 GB of 48.04 GB used, commit charge 39.57 GB of a 63.26 GB limit; Cached 16.38 GB; HardwareCorrupted 0B; installed 32GB, DDR5 6000 MT/s (rated 4800); 251 of 251 blocks online.

Unusual values and what they suggest.

  • Total well below installed (for example 24 GB of 32 GB): memory reserved for integrated graphics, or a stick not detected. A small gap (here 30.45 of 32 GB) is normal: firmware, the kernel and reserved areas take some.
  • Cached large and MemFree small: normal. Linux uses spare RAM as disk cache and gives it back when needed. Look at Available, not Free.
  • HardwareCorrupted above 0: the kernel took pages offline because of memory errors. Test your RAM (memtest86+) and lower memory overclocks.
  • Commit Charge close to the limit: programs may fail to get memory; add swap or RAM.
  • EDAC CE rising: correctable errors on ECC memory, an early warning of a failing stick.

Where Linux gets it. /proc/meminfo, /sys/devices/system/memory/, /sys/devices/system/edac/mc/, SMBIOS type 17.

Background. Swap (Windows: paging file) is disk or compressed memory (zram, zswap) used when RAM is full. Commit charge is how much memory programs have reserved, not how much they actually touch.

Memory timings

mem-tweak - Linux data - Needs root data

In plain words. Shows the memory speed. Detailed timings (CL, tRCD and so on) are not read, because on AMD they sit in memory-controller registers that SRS would have to write to reach.

What you see.

  • DRAM - type, size, form factor and ranks of the first stick.
  • Configured Speed - current data rate.
  • MEMCLK - real memory clock, half the data rate ("DDR: 2 transfers per clock").
  • Rated (JEDEC) Speed - the stick's base speed.
  • ryzen_smu - whether the third-party ryzen_smu driver is loaded.
  • Timing registers (UMC) - "not read": needs SMN register access; SRS stays read-only.
  • Two notes: primary / secondary timings (tCL, tRCD, tRP, tRAS, tRFC...) would come from the AMD memory controller (UMC) via SMN; FCLK / UCLK / MCLK are in the SMU PM table item amd-pmt.

Healthy / typical values. Author's PC: DDR5 16GB, ranks 1, 6000 MT/s, MEMCLK 3000 MHz, rated 4800 MT/s.

Unusual values and what they suggest. MEMCLK equal to half the rated speed (2400 MHz on a 6000 kit): EXPO / XMP is off. For timings use a tool that reads the memory controller (for example ZenTimings on Windows) or read them in the BIOS setup.

Where Linux gets it. SMBIOS type 17; /sys/kernel/ryzen_smu_drv presence.

Background. SMN (System Management Network) is AMD's internal register bus. UMC is the Unified Memory Controller. On AM5, FCLK (Infinity Fabric clock), UCLK (memory controller clock) and MCLK (memory clock) should be in a good ratio; UCLK = MCLK ("1:1") is fastest.

Overview

overview - Linux data

In plain words. SIV's classic overview header: one screen with the OS, board, user, uptime, power source, memory use, CPU and memory sticks. Refreshes every second.

What you see.

  • First line - OS name and kernel, board maker and model, host::user, language (LANG), time zone, BIOS version and date.
  • Second line - uptime as DD HH:MM:SS (days first), current date and time, [BIOS version date], and the power source: Mains Power or Battery Power, followed by Battery N% for each battery the system reports.
  • Resource table - "Resource Usage N%" (physical memory load), then three rows with Current, Committed and Maximum: System Physical Memory (RAM in use, total commit charge, usable RAM), System Paging File (swap in use, swap size), Commit Charge (limit) (committed memory, commit limit).
  • Linux kernel release.
  • CPUs / Cores / Chips / DIMMs - logical CPUs, physical cores, CPU packages, sticks installed.
  • CPU model name.
  • One line per installed stick: bank, slot, size, type, speed, maker and part number.

Healthy / typical values. Author's PC: CachyOS 7.3.0-... ASUS TUF GAMING X870-PRO WIFI7 W NEO MYPC::user en_US.UTF-8 EDT BIOS 1805 09/18/2026; uptime 21 h 46 min; Mains Power; Resource Usage 35%; CPUs 16 Cores 8 Chips 1 DIMMs 2.

Unusual values and what they suggest. The Committed figure on the physical-memory row is the total commit charge, so it can be larger than the RAM size; that is normal when swap exists. A "Battery" entry on a desktop usually comes from a wireless mouse, keyboard or UPS (uninterruptible power supply) that reports a battery to Linux.

Where Linux gets it. /etc/os-release, /sys/class/dmi/id, /proc/uptime, /sys/class/power_supply, /proc/meminfo, /sys/devices/system/cpu/*/topology, SMBIOS type 17.

Physical memory map

physical - Linux data

In plain words. The memory map the firmware gave Linux at boot: which address ranges are usable RAM and which are reserved for firmware, ACPI or devices.

What you see.

Field Meaning
# Entry number
Start / End First and last physical address (hex)
Size Length of the range
Type System RAM, Reserved, ACPI Tables (reclaimable after boot), ACPI Non-volatile Storage (kept for firmware), Persistent Memory, Unusable memory...

Then Total rows: size and count of entries per type. Then, with the srs-root cache, the top-level /proc/iomem list: the same address space with owners, including PCI windows, the IOMMU, I/O APICs, HPET and the graphics card's memory window. Without it, a note that resource owners need root.

Healthy / typical values. Author's PC: 23 entries; System RAM total 31.10 GB in 8 ranges, Reserved 13.68 GB (that is address space, mostly not real RAM), ACPI NVS 32.06 MB, ACPI Tables 8.82 MB. The biggest RAM range is 0x100000000-0x87DEFFFFF (29.97 GB above 4 GB). The iomem list shows PCI ECAM at 0xE0000000 (256 MB of PCIe configuration space) and a large window at the top for the graphics card (Resizable BAR).

Unusual values and what they suggest.

  • System RAM total far below installed RAM: a stick is not detected, or memory is set aside (integrated graphics, memmap= kernel option, crash kernel).
  • Unusable memory or Bad RAM entries: the firmware marked memory as faulty.
  • Reserved address space is not lost RAM: most of it is device windows and the "PCI hole" below 4 GB, which modern systems remap above 4 GB.

Where Linux gets it. /sys/firmware/memmap/* (start, end, type); owners from the srs-root iomem.txt (copy of /proc/iomem, whose addresses are hidden from normal users).

Background. This is the E820 / UEFI memory map. Physical addresses are also used by devices, so the address space is bigger than the installed RAM.

SPD (DIMMs)

spd - Linux data

In plain words. The SPD (Serial Presence Detect) is the small description each memory stick carries: maker, size, speeds, timings, and XMP / EXPO overclock profiles. This item shows the decoded SPD.

What you see. Two possible forms:

  • With the srs-root cache spd.txt: the text output of decode-dimms (from i2c-tools), unchanged. A full decode lists per stick the module maker, manufacture date, size and organisation, supported speeds and CAS latencies, primary timings, and any XMP / EXPO profiles.
  • Without it: an SMBIOS-based summary per installed stick: bank and slot, Module Manufacturer, Manufacturer ID (JEDEC), Part Number, Size, Type (type, form factor, detail), Rated Speed (SPD/JEDEC), Configured Speed, Ranks, SPD Hub (the spd5118 device). Two notes explain that the full decode comes from the cache and that SRS never reads the SPD chip directly. Then the "Needs root" hint.

When the cached decode-dimms run decoded no DIMMs ("Number of SDRAM DIMMs detected and decoded: 0", normal with DDR5), SRS says so and shows the SMBIOS summary instead.

Healthy / typical values. A full decode shows one block per stick. On the author's DDR5 PC decode-dimms decodes 0 DIMMs, so the page shows the SMBIOS summary of both sticks.

Unusual values and what they suggest. "0 DIMMs decoded" with DDR5: decode-dimms needs the spd5118 driver's eeprom file and a version of i2c-tools that understands DDR5. Updating i2c-tools, then running srs-root again, usually fixes it. Rated speed and part number are also in DIMMs.

Where Linux gets it. srs-root cache spd.txt (output of decode-dimms, which reads /sys/bus/i2c/drivers/spd5118/*/eeprom); fallback SMBIOS type 17.

Background. XMP (Intel Extreme Memory Profile) and EXPO (AMD Extended Profiles for Overclocking) are tested faster settings stored in the SPD. The BIOS applies them when you enable the profile.

SPD thermal

spd-temp - Linux data

In plain words. The same DDR5 stick temperature table as DIMM status/temperatures, under the SPD name. Refreshes every 2 seconds.

What you see. Sensor, Device, Slot, Temp, Min, Max, Crit, LCrit, Alarms, Enabled, exactly as described for DIMM status.

Healthy / typical values. Author's PC: A1 31.0 °C, B1 30.5 °C, limits 0 / 55 / 85 / 0 °C, no alarms.

Where Linux gets it. spd5118 hwmon attributes temp1_*.

System CMOS

system-cmos - Linux data - Needs root data

In plain words. The CMOS RAM is a small battery-backed memory next to the clock. SIV can dump it on Windows. SRS does not read it (that needs raw port access), so it reports what it can without that.

What you see.

  • CMOS RAM dump - "not read: needs /dev/nvram or port I/O (root), not in the srs-root cache".
  • /dev/nvram - present (root only) or absent (nvram module not loaded).
  • RTC driver - e.g. rtc_cmos PNP0B00:00.
  • CMOS battery - okay (green) or the warning the driver reports (red).
  • A pointer to CMOS / RTC status.

Healthy / typical values. Author's PC: /dev/nvram present (root only), rtc_cmos PNP0B00:00, battery okay.

Unusual values and what they suggest. Battery not okay: replace the coin cell (usually a CR2032) before BIOS settings and the clock get lost.

Where Linux gets it. /dev/nvram existence, /sys/class/rtc/rtc0/name, /proc/driver/rtc.

System EBDA

system-ebda - Linux data - Needs root data

In plain words. The EBDA (Extended BIOS Data Area) is a small block just below 640 KB that legacy BIOSes used for their own data. SRS does not read its contents, but shows what the memory map says about that area.

What you see.

  • EBDA contents - "not read: needs /dev/mem (root); srs never opens /dev/mem".
  • Conventional memory - the first memory-map entry (start - end, type).
  • EBDA (implied) - either "none reserved: the firmware map gives RAM up to 0x9FFFF", or the reserved range between the end of that RAM and 0x9FFFF.
  • Firmware - "UEFI (EBDA kept only for CSM/legacy compatibility)" or "Legacy BIOS".
  • With the srs-root cache: the /proc/iomem lines below 1 MB (Reserved, System RAM, PCI Bus, System ROM).

Healthy / typical values. Author's PC: conventional memory 0x0 - 0x9FFFF System RAM, no EBDA reserved, UEFI; iomem shows the System ROM at 0xF0000-0xFFFFF.

Unusual values and what they suggest. Nothing to fix here. An EBDA range on a UEFI PC means CSM (legacy boot support) is active.

Where Linux gets it. /sys/firmware/memmap/0/*, srs-root iomem.txt.

BIOS IDs

system-ids - Linux data - Needs root data

In plain words. The identity strings in SMBIOS: UUID, serial numbers, asset tags, and the memory sticks' serials. Useful for warranty claims and asset lists. Keep them private when you share reports.

What you see.

Field Meaning
System UUID Unique ID of this machine (green)
System Serial / Board Serial / Chassis Serial Serial numbers from SMBIOS types 1, 2, 3
System SKU / System Family Product variant and family
Board Asset Tag / Chassis Asset Tag Inventory tags (often blank)
DIMM Serial channel slot Serial of each installed memory stick
DMI modalias One-line summary Linux uses to match drivers to the board (bvn BIOS vendor, bvr version, bd date, svn system vendor, pn product name, rvn board vendor, rn board name, rvr board revision, cvn chassis vendor...)

Fields that need root and are not in the cache show "(needs root)", followed by the root hint.

Healthy / typical values. Author's PC: a UUID, Board Serial XXXX, and placeholder strings for the rest ("System Serial Number", "Default string", "SKU", "To be filled by O.E.M."), which is typical for a retail motherboard. DIMM serials: one real serial and one 00000000.

Unusual values and what they suggest. Placeholder strings are normal on self-built PCs. On a brand-name PC they can mean the board was replaced and the service centre did not program the IDs, which can break OEM Windows activation or warranty look-ups. An all-FF or all-0 UUID means the firmware did not set one.

Where Linux gets it. /sys/class/dmi/id/* (serials and UUID are root-only there), else the srs-root dmidecode.txt; DIMM serials from SMBIOS type 17; /sys/class/dmi/id/modalias.

TPM device

tpm-device - Linux data

In plain words. The TPM (Trusted Platform Module) as Linux sees it: version, driver, how it is connected, and its measurement banks.

What you see.

Field Meaning
TPM Version TPM 2.0 or TPM 1.2
Driver e.g. tpm_crb_acpi, tpm_tis
Interface CRB (Command Response Buffer) or TIS/FIFO
Implementation On AMD with CRB: "firmware TPM (AMD fTPM in the PSP, likely)"
ACPI Node / ACPI Path / ACPI Status The ACPI device behind it
Physical Presence Interface PPI version (how the OS asks the firmware to clear or enable the TPM)
PCR Banks Hash algorithms with PCR banks, e.g. sha256
Device Nodes /dev/tpm0 and /dev/tpmrm0 (the resource-managed node)
ACPI TPM2 table Size of the TPM2 table

PCR values are not read by default. tpm-device:pcr adds the 24 sha256 PCR values (PCR 0 to PCR 23). If there is no TPM: "No TPM (/sys/class/tpm empty)".

Healthy / typical values. Author's PC: TPM 2.0, tpm_crb_acpi, CRB, AMD fTPM, MSFT0101:00, \_SB_.TPM_, 0x0F PESF, PPI 1.3, bank sha256, /dev/tpm0 /dev/tpmrm0, TPM2 table 76 bytes.

Unusual values and what they suggest.

  • No TPM: enable fTPM (AMD) or PTT (Intel) in the BIOS setup.
  • Only a sha1 bank: old firmware or TPM 1.2; some disk encryption tools want sha256.
  • PCR values that change after a BIOS update or settings change are expected. If your disk encryption is sealed to PCRs, it will then ask for the recovery key.

Where Linux gets it. /sys/class/tpm/tpm0/* (tpm_version_major, device/driver, device/firmware_node, ppi/version, pcr-*), /sys/firmware/acpi/tables/TPM2 size.

Background. PCRs (Platform Configuration Registers) hold hashes of everything that ran during boot (firmware, boot loader, kernel). Disk encryption can be "sealed" so the key is only released when the PCRs match.

UEFI data

uefi-data - Linux data

In plain words. Lists every UEFI variable stored in the firmware's flash: boot entries, Secure Boot keys, and the board maker's own settings. Names and sizes only.

What you see. Variables grouped by vendor GUID (the 128-bit ID of whoever defined them). Each GUID line may carry a known label: "EFI Global Variable" (the standard boot variables such as BootOrder, Boot0000, SecureBoot, PK, KEK), "Image Security Database" (db allowed signatures, dbx revoked signatures), "systemd Boot Loader Interface" (variables set by systemd-boot or GRUB). Under each GUID: Variable name and Size in bytes.

Detail view (uefi-data:<Name-GUID>, the full file name): Attributes in hex with flags NV (non-volatile, survives power-off), BS (boot-services access), RT (runtime access, visible to the OS), TA (time-based authenticated, i.e. signed), the size, and a hex dump of up to 4 KB. Read-only.

Healthy / typical values. Author's PC: 159 variables. The standard group has Boot0000, Boot0001, BootCurrent, BootOrder, KEK, ConIn, ConOut; db is 11440 bytes and dbx 22314 bytes. Many vendor groups hold ASUS and AMD BIOS settings (Setup, AmdSetup..., AsusQFanSetupData, MyFav, StdDefaults...).

Unusual values and what they suggest.

  • A very large number of variables or a nearly full variable store can make firmware updates or new boot entries fail. Old Boot#### entries can be removed with efibootmgr.
  • An empty dbx (or a very small one) means the revocation list was never updated, which matters if you use Secure Boot.

Where Linux gets it. /sys/firmware/efi/efivars/ (each file is 4 bytes of attributes then the data).

UEFI information

uefi-info - Linux data

In plain words. The key UEFI boot settings: Secure Boot mode, boot menu timeout, language, which boot entry started this session, and the boot order.

What you see.

Field Meaning
UEFI Platform 64-bit or 32-bit UEFI
SecureBoot 1 (on) / 0 (off)
SetupMode 1 = no Platform Key installed, Secure Boot keys can be changed freely
AuditMode / DeployedMode Extra Secure Boot modes, when the firmware supports them
Timeout Firmware boot menu timeout in seconds
PlatformLang Firmware language
OsIndicationsSupported Hex mask of OS-to-firmware requests the firmware supports; SRS names BootToFwUI (reboot into setup), FileCapsule and CapsuleResultVar (firmware updates)
Boot Loader / Firmware Info / Firmware Type / Kernel Stub Strings from the systemd Boot Loader Interface, when the boot loader sets them
BootCurrent Boot entry used for this boot (green)
BootOrder Boot entries in the order the firmware tries them
Boot Entries One line per entry in BootOrder: Boot####, * if active, and its description

If the PC did not boot via UEFI: "Not booted via UEFI (/sys/firmware/efi absent)".

Healthy / typical values. Author's PC: 64-bit, SecureBoot 0 (off), SetupMode 0, timeout 1 s, en-US, Boot Loader GRUB 2.16, BootCurrent Boot0001 ("UEFI OS", the Linux entry), BootOrder 0001,0000,001D,001C,001E,001F, with a Windows Boot Manager entry and several USB-stick entries.

Unusual values and what they suggest.

  • SetupMode 1: no Platform Key is installed. Secure Boot cannot be enforced until keys are enrolled (normal right after "Clear Secure Boot keys").
  • BootCurrent not the first entry in BootOrder: the PC booted from a fallback, a one-time boot (boot menu) or the first entry failed.
  • Stale entries (removed drives, old distributions) can be cleaned with efibootmgr -b XXXX -B.

Where Linux gets it. /sys/firmware/efi/fw_platform_size and efivars SecureBoot, SetupMode, AuditMode, DeployedMode, Timeout, PlatformLang, OsIndicationsSupported, BootCurrent, BootOrder, Boot####, and the systemd Loader* / StubInfo variables.

Sensors / Cooling / Power (SRS Section Reference)

Back to the section index - Glossary

Where to find these items (SRS 2.0). In the main window they are on the Sensors page (Alt+8). Its tabs are Sensor status (with Zero and Hide unused), Hardware status, Cooling status (fans) and Power status; All N items lists the rest. The Overview's Is my PC OK? sums up the temperatures and alarms. You can also type an item's name or id into the search box (Ctrl+F). The rest of this introduction describes the classic view (Menu -> Classic View), with its Menu and panel buttons.

This group shows what your PC can measure about itself: temperatures, fan speeds, voltages, power use and batteries. It also covers the chips and firmware that supply those readings (the Super I/O chip, ASUS WMI, IPMI on servers) and the export and "setup" items that SIV offers for its own sensor tools. Open it from Menu -> Sensors / Cooling / Power -> item, or use the Sensors panel button. The panel has sub-buttons: Zero (reset the Minimum / Maximum columns), Status (Sensor status), Cooling (Cooling status), Power (Power status) and Hide (hide unused sensors). Everything here is read only: SRS never changes a fan speed, a limit or a register. Four items are only complete with root data from srs-root (Menu -> Run as root): ASUS ATK/WMI info, ASUS WMI ACPI methods, Super I/O LDNs and SIO debug.

All examples come from the author's PC: an ASUS TUF GAMING X870-PRO WIFI7 W NEO board (Nuvoton NCT6799 Super I/O chip), an AMD Ryzen 7 7800X3D, a Radeon RX 9070 XT, DDR5 memory, three NVMe drives and one SATA hard disk.
