AIO Link export

aio-export - Not present on most PCs

In plain words. An AIO (all-in-one) liquid cooler or a fan/RGB hub can report its own pump speed, liquid temperature and fan speeds over USB. SIV can read some of these hubs directly. SRS only checks whether Linux already has a kernel driver for one, and tells you if it found any.

What you see. This item, and all eleven "AIO Link ..." items below, print the same short report:

  • Status line - "No AIO Link Devices found on this system", or one line per hub found (hwmonN - driver name). When a hub is found, a note says its readings are part of Sensor status and Cooling status.
  • Checked - which kernel drivers were looked for: Corsair (Commander Pro corsair_cpro, Corsair PSUs corsair-psu), NZXT (nzxt-kraken2, nzxt-kraken3, nzxt-smart2), Aquacomputer (d5next, quadro, octo, highflownext), ASUS ROG Ryujin and Gigabyte Waterforce.
  • A note that USB HID cooler devices belong to CoolerControl or liquidctl. SRS never opens hidraw (the raw USB HID device files), so it cannot clash with those tools.

Healthy / typical values. On the author's PC: "No AIO Link Devices found". That is normal for any cooler without a Linux hwmon driver, and for an AIO whose pump is plugged into a motherboard header. In that case the pump shows up as an ordinary fan in Cooling status.

Unusual values and what they suggest. You own a supported hub but nothing is found: the driver module is not loaded, or another tool has claimed the device. Check lsmod for the driver name.

Where Linux gets it. /sys/class/hwmon/hwmon*/name, matched against the list of cooler drivers.

Background. Corsair iCUE LINK is Corsair's single-cable system for fans, pumps and lights. SIV talks to such hubs itself. On Linux the usual tools are liquidctl and CoolerControl, which drive the hub over USB HID. SRS stays out of their way on purpose.

ASUS ATK/WMI info

asus-info - Linux data - Needs root data

In plain words. ASUS boards hide some sensor and control functions behind firmware interfaces called ATK and ASUS WMI. This item shows which of those interfaces your board has, and whether any Linux ASUS sensor driver supports your exact board.

What you see.

Field Meaning Why it matters
Board vendor / Board / BIOS From the DMI (Desktop Management Interface) tables Driver support is decided per board name
ASUS WMI GUID 97845ED0-... (the ATK / ASUSWMI interface). Green if present If present, the ASUS WMI interface exists in firmware
ASUS sensor drivers One line per driver: asus_ec_sensors, asus_wmi_sensors, asus_atk0110, asus_wmi, asus_nb_wmi. Each says loaded / not loaded, then either "supports this board" or why not Tells you if an extra ASUS driver could add sensors
ASUS WMI blocks Table of WMI blocks that belong to ASUS firmware devices: GUID, Obj, Inst, ACPI parent, Driver, Description Shows what ASUS put in the firmware
ACPI tables / DSDT / SSDT Where the copied ACPI tables are, and which ones were copied Needed if you want to read the firmware code yourself

The reasons a driver line can give:

  • "N supported boards, this board is not listed" - the driver has a list of boards; yours is not on it.
  • "binds by ACPI device id, not by board (DMI)" - the driver loads on a firmware device, not a board name (true for asus_atk0110).
  • "module not built for this kernel" - your kernel has no such module file.
  • "modinfo failed" - SRS could not read the module's info.

WMI table columns (same as in ASUS WMI ACPI methods):

  • GUID - the 128-bit name of the interface.
  • Obj - the two-letter object id. MO is common for a data block holding a binary MOF (a description of the interface). ev D2 means an event, with notify id D2.
  • Inst - how many instances the block has.
  • ACPI parent - the PNP0C14:NN firmware device and its UID (for example AsusMbSwInterface).
  • Driver - the Linux driver bound to the block, or - for none.
  • Description - a name SRS knows for that GUID, if any.

Healthy / typical values. On the author's TUF GAMING X870-PRO WIFI7 W NEO (BIOS 1805): the ASUS WMI GUID is present on PNP0C14:02 AsusMbSwInterface; asus_ec_sensors says "60 supported boards, this board is not listed" and asus_wmi_sensors says "16 supported boards, this board is not listed". That is fine: board sensors come from the Super I/O chip instead (see Sensor status). Only the wmi-bmof driver is bound.

Unusual values and what they suggest.

  • "supports this board" but "not loaded": you could get extra readings (often chipset, VRM or water temperatures) by loading that module.
  • ACPI tables "Needs root: Menu > Run as root (srs-root)": the copy of the tables has not been made yet.

Where Linux gets it. /sys/class/dmi/id/*, /sys/bus/wmi/devices, modinfo -F alias (the dmi: board patterns), /sys/module, and the srs-root copy of /sys/firmware/acpi/tables.

Background. WMI (Windows Management Instrumentation) is a Windows interface. Board makers put WMI "blocks" inside the ACPI (Advanced Configuration and Power Interface) firmware so Windows tools can call them. Linux can see these blocks through the wmi bus. A driver must exist for each one before it does anything useful.

ASUS WMI ACPI methods

asus-wmi - Linux data - Needs root data

In plain words. A full list of every WMI firmware device and WMI block on the board, not only the ASUS ones. SRS lists them but does not run them.

What you see.

  • ACPI WMI devices (PNP0C14) - one line per WMI device: device name, UID (the firmware's own name for it, for example AsusLedControlWmi) and ACPI path (for example \ALCW).
  • WMI GUID blocks - the same table as in ASUS ATK/WMI info, but for all blocks.
  • A note: "WMI methods are not evaluated". Calling firmware methods from user space could change settings, so SRS never does it.
  • ACPI tables / DSDT / SSDT - as in ASUS ATK/WMI info.

Healthy / typical values. The author's board has six WMI devices (PNP0C14:00 to :05), including AsusLedControlWmi (RGB lights), AsusMbSwInterface (the main ASUS WMI interface), AsusMiniZipWmi and AsusWifiOptionWmi, plus 14 GUID blocks. Most have no Linux driver (-). That is normal.

Unusual values and what they suggest. "No WMI devices (/sys/bus/wmi/devices empty)": the wmi kernel module is not loaded, or the firmware has no WMI at all (common on older or server boards).

Where Linux gets it. /sys/bus/acpi/devices/PNP0C14* (uid, path), /sys/bus/wmi/devices, and the srs-root ACPI table copy.

Background. PNP0C14 is the standard ACPI id for a "WMI mapper" device. Each one holds a _WDG table that lists its GUID blocks. The method code lives in the DSDT and SSDT tables (the main and extra ACPI code tables).

ASUS ATK0110 debug

atk-debug - Not present on most PCs

In plain words. Older ASUS boards (roughly up to the early 2010s) gave sensor readings through a firmware device called ATK0110. This item checks for it.

What you see.

  • ACPI device - the ATK0110 device name if found, or "No ATK0110 ACPI device (used by older ASUS boards only)".
  • asus_atk0110 module - loaded / not loaded.
  • Checked - /sys/bus/acpi/devices/ATK0110*.

Healthy / typical values. Modern boards, like the author's X870, have no ATK0110. "Not present" is the expected answer.

Where Linux gets it. /sys/bus/acpi/devices, /sys/module/asus_atk0110.

Battery

battery - Not present on most PCs

In plain words. Lists every battery or UPS that Linux knows about. On a desktop that is often only the batteries inside wireless controllers, mice and headsets.

What you see. One block per battery, named after the Linux power-supply entry. Each block shows only the fields the driver provides:

Field Meaning
type Battery or UPS
scope System (powers the PC) or Device (powers a peripheral, like a game pad)
online 1 if on external power
status Charging, Discharging, Full, Not charging
capacity Charge level in %
capacity_level A rough level (Full, Normal, Low, Critical) when no % is given
health Good, Overheat, Dead and so on
technology Li-ion, Li-poly ...
manufacturer / model_name Who made it
cycle_count Charge cycles so far (battery wear)
voltage_now, current_now, power_now Live V, A, W
energy_now / energy_full / energy_full_design Wh now, Wh when full today, Wh when new
charge_now / charge_full / charge_full_design the same in mAh, for drivers that report charge

The serial number is never shown. A last line, Checked, says where SRS looked.

Healthy / typical values. The author's desktop has no system battery. It shows one Nintendo Switch controller battery: type Battery, scope Device, status Discharging, capacity_level Full.

Unusual values and what they suggest. On a laptop, energy_full well below energy_full_design means a worn battery (for example 70% of design = 30% wear). Health other than Good is worth acting on.

Where Linux gets it. /sys/class/power_supply/* (entries of type Battery or UPS).

Cooling status (fans)

cooling - Linux data

In plain words. One line per fan header: how fast the fan spins, how hard the board drives it, who is in control, which temperature it follows and the fan curve the chip uses.

What you see.

Column Meaning Why it matters
Fan Fan name (driver label if any, else fanN, or pwmN for an output with no speed sensor) Matches the header number in the chip, not always the board's printed name
Current Speed now, in RPM (revolutions per minute) The main health sign
Minimum / Maximum Lowest / highest speed SRS has seen since start or since Zero Shows whether the fan ramps up
Target Target speed, if the chip uses one Shown for non-Super-I/O chips, and for Super I/O fans only in Fan Speed Cruise mode
Duty How hard the header drives the fan: % and the raw value 0-255 in brackets 100% (255) is full power
Mode PWM (4-pin signal control) or DC (3-pin voltage control) A 4-pin fan on a DC header still works, but control is coarser
Control The chip's control mode number and name (see below), or "firmware / driver" when the driver gives no mode Who decides the fan speed
Temperature source The temperature input the fan follows: number and label If this is a wrong or floating input, the fan reacts to nothing
Curve Fan curve points as temperature:duty What the board will do as things heat up

Control mode names for Nuvoton (NCT) and Winbond (W83) chips: 0 off (full speed), 1 manual (software), 2 Thermal Cruise, 3 Fan Speed Cruise, 4 Smart Fan III, 5 Smart Fan IV. Other chips: 0 full speed / off, 1 manual (software), 2 and up automatic (hardware). The curve is only shown for automatic modes.

Fans reading 0 RPM are greyed. With Hide on, they are left out.

Under the table, Thermal cooling devices groups the kernel's cooling devices by type and state, for example "16 devices Processor state 0/3" (16 CPU threads, throttle step 0 of 3, so no throttling).

Healthy / typical values. On the author's NCT6799, all seven headers run in mode 5 Smart Fan IV and follow input 8 "PECI/TSI Agent 0 Calibration" (the CPU temperature as the chip sees it). fan1 runs at 874 RPM at 45% duty with the curve 20°C:35% 30°C:35% 40°C:35% 45°C:50% 125°C:100%. fan7 runs at 3325 RPM at 100% - a pump-style reading. The Radeon's own fan runs at 553 RPM, 15% duty, with a Target of 553 RPM, controlled by its firmware.

Unusual values and what they suggest.

  • 0 RPM with duty above 0%: nothing is plugged into that header, the fan has a zero-RPM mode, or the fan is stuck. On the author's PC, fan4 (68%) and fan6 (100%) read 0 RPM because nothing is plugged in.
  • A fan stuck at 100% with a flat curve (0°C:100% 100°C:100% ...): the BIOS is set to full speed for that header. Often chosen for pumps.
  • Speed never changes under load: the temperature source may be an unconnected input, or the curve is flat.
  • Very low RPM at high duty on a fan that used to be faster: dust, a worn bearing, or a fan that needs more starting voltage.
  • Mode DC on a 4-pin fan: switch the header to PWM in the BIOS for finer control.

Where Linux gets it. /sys/class/hwmon/hwmon*/fanN_input, pwmN, pwmN_mode, pwmN_enable, pwmN_temp_sel, pwmN_auto_pointN_temp/pwm, fanN_target; /sys/class/thermal/cooling_device*.

Background. PWM (Pulse Width Modulation) switches the fan's power on and off very fast. The "duty" is the share of time it is on. A fan curve is a list of points: at this temperature, use this duty. The chip draws straight lines between the points.

Sensor formula setup

formula-setup - Linux data

In plain words. Shows any rename, formula or "ignore" rule from your lm-sensors config that applies to the sensor chips in your PC. SIV keeps its own formula table; on Linux the same job is done by /etc/sensors3.conf and /etc/sensors.d/*.

What you see. A table with one row for each matching rule:

Column Meaning
SIV Device Name The chip name (for example nct6799)
User Name The new label from a label line
Formula A compute formula (read, write), or set = value (applied only by sensors -s), or ignore
Units Units of that sensor (°C, RPM, V, W, J, A, %, Hz)
SIV Device ID hwmonN/feature, for example hwmon4/in4
Source File and line number, for example sensors3.conf:233

If no rule matches, SRS says so and lists every chip with its full lm-sensors name, so you know what name to write in a chip line.

Healthy / typical values. On the author's PC: "No label / compute / set / ignore statements match the chips present", followed by the 13 chips (nct6799-isa-0290, k10temp-pci-00c3, ...). That is normal: the stock sensors3.conf has no section for the NCT6799.

Unusual values and what they suggest. A rule you wrote does not show: the chip pattern does not match the name shown here. Copy the name from this list.

Where Linux gets it. /etc/sensors3.conf (or /etc/sensors.conf) and /etc/sensors.d/*, matched to /sys/class/hwmon chips. SRS only reads these files.

Background. In lm-sensors config, label in4 "+12V" renames a reading, compute in4 @*12, @/12 scales it (the @ is the raw value; the first formula converts the reading, the second converts back for writing limits), ignore hides it, and set writes a limit when you run sensors -s.

Hardware status

hw-status - Linux data

In plain words. A one-screen summary of every sensor chip: how many readings of each type it has, how many are not connected, and how many are in alarm. Plus the case-open switch and the list of loaded monitoring drivers.

What you see.

Column Meaning
Chip Driver name of the chip (nct6799, k10temp, amdgpu ...)
Sensors name Full lm-sensors name, for example nct6799-isa-0290
Device The kernel device it hangs off (PCI address, platform device, NVMe name ...)
Temp / Fans / Volts / Power / PWM How many readings of each type
Other Energy, current, humidity and clock readings together
NC Readings judged "not connected" (see Sensor status)
Alarms Readings with an alarm flag set (red if any, green if none)

Below the table:

  • <chip> intrusionN - the chassis intrusion switch: "Closed", or "Intrusion latched (set since last clear, not live; ...)".
  • <chip> beep - whether the chip's alarm beeper is Enabled or Disabled.
  • Monitoring modules - which known sensor drivers are loaded.

Healthy / typical values. The author's PC has 13 chips. The NCT6799 has 13 temperatures, 7 fans, 18 voltages and 7 PWM outputs, with 9 not connected and 0 alarms. k10temp has 2 temperatures, zenergy 9 energy readings, amdgpu 3 temperatures, 1 fan, 1 voltage, 1 power, 1 PWM and 2 clocks. Each NVMe drive has 3 temperatures. Modules: nct6775 nct6775_core k10temp zenergy drivetemp spd5118 amdgpu ryzen_smu.

Unusual values and what they suggest.

  • Alarms above 0: open Sensor status to see which reading.
  • "Intrusion latched": the case-open flag was set at some point and nobody cleared it. It is not live. It is often set after a CMOS reset or on boards with no intrusion header wired. On the author's PC intrusion0 is latched and intrusion1 is Closed.
  • A chip you expect is missing: its driver is not loaded (for example no nct6775, so no board fans).

Where Linux gets it. /sys/class/hwmon/hwmon* (all attributes), intrusionN_alarm, beep_enable, /proc/modules.

Background. "hwmon" is the Linux hardware-monitoring framework. Every sensor driver puts its readings in a folder /sys/class/hwmon/hwmonN using the same file names, so any tool can read any chip.

IPMI dump

ipmi-dump - Not present on most PCs

In plain words. IPMI (Intelligent Platform Management Interface) is a server feature. A small separate computer on the board, the BMC (Baseboard Management Controller), watches sensors and lets admins manage the machine remotely. In SIV this item dumps the BMC's records. SRS only checks if a BMC is there.

What you see. (All four IPMI items print the same check.)

  • Status - "No IPMI BMC found on this system", or "IPMI device present (not opened)".
  • /dev/ipmi0 - present / absent (the device file used to talk to the BMC).
  • /sys/class/ipmi - present / absent.
  • ipmi_si / ipmi_devintf - the two kernel modules, loaded / not loaded.
  • ipmitool - installed / not installed.

Healthy / typical values. Desktop boards, like the author's, have no BMC: everything reads absent.

Unusual values and what they suggest. On a server where you expect a BMC: load ipmi_si and ipmi_devintf, then use ipmitool sdr (sensor records) or ipmitool sel list (event log). SRS does not open the device itself.

Where Linux gets it. /dev/ipmi0, /dev/ipmi/0, /sys/class/ipmi, /sys/module/ipmi_*.

IPMI status

ipmi-info - Not present on most PCs

In plain words. In SIV: the BMC's identity and health. In SRS: the same "is there a BMC" check as IPMI dump. "Not present" means the board has no server management controller, which is normal for desktops.

IPMI time

ipmi-time - Not present on most PCs

In plain words. In SIV: the BMC's own clock, used to time-stamp its event log. In SRS: the same presence check as IPMI dump. On a server, ipmitool sel time get shows that clock.

IPMI wait

ipmi-wait - Not present on most PCs

In plain words. In SIV: timing of requests to the BMC. In SRS: the same presence check as IPMI dump. Nothing to wait for when there is no BMC.

kWh cost

kwh-cost - Linux data

In plain words. Turns the power your parts are drawing right now into money: per hour, per day and per year, as if the PC ran like this all the time.

What you see.

  • Rate - price per kWh (kilowatt-hour). Default $0.1500. Set your own with the environment variables SRS_KWH_COST (for example 0.32) and SRS_CURRENCY (for example €).
  • A table: Component, Power (W), per Hour, per Day, per Year.
    • CPU line: the RAPL package power (CPU package-0 (RAPL)), or if there is none, the zenergy Esocket reading.
    • One line for each other hwmon power sensor (the GPU shows as GPU PPT).
  • Total Power (measured) - the sum, with its cost.
  • A note that only parts with power sensors are counted.

Healthy / typical values. On the author's PC at light load: CPU 49.60 W and GPU 36.00 W, total 85.60 W, which is $0.31 per day or $112.48 per year at $0.15/kWh.

Unusual values and what they suggest. The total is always lower than the wall socket reading. The board, drives, fans, RAM and the power supply's own losses are not measured. A wall power meter shows the real figure; expect it to be clearly higher than this total.

Where Linux gets it. /sys/class/powercap/*/energy_uj (RAPL), hwmon energy*_input (zenergy) and power*_input / power*_average (for example amdgpu). Power is worked out from two energy readings about 0.2 s apart.

Background. 1 kWh is 1000 W used for one hour. A PC drawing 100 W all day uses 2.4 kWh per day.

LCD panel setup

lcd-panel - Not present on most PCs

In plain words. SIV can show its readings on small external screens, such as LCDSysInfo USB panels or the screen on some AIO coolers. SRS does not drive such screens.

What you see. "No supported external LCD panel (LCDSysInfo / AIO LCD) found" and a note that case and AIO displays are driven over USB HID by their own tools and are not probed.

Healthy / typical values. This message is the normal answer on every Linux PC.

Super I/O LDNs

ldn-info - Linux data - Needs root data

In plain words. The Super I/O is a small chip on the motherboard that reads fans, voltages and board temperatures. It is split into "logical devices". This item shows which chip you have, where its hardware-monitor part lives, and what the kernel said when it found it.

What you see.

  • Chip - the Super I/O driver name, for example nct6799.
  • Platform device - the kernel device, for example nct6775.656. The number is the base address in decimal (656 = 0x290).
  • HWM base (LDN 0x0B) - the I/O address of the hardware-monitor logical device, for example 0x0290.
  • hwmon - the sysfs folder, for example /sys/class/hwmon/hwmon4.
  • Driver - nct6775 + nct6775_core (loaded) when the Nuvoton driver is in use.
  • I/O ports - lines from the I/O port map that mention the chip or its address. Without root data the addresses are hidden (shown as zeros), so SRS uses the srs-root copy.
  • Kernel log - the driver's start-up message (from the srs-root copy of the kernel log).
  • A note that the LDN configuration registers are not read: SRS never does raw port I/O.

Healthy / typical values. On the author's PC: chip nct6799 at HWM base 0x0290; I/O ports 0290-029f : PNP0C02:03; kernel log nct6775: Found NCT6796D-S/NCT6799D-R or compatible chip at 0x2e:0x290.

Unusual values and what they suggest.

  • "No Super-I/O hardware monitor driver bound": no fan or board readings at all. Load nct6775 (Nuvoton) or it87 (ITE). On some boards the firmware reserves the address range and the driver refuses to load; the common workaround is the kernel option acpi_enforce_resources=lax, used at your own risk.
  • "Needs root: Menu > Run as root (srs-root)" under I/O ports or Kernel log: run srs-root once.

Where Linux gets it. /sys/class/hwmon/*/device (platform device), /proc/ioports or the srs-root ioports.txt, the srs-root dmesg.txt, /sys/module/nct6775.

Background. The chip is reached through two "config" ports, 0x2E/0x2F (or 0x4E/0x4F). Each logical device (serial port, keyboard, hardware monitor ...) has a number, the LDN (Logical Device Number). On Nuvoton chips the hardware monitor is LDN 0x0B. The kernel log's 0x2e:0x290 means "config port 0x2E, hardware monitor at 0x290". A PNP0C02 entry is an ACPI "motherboard resources" device that reserves the range.

AIO Link devices

link-devices - Not present on most PCs

In plain words. In SIV: the list of devices on an AIO / fan hub chain. In SRS: the same cooler driver check as AIO Link export. If a supported hub is found it is listed here as hwmonN - driver name.

AIO Link dump

link-dump - Not present on most PCs

In plain words. In SIV: a raw data dump from the hub. SRS never reads raw USB data from coolers, so it shows the same driver check as AIO Link export.

AIO Link fans

link-fans - Not present on most PCs

In plain words. In SIV: fan speeds reported by the hub. In SRS: the same check as AIO Link export. Fans of a hub with a Linux driver appear in Cooling status.

AIO Link LEDs

link-leds - Not present on most PCs

In plain words. In SIV: the hub's RGB lighting channels. In SRS: the same check as AIO Link export. For lighting on Linux, tools like OpenRGB or liquidctl are used.

AIO Link limits

link-limits - Not present on most PCs

In plain words. In SIV: warning limits stored in the hub. In SRS: the same check as AIO Link export. Limits of a driver-supported hub show in the Limits column of Sensor status.

AIO Link power

link-power - Not present on most PCs

In plain words. In SIV: power drawn through the hub (and, for Corsair PSUs, PSU rails). In SRS: the same check as AIO Link export. A corsair-psu driver's readings would show in Power status.

AIO Link setup

link-setup - Not present on most PCs

In plain words. In SIV: settings for the hub link. SRS has nothing to set up and shows the same check as AIO Link export.

AIO Link status

link-status - Not present on most PCs

In plain words. In SIV: live status of each linked device. In SRS: the same check as AIO Link export.

AIO Link test

link-test - Not present on most PCs

In plain words. In SIV: a communication test with the hub. SRS never talks to the hub directly, so it shows the same check as AIO Link export.

AIO Link update

link-update - Not present on most PCs

In plain words. In SIV: hub firmware details. SRS does not touch cooler firmware and shows the same check as AIO Link export. Use the maker's tool to update hub firmware.

Power status

power - Linux data

In plain words. Every power and energy reading in the PC: the CPU's own energy counters, power readings from drivers such as the GPU, and any batteries or other power supplies.

What you see. Three blocks:

  1. RAPL energy (powercap) - one row per energy zone: zone name and folder, power now (W), total energy counted so far (J, joules), and any power limits the zone reports (name N W).
  2. hwmon power and energy - one row per hwmon power, energy or current reading: chip and label, value, then either total energy (J) or the sysfs file name. GPU power rows also show cap (current power limit), max (highest limit allowed) and default (factory limit).
  3. Power supplies - every entry in /sys/class/power_supply, with the same fields as Battery (mains adapters too, not only batteries).

Healthy / typical values. On the author's 7800X3D near idle: package-0 52.77 W, core 1.91 W. zenergy shows each core at about 2-4 W and Esocket0 at 52.22 W. The Radeon shows amdgpu PPT 35.00 W cap 374 W max 374 W default 304 W - the power limit has been raised from the 304 W default to the 374 W maximum. The only power supply is a game controller battery.

Unusual values and what they suggest.

  • Package power far above core power at idle is normal on Ryzen desktop chips: the I/O die, memory controller and cache use a lot of the package power.
  • cap lower than default on a GPU: something (a tuning tool or a profile) has lowered the power limit, which can cut performance.
  • "No powercap energy zones": the intel_rapl powercap driver is not loaded (it is also used for AMD).
  • A watt value of -: the counter could not be read twice in time; open the item again.

Where Linux gets it. /sys/class/powercap/*/energy_uj and constraint_N_*; hwmon power*_average, power*_input, power*_cap*, energy*_input, curr*_input; /sys/class/power_supply.

Background. RAPL (Running Average Power Limit) is a CPU feature that counts the energy used. The counter only goes up; power is the change in energy divided by the time between two readings. Linux names the zones intel-rapl even on AMD CPUs. zenergy is an extra (out-of-tree) driver that reads the same AMD counters per core. PPT (Package Power Tracking) is AMD's name for the power the GPU or CPU is allowed to draw.

PWM export

pwm-export - Linux data

In plain words. A CSV (comma-separated values) snapshot of every fan control output, ready to paste into a spreadsheet.

What you see. A header line, then one line per PWM output:

Column Meaning
hwmon The hwmon folder (hwmon4)
chip Full chip name (nct6799-isa-0290)
pwm Output name (pwm1)
raw Raw drive value 0-255
duty_pct Duty in %
enable Control mode number (see Cooling status)
mode 1 = PWM, 0 = DC
temp_sel Number of the temperature input the fan follows
fan_rpm Speed of the fan with the same number

-1 means the driver does not provide that value. A note says values are read only.

Healthy / typical values. From the author's PC: hwmon4,nct6799-isa-0290,pwm1,133,52.2,5,1,8,955 (52% duty, Smart Fan IV, PWM mode, following input 8, 955 RPM). The GPU line is hwmon9,amdgpu-pci-0300,pwm1,40,15.7,-1,-1,-1,554: the amdgpu driver gives no mode or source here.

Where Linux gets it. hwmon pwmN, pwmN_enable, pwmN_mode, pwmN_temp_sel, fanN_input.

QST status

qst-status - Not present on most PCs

In plain words. QST (Intel Quiet System Technology) was fan control built into the Intel management engine on some Intel desktop boards around 2007-2010. SIV can read it. SRS reports "Not present on this system" (Checked: n/a (Intel QST)). Modern boards, and all AMD boards, use the Super I/O or the embedded controller instead.

Sensor export

sen-export - Linux data

In plain words. A CSV snapshot of every sensor reading, for spreadsheets or logs.

What you see. Header hwmon,chip,feature,label,value,unit,minimum,maximum,status, then one line per reading:

  • hwmon, chip - where it comes from.
  • feature - the hwmon name (temp3, fan1, in0, energy9 ...).
  • label - the name in quotes (driver label, lm-sensors label, a standard pin name, or the feature name).
  • value - with 3 decimals, after any lm-sensors formula. Energy readings are exported as watts.
  • unit - C, RPM, V, W, A, %, MHz.
  • minimum, maximum - lowest and highest values seen since start or since Zero.
  • status - ok, alarm, or not-connected (a floating or unwired input; these lines are greyed).

Healthy / typical values. From the author's PC: hwmon5,k10temp-pci-00c3,temp1,"Tctl",56.375,C,56.375,57.625,ok and hwmon4,nct6799-isa-0290,temp3,"AUXTIN0",86.000,C,86.000,86.000,not-connected.

Unusual values and what they suggest. Filter out not-connected lines before you graph or average anything. They are not real temperatures (see Sensor status).

Where Linux gets it. All of /sys/class/hwmon/hwmon*.

Sensor status

sensors - Linux data

In plain words. The main sensor page. Every temperature, fan, voltage, power, energy, clock and PWM reading from every chip, with the lowest and highest values seen, the chip's limits and a plain status. It refreshes about once a second.

What you see.

A top line: "Minimum / Maximum since (Zero resets) Hide unused: on/off".

Then one block per chip. The chip line shows: driver name, full lm-sensors name, hwmon folder and the kernel device path. Chips are sorted: Super I/O first, then CPU, GPU, memory, drives, everything else. Inside each chip, readings are grouped under Temperatures, Fans, Voltages, Power, Energy, Currents, Humidity, Clocks and PWM duty.

Column Meaning Why it matters
Sensor The label (from the driver, your lm-sensors config, a standard pin name, or just in4) Tells you what it measures
Current Value now (°C, RPM, V, W, A, %, MHz)
Minimum / Maximum Lowest / highest seen since SRS started or since Zero Catches spikes you were not watching
Limits The chip's own limits: min, max, crit (critical); cap for power; total N J for energy What the chip or driver treats as too high
Status See the list below The quick answer
Source The sysfs file read, plus (compute) if an lm-sensors formula was applied, or (pin) for a standard pin name Lets you check the raw value yourself

Status values, checked in this order:

  • not connected (...) - the input is not wired to anything. Greyed. The reasons are explained below.
  • ignored (sensors.conf) - your lm-sensors config says to ignore it. Greyed.
  • ALARM (red) - the chip has set an alarm flag for this reading.
  • CRITICAL (red) - at or above the crit limit.
  • HIGH (orange) - above max (not used for power).
  • LOW (orange) - below min (not used for temperatures).
  • unused (grey) - reads exactly 0, for example an empty fan header.
  • OK (green).

A voltage or fan alarm is ignored when the chip has no limits set (both 0). Those alarm flags mean nothing.

At the bottom: a count line ("13 chips, 79 sensors, 79 shown, 0 hidden, 9 not connected, 0 in alarm"), plus notes explaining greyed rows and (pin) names.

Zero clears the Minimum / Maximum columns and restarts the "since" time. Hide removes rows that are not connected, ignored, or reading 0.

Healthy / typical values. From the author's PC, near idle:

  • CPU: k10temp Tctl 56.4°C, Tccd1 52.4°C (it has peaked at 57.6°C and 56.5°C). The Super I/O's TSI0_TEMP (56.8°C) is the same CPU temperature, read over the CPU's SB-TSI interface.
  • Board: SYSTIN 22.0°C and CPUTIN 30.0°C, both with max 80 crit 125.
  • Vcore 1.120 V (range 1.096-1.144 V), +3.3V 3.312 V, 3VSB 3.408 V, Vbat 3.344 V.
  • GPU: edge 25.0°C, junction 29.0°C, memory 50.0°C, PPT 37.00 W (cap 374), sclk 311 MHz.
  • DDR5 modules (spd5118): 31.0°C and 30.5°C, max 55 crit 85.
  • NVMe Composite: 34.9, 37.9 and 39.9°C. SATA disk (drivetemp): 38.0°C. USB controller in the chipset (prom21_xhci): 51.9°C. Network chip PHY (r8169): 55.0°C, max 120.

Unusual values and what they suggest.

  • AUXTIN reading 66-86°C and never moving. This confuses many people. See "Not connected inputs" below. On the author's board AUXTIN0 reads 86°C, AUXTIN3 84°C and AUXTIN4 70°C. They are not real and nothing is overheating.
  • PCH_... temperatures at 0.0°C: AMD boards have no Intel-style PCH (Platform Controller Hub) feeding this chip, so these read 0. SRS marks them "not connected (PCH reading 0)".
  • CPU temperature (Tctl) above 90°C under normal load: check the cooler mounting, paste and fan curve. Ryzen 7000 chips are designed to run up to 89-95°C under full load, but not at light load.
  • GPU junction more than about 20-25°C above edge under load: possible poor paste or pad contact.
  • NVMe Composite near its max: the drive will slow itself down (thermal throttle). Add a heatsink or airflow.
  • Vcore that never drops at idle: power saving may be off in the BIOS.
  • Vbat below about 3.0 V: the CMOS coin cell is getting weak. While the PC is on, some boards feed this input from standby power, so a good reading does not prove the coin cell is fine.
  • A plain inN voltage with an odd value (0.344 V, 1.472 V): see "Voltages" below.

Not connected inputs (floating AUXTIN). A Super I/O chip has many temperature inputs. Each one is built for a thermistor: a small part whose resistance changes with heat. The chip measures the voltage at the pin and turns it into °C using a fixed table. The board maker decides which inputs get a real thermistor. The rest are left unwired. An unwired pin is "floating": its voltage drifts to some level set by leakage and noise, not by heat. The chip still turns that voltage into a temperature, so you get a number that looks real but is not. Signs of a floating input:

  • It stays the same, or nearly so: Minimum = Current = Maximum, even under heavy load.
  • It does not match anything nearby (86°C while the board and CPU are at 22-30°C).
  • It may be very low (1-12°C, colder than the room) instead of high.
  • Its alarm flag may be set because the fake value is above the 80°C max. Tools such as sensors then show ALARM. SRS shows it greyed as not connected and does not count it as an alarm.

SRS marks these as follows:

  • probably not connected (floating high) - an AUXTIN input reading more than 25°C above the board's own SYSTIN / CPUTIN readings (a real probe on a board header reads near those). On the author's ASUS TUF GAMING X870-PRO these are AUXTIN0, AUXTIN3 and AUXTIN4 of the NCT6799 (66-86°C while SYSTIN / CPUTIN read 22-29°C).
  • not connected (floating low) - any AUXTIN input reading below 15°C (AUXTIN1, AUXTIN2, AUXTIN5 here).
  • not connected (implausible) - any Super I/O temperature at or below 0°C or at or above 120°C.
  • not connected (PCH reading 0) - PCH inputs reading exactly 0.

If you plug a probe into the board's optional thermistor header (often labelled T_SENSOR), one AUXTIN input will start to follow real temperatures and is no longer greyed. To make sure SRS treats an input as connected, give it a label in /etc/sensors.d/ (inputs labelled there are never marked floating).

Voltages and (pin). The Nuvoton driver gives voltage inputs no names. SRS names the five that are the same on every NCT67xx chip: in0 Vcore, in2 AVCC, in3 +3.3V, in7 3VSB, in8 Vbat, marked (pin). The other inN inputs are wired differently on each board. The chip can only measure small voltages (about 2 V at most), so rails such as +12 V and +5 V reach it through a resistor divider. SRS shows the raw pin voltage and does not apply the divider. An lm-sensors compute line can scale it, and the result shows as (compute).

Where Linux gets it. Every /sys/class/hwmon/hwmon* folder: *_input, *_label, *_min, *_max, *_crit, *_alarm, power*_average, power*_cap, energy*_input (sampled to watts), pwmN; labels, formulas and ignores from /etc/sensors3.conf and /etc/sensors.d/*.

Background.

  • Tctl is the AMD "control" temperature that the CPU uses for fan and boost decisions. Tccd1 is the temperature of the first CCD (core complex die, the chip with the cores).
  • "PECI/TSI Agent 0 Calibration" is the CPU temperature as the Super I/O sees it, after the board's own adjustment. Board fan curves usually follow it. SB-TSI is AMD's sideband temperature interface.
  • GPU edge is the die's edge sensor, junction is the hottest spot on the die, and mem is the video memory.
  • NVMe Composite is the drive's own summary temperature. Sensor 1 and 2 are extra sensors (often the controller and the flash).

SIO debug

sio-dbg - Linux data - Needs root data

In plain words. A raw list of every value the Super I/O driver exposes, in the driver's own units. It is the "under the bonnet" view behind Sensor status and Cooling status.

What you see.

  • Chip and Source - the chip name and its hwmon folder.
  • A note: these are register-derived driver values, read only. Raw register dumps would need /dev/port and are not done.
  • Then one name value line for every file in the folder, sorted by name. Raw units: milli-degrees (46000 = 46°C), millivolts (1120 = 1.120 V), RPM, PWM 0-255, times in milliseconds.

The main families:

Attribute Meaning
tempN_input, _label Temperature and its name
tempN_max, _max_hyst, _crit Warning limit, the value it must fall back below to clear, critical limit
tempN_offset Correction added by the chip
tempN_type Sensor type; 4 = thermistor
tempN_alarm, _beep Alarm flag; whether the alarm beeps
inN_input, _min, _max, _alarm, _beep Voltage inputs and their limits
fanN_input, _min, _pulses, _target, _tolerance, _alarm, _beep Fan speed, low limit, tacho pulses per turn, target and allowed error for speed modes
pwmN, _enable, _mode, _temp_sel Drive value, control mode, PWM/DC, temperature source
pwmN_auto_pointN_temp, _pwm The fan curve points
pwmN_floor, _start, _stop_time Lowest duty allowed, duty used to start a stopped fan, delay before stopping
pwmN_step_up_time, _step_down_time How fast the duty may change
pwmN_target_temp, _temp_tolerance, _crit_temp_tolerance Settings for Thermal Cruise mode
pwmN_weight_* A second temperature that can add to the fan duty
intrusionN_alarm, _beep Case-open switch
beep_enable, name Master beeper switch; chip name

Healthy / typical values. On the author's NCT6799: temp1_label SYSTIN, temp1_input 22000, temp1_max 80000, temp1_type 4; pwm1 131, pwm1_enable 5, pwm1_temp_sel 8; pwm1_auto_point4_temp 45000 with pwm1_auto_point4_pwm 127; fan1_pulses 2; in0_input 1120, in0_max 1744.

Unusual values and what they suggest.

  • in10_alarm 1 to in16_alarm 1 with _min 0 and _max 0: the BIOS set no limits for these inputs, so the chip flags them. These alarms mean nothing, and Sensor status ignores them.
  • temp3_alarm 1 and temp6_alarm 1: the floating AUXTIN0 and AUXTIN3 inputs read above their 80°C max. Again not real.
  • fanN_target values look odd unless that fan is in mode 3 (Fan Speed Cruise). The chip only uses them in that mode.
  • fanN_pulses wrong for your fan (most fans give 2 pulses per turn): the RPM reading will be double or half.

Where Linux gets it. Every readable file in the Super I/O's /sys/class/hwmon/hwmonN folder.

Synthetic sensors setup

synthetic - Linux data

In plain words. SIV lets you build your own "computed" sensors. On Linux the matching feature is the lm-sensors compute line. This item lists every compute line in your config and, if the chip is present, shows the raw and computed value side by side.

What you see.

  • Config files - which files were read (/etc/sensors3.conf, /etc/sensors.d/*), or "none".
  • A table:
Column Meaning
Source File and line, for example sensors3.conf:233
Chip match The chip pattern from the chip line (... if there are more), or the real chip name if it matches one in your PC
Feature The reading it applies to (in6)
Formula (read, write) The two formulas; @ is the raw value
Raw The raw reading (only for present chips)
Computed The result, or n/a if the formula could not be worked out
  • A summary: number of compute statements and the list of chips present.
  • A note: greyed rows are for chips not in this PC. Add your own in /etc/sensors.d/<name>.conf.

Healthy / typical values. On the author's PC: 19 compute statements from the stock /etc/sensors3.conf, all for other chips (pc87365, w83627thf, nct6106, f71808e ...), so all rows are greyed and Raw / Computed are empty.

Unusual values and what they suggest. Your own line shows greyed: the chip pattern does not match. Use the full names from the summary line or from Sensor formula setup.

Where Linux gets it. /etc/sensors3.conf (or /etc/sensors.conf) and /etc/sensors.d/*, applied to /sys/class/hwmon readings.

Background. Example for a +12 V rail measured through a divider that divides by 12: chip "nct6799-*" then compute in4 @*12, @/12 and label in4 "+12V". Find the right factor in your board's documentation or by comparing with the BIOS hardware monitor.

Thermal zones

thermal-zones - Not present on most PCs

In plain words. Thermal zones are temperature areas defined by the firmware (ACPI), mostly on laptops. Each zone has trip points: temperatures where the system slows down, starts a fan, or shuts down.

What you see.

  • One row per zone: zone name (thermal_zone0), type, temperature, and the governor policy that acts on it.
  • Under each zone, its trip points: type (active, passive, hot, critical) and temperature.
  • If there are none: "No ACPI / thermal_zone* zones exposed by this firmware".
  • Cooling devices - how many cooling devices exist (details in Cooling status).
  • Checked - /sys/class/thermal.

Healthy / typical values. Many desktop boards have no zones, like the author's PC ("No ACPI / thermal_zone* zones", 16 cooling devices). That is normal; the CPU protects itself anyway.

Unusual values and what they suggest. On a laptop, a critical trip only a few degrees above the current temperature means the machine is about to shut down to protect itself.

Where Linux gets it. /sys/class/thermal/thermal_zone* (type, temp, policy, trip_point_N_type/temp).

UPS export

ups-export - Not present on most PCs

In plain words. A UPS (Uninterruptible Power Supply) is a battery box that keeps the PC running in a power cut. SIV can export UPS data. SRS shows which UPS tools are installed and any UPS or battery that Linux reports.

What you see.

  • apcupsd (apcaccess) - installed (not queried) / not installed.
  • Network UPS Tools (upsc) - installed (not queried) / not installed.
  • Battery and UPS entries from /sys/class/power_supply, with the same fields as Battery.
  • "No UPS data to export".

Healthy / typical values. On the author's PC: apcupsd is installed but not queried, NUT is not installed, and the only entry is a game controller battery.

Unusual values and what they suggest. You have a USB UPS but no entry shows: many UPS units are handled only by apcupsd or NUT and do not appear in /sys/class/power_supply. Ask those tools directly (apcaccess status or upsc <name>).

Where Linux gets it. /usr/bin/apcaccess, /usr/bin/upsc (presence only), /sys/class/power_supply.

Volumes / Drives (SRS Section Reference)

Back to the section index - Glossary

Where to find these items (SRS 2.0). In the main window they are on the Storage page (Alt+6). Its tabs are Disk drives, Volumes, SMART drives, Partitions, Disk performance and USB disk drives; All N items lists the rest. The Overview checks drive health and drive temperature. You can also type an item's name or id into the search box (Ctrl+F). The rest of this introduction describes the classic view (Menu -> Classic View), with its Menu and panel buttons.

This group covers everything about storage: the physical drives in the PC, how they are split into partitions, which filesystems are on them, where those filesystems are mounted, how busy the drives are, and how healthy they are. Open any item with Menu -> Volumes / Drives -> item. The panel button Volumes opens the volume list straight away; next to it, Drive / shows the full detail of the root filesystem (volumes:/) and FS shows the filesystem statistics of the root filesystem (ntfs:/). Most items read only files the kernel already makes public, so they work as a normal user. The drive health items (SMART drives, SMART all drives, SMART drive monitor) and the NVMe controller items need root data: use Menu -> Run as root (srs-root) once, and SRS shows the cached results from then on. SMART on USB-attached disks is skipped unless you set SRS_SMART_USB=1 before running srs-root.

A note on units: SRS shows sizes in powers of 1024 but writes them as "GB" and "TB". So a "1 TB" drive (10^12 bytes on the box) shows as 931.51GB. The Drive geometry item shows both styles side by side.

SRS (srs-sysinfo) is a Linux system information viewer inspired by SIV64X (System Information Viewer). SIV is the work of Ray Hinchliffe, RH Software. SRS is not affiliated with or endorsed by RH Software and contains no SIV code or data. Item names follow SIV, which is why some titles name Windows things (NTFS, stornvme, Storage Spaces); SRS shows the nearest Linux equivalent.
