A note on the examples: real addresses from the author's PC have been replaced. The home network is shown as 192.168.1.x (router 192.168.1.1, wired card 192.168.1.20, Wi-Fi 192.168.1.21). MAC addresses, link-local IPv6 addresses and Wi-Fi names are shown as XX:XX:..., fe80::XXXX and "HomeWiFi".

Network adapters

adapters - Linux data

In plain words. One block per network adapter (real or virtual), with its addresses, how it got them, its DNS servers, gateway and the multicast groups it listens to. This is the Linux version of Windows' ipconfig /all.

What you see.

Top line (whole PC):

Field Meaning Why it matters
Linux IP Configuration Your OS name and kernel. Context.
Host The computer's host name. How other machines may know you.
Domain DNS (Domain Name System) domain or search domain, "-" if none. Home PCs usually have none.
DNS IP Address DNS servers from /etc/resolv.conf, one per line. Who turns names into addresses.
Routing / Proxy "Enabled/Disabled" for IP forwarding, then for a proxy in the environment. Forwarding on means the PC can pass packets between adapters (Docker and VMs turn it on).

Then one block per adapter (physical first, then virtual, loopback last). Each block has at least three rows:

Column Meaning Why it matters
Adapter / Description Row 1: interface name. Row 2: driver. Under the block: full description (PCI name, USB product, or "Bridge (virtual, driver bridge)"). Tells you which chip and driver handle the port.
Type (Index) Row 1: Ethernet, Wi-Fi, Bridge, TUN, TAP, veth, Loopback, PPP, etc., plus the kernel's interface index. Row 2: MAC address. The index is a stable number tools use instead of the name.
Speed Row 1: link speed (only when up). Row 2: MTU. Row 3: state (up, down, unknown, dormant). Wrong speed or "down" is the first thing to check when the network is slow or dead.
Adapter Address Each IPv4 and IPv6 address with its prefix length (for example 192.168.1.20/24). The address other machines use to reach this adapter.
Prefix Origin Where the network part came from: DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol: the router hands out the address), Manual, RouterAdv (IPv6 router advertisement), WellKnown (loopback, link-local). Shows if an address was handed out or typed in.
Suffix Origin Where the host part came from: DHCP, Manual, Link (built from the MAC), Random (privacy address), WellKnown. "Random" means IPv6 privacy addresses are on.
DAD State Duplicate Address Detection: Preferred (fine), Tentative (still checking), Duplicate (another device has it), Deprecated (being phased out). "Duplicate" is a real address conflict.
DNS and Gateway DNS servers for this adapter (from NetworkManager, else resolv.conf), then GW = default gateway (IPv4, then IPv6). Only adapters with a default route show a GW.
Multicast Address Multicast groups the adapter has joined, up to four (then "+N more"). Normal: 224.0.0.1 (all hosts), 224.0.0.251 (mDNS), 239.255.255.250 (SSDP/UPnP: Simple Service Discovery Protocol / Universal Plug and Play), ff02::1.

You can open one adapter on its own with adapters:<name>, for example adapters:em1.

Healthy / typical values. On the author's PC the 2.5 GbE wired port em1 (Realtek RTL8126, driver r8169) shows Ethernet (3), 2.5 Gbps, MTU 1500, up, a DHCP address 192.168.1.20/24 in state Preferred, a link-local fe80::XXXX/64 (WellKnown / Link), DNS 192.168.1.1 and GW 192.168.1.1. Virtual adapters (VMware vmnet1/vmnet8, libvirt virbr0, Docker docker0, a veth pair, a TAP device) have Manual addresses and no gateway. Docker bridges and veth report a fake 10.0 Gbps. lo is Loopback (1) with 127.0.0.1/8 and ::1/128, MTU 65536.

Unusual values and what they suggest.

  • Wired link at 100 Mbps or 10 Mbps on a gigabit card: bad cable (a broken pair), old switch port, or a power-saving setting.
  • An address starting 169.254.: DHCP failed and Linux gave itself a fallback address.
  • DAD State "Duplicate": two devices have the same IP. Check for a static address clashing with the router's DHCP range.
  • Two adapters (wired and Wi-Fi) in the same subnet, both with a gateway: works, but the one with the lower route metric wins (see Routing table).
  • Physical adapter state "down" with no cable plugged in is normal.

Where Linux gets it. /sys/class/net/<if>/ (type, operstate, speed, mtu, address), ip -o addr show, nmcli device show, /etc/resolv.conf, /proc/net/route, /proc/net/igmp and /proc/net/igmp6.

Background. A prefix length (the "/24") says how many leading bits are the network part. /24 means the first three numbers (192.168.1) are the network and the last number picks the host. Multicast is one-to-many traffic: a device joins a group address and receives anything sent to it, which is how printers and media players announce themselves.

ARP table

arp-table - Linux data

In plain words. The list of nearby devices your PC has recently talked to on the local network, with their hardware (MAC) addresses. Below it, the services those devices announce over mDNS (printers, speakers, phones).

What you see.

Neighbour table:

Column Meaning
IP Address The neighbour's IPv4 or IPv6 address.
Physical Address Its MAC address ("-" if not resolved).
HW Type "Ethernet" for IPv4 ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) entries, "IPv6 NDP" (Neighbor Discovery Protocol) for IPv6.
Flags IPv4: Dynamic (learned), Static (set by hand), Incomplete (asked, no answer yet). IPv6: the kernel state, such as REACHABLE, STALE, DELAY, PROBE, FAILED, PERMANENT.
Adapter Which of your interfaces it was seen on.

mDNS / DNS-SD services (read from avahi's cache; SRS sends no new queries):

Column Meaning
1 Your interface the announcement arrived on.
2 IPv4 or IPv6.
3 The service's name (for example a printer's name). Names keep avahi's escape codes, so \032 is a space and \064 is "@".
4 Service type, such as "Internet Printer", "AirPlay Remote Video", _kdeconnect._udp, _adb._tcp.
5 Domain, normally local.

Healthy / typical values. On the author's PC the router 192.168.1.1 appears as Dynamic on both em1 and wlan0, plus a few other home devices. IPv6 entries show STALE (seen a while ago, still usable) and the odd FAILED. The mDNS list shows a smart TV ("AirPlay Remote Video"), a Lexmark printer and scanner (Internet Printer, _uscan._tcp), KDE Connect and a phone with ADB enabled. The same service usually appears once per interface.

Unusual values and what they suggest.

  • The router's IP shows two different MAC addresses over time: possible ARP spoofing (someone pretending to be the router), or you swapped the router.
  • Many Incomplete or FAILED entries: devices that went offline, or a scan of the subnet.
  • "Neighbour table is empty" on a connected PC: you have not talked to anything yet, or the adapter is down.
  • "avahi-daemon cache empty or avahi not running": avahi is off, so no mDNS list.

Where Linux gets it. /proc/net/arp, ip -o -6 neigh show, and avahi-browse -a -t -p -c (cache only).

Background. IP addresses are for routing; on the local cable the hardware needs a MAC address. ARP (IPv4) and NDP (IPv6) ask "who has 192.168.1.1?" and remember the answer for a short time. mDNS (multicast DNS) lets devices announce names and services on the LAN (local area network) without a DNS server.

Bluetooth radios

bluetooth - Linux data

In plain words. Your Bluetooth controller(s): what chip it is, which driver runs it, whether it is blocked, and the settings and services the Bluetooth daemon reports.

What you see. Per controller (hci0, hci1...), from sysfs:

  • Bus - usb or pci plus the port. Most built-in Bluetooth is a USB device even on a Wi-Fi card.
  • Driver - usually btusb.
  • USB ID - vendor:product and revision (USB only).
  • USB device - manufacturer and product strings.
  • rfkill - the radio kill switch: soft-blocked (turned off in software) and hard-blocked (a physical switch or BIOS).

Then, from bluetoothctl show, one block per controller:

  • Controller line - its Bluetooth address and type (public/random).
  • Manufacturer, Version - Bluetooth SIG company ID and the core spec version code (for example 0x0c = Bluetooth 5.3).
  • Name, Alias - the name other devices see.
  • Class - the device class code (desktop computer, etc.).
  • Powered, PowerState - is the radio on.
  • Discoverable, DiscoverableTimeout, Pairable - can others find and pair with it (timeout 0 = no time limit).
  • Services (UUID) - the profiles it offers (Audio Sink/Source, A/V Remote Control, Phonebook Access, etc.).
  • Modalias - the ID of the Bluetooth stack (BlueZ).
  • Discovering - is a scan running now.
  • Roles - central (connects to devices) and/or peripheral (devices connect to it).
  • Advertising Features block - Bluetooth Low Energy advertising limits: instances, what can be included, secondary PHYs (1M, 2M, Coded), min/max transmit power, max advert length.

Healthy / typical values. On the author's PC: hci0, Bus usb 8-11:1.0, Driver btusb, USB ID 13d3:3617, "Realtek Bluetooth Radio" (the Bluetooth half of the RTL8922AE Wi-Fi 7 card), rfkill "soft-blocked no, hard-blocked no", Powered yes, Version 0x0c (12), roles central and peripheral, TX power -11 to 16 dBm.

Unusual values and what they suggest.

  • soft-blocked yes: aeroplane mode or a desktop toggle turned Bluetooth off; rfkill unblock bluetooth turns it on.
  • hard-blocked yes: a laptop switch or BIOS setting.
  • "No Bluetooth controllers in /sys/class/bluetooth": no adapter, it is disabled in BIOS, or firmware failed to load (check dmesg).
  • "bluetoothctl: no controllers reported": the hardware is there but bluetoothd (bluetooth.service) is not running.
  • Discoverable yes all the time: anyone nearby can see the PC. Fine at home, less so in public.

Where Linux gets it. /sys/class/bluetooth/hci*, bluetoothctl list and bluetoothctl show.

Background. rfkill is the kernel's on/off switch for every radio (Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, mobile). A UUID here is a standard number for a Bluetooth profile; the short ones (like 110b = Audio Sink) are defined by the Bluetooth SIG.

Bluetooth IDs

bluetooth-ids - Linux data

In plain words. The ID codes of your Bluetooth controller and of every device you have paired.

What you see.

Column Meaning
Device hci0 etc. for a controller, "paired device" for a known device.
Address "(controller)", or the device's Bluetooth address.
Name Device name.
Modalias / ID For a controller, usb:vVVVVpPPPPdDDDD (vendor, product, device release). For a device, its bluetooth: or usb: modalias, if it sends one.
Class / Icon The device class code and the icon name BlueZ picks (phone, audio-headset, input-mouse...).

A footer counts controllers and known devices.

Healthy / typical values. On the author's PC: hci0 with usb:v13D3p3617d0000, and one paired phone with class 0x005a020c and icon phone.

Unusual values and what they suggest. A device with Modalias "-" just did not send one (common for cheap devices). A long list of old devices you no longer own can be removed in your desktop's Bluetooth settings.

Where Linux gets it. /sys/class/bluetooth/<hci>/device/modalias, bluetoothctl devices, bluetoothctl info <address>. No discovery scan is run.

Background. A modalias is a short ID string the kernel uses to pick a driver automatically.

Bluetooth device tree

blue-tree - Linux data

In plain words. A simple tree: each controller, and under it the devices it knows, with their status.

What you see.

  • Controller lines from bluetoothctl list (address, name, [default] for the default one).
  • One branch per known device: name, address, icon (device type).
  • Under a device, its status words: paired, trusted, and CONNECTED if connected right now.

Healthy / typical values. On the author's PC: controller "MYPC [default]" with one phone, "paired trusted" (not connected at that moment).

Unusual values and what they suggest. Paired but not trusted means the device has to be confirmed each time it connects. "bluetoothd not answering; devices unknown" means the controller exists but the Bluetooth service is stopped. "No known devices" means nothing was ever paired.

Where Linux gets it. bluetoothctl list, bluetoothctl devices, bluetoothctl info.

Network browse masters

browsers - Linux data

In plain words. Which machine on your LAN keeps the list of Windows-style computers ("Network Neighbourhood"), and how your own Samba is set up to take part.

What you see.

  • nmbd - is Samba's NetBIOS name daemon running.
  • workgroup, local master, preferred master, domain master, os level - your Samba settings for the browser election (os level 0 means "never try to win").
  • A table of machines in nmbd's browse list that are Master Browsers: Name, Workgroup, Type (the server type bits: Workstation, Server, PrintQ, Unix, NT, NT Server, Potential/Backup/Master Browser, Domain Master, DC, Time, and others), Comment.

Healthy / typical values. On the author's PC nmbd is running, workgroup WORKGROUP, all master options No, os level 0. The master browser is the router (a GL.iNet GL-BE9300), with type "Workstation, Server, PrintQ, Unix, NT, NT Server, Master Browser, Domain Master".

Unusual values and what they suggest.

  • "browse list not present - nmbd is not running": Samba's name service is off, so there is no list. Normal on PCs that do not share files.
  • No master browser at all: Windows PCs may not see each other by name. Modern Windows uses WS-Discovery (Web Services Discovery) instead, so this matters less today.
  • Two machines both claiming Master Browser: an election fight, often from two Samba boxes both set to "preferred master = yes".

Where Linux gets it. testparm -s for settings, /var/cache/samba/browse.dat (nmbd's cached list). SRS sends no NetBIOS queries.

Background. NetBIOS browsing is the old Windows way to list computers. One machine per workgroup wins an election and becomes the master browser; others ask it for the list.

TCP/IP counters

counters - Linux data

In plain words. Live traffic rates for every adapter, then the kernel's protocol counters for IP, ICMP, TCP and UDP since boot.

What you see.

Rates table (refreshes every second in the window):

Column Meaning
Adapter Interface name.
Rx /s, Tx /s Bytes received / sent per second.
Rx pkt/s, Tx pkt/s Packets per second.
Rx total, Tx total Totals since the adapter came up.
State up, down, unknown.

The footer says how long the measuring window was ("rates over the last 0.50 s"). On first open in the window it says "rates appear after the next refresh". In a saved report SRS takes a half-second sample so the rates are real.

Then the /proc/net/snmp tables. Each has a heading (Ip, Icmp, IcmpMsg, Tcp, Udp, UdpLite) and one counter per line. Zero counters are greyed. Key ones:

  • Ip: Forwarding (1 = router mode on, 2 = off), DefaultTTL, InReceives, InHdrErrors, InDiscards, OutRequests, OutNoRoutes, fragment and reassembly counts.
  • Icmp / IcmpMsg: ping and error messages in and out (InType0 = echo reply, InType3 = destination unreachable, InType8 = echo request).
  • Tcp: ActiveOpens (connections you started), PassiveOpens (connections to your servers), AttemptFails, EstabResets, CurrEstab (open now), InSegs, OutSegs, RetransSegs (resent), InErrs, OutRsts.
  • Udp: InDatagrams, NoPorts (sent to a port nobody listens on), InErrors, RcvbufErrors and SndbufErrors (buffer full).

Healthy / typical values. On the author's PC, idle: em1 about 1.9 KB/s in and 1.2 KB/s out, 14.19 GB received since boot; lo about 1 KB/s each way. Tcp CurrEstab 19, RetransSegs 2,142 out of 3.8 million OutSegs (well under 1%). Udp RcvbufErrors 0.

Unusual values and what they suggest.

  • RetransSegs above about 1-2% of OutSegs: packet loss somewhere (Wi-Fi interference, bad cable, overloaded router).
  • InCsumErrors or InHdrErrors rising: damaged packets, often a bad cable or failing NIC.
  • Udp RcvbufErrors rising: a program cannot read fast enough (game servers, streaming); the receive buffer is too small.
  • Big AttemptFails compared with ActiveOpens: many connections refused or timed out, for example a blocked port or a dead server.
  • Ip Forwarding 1 on a desktop: normal if you run Docker or VMs, otherwise check why.

Where Linux gets it. /sys/class/net/<if>/statistics/ sampled twice, and /proc/net/snmp.

Background. TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) is the reliable, ordered connection used by web, SSH and most apps; lost pieces are resent. UDP (User Datagram Protocol) just fires packets with no resend, used by DNS, games and voice. ICMP (Internet Control Message Protocol) carries ping and error replies.

DNS cache

dns-cache - Linux data, Needs root data

In plain words. Is there a local DNS cache on this PC, and what is in it.

What you see.

  • One line per known caching program that is running, with its process ID: systemd-resolved, dnsmasq, nscd, unbound, named (BIND), kresd, dnscrypt-proxy, stubby, pdns_recursor, AdGuardHome. "none running" if none.
  • If systemd-resolved runs: the cache contents from resolvectl show-cache. That command is root-only, so without srs-root you get "Needs root: Menu > Run as root (srs-root)".
  • If systemd-resolved does not run: a note that glibc itself does not cache lookups, and that dnsmasq copies are often the ones libvirt or containers start for their own bridges.

Healthy / typical values. On the author's PC, dnsmasq running (pid ...) and systemd-resolved not running. Here dnsmasq is a real system cache: /etc/resolv.conf points at 127.0.0.1, where dnsmasq listens (see DNS ports). SRS lists cache contents only for systemd-resolved, so the dnsmasq cache itself is not shown.

Unusual values and what they suggest. Two different caches running at once (for example systemd-resolved and dnsmasq both on port 53) can fight; one usually fails to start. No cache at all is fine; lookups just go straight to your router or DNS provider each time.

Where Linux gets it. Process names in /proc/*/comm; resolvectl show-cache (root).

Background. A DNS cache remembers answers ("example.com is at ...") for their time-to-live, so repeated lookups are instant and work for a while even if the upstream server is slow.

DNS names

dns-names - Linux data

In plain words. All the names this computer and your user account go by.

What you see.

Row Meaning
NetBIOS Name Windows-network name (from Samba, or the host name in capitals, max 15 characters).
DNS Domain The PC's DNS domain, often empty at home.
DNS Host Name The host name.
Full DNS Name Host name plus domain (the FQDN, fully qualified domain name).

The two columns, Computer Name and Computer Physical Name, are the same on Linux (Windows can differ on clusters).

Then the user block:

  • Display Username - your login name.
  • Legacy Account Name - NETBIOSNAME\user, the Windows-style form.
  • Full Name (GECOS) - the real name stored in /etc/passwd (only if set).
  • User ID - your numeric UID.

Then /etc/hostname, and from hostnamectl: StaticHostname, PrettyHostname, Chassis (desktop, laptop, vm...), Deployment and Location, when set.

Healthy / typical values. On the author's PC: NetBIOS Name MYPC, no DNS domain, Full DNS Name MYPC, user user, legacy name MYPC\user, User ID 1000, Chassis desktop.

Unusual values and what they suggest. /etc/hostname different from DNS Host Name: the name was changed without a reboot, or something (DHCP, a VM tool) set a temporary name. A host name longer than 15 characters is cut short in the NetBIOS name, which can confuse Windows shares.

Where Linux gets it. gethostname(), getdomainname(), /etc/resolv.conf, testparm (netbios name), /etc/passwd, /etc/hostname, hostnamectl --json=short.

DNS ports

dns-ports - Linux data

In plain words. Every socket on a DNS-related port: local DNS servers listening, and your open connections to DNS servers.

What you see.

Column Meaning
Proto UDP, UDP6, TCP, TCP6.
Address The local address (for a listener) or the remote server address.
Port 53 (DNS), 853 (DNS over TLS), 5353 (mDNS), 5355 (LLMNR, Link-Local Multicast Name Resolution).
Service Name from /etc/services (domain, mdns...).
State Listen, Local, or "To server" (an outgoing query).
Process (PID) The program, if SRS can see it. Programs of other users (including root) show "-" unless you run srs-root.

Below that: the DNS servers from /etc/resolv.conf (each on port 53), resolver options, and whether systemd-resolved is running (its stub listens on 127.0.0.53).

Healthy / typical values. On the author's PC dnsmasq listens on 127.0.0.1:53 (UDP and TCP) and on the libvirt and retro-VM bridge addresses; avahi listens on 0.0.0.0:5353 (mDNS). resolv.conf lists 127.0.0.1 with options timeout:2 attempts:3.

Unusual values and what they suggest.

  • Something listening on port 53 on your LAN address (not 127.x or a VM bridge): your PC is acting as a DNS server for the network. Fine if intended.
  • resolv.conf points at 127.0.0.53 but systemd-resolved is "not running": DNS will fail.
  • Nothing listening on 127.0.0.1:53 while resolv.conf says 127.0.0.1: your local cache died, so names stop resolving.

Where Linux gets it. /proc/net/udp, udp6, tcp, tcp6, process sockets under /proc/*/fd, /etc/resolv.conf.

DNS usage

dns-usage - Linux data

In plain words. How name lookups are set up on this PC, or, with systemd-resolved, its lookup statistics.

What you see. If systemd-resolved runs, the output of resolvectl statistics: transactions, cache size, cache hits and misses, DNSSEC verdicts. Otherwise a note, then:

  • Name servers - how many are in resolv.conf.
  • Search list - domains tried after short names.
  • Resolver options - resolv.conf options (timeout, attempts, edns0...).
  • NSS hosts order - the hosts: line of /etc/nsswitch.conf, the order Linux tries: files (/etc/hosts), mdns, resolve, dns, myhostname, wins...
  • /etc/hosts entries - number of non-comment lines.
  • /etc/gai.conf - present, or absent (default IPv6-first rules).

Healthy / typical values. On the author's PC: 1 name server, no search list, timeout:2 attempts:3, NSS order mymachines mdns_minimal resolve files myhostname dns wins, 9 hosts entries, gai.conf present.

Unusual values and what they suggest. A huge /etc/hosts (thousands of lines from an ad blocker) slows every lookup because it is read top to bottom; a local DNS cache is faster for that. With resolved statistics, a low cache-hit rate is normal for browsing many new sites; many DNSSEC "bogus" verdicts suggest a broken upstream server or a clock that is far off.

Where Linux gets it. resolvectl statistics, /etc/resolv.conf, /etc/nsswitch.conf, /etc/hosts, /etc/gai.conf.

Background. NSS (Name Service Switch) is glibc's plug-in list that decides where names are looked up, and in what order.

Domains / workgroups

domains - Linux data

In plain words. Which Windows workgroup or domain, Kerberos realm and DNS domain this PC belongs to, plus the workgroups seen on your LAN.

What you see.

  • SMB workgroup - Samba's workgroup (WORKGROUP is the Windows default).
  • Kerberos realm - for Active Directory joins.
  • Samba security - USER (normal standalone), ADS (Active Directory member), etc.
  • NIS domain - old Unix network login domain, usually "-".
  • DNS domain, DNS search list - from resolv.conf.
  • AD/realmd join - "keytab present" if /etc/krb5.keytab exists (joined to a domain), else "not joined".
  • A table of domains/workgroups in nmbd's browse list: name, workgroup, type, comment (usually the master browser's name).

Healthy / typical values. On the author's PC: workgroup WORKGROUP, security USER, not joined; the LAN list shows WORKGROUP with type "NT, Domain Enum", led by the router.

Unusual values and what they suggest. A workgroup name different from your other PCs means they will not list each other in the old browse view. "keytab present" on a home PC is unusual and means it was once joined to a company domain.

Where Linux gets it. testparm (workgroup, realm, security), getdomainname(), /etc/resolv.conf, /etc/krb5.keytab, /var/cache/samba/browse.dat.

Firewall

firewall - Linux data, Needs root data

In plain words. Is the firewall running, and what each active zone allows in.

What you see.

  • firewalld state - running, not running, or "not installed".
  • Panic mode - "yes" means all traffic is being blocked.
  • Default zone - the zone new interfaces fall into.
  • One block per active zone (the heading says "(active)" and "(default)" where true). Each line is a zone setting that has a value: target (ACCEPT, default, %%REJECT%%, DROP), ingress/egress priority, icmp-block-inversion, interfaces, sources, services, ports, protocols, forward, masquerade, forward-ports, rich rules.
  • nftables ruleset - the raw kernel rules need root (nft list ruleset), so this line points you to srs-root.

Healthy / typical values. On the author's PC firewalld is running, panic mode no, default zone public (interfaces em1 and wlan0, services dhcpv6-client, kdeconnect, ssh). Extra zones exist for Docker (target ACCEPT), libvirt (dhcp, dns, ssh, tftp), a retro-VM bridge (target %%REJECT%% with only NFS (Network File System), Samba and AFP (Apple Filing Protocol) allowed) and a trusted zone for Waydroid.

Unusual values and what they suggest.

  • Your LAN interfaces in zone trusted or a zone with target ACCEPT: everything is allowed in. Fine for VM bridges, risky for the adapter that faces the internet or a public Wi-Fi.
  • Services open that you do not use (ssh, samba, cockpit): close them to reduce what others can reach.
  • "not installed": you may use plain nftables, ufw, or no firewall at all. Check with root.
  • Panic mode yes: someone ran firewall-cmd --panic-on; the network will look dead.

Where Linux gets it. firewall-cmd --state, --query-panic, --list-all-zones (read-only queries); nft list ruleset needs root.

Background. firewalld groups rules into zones. Each network interface belongs to one zone, and the zone decides which incoming services are allowed. Masquerade is NAT (network address translation): sharing one address for many devices behind it.

Network interface statistics

interface - Linux data

In plain words. The kernel's error and traffic counters for every adapter since it came up.

What you see.

Column Meaning
Interface Name.
Rx Bytes / Rx Packets Received data and packets.
Rx Err Received frames with errors (bad checksum, wrong length).
Rx Drop Received but thrown away (no room in the queue, or unwanted traffic).
Tx Bytes / Tx Packets Sent.
Tx Err / Tx Drop Failed or dropped sends.
Multicast Multicast packets received.
Collisions Half-duplex collisions; should be 0 on modern full-duplex links.
Carrier chg How many times the link went up or down.

Healthy / typical values. On the author's PC em1 shows 14.19 GB and 11.8 million packets in, 0 errors, 0 drops, Carrier chg 2 (link came up at boot). Bridges with no members show some Tx Drop (711 on one bridge), which is harmless: packets sent to an empty bridge go nowhere.

Unusual values and what they suggest.

  • Rx Err rising on a wired port: bad cable, bad connector, or electrical noise. Try another cable or port.
  • Collisions above 0: the link fell back to half duplex; usually an auto-negotiation problem with an old switch.
  • Carrier chg climbing while you watch: the link keeps dropping. Loose cable, power-saving (EEE, Energy-Efficient Ethernet), or a flaky driver.
  • Rx Drop on a busy server: the receive ring is too small or the CPU is too slow to keep up.

Where Linux gets it. /sys/class/net/<if>/statistics/* and carrier_changes (the same numbers as /proc/net/dev and ip -s link).

IP address

ip-address - Linux data

In plain words. Every IP address on every adapter, with its scope, flags and lifetime.

What you see.

Column Meaning
Adapter Interface name ("(no addresses)" if it has none).
Address IPv4 or IPv6 address.
Prefix Prefix length, such as /24 or /64.
Scope host (only this PC, like 127.0.0.1), link (only this cable/Wi-Fi, like fe80::), global (routable).
Flags dynamic (from DHCP or SLAAC, stateless address autoconfiguration, where IPv6 builds its own address from router adverts), noprefixroute, temporary (privacy address), stable-privacy, tentative, deprecated, dadfailed, mngtmpaddr... "-" if none.
Lifetime (valid/preferred) Seconds until the lease runs out (valid) and until it stops being used for new connections (preferred), or "forever".

Open one adapter with ip-address:<name>.

Healthy / typical values. On the author's PC em1 has 192.168.1.20 /24 global dynamic noprefixroute with about 37,900 seconds left (a 12-hour DHCP lease), and a link-local fe80::XXXX /64 lasting forever. VM bridges have static addresses lasting forever.

Unusual values and what they suggest. A lifetime counting down to near 0 without renewing means DHCP renewals are failing. dadfailed means address conflict. No global IPv6 address while your provider supports IPv6: the router is not sending router advertisements, or IPv6 is off.

Where Linux gets it. ip -o addr show.

Background. A DHCP lease is an address the router lends you for a set time. Your PC renews it halfway through. Link-local addresses (fe80:: for IPv6, 169.254. for IPv4) only work on the local segment and are made automatically.

LAN Manager share setup

lm-setup - Linux data

In plain words. Your Samba (Windows file sharing) configuration, as Samba itself reads it.

What you see. The effective smb.conf from testparm -s, section by section:

  • [global] - server-wide settings: workgroup, server string, security, interfaces and bind interfaces only, hosts allow/deny, min/max protocol, map to guest, logging, printing, usershare limits, wins support, idmap.
  • One section per share ([homes], [printers], and your own shares) - path, comment, read only, guest ok, guest only, force user, valid users, create mask, directory mask, inherit acls, printable.

Only settings that differ from the defaults are printed. Values of any setting whose name contains TOKEN, KEY, SECRET, PASS, AUTH, COOKIE or PSK are hidden as **** (except plain Yes/No).

Healthy / typical values. On the author's PC: security USER, standalone server, minimum protocol SMB2 for client and server, Samba bound only to lo and the home subnet, hosts allow limited to the LAN and 127.0.0.1, hosts deny = 0.0.0.0/0. Shares include [homes], several file shares and a printer.

Unusual values and what they suggest.

  • guest ok = Yes with read only = No: anyone on the network can write there without a password. Only safe on a trusted LAN with hosts allow set.
  • A share with path = /: the whole disk is shared. Limit with valid users or remove it if not needed.
  • server min protocol = NT1 (SMB1): very old and insecure protocol; only enable for retro machines that need it.
  • "Samba is not installed or smb.conf is unreadable": no Samba, nothing shared this way.

Where Linux gets it. testparm -s --suppress-prompt (reads /etc/samba/smb.conf).

Background. SMB (Server Message Block) is the Windows file-sharing protocol; Samba is its Linux implementation. "LAN Manager" is the old name from the 1980s Microsoft/IBM network software.

MAC addresses

mac-address - Linux data

In plain words. The hardware address of every adapter, whether it is the factory one, and which company made the chip.

What you see.

Column Meaning
Adapter Interface name.
MAC Address The address in use now.
Permanent The factory address burned into the card (physical adapters only, from ethtool -P), "-" for virtual ones.
Assigned How the current address was set: permanent (factory), random (made up at start), stolen (copied from another device, as bonds do), set by user (changed by software or NetworkManager).
Broadcast The link broadcast address (ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff on Ethernet and Wi-Fi).
Vendor (OUI) Maker looked up from the first half of the address, or "(locally administered)" for made-up addresses.

Healthy / typical values. On the author's PC the wired port is "permanent" with vendor ASUSTek (the motherboard maker), the Wi-Fi card shows AzureWave Technology (the module maker), the USB adapter shows Realtek, VMware adapters show VMware, and bridges, TAP, Docker and veth are "(locally administered)" with "set by user". lo is all zeros.

Unusual values and what they suggest.

  • Wi-Fi with Assigned "random" or "set by user" and a current address different from Permanent: MAC randomisation is on (a privacy feature). Normal, but your router will see a "new device" per network.
  • Two adapters with the same MAC on one network: they will fight; usually a cloned VM.
  • A vendor that does not match the card you bought: the card was rebranded, or the address was changed.

Where Linux gets it. /sys/class/net/<if>/address, addr_assign_type, broadcast; ethtool -P; vendor from /usr/share/hwdata/oui.txt.

Background. A MAC address (Media Access Control) is the 6-byte hardware address used on the local network. The first three bytes are the OUI (Organizationally Unique Identifier), bought by the maker. If the second-lowest bit of the first byte is set, the address is locally administered: made up by software, not by a factory.

Modem API

modem-api - Not present on most PCs

In plain words. On Windows this lists the telephony (TAPI) modem interface. Linux has no such API; SRS shows what ModemManager knows instead. The page title reads "Modems" because it shares its output with the next item.

What you see. Either the mmcli -L list of modems (mobile broadband sticks, built-in LTE/5G modules), or "ModemManager reports no modems", or "ModemManager (mmcli) not available".

Healthy / typical values. On the author's PC: "ModemManager reports no modems". This is normal for any desktop without a mobile data module.

Where Linux gets it. mmcli -L (ModemManager).

Modems

modems - Not present on most PCs

In plain words. Mobile broadband modems (4G/5G USB sticks, built-in WWAN (wireless wide area network) cards) known to ModemManager.

What you see. Each modem line from mmcli -L (its path, maker and model), or "ModemManager reports no modems" / "ModemManager (mmcli) not available". Old serial dial-up modems are not listed; Linux has no general way to enumerate those.

Healthy / typical values. "ModemManager reports no modems" on a desktop. That just means there is no mobile modem, not that anything is wrong.

Unusual values and what they suggest. A laptop with a WWAN card that shows no modem: the card may be disabled in BIOS, rfkill-blocked, or need a firmware unlock (FCC lock) before ModemManager will use it.

Where Linux gets it. mmcli -L (ModemManager).

My browser / IP location

my-browser - Linux data

In plain words. Which web browser opens your links. The Windows version also looks up your public IP's location online; SRS does not, because it makes no internet requests.

What you see.

  • Default web browser - from xdg-settings (a .desktop file name).
  • https handler - the app registered for https: links (xdg-mime).
  • $BROWSER - the BROWSER environment variable, used by many terminal programs.
  • IP geolocation - always "not looked up - srs makes no internet requests".

Healthy / typical values. On the author's PC the default browser and https handler are the same Floorp .desktop file, while $BROWSER is set to a different browser (firedragon).

Unusual values and what they suggest. Default browser and https handler disagree: some apps open links in one browser and some in the other. Fix it in your desktop's Default Applications settings. A $BROWSER that differs, as here, only affects programs that read that variable.

Where Linux gets it. xdg-settings get default-web-browser, xdg-mime query default x-scheme-handler/https, the environment.

My IP address

my-ip-address - Linux data

In plain words. The address your PC uses when it talks to the outside world, and all your routable addresses.

What you see.

  • Outgoing IPv4 source - the address the kernel would use for a packet to the internet. SRS finds this with a route lookup for the documentation address 192.0.2.1; nothing is sent.
  • Default gateway - your router address and the adapter it is reached through.
  • Public (WAN) address - "not looked up - srs makes no internet requests". Your router's status page or any "what is my IP" site shows it. WAN (wide area network) means the internet side of your router.
  • Global-scope addresses - every global address per adapter, with prefix and flags.

Healthy / typical values. On the author's PC: outgoing source 192.168.1.20 (the wired port), gateway 192.168.1.1 dev em1, and global addresses on em1, wlan0 and the VM/Docker bridges.

Unusual values and what they suggest. Outgoing source is the Wi-Fi address while a cable is plugged in: the Wi-Fi route has the better metric, so traffic goes over the slower link. Outgoing source on a VPN (virtual private network) interface (tun0, wg0): all traffic goes through the VPN, as intended for a full-tunnel VPN. "-" means no route to the internet.

Where Linux gets it. ip -o route get 192.0.2.1, /proc/net/route, ip -o addr show.

Background. At home your PC has a private address (192.168.x.x, 10.x, 172.16-31.x). The router swaps it for your one public address on the way out (NAT), so websites never see the private one.

Network cards

net-cards - Linux data

In plain words. The physical network hardware: chip name, bus slot, IDs, driver, firmware and link details. Virtual adapters are left out (see Network adapters).

What you see. One block per physical adapter:

  • Description - PCI device name, or USB maker and product.
  • Bus - pci with the slot address, or usb with the port path.
  • PCI ID - vendor:device and subsystem vendor:device (PCI cards). The subsystem tells you the board maker.
  • PCIe link - lane count and speed the card is running at now.
  • USB ID - vendor:product and the USB link speed in Mbps (USB adapters).
  • Driver, Driver version, Firmware, Expansion ROM (if the card has a boot ROM) - from ethtool -i.
  • MAC address.
  • Link - state; when up, also speed and duplex.
  • MTU - with the transmit queue length.
  • Wireless PHY - for Wi-Fi cards, the radio name (phy0...).

Open one card with net-cards:<name>.

Healthy / typical values. On the author's PC:

  • em1: Realtek RTL8126 5GbE, PCI ID 10ec:8126, subsystem 1043 (ASUS), PCIe link x1 8.0 GT/s, driver r8169, firmware rtl8126a-3, link up 2.5 Gbps full duplex, MTU 1500.
  • wlan0: Realtek RTL8922AE Wi-Fi 7, PCIe x1 5.0 GT/s, driver rtw89_8922ae, firmware 0.35.80.3, Wireless PHY phy0.
  • enp115s0u2u4u4: a Realtek USB gigabit adapter (0bda:8153, driver r8152) on a 5000 Mbps USB port, link down.

Unusual values and what they suggest.

  • A 5 GbE card linked at 2.5 Gbps: the switch or router port is only 2.5 GbE (as here), or the cable is Cat5. Not a fault.
  • PCIe link slower than the card supports (for example 2.5 GT/s on a 10 GbE card): slot shares lanes or is set to an older PCIe generation in BIOS. Can cap throughput on fast cards.
  • A USB adapter on a 480 Mbps (USB 2) port: a gigabit adapter will top out around 300 Mbps. Move it to a blue/USB 3 port.
  • Half duplex on a modern link: auto-negotiation failed. Check the cable and switch.
  • Firmware missing or very old: some features (and bug fixes) need the linux-firmware package updated.

Where Linux gets it. /sys/class/net/<if>/device/ (vendor, device, subsystem IDs, current_link_width, current_link_speed), lspci -nn, ethtool -i.

Background. Duplex is whether both ends can send at the same time (full) or must take turns (half). MTU (Maximum Transmission Unit) is the biggest packet the link carries, 1500 bytes on normal Ethernet.

Network provider names

net-names - Windows-only (Linux equivalent shown)

In plain words. On Windows this lists "network providers" (the plug-ins that let Explorer open \\server\share paths). Linux has no such list, so SRS shows the network file-system tools installed and the network shares mounted right now.

What you see.

  • Network providers available - which client tools exist: Samba client (smbclient), CIFS kernel mounts (mount.cifs), NFS client, SSHFS, GVfs SMB, KIO (KDE's smb:/ sftp:/ fish:/), CUPS network printing (lpstat). Each with its path.
  • Mounted network file systems - source, mount point, and type for every cifs, smb3, nfs, nfs4, fuse.sshfs, 9p, davfs, fuse.rclone, fuse.gvfsd-fuse, ceph or glusterfs mount. Any user:password in a source is masked.

Healthy / typical values. On the author's PC all seven tools are present, and three network mounts are active: an NFS4 share, GVfs's FUSE mount at /run/user/1000/gvfs, and a CIFS mount of the router's USB disk.

Unusual values and what they suggest. A network mount you did not expect: something (fstab, a file manager, an automounter) mounted it. A mount whose server is gone can make file managers and df hang. "none mounted" is normal.

Where Linux gets it. Tool paths on disk; /proc/self/mounts.

Network

network - Linux data

In plain words. The one-page summary of your networking: host name, adapters, gateway, DNS, forwarding and TCP tuning, then one line per adapter.

What you see.

  • Host name.
  • Adapters - total, how many physical and virtual, and how many are up (state "up" or "unknown"; loopback and some virtual adapters always report "unknown").
  • IPv4 default gateway - router address and adapter.
  • IPv6 default route - or "none".
  • DNS servers - from /etc/resolv.conf.
  • DNS search - if set.
  • IP forwarding - on/off for IPv4 and IPv6.
  • TCP congestion control - the algorithm that decides how fast TCP sends (cubic, bbr, bbr3...).
  • Default qdisc - the default queueing discipline (fq, fq_codel, pfifo_fast...).

Then a table: Adapter, Type, State, Speed, MAC Address, IPv4 (all addresses with prefix), Driver. The last line names the motherboard maker, model, BIOS version and BIOS date (for example "ASUSTeK COMPUTER INC. TUF GAMING X870-PRO WIFI7 W NEO BIOS 1805").

Healthy / typical values. On the author's PC: host MYPC, "11 (3 physical, 8 virtual), 7 up", gateway 192.168.1.1 dev em1, no IPv6 default route, DNS 127.0.0.1 (a local dnsmasq), IPv4 forwarding on (needed by Docker and VMs), TCP congestion control bbr3, default qdisc fq.

Unusual values and what they suggest.

  • IPv4 default gateway "none": no internet route. Check the cable/Wi-Fi and DHCP.
  • IPv6 default route "none" while your provider offers IPv6: router advertisements are not arriving or IPv6 is disabled on the router.
  • DNS servers "none": names will not resolve at all.
  • BBR with a qdisc other than fq on older kernels: BBR worked best with fq pacing; modern kernels pace internally, so this matters less now.

Where Linux gets it. /sys/class/net, ip -o addr show, /proc/net/route, ip -o -6 route show default, /etc/resolv.conf, /proc/sys/net/ipv4/ip_forward, /proc/sys/net/ipv6/conf/all/forwarding, /proc/sys/net/ipv4/tcp_congestion_control, /proc/sys/net/core/default_qdisc.

Background. Congestion control is how TCP guesses the safe sending speed. Classic algorithms (cubic) slow down when packets are lost; BBR measures bandwidth and delay instead and often does better on lossy or long links. A qdisc (queueing discipline) is the kernel's waiting line for outgoing packets; fq (fair queue) shares the link fairly between connections.

Network profiles

profiles - Linux data

In plain words. Every connection NetworkManager has saved: wired, Wi-Fi, VPN, bridges, Bluetooth tethering.

What you see.

Column Meaning
Profile The connection name. For Wi-Fi this is usually the network name.
Type 802-3-ethernet (wired), 802-11-wireless (Wi-Fi), vpn, wireguard, bridge, tun, loopback, bluetooth, gsm...
Device The adapter using it now, or "-" if not active.
Auto Does it connect automatically.
Last used When it was last activated, or "never".
UUID The profile's unique ID, used by nmcli connection up <uuid>.

Healthy / typical values. On the author's PC: "Wired connection 3" on em1, the home Wi-Fi profile on wlan0, profiles for lo and two bridges and a TAP device, plus inactive ones: older wired profiles, two other Wi-Fi networks, a VPN profile, and a Bluetooth phone-tethering profile.

Unusual values and what they suggest. Several "Wired connection N" profiles for one port: NetworkManager made a new one each time the adapter or its MAC changed; the old ones can be deleted. A Wi-Fi profile with Auto yes for a public network you no longer visit: your PC will join it whenever it sees that name. Remove it.

Where Linux gets it. nmcli -t connection show.

Network protocols

protocols - Linux data

In plain words. The socket types the kernel has loaded right now, how many sockets of each are open, and how much memory they use.

What you see.

Column Meaning
Protocol TCP, UDP, TCPv6, UDPv6, UNIX, UNIX-STREAM, NETLINK, PACKET, RAW, PING, MPTCP, XDP, MCTP, Bluetooth ones (HCI, L2CAP, SCO, RFCOMM, BNEP), ALG (kernel crypto), and others.
Size Bytes per socket structure in the kernel.
Sockets Number open now.
Memory Memory pages used by this protocol's buffers (-1 = not tracked).
Press Memory pressure: "no" (fine), "yes" (the kernel is limiting buffers), "NI" (not implemented for this protocol).
Module Kernel module that provides it ("kernel" if built in).

A footer counts the protocols and the IP protocol numbers defined in /etc/protocols.

Healthy / typical values. On the author's PC 22 protocols: about 1,500 UNIX-STREAM sockets (normal for a desktop; apps talk to each other this way), 50 TCP, 53 UDP, 88 NETLINK, and Press "no" for TCP.

Unusual values and what they suggest. Press "yes" for TCP: the system is short of socket memory, often a server with very many connections; raise net.ipv4.tcp_mem. Thousands of TCP sockets on a desktop: a program is leaking connections.

Where Linux gets it. /proc/net/protocols; /etc/protocols.

Background. A socket is a program's handle for one network conversation (or local channel). Netlink sockets are how tools like ip talk to the kernel; UNIX sockets are local-only pipes between programs.

Proxy config

proxy - Linux data

In plain words. Whether apps are told to send web traffic through a proxy server, and where that setting comes from.

What you see. Three or four blocks:

  • Environment (this process) - http_proxy, https_proxy, ftp_proxy, all_proxy, no_proxy (both lower and upper case), or "none set (direct connection)".
  • /etc/environment - any proxy lines there, or "none".
  • KDE (kioslaverc [Proxy Settings]) - ProxyType (No proxy, Manual, PAC script, WPAD auto-detect, System environment) and the other keys in that section, such as httpProxy and NoProxyFor. Secret-looking keys are hidden.
  • GNOME proxy mode - from gsettings, if available ('none', 'manual', 'auto').

Any user:password@ in a proxy URL is shown as ****.

Healthy / typical values. On the author's PC: no environment proxy, none in /etc/environment, KDE ProxyType "No proxy" (an old httpProxy value of http://127.0.0.1:9099 is still stored but unused), GNOME mode 'none'.

Unusual values and what they suggest. A proxy set that you did not configure: some VPN or "privacy" tools, and some malware, set one to route your traffic. A proxy in KDE but not in the environment means KDE apps use it while terminal tools and many other apps do not.

Where Linux gets it. The process environment, /etc/environment, ~/.config/kioslaverc, gsettings get org.gnome.system.proxy mode.

Background. A proxy is a middle server that makes web requests for you. A PAC (proxy auto-config) script picks the proxy per address; WPAD finds that script automatically.

Routing table

routing - Linux data

In plain words. The kernel's map of "to reach this network, go this way".

What you see. First, whether IPv4 routing (forwarding between adapters) is Enabled or Disabled. Then the IPv4 table:

Column Meaning
Destination Network address, or "default" for everything else.
Netmask Which part is the network (255.255.255.0 = /24).
Gateway Next router to hand packets to, or "on-link" (the destination is directly on that adapter).
Flags U = route is up, G = uses a gateway, H = route to a single host, ! = reject route.
Metric Cost; when two routes match, the lower metric wins.
MTU Per-route MTU, "-" if not set.
Adapter Interface used.

Then IPv6 routes: each line of ip -6 route show table all as text. Normal routes are coloured; local and multicast housekeeping routes are greyed.

Healthy / typical values. On the author's PC: two default routes via 192.168.1.1, one on em1 with metric 100 and one on wlan0 with metric 600, so the wired port wins. On-link routes for the home subnet and each VM/Docker bridge. IPv6 shows only link-local fe80::/64 routes (no IPv6 internet).

Unusual values and what they suggest.

  • No "default" line: no internet access, only local networks.
  • Two default routes with the same metric: traffic may flip between adapters.
  • A default route on a VPN adapter (tun0, wg0): all traffic goes through the VPN.
  • Two routes for the same subnet on different adapters (for example a VM bridge reusing your home subnet): local traffic can go to the wrong place.

Where Linux gets it. /proc/net/route, /proc/sys/net/ipv4/ip_forward, ip -o -6 route show table all.

Background. A gateway is the router that forwards your packets to other networks. A metric is a priority number: NetworkManager gives wired links 100 and Wi-Fi 600 so cables are preferred.

Servers

servers - Linux data

In plain words. Every service on this PC that is waiting for incoming connections, and the SMB (Windows sharing) servers seen on your LAN.

What you see.

Local listening services:

Column Meaning
Proto TCP, TCP6, UDP, UDP6.
Bound Address 0.0.0.0 or :: = all addresses (reachable from the network, unless the firewall blocks it); 127.0.0.1 or ::1 = this PC only (greyed); a specific address = only that adapter.
Port Port number.
Service Standard name from /etc/services, blank if none.
Process (PID) The program, if visible. Other users' programs show "-" unless you run srs-root.

SMB servers seen on the LAN: Name, Workgroup, Type and Comment from nmbd's browse list (see Network browse masters).

Healthy / typical values. On the author's PC, a fairly busy home server: ssh (22), dnsmasq (53), rpcbind (111), Samba (139, 445), AFP (548) for retro Macs, CUPS printing (631), NFS (2049, mountd 20048), WS-Discovery (5357), syncthing on 127.0.0.1:8384, and a few local helpers. The router shows up as an SMB server.

Unusual values and what they suggest.

  • A service on 0.0.0.0 you did not know about: it is reachable from your network. Check what it is and whether the firewall blocks it.
  • A database or admin panel on 0.0.0.0 instead of 127.0.0.1: often a misconfiguration.
  • Note that /etc/services names are just the registered meaning of the number, not the real program. Port 2049 shows as "shilp" but is NFS, and 8080 is labelled "http-alt" whatever runs there.

Where Linux gets it. /proc/net/tcp, tcp6, udp, udp6 (listening sockets), /proc/*/fd for owners, /var/cache/samba/browse.dat.

Background. A port is a number (0-65535) that picks which program on a machine gets a packet. A listening socket is a program waiting for others to connect.

TCP V4 ports

tcp-ip4-ports - Linux data

In plain words. Every IPv4 TCP socket: servers waiting for connections and every open connection, with the program that owns it.

What you see.

Column Meaning
Local Address / Port / Service Your side of the socket.
Remote Address / Port / Service The other side; 0.0.0.0 * for a listener.
State Listen, Established, SYN Sent, SYN Received, FIN Wait 1, FIN Wait 2, Time Wait, Closed, Close Wait, Last ACK, Closing, New SYN Recv.
User Account that owns the socket.
Process (PID) Program and process ID; "-" for other users' programs without root; "(kernel/time-wait)" for sockets no program owns any more.

Listeners are listed first, sorted by port. The footer counts sockets, listening and other.

Healthy / typical values. On the author's PC 51 sockets: 38 listening, 13 other. For example 127.0.0.1 8384 ... Listen user syncthing (18116) and outgoing https (443) connections in state Established, plus a few in Time Wait.

Unusual values and what they suggest.

  • Many Close Wait sockets for one program: that program is not closing connections (a bug); it will slowly run out of sockets.
  • Hundreds of Time Wait: normal on a busy web client or server; they clear after about a minute.
  • Many SYN Received from different addresses: someone is flooding your server (SYN flood).
  • An Established connection to an address you do not recognise, owned by an unknown program: worth looking up.

Where Linux gets it. /proc/net/tcp; owners from /proc/<pid>/fd socket links.

Background. TCP connections go through states: a client sends SYN, the server answers, and the connection is Established. Closing passes through FIN Wait / Close Wait, and the side that closes first waits in Time Wait so late packets are not mistaken for a new connection.

TCP V6 ports

tcp-ip6-ports - Linux data

In plain words. The same as TCP V4 ports but for IPv6 TCP sockets.

What you see. The same columns and states as TCP V4 ports, with IPv6 addresses. :: means "all addresses", ::1 is this PC only. Addresses like ::ffff:192.168.1.20 are IPv4 connections accepted by an IPv6 socket (IPv4-mapped addresses).

Healthy / typical values. On the author's PC 30 sockets: 23 listening, 7 other. For example KDE Connect (kdeconnectd) listening on :: 1716 and connected to a phone over an IPv4-mapped address, syncthing on 22000, and CoolerControl talking to its daemon on ::1.

Unusual values and what they suggest. As for TCP V4. Also, a service listening only on :: may still accept IPv4 through mapped addresses, so it can be more reachable than it looks.

Where Linux gets it. /proc/net/tcp6; owners from /proc/<pid>/fd.

Network transports

transports - Linux data

In plain words. A count of sockets in use per transport type, and which address families have socket tables. Windows lists NetBIOS transport bindings here; Linux has none.

What you see.

  • From /proc/net/sockstat and sockstat6: sockets used, TCP (inuse, orphan, tw = time-wait, alloc, mem), UDP, UDPLITE, RAW, FRAG (packets being reassembled), and the IPv6 versions.
  • Address families with registered sockets - which of unix, packet, netlink, raw, tcp, udp, icmp, sctp, bluetooth, can, vsock, xdp and others have a table in /proc/net.
  • A note that SMB/NetBIOS on Linux simply runs over TCP 139/445 and UDP 137/138.

Healthy / typical values. On the author's PC: 1,937 sockets used, TCP inuse 50, orphan 0, tw 1, UDP inuse 53, FRAG inuse 0.

Unusual values and what they suggest. A large TCP "orphan" count: connections closed by programs but not yet finished in the kernel; many orphans can mean a DoS (denial-of-service) attack or a buggy server. TCP mem near the limit: see Press in Network protocols.

Where Linux gets it. /proc/net/sockstat, /proc/net/sockstat6, the /proc/net directory.

UDP V4 ports

udp-ip4-ports - Linux data

In plain words. Every IPv4 UDP socket, with its owner.

What you see. The same columns as TCP V4 ports. UDP has no real connection, so State is "Listen" (bound and waiting) or "Connected" (fixed to one remote address).

Healthy / typical values. On the author's PC 53 sockets, 51 listening: dnsmasq (53), DHCP server (67, bootps) for the VM bridges, rpcbind (111), Samba's NetBIOS name and datagram services (137, 138) on each address including broadcast addresses, WS-Discovery (3702) on each address plus the multicast group 239.255.255.250, avahi mDNS (5353), and syncthing discovery (21027).

Unusual values and what they suggest. A program listening on 0.0.0.0 with a port you do not recognise. Games and voice apps open random high ports while running; that is normal. Port 1900 (SSDP) or 5353 bound by many apps is also normal.

Where Linux gets it. /proc/net/udp; owners from /proc/<pid>/fd.

UDP V6 ports

udp-ip6-ports - Linux data

In plain words. The same as UDP V4 ports but for IPv6 UDP sockets.

What you see. The same columns. Addresses starting ff02:: are IPv6 multicast groups (for example ff02::c for WS-Discovery); fe80:: addresses are link-local, one per adapter.

Healthy / typical values. On the author's PC 29 sockets, all listening: wsdd on each adapter's link-local address and ff02::c, avahi on :: 5353, KDE Connect on 1716, syncthing on 21027 and 22000.

Unusual values and what they suggest. As for UDP V4.

Where Linux gets it. /proc/net/udp6; owners from /proc/<pid>/fd.

Wi-Fi SSIDs

wi-fi - Linux data

In plain words. Your Wi-Fi card's current connection (channel, signal, speed), and the networks NetworkManager last saw. SRS never starts a new scan.

What you see. Per wireless adapter, from iw dev <if> info:

  • addr - its MAC address. ssid - the network it is on. type - managed (normal client), AP, monitor... wiphy - radio number. channel - channel number, frequency, width. txpower - transmit power.

Then from iw dev <if> link:

  • Connected to - the access point's address, or Link: Not connected.
  • SSID, freq - network and frequency in MHz.
  • RX / TX - bytes and packets on this link.
  • signal - received strength in dBm.
  • rx bitrate / tx bitrate - the current data rate and how it is built: width, standard (HT = Wi-Fi 4, VHT = Wi-Fi 5, HE = Wi-Fi 6, EHT = Wi-Fi 7), MCS (coding level), NSS (number of spatial streams), GI (guard interval).
  • bss flags, dtim period, beacon int - access point timing details.
  • On Wi-Fi 7 multi-link connections, extra Link and MLD lines per link.

Then /proc/net/wireless - the old wireless-extensions quality line (many modern drivers leave it empty, giving "no associated interfaces").

Then Visible networks from NetworkManager's cache:

Column Meaning
(first) * = the one you are on.
SSID Network name, "(hidden)" if it does not broadcast one.
BSSID The access point's radio address.
Chan, Band Channel and band: 2.4 GHz, 5 GHz or 6 GHz.
Rate Max rate NetworkManager reports.
Signal, Bars Strength in percent (green 60% and up, orange 30-59%, red below 30%) and as bars.
Security WPA2, WPA3, WPA1, "open"...

Healthy / typical values. On the author's PC wlan0 (Wi-Fi 7 card) is on channel 36, 5180 MHz, 160 MHz wide, txpower 20 dBm, signal -28 dBm (excellent; the router is close), tx bitrate 2882.3 MBit/s using EHT-MCS 13 with 2 streams, security WPA3, 92%. The rx bitrate was only 6 MBit/s because the link was idle at that moment; it rises with traffic.

Unusual values and what they suggest.

  • Signal weaker than about -70 dBm: slow and unstable. Move closer, or use 5 GHz only where coverage is good.
  • Connected on 2.4 GHz with a 5/6 GHz-capable router nearby: slower; the bands may share one name and the PC chose the far-reaching one.
  • 20 MHz channel width on 5 GHz: the router or regulatory setting is limiting width.
  • Security "open" or WPA1 on your own network: change it to WPA2 or WPA3.
  • "NetworkManager has no cached scan results": no scan has happened yet; open your Wi-Fi menu to trigger one.

Where Linux gets it. iw dev <if> info, iw dev <if> link, /proc/net/wireless, nmcli device wifi list --rescan no.

Background. SSID (Service Set Identifier) is the network name; BSSID is the radio address of one access point. dBm is signal power on a log scale: -30 is excellent, -67 is good for video calls, -80 is barely usable. MCS (Modulation and Coding Scheme) is the encoding step; higher means faster but needs a cleaner signal.

WLAN profiles

wlan - Linux data, Needs root data

In plain words. The saved Wi-Fi networks only, with their name, mode and type of security. Passwords are never shown.

What you see. The same columns as Network profiles, but the last column is SSID / Security / IPv4: the network name, then in brackets the mode (infrastructure = normal router, adhoc, ap = hotspot), the key management (none/open, wpa-psk = WPA2 password, sae = WPA3 password, wpa-eap = enterprise login, owe = enhanced open), and the IPv4 method (auto = DHCP, manual, shared, disabled).

The footer says keys are never shown: reading them needs root or a secret agent, and SRS does not ask for them.

Healthy / typical values. On the author's PC three saved Wi-Fi networks: the home network ([infrastructure, sae, ipv4 auto], WPA3), a university profile (wpa-eap, enterprise login), and one more WPA3 network last used weeks ago.

Unusual values and what they suggest. A saved network with security "open" and Auto yes: your PC will join any network that copies that name, which is how fake hotspots work. Profiles from long ago can be deleted. wpa-psk (WPA2) on your own router is fine, but switch to sae (WPA3) if all your devices support it.

Where Linux gets it. nmcli connection show and nmcli connection show <uuid> (ssid, mode, key-mgmt, ipv4.method). Full profiles, including secrets, live in /etc/NetworkManager/system-connections, which is root-only.

Background. WPA2 and WPA3 are Wi-Fi security standards. WPA3's SAE (Simultaneous Authentication of Equals) protects the password even if someone records your traffic.

Linux (SIV's Windows items) (SRS Section Reference)

Back to the section index - Glossary

Where to find these items (SRS 2.0). In the main window they are on the Operating system page (Alt+-). Its first tab is General Info (SIV's "Windows" panel; the classic Linux button), then Drivers, Processes, Startup programs, Installed software, Environment and Users; All N items lists the rest. You can also type an item's name or id into the search box (Ctrl+F). The rest of this introduction describes the classic view (Menu -> Classic View), with its Menu and panel buttons.

This group holds the items that SIV64X (System Information Viewer, by Ray Hinchliffe, RH Software) files under "Windows": the operating system itself, its services, drivers, users, memory, time, fonts, languages and crash handling. SRS (srs-sysinfo) is an independent Linux program. It is not affiliated with or endorsed by RH Software and contains no SIV code or data. Most Windows ideas have a close Linux twin, so each item shows that twin: services become systemd units, drivers become kernel modules, the registry becomes the files in /etc and ~/.config, and Windows Error Reporting (WER) becomes coredumpctl. Open an item with Menu -> Linux (SIV Windows items) -> item, or press the Linux button in the classic main window (SIV's "Windows" button). That button opens the overview panel; its sub-buttons are Machine, Sensors, USB Bus, Processors, Volumes, PCI Bus, ALL Dev and Graphics. Only Open server files needs root data from the srs-root helper (Menu -> Run as root) to be complete; Sessions and Product IDs each have one line that also fills in only after srs-root has run.

How to read the saved text. In a saved report (sysreport-search '-save=[id]'), [=] is a ticked box and [_] is an empty box. The GUI draws them as real check boxes. Some items take an argument after a colon, such as driver-vsn:amdgpu. You can type that form in the GUI or save it from the command line, for example sysreport-search '-save=[signing:amdgpu]'.

"This process" items. Several items (Environment, the DLL items, Process heap, Memory heap, Memory mapping, Virtual memory, Privileges, Handles, and part of Scheduling) describe SRS's own running process. SIV does the same thing on Windows. They show what any normal program on your desktop gets: its libraries, memory, limits and rights.

ASUS control service

acs-srv - Not present on most PCs

In plain words. On Windows, ASUS laptops and some desktops run an "ASUS control service" (Armoury Crate and friends). Linux has no such service. SRS shows the nearest Linux pieces instead.

What you see.

  • Windows service - always "not applicable on Linux - showing the Linux analogue".
  • Unit lines asusd.service, supergfxd.service - two columns: Active state (active, inactive, failed) and Enabled state (enabled, disabled, masked, static, or not-found / "not installed"). asusd is the asusctl daemon for ASUS ROG/TUF laptops (fan curves, keyboard light, charge limit). supergfxd switches laptop graphics modes.
  • Module lines asus_wmi, asus_nb_wmi, asus_ec_sensors, asus_wmi_sensors, asus_armoury - "loaded" or "not loaded". These are kernel drivers that talk to ASUS firmware: hot keys, fan and temperature sensors, BIOS settings.

Healthy / typical values. On the author's ASUS TUF X870 desktop board every module is "not loaded" and asusd is inactive / masked. That is normal for a desktop. On an ASUS laptop you would expect asus_nb_wmi loaded and, if you installed asusctl, asusd active.

Unusual values and what they suggest. An ASUS laptop with asus_nb_wmi "not loaded": Fn hot keys and fan modes will not work; check that the kernel was built with the driver. asus_ec_sensors not loaded on a supported ROG/TUF desktop board: board sensors (chipset, VRM temperature) will be missing from the Sensors items.

Where Linux gets it. systemctl is-active / is-enabled for each unit; /sys/module/<name> for each module.

Background. A systemd unit is Linux's version of a Windows service entry. "Masked" means it has been blocked on purpose and cannot start, even by hand.

Boot mode options

boot-mode - Linux data

In plain words. How this PC started: UEFI or old BIOS, Secure Boot on or off, which boot loader, and which "target" (Linux's version of a boot mode) it boots into.

What you see.

  • Firmware - "UEFI" or "Legacy BIOS (CSM)". CSM (Compatibility Support Module) is the old-BIOS emulation inside UEFI firmware.
  • UEFI platform size - 64-bit or 32-bit UEFI. Some cheap tablets have 32-bit UEFI on a 64-bit CPU, and that needs a special boot loader.
  • Secure Boot - the line from mokutil --sb-state, e.g. "SecureBoot enabled" / "SecureBoot disabled".
  • Default target - the systemd target used at boot. graphical.target = desktop login; multi-user.target = text console only.
  • Kernel command line - the options the boot loader passed to the kernel.
  • Boot loader (bootctl status) - the System block from bootctl: firmware arch, Secure Boot, TPM2 support, measured boot, "Boot into FW" (can the OS reboot you straight into BIOS setup), platform language, and the boot loader product.
  • Safe-mode equivalents (systemd) - a fixed cheat sheet. Add systemd.unit=rescue.target (like Windows Safe Mode), emergency.target (bare root shell, read-only root) or multi-user.target (like Safe Mode with Networking, no desktop) to the kernel command line for one boot.

Healthy / typical values. Author's PC: UEFI, 64-bit, SecureBoot disabled, graphical.target, boot loader "GRUB 2.16", TPM2 Support yes. The command line starts BOOT_IMAGE=/@/boot/vmlinuz-linux73-tkg-bore-llvm root=UUID=XXXX rw rootflags=subvol=@ ... followed by tuning options such as amd_pstate=active preempt=full.

Unusual values and what they suggest. "Legacy BIOS (CSM)" on a modern board: the disk was installed in old mode. You cannot use Secure Boot, and Windows 11 dual-boot needs UEFI. Default target multi-user.target on a desktop: the PC will boot to a text login. Options you do not recognise on the command line (such as mitigations=off) change security or performance. Check the GRUB or systemd-boot config before you copy them.

Where Linux gets it. /sys/firmware/efi (present = UEFI), /sys/firmware/efi/fw_platform_size, mokutil --sb-state, systemctl get-default, /proc/cmdline, bootctl status.

Background. UEFI (Unified Extensible Firmware Interface) replaced the PC BIOS. Secure Boot is a UEFI feature that only runs boot loaders signed with trusted keys. A systemd target is a named group of services. Booting into a target is like picking a Windows boot mode.

Corsair Link 4 service

cl4-srv - Not present on most PCs

In plain words. Corsair Link 4 was Corsair's Windows service for fans, pumps and power supplies. On Linux, the same hardware is run by CoolerControl, liquidctl or kernel hwmon drivers. SRS shows those. This item prints the same probe as Corsair service.

What you see.

  • Windows service - "not applicable on Linux - showing the Linux analogue".
  • Units coolercontrold.service, coolercontrol-liqctld.service, liquidcfg.service - Active state and Enabled state.
  • Modules corsair_cpro (Commander Pro), corsair_psu (Corsair HXi/RMi power supplies), nzxt_kraken3, nzxt_smart2 - "loaded" / "not loaded".
  • Processes coolercontrold, coolercontrol-l (the liquidctl helper; the kernel cuts process names to 15 characters), liquidctl - "running PID n" or "not running".

Healthy / typical values. Author's PC: coolercontrold.service active enabled, process coolercontrold running. No Corsair or NZXT kernel modules are loaded because no such device is attached.

Unusual values and what they suggest. A Corsair PSU on USB but corsair_psu "not loaded": power-supply sensors will be missing. Try modprobe corsair_psu or let CoolerControl read it. coolercontrold enabled but not running: the daemon crashed. Check journalctl -u coolercontrold.

Where Linux gets it. systemctl is-active / is-enabled, /sys/module/<name>, the process list in /proc.

Background. hwmon is the kernel's hardware-monitoring framework. Each sensor chip appears under /sys/class/hwmon, and tools like CoolerControl read and control it there.

Shell CLSIDs

clsid - Windows-only (Linux equivalent shown)

In plain words. In Windows, a CLSID (class ID) is a registry number that ties a file type or shell object to a program. Linux has no CLSIDs. The nearest thing is the default-application list, which says which app opens which file type or link type.

What you see.

  • Table MIME Type / Scheme - Default Handler (.desktop): one row per line in the [Default Applications] part of ~/.config/mimeapps.list. Lines starting x-scheme-handler/ (links such as mailto: or https:) are tinted differently.
  • System .desktop entries - how many files are in /usr/share/applications.
  • User .desktop entries - how many are in ~/.local/share/applications.
  • If you have no defaults: "no user defaults in ~/.config/mimeapps.list".

Healthy / typical values. Author's PC: application/pdf -> okularApplication_pdf.desktop;, application/ogg -> vlc.desktop;, application/vnd.flatpak -> org.kde.discover.desktop;. A trailing ; is normal; the format allows a list.

Unusual values and what they suggest. A handler whose .desktop file no longer exists (the app was removed): double-clicking that file type does nothing or asks every time. Fix it in System Settings -> Default Applications or File Associations.

Where Linux gets it. ~/.config/mimeapps.list; the counts are directory listings of /usr/share/applications and ~/.local/share/applications.

Background. A MIME type (Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions type) is a standard name for a kind of file, such as image/png. A .desktop file is a small text file that describes an app: its name, icon, command, and the MIME types it can open.

Code pages

codepage - Linux data

In plain words. A code page is an old table that maps byte values to letters. Windows still lists dozens of them. Linux uses UTF-8 almost everywhere, but its iconv library can still convert the old ones. This item checks each Windows code page against it.

What you see.

  • Page ID - the Windows code page number (437, 850, 1252, 65001...).
  • Description - what it is, e.g. "OEM United States", "ANSI Latin 1", "Mac Roman", "Unicode UTF-8".
  • glibc iconv - the name glibc uses for it (CP437, IBM037, ISO-8859-15, MACINTOSH...), or - if none was found.
  • Supported - ticked if glibc can convert that page to UTF-8.
  • Footer: "N of 70 supported; locale charset X" and the number of glibc charmaps in /usr/share/i18n/charmaps.

Healthy / typical values. Author's PC: "58 of 70 supported; locale charset UTF-8", 233 charmaps. The gaps are pages glibc does not ship, such as 720 (Arabic Transparent ASMO) and several Mac pages.

Unusual values and what they suggest. Very few pages supported (say under 10): the glibc gconv modules are missing or were trimmed, for example in a minimal container. Old text files and some emulators will then show garbled letters. A locale charset of ANSI_X3.4-1968 means plain ASCII: no LANG is set, so programs cannot print accented letters.

Where Linux gets it. glibc iconv_open() tested for each name; /usr/share/i18n/charmaps; the charset part of LC_ALL / LC_CTYPE / LANG.

Background. "OEM" pages (437, 850...) are the old DOS character sets. "ANSI" pages (1250-1258) are the old Windows ones. UTF-8 (page 65001) can hold every Unicode character, which is why Linux uses it by default.

TAPI country list

country - Linux data

In plain words. On Windows, TAPI (Telephony API) keeps a country list with dialling codes. Linux has no TAPI. SRS lists the ISO 3166 country table from the time-zone database instead, with the number of time zones in each country.

What you see.

  • Code - the two-letter ISO 3166 country code. Your own country (from your locale) is shown in green.
  • Country - the country name.
  • Zones - how many time-zone entries zone.tab lists for it.
  • Representative Time Zone - the first zone listed for that country.
  • Footer: "N countries; current locale territory XX".

Healthy / typical values. Author's PC: 249 countries, current territory US. Examples: AR Argentina 12 America/Argentina/Buenos_Aires, AQ Antarctica 10 Antarctica/McMurdo.

Unusual values and what they suggest. "current locale territory -": your LANG has no country part (for example C.UTF-8), so programs fall back to default number, date and paper formats. Error "iso3166.tab not readable": the tzdata package is missing or damaged.

Where Linux gets it. /usr/share/zoneinfo/iso3166.tab and /usr/share/zoneinfo/zone.tab (both from tzdata); the territory comes from LC_ALL or LANG.

Corsair service

cue-srv - Not present on most PCs

In plain words. The Windows "Corsair Service" belongs to iCUE (Corsair Utility Engine). Linux has no iCUE. SRS shows the same Linux analogue as Corsair Link 4 service: CoolerControl and liquidctl units, Corsair and NZXT hwmon modules, and their processes.

What you see. Exactly the same lines as cl4-srv: three units with Active and Enabled state, four modules loaded / not loaded, three processes running / not running.

Healthy / typical values. Author's PC: coolercontrold.service active enabled, process running, no Corsair/NZXT modules loaded.

Unusual values and what they suggest. Corsair RGB keyboards and mice are not covered here. On Linux they are driven by OpenRGB or ckb-next, which this probe does not check.

Where Linux gets it. systemctl, /sys/module, /proc.

Base DLLs

dll - Linux data

In plain words. A DLL (dynamic-link library) is Windows' shared code file. The Linux version is the shared object (.so file). This item lists every file mapped into SRS's own process: the program, its libraries, and some data files.

What you see.

  • Image - the running program file.
  • Dynamic loader - the program that loads shared libraries at start, normally /usr/lib/ld-linux-x86-64.so.2.
  • glibc - the C library version.
  • Table:
    • Base / End - lowest and highest memory address the file occupies, in hex.
    • Size - End minus Base.
    • Module - file name.
    • Version / Path - for name.so.N files, "VN" is the number after .so. (the soname major number), then the full path.
  • Footer: "N mapped files (executable, shared libraries, locale/data files)".

Healthy / typical values. Author's PC: glibc 2.44, 9 mapped files. These are sysreport-search (1.38MB), libc.so.6 (V6, 2.25MB), libm.so.6, the loader (V2), /etc/ld.so.cache, and glibc gconv converters such as UTF-16.so. The converters appear because other items have already used iconv.

Unusual values and what they suggest. A library from an unexpected place (for example /home/... or /tmp/... instead of /usr/lib): something is setting LD_LIBRARY_PATH or LD_PRELOAD. Check Known DLLs. The GUI process (srs-gui) maps many more files (GTK and friends) than the command-line run.

Where Linux gets it. /proc/self/maps, readlink /proc/self/exe, gnu_get_libc_version().

Background. The soname number (the 6 in libc.so.6) changes only when a library breaks compatibility. It is not the library's release version.

DLLs by address

dll-addr - Linux data

In plain words. The same table as Base DLLs, in memory-address order and without the header lines.

What you see. Base, End, Size, Module, Version / Path, and the "N mapped files" footer, exactly as in dll.

Healthy / typical values. The program itself sits low (around 6023822F3000 on the author's PC) and the libraries sit high (7A58...). The exact numbers change on every run.

Unusual values and what they suggest. Addresses that are the same on every run would mean ASLR is off; see randomize_va_space in Virtual memory.

Where Linux gets it. /proc/self/maps.

Background. ASLR (Address Space Layout Randomization) loads programs and libraries at random addresses each time. That makes many attacks harder.

Known DLLs

dll-known - Linux data

In plain words. Windows keeps a list of "Known DLLs" that always load from the system folder. Linux has a cache of every library the loader knows about, plus the list of folders it searches. This item shows both.

What you see.

  • ld.so.cache - the first line of ldconfig -p, e.g. "12521 libs found in cache `/etc/ld.so.cache'".
  • LD_LIBRARY_PATH - extra library folders set in your environment, or <not set>.
  • LD_PRELOAD - libraries forced into every program, or <not set>.
  • /etc/ld.so.preload - shown only if the file exists. It forces libraries into every program system-wide.
  • Search directories - each folder from /etc/ld.so.conf and /etc/ld.so.conf.d/*.conf, with the file that added it.
  • Core system libraries (ldconfig -p) - cache entries for key libraries (libc, libm, libstdc++, libz, libssl, libsystemd, libdrm, libGL, libEGL, libvulkan, libX11, libwayland-client, libasound, libpulse...), both 64-bit (libc6,x86-64) and 32-bit (libc6).

Healthy / typical values. Author's PC: 12521 libraries, both variables not set. Extra folders come from installed packages, e.g. /opt/rocm/lib (rocm.conf), /usr/lib32 (lib32-glibc.conf).

Unusual values and what they suggest. LD_PRELOAD set when you did not set it, or a /etc/ld.so.preload you do not recognise: something injects code into every program. That is sometimes a tool (a game overlay, a memory allocator) and sometimes malware. Find out which package owns it. A newly installed library that is missing from the cache: run sudo ldconfig.

Where Linux gets it. ldconfig -p, /etc/ld.so.conf, /etc/ld.so.conf.d/, /etc/ld.so.preload, environment variables.

DLLs by name

dll-name - Linux data

In plain words. The same table as Base DLLs, sorted by file name (A-Z, ignoring case).

What you see. Base, End, Size, Module, Version / Path, and the footer. Author's PC: gconv-modules.cache, ISO8859-13.so, ISO8859-15.so, ld-linux-x86-64.so.2, ld.so.cache, libc.so.6, libm.so.6, sysreport-search, UTF-16.so.

Healthy / typical values / unusual values. As for Base DLLs. Sorting by name makes it easy to spot two copies of the same library from different folders.

Where Linux gets it. /proc/self/maps.

Drivers

drivers - Linux data

In plain words. Windows drivers become Linux kernel modules: pieces of the kernel that are loaded on demand. This item lists every loaded module, the same list as lsmod.

What you see.

  • Module Name - the module name (A-Z).
  • Size - memory the module uses.
  • Used - how many other modules or users hold it.
  • State - Live (normal), Loading or Unloading (anything other than Live is shown in orange).
  • Taint - letters from the kernel if this module "taints" the kernel: O = out-of-tree (built outside the kernel source), E = unsigned, P = proprietary licence. Blank = clean.
  • Used By - the modules that depend on it.
  • Footer: "N loadable modules loaded, M built into kernel (modules.builtin)".
