COM port resource arbiter

arbiter - Windows-only (Linux equivalent shown)

In plain words. Windows has an "arbiter" that hands out I/O addresses and IRQs (interrupt lines) to COM (serial) ports. Linux has no such component. SRS shows the serial port list instead, plus the I/O ranges that the serial driver has claimed.

What you see.

  • The full Serial COM ports table (Port, I/O, IRQ, UART, Base clock, Device), the placeholder count line and the TTY driver list.
  • COM resources (Linux equivalent of the COM port arbiter) - every line of the I/O port map that mentions serial, e.g. 03f8-03ff serial. This is the address range the port really uses.

Healthy / typical values. On the author's PC: one real port, ttyS0 at 0x3F8, IRQ 4, and the claimed range 03f8-03ff serial. COM1 has used these values since the IBM PC.

Unusual values and what they suggest. No serial range while a port is listed means the driver has not claimed it yet. Two devices on the same range would be a firmware conflict, but that is very rare today.

Where Linux gets it. /sys/class/tty, /proc/tty/drivers, /proc/ioports (addresses need the srs-root cache).

Chipsets

chipsets - Linux data

In plain words. This is a short list of the "glue" chips on the motherboard: host bridges, the IOMMU, the chipset's PCIe switch and its ports, the SMBus controller and the LPC bridge.

What you see. One line per device. The label on the left is the role SRS gives it:

Label Meaning
Host Bridge PCI class 0600. The link between the CPU and the PCI bus. On AMD this includes the Root Complex, the "Dummy Host Bridges" and the eight Data Fabric functions (00:18.0-7).
IOMMU Class 0806. The input-output memory management unit. It controls which memory each device may reach by DMA (Direct Memory Access).
ISA/LPC Bridge Class 0601. It connects the legacy LPC bus (Super I/O chip, TPM, BIOS flash).
SMBus Controller Class 0C05. The controller for the small management bus that reads DIMM SPD chips and sensors.
Chipset Bridge A PCI bridge whose name contains "Chipset", such as one port of the chipset's PCIe switch.
Chipset Function Any other device named "Chipset", such as the chipset's USB or SATA controller.

After the label comes the PCI address, the vendor and device names, [VVVV:DDDD rev RR] and the driver if one is bound. The last line is the board name and BIOS version.

Healthy / typical values. On the author's ASUS TUF GAMING X870-PRO WIFI7 W NEO (Ryzen 9000 "Granite Ridge" CPU): the Root Complex 1022:14D8 with driver ryzen_smu, the IOMMU 1022:14D9, and the "600 Series Chipset PCIe Switch Upstream Port" 1022:43F4 with its downstream ports 1022:43F5 (X870 boards use the same Promontory 21 chip). The chipset USB controller 1022:43FC and SATA controller 1022:43F6 also appear, plus 00:18.3 Data Fabric Function 3 with driver k10temp (the CPU temperature driver).

Unusual values and what they suggest. If the SMBus controller has no driver, piix4_smbus is not loaded, and RAM and RGB tools will not find their devices. If there are no "Chipset" lines on a board that has a chipset, the PCI ID database is old (see PCI ID database).

Where Linux gets it. /sys/bus/pci/devices/*/class, vendor, device, revision, driver, with names from /usr/share/hwdata/pci.ids.

Background. On a modern AMD desktop the memory controller and most PCIe lanes are in the CPU. The "chipset" is a separate chip joined to the CPU by a PCIe x4 link. It acts like a PCIe switch with extra USB and SATA controllers built in.

System device classes

class - Linux data

In plain words. Linux sorts every device into a "class" by what it does (block disks, network, sound, input, hwmon sensors...). This item lists each class and the devices in it.

What you see. One row per directory in /sys/class:

  • Class name - such as block, drm (graphics), hwmon, net, tty.
  • Count - how many entries the class has.
  • Members - their names, cut off with ... after about 150 characters.

Healthy / typical values. On the author's PC: block 27 (loop devices, three NVMe drives and their partitions, SATA disks), cpuid 16 (one per logical CPU), drm 8 (card0, its four connectors, a writeback connector, renderD128, version), bluetooth 1 hci0. Many classes are 0, which is normal. They exist because the kernel supports them, not because hardware is present.

Unusual values and what they suggest. A count of 0 where you expect hardware, such as net without your network card or drm without card0, means the driver did not load. Check Device owners.

Where Linux gets it. /sys/class/*.

Background. A sysfs "class" is a view by function. The same device also appears under its bus (/sys/bus/pci/...) and at its place in the device tree (/sys/devices/...).

Remote system classes

class-remote - Windows-only (Linux equivalent shown)

In plain words. SIV on Windows can read the device classes of another PC over the network, through the remote registry. Linux has nothing like that.

What you see. Status: Windows-only item in SIV and Linux equivalent: none (remote registry); nearest ssh + /sys/class. To see another Linux PC's classes, log in with ssh and look at /sys/class, or run SRS there.

Co-device installers

codevice - Windows-only (Linux equivalent shown)

In plain words. Windows "co-installers" are small helper programs that run when a driver is installed. The closest thing on Linux is udev rules. These are text files that say what to do when a device appears: set permissions, make symlinks, load firmware, start a service.

What you see. Three folders, each with its file count and then every rule file in it:

  • /usr/lib/udev/rules.d - rules shipped by packages.
  • /etc/udev/rules.d - your own rules. A file with the same name here overrides the package one.
  • /run/udev/rules.d - temporary rules made at run time.

Healthy / typical values. On the author's PC: 290 package rules (e.g. 30-amdgpu-pm.rules, 10-rtl-sdr.rules, 01-asrock-LED-controller.rules) and 1 run-time rule (30-drm-awaiter.rules). The number at the front sets the order. Lower numbers run first.

Unusual values and what they suggest. A rule left behind by a removed program can still change device permissions. If a USB gadget works only as root, look here for a rule that should give access to your user and is missing.

Where Linux gets it. A file listing of the three rules.d folders.

Compatible IDs

compatible - Linux data

In plain words. Every device has a "modalias". This is one long ID string that Linux matches against each driver's list of supported hardware to pick the right driver. It is the Linux version of Windows "Compatible IDs".

What you see. Three groups, one line each:

  • PCI devices (teal label = PCI address) - e.g. pci:v00001022d000014D8sv00001043sd00008877bc06sc00i00.
  • USB interfaces (label = interface name such as 1-2:1.0) - e.g. usb:v2109p2817d0623dc09dsc00dp02ic09isc00ip02in00 (a VIA USB hub).
  • ACPI devices (label = ACPI name such as ACPI0007:00) - e.g. acpi:ACPI0007:.

How to read a PCI modalias:

Part Meaning
v00001022 Vendor ID 1022 (AMD)
d000014D8 Device ID 14D8
sv00001043 Subsystem vendor 1043 (ASUS, the board maker)
sd00008877 Subsystem device 8877 (the board's own number for this part)
bc06 sc00 i00 Base class 06 (bridge), subclass 00 (host), programming interface 00

For USB: v=vendor, p=product, d=device release, dc/dsc/dp=device class/subclass/protocol, ic/isc/ip=interface class/subclass/protocol, in=interface number.

Healthy / typical values. On the author's PC the Radeon RX 9070 XT reads pci:v00001002d00007550sv00001EAEsd00008811bc03sc00i00: AMD/ATI chip 7550, built by subsystem vendor 1EAE (XFX), class 03 (display).

Unusual values and what they suggest. A subsystem of sv00000000sd00000000 is normal for internal bridges. On a plug-in card it means the maker did not program one. You can add a filter after the item name (e.g. compatible:03:00) to show only matching devices.

Where Linux gets it. /sys/bus/pci/devices/*/modalias, /sys/bus/usb/devices/*:*/modalias, /sys/bus/acpi/devices/*/modalias.

Device IDs

device-ids - Linux data

In plain words. This shows every PCI and USB device's ID, and how SRS turned that ID into a name. It shows which entry in the ID database matched.

What you see.

Column Meaning
Device The PCI address (03:00.0) or the USB device name (5-1, usb3).
Lookup Key For PCI: Vendor:Device:SubVendor:SubDevice:Revision. Internal parts with no subsystem use Vendor:Device:Revision. For USB: Vendor:Product.
Matched Which step of the lookup chain found a name. For PCI: rung 0 is the most exact. For USB: V:D (vendor and product found), V (only the vendor is known) or none.
Name The vendor name, then the device name from the step that matched.

The PCI lookup chain for a full key goes from most to least exact: rung 0 V:D:S:s:RR -> rung 1 V:D:S:s -> rung 2 V:D:RR -> rung 3 V:D -> rung 4 V. For a short key (no subsystem) it is rung 0 V:D:RR -> rung 1 V:D -> rung 2 V.

Double-click any key to open it in Device ID Lookup, which shows every step of the chain side by side.

Healthy / typical values. On the author's PC most PCI rows match at rung 3 (the generic vendor:device name). The Samsung SSD matches at rung 1: key 144D:A80A:144D:A801, where the subsystem entry gives the retail name "SSD 980 PRO" instead of the chip name. Internal bridges like 1022:14DA:00 match at rung 1 (their short-key V:D). On the USB side the Razer mouse 1532:005C is V:D "DeathAdder Elite". Some devices are only V (the SteelSeries keyboard 1038:1612) or none (9129:1583).

Unusual values and what they suggest. none on PCI means the vendor is missing from the database. This happens with brand-new hardware or a very old pci.ids. Update the hwdata package. V or none on USB is common for cheap gadgets and is harmless. The device's own name strings still show in Device owners.

Where Linux gets it. sysfs vendor, device, subsystem_vendor, subsystem_device, revision and idVendor/idProduct, looked up in /usr/share/hwdata/pci.ids and usb.ids.

Background. A PCI device carries two pairs of IDs. The vendor/device ID names the chip (who made the silicon). The subsystem vendor/device ID names the product built around it (who made the card or board). The same Navi 48 chip 1002:7550 shows up with a different subsystem on every card brand. The revision ID tells chip steppings apart.

All devices

devices - Linux data

In plain words. This is every device udev knows about: real hardware, virtual devices and kernel helpers. It is the Linux equivalent of Device Manager with "show hidden devices" on.

What you see.

Column Meaning
Device The device path under /sys/devices (the leading /devices/ is dropped), such as pci0000:00/0000:00:01.2/0000:04:00.0/nvme/nvme0/nvme0n1.
Subsystem The bus or class it belongs to: pci, usb, block, net, acpi, workqueue...
Driver The bound driver, if any.
Node Its /dev node, if any (e.g. nvme0n1, bus/usb/002/002).

At the end: Total of N devices in the udev database.

Healthy / typical values. On the author's PC: 1583 devices. The list starts with the ACPI tree (LNXSYSTM:00/...) and ends with virtual/workqueue/... entries. Hundreds of rows with no driver are normal. Most entries are containers, ports or virtual objects.

Unusual values and what they suggest. A real device (PCI or USB) with an empty Driver column has no driver. A missing device that you can see in lspci means udev has not processed it. This is rare, and restarting systemd-udevd fixes it.

Where Linux gets it. udevadm info --export-db (read only).

Device owners

dev-owner - Linux data

In plain words. For each PCI and USB device, this shows which driver "owns" it and which kernel module that driver lives in.

What you see.

Column Meaning
Device The PCI address or USB device name.
Driver For PCI, the bound driver or (none). For USB, every interface driver, comma-separated (e.g. usbhid, usbfs).
Module For PCI, the module file the driver comes from, or built-in if it is compiled into the kernel. It is blank when there is no driver, and blank for USB.
Description For PCI, the device name. For USB, the maker and product strings the device reports about itself. Root hubs show xHCI Host Controller - <controller name>.

Healthy / typical values. On the author's PC: GPU 03:00.0 -> amdgpu, NVMe drives -> nvme, the 5GbE card -> r8169, PCIe bridges -> pcieport (module pcieportdrv), USB hubs -> hub, the webcam -> uvcvideo, the Bluetooth radio -> btusb. The IOMMU and "Dummy Host Bridges" show (none). That is normal, because they need no driver.

Unusual values and what they suggest.

  • A plug-in card or USB gadget with (none) has no driver: it is unsupported, or its module is not loaded.
  • usbfs means a user-space program (OpenRGB, a game launcher, a printer driver) has claimed the interface directly. This is expected for RGB keyboards and printers.
  • Garbled description text (stray symbols) comes from the device's own firmware strings, not from SRS.

Where Linux gets it. /sys/bus/pci/devices/*/driver, .../driver/module, /sys/bus/usb/devices/*:*/driver, plus the USB manufacturer and product files.

Device property keys

devpropkey - Linux data

In plain words. udev stores key=value "properties" for each device. This item lists every property name in use and how many devices have it. Use it to find a key you can then look up with Device property.

What you see. One line per key, A-Z, with N devices. The last line is Total of K keys across D devices.

Healthy / typical values. On the author's PC: 298 keys across 1583 devices. Common ones: DEVPATH (every device), DEVNAME (370 devices with a /dev node), DRIVER (258), HID_ID and HID_NAME (18), BUSNUM/DEVNUM (40 USB devices).

Where Linux gets it. The E: lines of udevadm info --export-db.

Background. Keys such as ID_VENDOR_FROM_DATABASE come from udev's hardware database (hwdb). Keys such as ID_SERIAL and ID_PATH come from udev helper programs. Desktop software uses them to decide how to treat a device.

Embedded controller I/O

embedded - Linux data - Needs root data

In plain words. The EC (Embedded Controller) is a small microcontroller on the motherboard. It handles things like power buttons, battery and fans on laptops, and some sensors on desktops. This item shows where it lives. It does not read it.

What you see.

  • ACPI device - PNP0C09:00 (ACPI Embedded Controller), or "No ACPI PNP0C09 device".
  • Namespace path - its place in the firmware's ACPI tables, e.g. \_SB_.PCI0.SBRG.EC0_.
  • Bound to - the Linux device it is attached to, or (ACPI core EC driver).
  • ECDT table - present if the firmware gives an early EC description table, otherwise absent (EC described in DSDT only).
  • ec_sys debugfs - whether the ec_sys debug module (which lets root read EC RAM) is loaded.
  • The EC's I/O ports from the port map: on PCs, 0062 = EC data and 0066 = EC command.

Healthy / typical values. On the author's desktop the EC is at \_SB_.PCI0.SBRG.EC0_, there is no ECDT, ec_sys is not loaded, and the ports are 0062 and 0066. That is a standard layout.

Unusual values and what they suggest. No EC at all is fine on many desktops. On a laptop, a missing EC explains missing battery or fan readings. SRS never reads EC RAM, because traffic on 0x62/0x66 can collide with the firmware.

Where Linux gets it. /sys/bus/acpi/devices/PNP0C09:00, /sys/firmware/acpi/tables/ECDT, /proc/ioports (addresses from the srs-root cache).

System enum (device tree)

enum - Linux data

In plain words. These are the same devices as All devices, drawn as an indented tree, so you can see what is plugged into what.

What you see. One line per device: its short name, indented by depth, then [subsystem]. Top-level entries are in bold. For example:

  LNXSYSTM:00  [acpi]
    LNXPWRBN:00  [acpi]
    LNXSYBUS:00  [acpi]
      ACPI0010:00  [acpi]
        ACPI0007:00  [acpi]

Healthy / typical values. On the author's PC the tree starts with the ACPI root and its 16 processor objects (ACPI0007:00 to 0f, one per logical CPU). Then come the PCI tree (pci0000:00), platform devices and the virtual devices. There are about 1580 lines.

Unusual values and what they suggest. If a device sits under an unexpected parent (an NVMe drive under the chipset instead of the CPU, say), it is in an M.2 slot wired to the chipset. That slot is slower and shares bandwidth.

Where Linux gets it. udevadm info --export-db, sorted by device path.

Remote system enum

enum-remote - Windows-only (Linux equivalent shown)

In plain words. SIV on Windows can list another PC's device tree through the remote registry. Linux has no such feature.

What you see. Status: Windows-only item in SIV and Linux equivalent: none (remote registry); nearest ssh + udevadm. On the other PC, run udevadm info --export-db over ssh, or run SRS there.

FireWire

firewire - Not present on most PCs

In plain words. FireWire (IEEE 1394) is an older high-speed bus, used for DV camcorders and pro audio interfaces. Modern boards do not have it.

What it would show. One 1394 controller line per FireWire card (PCI class 0C00), and whether /sys/bus/firewire exists.

What "not present" means. On the author's PC: /sys/bus/firewire absent and "No PCI class 0C00 (FireWire) controller present." Nothing is wrong. You would need an add-in card.

Ghost (non-present) devices

ghost-devices - Windows-only (Linux equivalent shown)

In plain words. Windows keeps every device ever plugged in, even after it is gone. These are "ghost devices". Linux forgets a device when it is removed. SRS checks the closest thing: udev records in /run/udev/data whose device no longer exists.

What you see. One orange line per stale record: stale udev record (device not present). Or, if there are none: "No stale entries in /run/udev/data: Linux drops records when devices go away." A second note explains the Windows difference.

Healthy / typical values. No stale entries, as on the author's PC.

Unusual values and what they suggest. A few stale records after hot-unplugging can happen and are harmless. They vanish at reboot, because /run is in memory.

Where Linux gets it. /run/udev/data compared with /sys/dev, /sys/bus and /sys/class.

HID all devices

hid-all - Linux data

In plain words. HID (Human Interface Device) is the standard way keyboards, mice, game pads, RGB controllers and security keys talk to the PC. This item gives a full card for each HID device.

What you see. For each device, a title line <bus>:<VID>:<PID>.<instance> <name>, then:

Field Meaning
Bus The bus number and name (0003 USB, 0005 Bluetooth, 0018 I2C, 0006 Virtual...), then VID_xxxx PID_xxxx.
usb.ids For USB devices only: the vendor and product names from the USB ID database.
Driver The HID driver: hid-generic, or a special one like logitech-djreceiver, razermouse, nintendo.
Physical Where it is attached, e.g. usb-0000:0b:00.0-8.4.4/input1:1 (controller, port path, interface).
Unique ID The device's own unique ID or serial, if it reports one (shown only when present).
Parent The USB interface or other device it hangs off.
Report descriptor The size in bytes of the descriptor that tells the PC what buttons, axes and LEDs the device has.
hidraw node The raw access node (hidrawN). It is listed but never opened.
Input devices The inputN devices the kernel made from it (the keyboard and mouse events your desktop reads).
Modalias The driver-matching ID, e.g. hid:b0003g0102v0000046Dp00004057.

Healthy / typical values. On the author's PC: a Logitech mouse 046D:4057 behind a Nano Receiver 046D:C52F (driver logitech-hidpp-device, parent 0003:046D:C52F.000F, report descriptor 192 bytes, Unique ID XXXX). Also a Nintendo Switch Pro Controller with driver nintendo, and a Razer DeathAdder with driver razermouse.

Unusual values and what they suggest.

  • A game pad on hid-generic instead of its own driver may lose rumble, LEDs or the gyro.
  • No Input devices on a keyboard or mouse interface is normal for vendor-only interfaces (RGB, macro setup). It is a problem only if typing does not work.
  • A tiny report descriptor (a few bytes) can mean a broken or half-initialised device.

Where Linux gets it. /sys/bus/hid/devices/* (uevent, report_descriptor, hidraw/, input/).

Background. One physical USB device often exposes several HID interfaces. A gaming keyboard can have one for keys, one for media keys and one for lighting, so it shows up several times here.

HID bus

hid-bus - Linux data

In plain words. This is a one-line-per-device table of the HID bus. It is the HID Bus button in the USB Bus panel.

What you see.

Column Meaning
HID Device bus:VID:PID.instance, e.g. 0003:1532:005C.0001.
Bus USB, Bluetooth, I2C, SPI, Virtual, Host or Other.
Name The name the device reports.
Driver The HID driver bound to it.
Nodes The hidrawN node and any inputN devices.

The last line is Total of N HID devices. You can filter, e.g. hid-bus:1532.

Healthy / typical values. On the author's PC: 15 HID devices. The SteelSeries Apex 7 keyboard appears four times (four interfaces), the ASUS AURA LED controller twice, and the Razer DeathAdder three times. There is also a "Virtual FIDO/U2F security Key" 0003:FFFF:FFFF made by software.

Unusual values and what they suggest. A device you can see on the USB bus but not here is not a HID device, or its HID driver failed. Check the kernel log.

Where Linux gets it. /sys/bus/hid/devices.

HID tree

hid-tree - Linux data

In plain words. This groups HID devices under the USB device they belong to, so you can see which interfaces of one gadget are HID.

What you see. For each USB device that has HID interfaces, a header line <usb name> VID:PID <description>, then one line per HID interface: |__ <usb interface> <HID device> [driver] <input devices>. HID devices that are not on USB (Bluetooth, I2C touchpads, virtual) are listed at the end with their bus name.

Healthy / typical values. On the author's PC:

5-2  1038:1612 SteelSeries SteelSeries Apex 7
  |__ 5-2:1.0  0003:1038:1612.0006  [hid-generic] input6
  |__ 5-2:1.2  0003:1038:1612.0008  [hid-generic] input7

Double-click a VID:PID such as 1038:1612 to open it in Device ID Lookup. If the lookup window opens on the PCI bus, switch it to USB.

Where Linux gets it. /sys/bus/hid/devices matched to /sys/bus/usb/devices.

Device interfaces

interfaces - Linux data

In plain words. On Windows, "device interfaces" are the named access points programs open. On Linux the matching idea is the /sys/class entries, so this item shows the same table as System device classes (its window title says so too).

What you see. Class name, count, members (see System device classes). For more detail use the extended form Device interfaces (extended).

Where Linux gets it. /sys/class.

Device interfaces (extended)

interfacex - Linux data

In plain words. This lists every single /sys/class entry with its device number, the hardware behind it and its driver.

What you see.

Column Meaning
class/name e.g. drm/card0, hidraw/hidraw0, block/nvme0n1.
dev_t The major:minor device number, if it has a /dev node (e.g. 226:0).
Device The hardware it belongs to (e.g. PCI 0000:03:00.0, HID 0003:1532:005C.0001, nvme0).
Driver That hardware's driver.

Healthy / typical values. On the author's PC: drm/card0 226:0 0000:03:00.0 amdgpu and hidraw/hidraw0 243:0 0003:1532:005C.0001 razermouse. Many entries (bdi, virtual ones) have empty columns. That is normal.

Where Linux gets it. /sys/class/*/*/dev, .../device, .../device/driver.

Background. A dev_t is the pair of numbers the kernel uses to find a device file. The major picks the driver (259 = NVMe/block extended, 226 = DRM graphics). The minor picks one device.

Interface IDs

int-ids - Linux data

In plain words. These are only the /sys/class entries that have a device file, with their device number and /dev path.

What you see. class/name, dev_t (major:minor) and the /dev/... node name from udev.

Healthy / typical values. On the author's PC: block/nvme0n1 259:5 /dev/nvme0n1, block/sda 8:0 /dev/sda. Block disks use major 8 for SATA/SCSI and 259 for NVMe.

Unusual values and what they suggest. An entry with a dev_t but no /dev path means udev did not make the node. Programs will not find the device.

Where Linux gets it. /sys/class/*/*/dev, plus the N: (node) line in the udev database.

Interface names

int-names - Linux data

In plain words. This shows the friendly symlink udev made for each /sys/class entry, such as /dev/disk/by-label/EFI.

What you see. class/name and the first udev symlink for it (relative to /dev), or - if there is none.

Healthy / typical values. On the author's PC: block/loop0 disk/by-diskseq/142, block/nvme0n1p1 disk/by-path/pci-0000:04:00.0-nvme-1-part/by-label/EFI. Most non-disk entries show -.

Unusual values and what they suggest. A disk with no by-id or by-uuid names can make /etc/fstab entries that use those names fail at boot.

Where Linux gets it. The S: (symlink) lines of the udev database.

Interface owner

int-owner - Linux data

In plain words. This shows which driver and kernel module own each /sys/class entry.

What you see. class/name, Driver (or -), Module (or built-in), Device (the parent hardware).

Healthy / typical values. On the author's PC: drm/card0 amdgpu amdgpu 0000:03:00.0, input/input25 razermouse razermouse 0003:1532:005C.0001.

Where Linux gets it. /sys/class/*/*/device/driver and .../driver/module.

ASUS I/O

io-asus - Linux data - Needs root data

In plain words. ASUS boards keep their fan and voltage sensors in a Super I/O chip and, on some models, the EC. This item shows which ASUS-related drivers are present. The sensor values themselves are in the Sensors group.

What you see.

  • Board - the board vendor and name from SMBIOS (System Management BIOS).
  • hwmonN - each Nuvoton (nct...) or ASUS hwmon chip, with a pointer to [sensors].
  • asus-wmi and asus_ec_sensors - loaded or not loaded.
  • I/O port ranges claimed by nct, asus or it87 drivers, or "no matching entries".

Healthy / typical values. On the author's ASUS TUF GAMING X870-PRO WIFI7 W NEO: hwmon4 nct6799, with asus-wmi and asus_ec_sensors not loaded. "No matching entries" in the port map is normal, because the nct6775 driver's port shows up under the Super I/O name, not under "nct".

Unusual values and what they suggest. No nct chip on an ASUS board usually means the nct6775 module is not loaded, or the board needs acpi_enforce_resources=lax. asus_ec_sensors adds extra readings (chipset temperature, water flow) on supported ROG/TUF models.

Where Linux gets it. /sys/class/dmi/id/board_*, /sys/class/hwmon/*/name, /sys/module/*, /proc/ioports (srs-root cache).

I/O port dump

io-dump - Linux data - Needs root data

In plain words. SIV can dump the raw contents of the PC's I/O ports. SRS deliberately does not, because reading some ports can confuse the SMBus or EC. It shows which driver owns which port range instead.

What you see. A note saying why /dev/port is not read, then the full I/O port map (the same as I/O ports).

Where Linux gets it. /proc/ioports (srs-root cache for real addresses).

I/O GPIO

io-gpio - Linux data - Needs root data

In plain words. GPIO (General Purpose Input/Output) pins are simple on/off signals the chipset uses for LEDs, buttons, and enabling or resetting other chips. This item lists the GPIO controllers.

What you see. One line per GPIO chip: gpiochipN <ACPI device> <name> driver <driver>, then a note that pin states are not read, and how root can see them (cat /sys/kernel/debug/gpio).

Healthy / typical values. On the author's PC: gpiochip0 AMDI0030:00 AMD GPIO Controller driver amd_gpio (the FCH (Fusion Controller Hub) pins) and gpiochip1 AMDIF031:00 AMD GPIO Controller driver pt-gpio (the chipset's pins).

Unusual values and what they suggest. "no GPIO chips" on an AMD board means pinctrl_amd is not loaded. Some laptops need it for the touchpad interrupt.

Where Linux gets it. /sys/bus/gpio/devices.

I/O PM2 MMIO

io-mmio - Linux data - Needs root data

In plain words. AMD chipsets put their power-management, SMBus, GPIO and pin-mux registers in one memory-mapped block at 0xFED80000. This item shows the memory-map lines around it. MMIO (Memory-Mapped I/O) means hardware registers that look like memory addresses.

What you see. A note (registers are not read; no /dev/mem), then every line of the physical memory map that mentions AMDI devices, IOAPIC, HPET, Local APIC, amd_iommu, pnp or Reserved.

Healthy / typical values. On the author's PC: fec00000-fec003ff IOAPIC 0, fed00000-fed003ff HPET 0, fed81500-fed818ff AMDI0030:00 (the GPIO block inside the FCH region), f7600000-f767ffff amd_iommu, and several Reserved ranges for firmware.

Where Linux gets it. /proc/iomem (srs-root cache; non-root readers see zeros).

nForce I/O

io-nforce - Not present on most PCs

In plain words. These would be the I/O registers of NVIDIA nForce chipsets (about 2001-2008). No current PC uses one.

What you see. Status: Not present on this system, Checked: n/a (no NVIDIA nForce chipset).

I/O ports

io-ports - Linux data - Needs root data

In plain words. x86 PCs have a separate 64K "I/O port" address space, left over from the original PC. This is the map of who owns which ports.

What you see. One line per range: start-end owner, indented to show nesting (a range inside a bigger one). Owners are drivers or firmware devices.

Healthy / typical values. From the author's PC, all classic PC values:

Range Owner
0020-0021, 00a0-00a1 pic1, pic2 (the two old interrupt controllers)
0040-0043 timer0 (the PIT, the original PC timer)
0060, 0064 keyboard (the PS/2 controller)
0062, 0066 EC data, EC cmd
0070-0071 rtc0 (the CMOS real-time clock)
0cf8-0cff PCI conf1 (the old way to reach PCI configuration)
0290-029f reserved by the firmware (PNP0C02) for the Super I/O hardware monitor (the nct6775.656 device: 656 = 0x290)
0800-0827 ACPI PM1, PM timer and GPE blocks
0b00-0b28 piix4_smbus

Unusual values and what they suggest. If the addresses show as 0000-0000, you are not root and there is no srs-root cache. The orange line tells you how to fill it. Two drivers on one range can mean a firmware resource conflict (the kernel log says "resource busy").

Where Linux gets it. /proc/ioports.

IrDA ports

irports - Not present on most PCs

In plain words. IrDA was infrared data transfer, used on old laptops and phones. Linux removed IrDA support in kernel 4.17.

What you see. Status: Not present on this system, Checked: n/a (no IrDA).

ISA bus

isa-bus - Linux data

In plain words. The ISA (Industry Standard Architecture) bus is gone, but its job lives on in the LPC bus. LPC is a slim bus that links the chipset to the Super I/O chip, TPM, serial port and BIOS flash. This item shows the LPC bridge and what sits behind it.

What you see.

  • LPC bridge - the PCI class 0601 device, with its driver (often (none), which is normal).
  • ISA bus devices - how many old-style ISA drivers are probing (usually 0).
  • LPC devices enumerated by ACPI PnP - the same resource map as PnP manager.
  • Super I/O - hwmon chips from Nuvoton (nct), ITE (it8) or Fintek (f718), with their platform device.

Healthy / typical values. On the author's PC: LPC bridge 0000:00:14.3 FCH LPC Bridge, 0 ISA devices, one PnP device (PNP0501 COM port at io 0x3f8-0x3ff, irq 4), and the Super I/O hwmon4 nct6799 (nct6775.656).

Where Linux gets it. /sys/bus/pci/devices (class 0601), /sys/bus/isa/devices, /sys/bus/pnp/devices, /sys/class/hwmon.

Background. The Super I/O chip handles the slow, old-style jobs: the serial port, PS/2 and fan/voltage monitoring. On most desktop boards it is the chip SRS reads fan speeds from.

MCA bus

mca-bus - Not present on most PCs

In plain words. MCA (Micro Channel Architecture) was IBM's PS/2 expansion bus from 1987. Linux dropped it long ago.

What you see. Status: Not present on this system, Checked: n/a (no MicroChannel).

Chipset MCH

mch - Linux data - Needs root data

In plain words. On older Intel PCs the MCH (Memory Controller Hub, the "northbridge") held the memory controller. AMD has no MCH. The nearest thing is the Root Complex at 00:00.0, so SRS shows that device in full.

What you see. The full PCI card for 0000:00:00.0:

Field Meaning
Location [ bus - device - function ] in SIV style.
IDs VEN_ DEV_ SUBSYS_ REV_ in Windows style.
Lookup key The key used for the name lookup. Double-click it for Device ID Lookup.
Class The 6-digit class code with its class and sub-class names.
Subsystem Subsystem vendor:device and the vendor name.
Parent bridge The upstream bridge, or root bus.
Driver The driver and module.
IRQ, NUMA node, Local CPUs The interrupt, memory node (-1 = single node) and the CPUs closest to it.
PCIe link, Power state, IOMMU group Shown when the device has them.
BAR / ROM lines Its memory windows, if any.
Modalias The driver-matching ID.

Then a note on why AMD has no MCH, then (with the srs-root cache) the lspci -vvv text and the hex dump of its configuration space.

Healthy / typical values. On the author's PC: 1022:14D8, subsystem 1043:8877 ASUSTeK Computer Inc., class 060000 Bridge / Host bridge, driver ryzen_smu, NUMA node -1, local CPUs 0-15, power state D0.

Where Linux gets it. /sys/bus/pci/devices/0000:00:00.0/*; configuration space from the srs-root cache (pci-all.txt).

Background. On Ryzen the memory controllers (UMC, Unified Memory Controller) are part of the CPU's Data Fabric. Their settings are reached through SMN (System Management Network), which SRS never touches, because doing so can hang the CPU's management firmware. For memory timings see the memory items.

Chipset MRH

mrh - Not present on most PCs

In plain words. The MRH (Memory Repeater Hub) was an Intel 820/840-era chip (1999-2000) that let RDRAM boards use SDRAM. No current PC has one.

What you see. Status: Not present on this system, Checked: n/a (Intel memory repeater hub).

NPU names

npu-names - Not present on most PCs

In plain words. An NPU (Neural Processing Unit) is an AI accelerator. AMD Ryzen AI laptop chips have one (XDNA). Linux lists such devices under /sys/class/accel.

What you see.

  • /sys/class/accel N devices.
  • amdxdna loaded / not loaded (the AMD NPU driver).
  • A note: "Desktop Ryzen 9000 (Granite Ridge) has no XDNA NPU."

What "not present" means. 0 devices on a desktop Ryzen is correct. On a Ryzen AI laptop with 0 devices, install or load amdxdna (kernel 6.14 or newer).

PCI all

pci-all - Linux data - Needs root data

In plain words. This is everything SRS knows about every PCI device, in one long report.

What you see.

  • With the srs-root cache: "Full configuration space (lspci -vvvnnxxx, srs-root cache)", then for each device the full lspci -vvv text (Control/Status flags, capabilities, link status, ASPM, AER) and a hex dump of its configuration space (256 bytes, or 4096 for PCIe).
  • Without it: the same per-device card as Chipset MCH for every device (Location, IDs, Lookup key, Class, Subsystem, Parent bridge, Driver, IRQ, NUMA node, Local CPUs, PCIe link, Power state, IOMMU group, BARs, Modalias), then an orange line saying extended configuration space needs root.

Healthy / typical values. On the author's PC the root cache holds about 3700 lines for 54 devices. Useful lines in the lspci text: LnkCap (what the link can do), LnkSta (what it is doing now) and Kernel driver in use.

Unusual values and what they suggest. LnkSta showing (downgraded). Uncorrectable error bits set under AER (Advanced Error Reporting). DevSta: CorrErr+ that keeps coming back points to a weak link: reseat the card, or set the slot to a lower PCIe generation in the BIOS.

Where Linux gets it. sysfs per device; the root cache holds lspci -vvvnnxxx output.

PCI BARs

pci-bars - Linux data

In plain words. A BAR (Base Address Register) is a window of addresses that a PCI device claims so the CPU can talk to it. This item lists every window: where it is, how big it is and what kind it is.

What you see.

Column Meaning
Location The PCI address.
BAR BAR 0-BAR 5, or ROM (the option ROM / VBIOS window).
Start / End The address range (hex).
Type Memory or I/O, plus Prefetch (safe to read ahead and cache) and 64-bit (can sit above 4 GB), and the size.
Device The device name.

At the end: < 4GB Total and > 4GB Total, the memory BAR space below and above the 4 GB line. You can filter by slot, e.g. pci-bars:03:00.0.

Healthy / typical values. On the author's PC the Radeon RX 9070 XT's BAR 0 is Memory Prefetch 64-bit 16GB at 0x1F800000000. That is the whole 16 GB of VRAM visible to the CPU. Totals: 6.70 MB below 4 GB and 16.25 GB above.

Unusual values and what they suggest. If a modern graphics card's big BAR is only 256MB, Resizable BAR (Smart Access Memory) is off. To turn it on, enable "Above 4G Decoding" and "Re-Size BAR" in the BIOS. This can help some games. A BAR with no address (all zeros) was not assigned: the kernel ran out of address space for it, and the kernel log will say "can't assign".

Where Linux gets it. /sys/bus/pci/devices/*/resource (start, end and flags for each BAR).

PCI bus

pci-bus - Linux data

In plain words. This is the main PCI view: every PCI and PCIe device in a tree, with its name, type, driver and link speed. It is the PCI Bus button on the classic main window, and the PCI bus tab of the USB & PCI devices page.

What you see.

Column Meaning
PCI Location bus:device.function, indented under the bridge it sits behind.
Vendor and Device Names from the PCI ID database.
Device Class e.g. VGA compatible controller, Non-Volatile memory controller, PCI bridge.
Driver The bound driver, or -.
Link For PCIe devices: xW S GT/s PCIe (max xW S GT/s PCIe), the current width and speed, then the maximum. It is blank for devices with no PCIe link.

Footer: Total of N PCI devices (B bridges) in T seconds using <pci.ids> Date ... Version ..., then the board and BIOS line.

The panel buttons go to Device properties, PnP devices, PCI devices and the drive, UAA (audio) and all-device views.

Healthy / typical values. On the author's PC (54 devices, 35 bridges):

  • GPU 03:00.0 Navi 48 -> amdgpu, x16 32.0 GT/s PCIe (max x16 32.0 GT/s PCIe). That is the full PCIe 5.0 x16, through the card's own internal switch (01:00.0/02:00.0).
  • Samsung 980 PRO 04:00.0 on the CPU's M.2 slot: x4 16.0 GT/s (PCIe 4.0 x4, its maximum).
  • Chipset uplink 00:02.1 -> 05:00.0: x4 16.0 GT/s. Everything behind the chipset shares this.
  • Realtek 5GbE 08:00.0: x1 8.0 GT/s. Wi-Fi 7 09:00.0: x1 5.0 GT/s.

Unusual values and what they suggest.

  • Current width lower than max (e.g. x8 ... (max x16 ...) on a graphics card): the card is in a slot wired for fewer lanes, the slot shares lanes with an M.2 drive or a second slot, or the contacts are dirty or the card is not fully seated.
  • Current speed lower than max: often harmless. Graphics cards drop to 2.5 GT/s at idle to save power, so check under load. A bridge port also trains down to the slowest partner: on the author's PC port 06:07.0 reads x1 5.0 GT/s (max x1 8.0 GT/s) because the Wi-Fi card behind it tops out at 5.0. A device that never reaches its maximum under load has a signal problem: a riser cable, or a slot forced to a lower generation in the BIOS.
  • A device with Driver - that should have one (network, storage, graphics) is not supported by your kernel.

Double-click a device row's ID in PCI devices or Device IDs to open Device ID Lookup.

Where Linux gets it. /sys/bus/pci/devices/* (vendor, device, class, driver, current_link_speed, current_link_width, max_link_speed, max_link_width) and pci.ids.

Background - PCIe link speed and width. A PCIe link is made of lanes. Each lane is a pair of wires in each direction. Width (x1, x4, x8, x16) is how many lanes. Speed is how fast each lane runs, in GT/s (gigatransfers per second). Each PCIe generation doubles the speed:

Speed Generation About per lane x4 x16
2.5 GT/s PCIe 1.x 250 MB/s 1 GB/s 4 GB/s
5.0 GT/s PCIe 2.0 500 MB/s 2 GB/s 8 GB/s
8.0 GT/s PCIe 3.0 985 MB/s 3.9 GB/s 15.8 GB/s
16.0 GT/s PCIe 4.0 1.97 GB/s 7.9 GB/s 31.5 GB/s
32.0 GT/s PCIe 5.0 3.94 GB/s 15.8 GB/s 63 GB/s

The link runs at the best speed and width that both ends support. Bridges and switches (upstream and downstream ports) fan one link out to several devices, and those devices share the upstream bandwidth.

PCI devices

pci-dev - Linux data

In plain words. This is a flat list of every PCI device with its ID and class code, like lspci -nn. Add a slot to see one device in full. It is the PCI Dev button in the PCI Bus panel.

What you see.

  • List form: 0000:03:00.0 1002:7550 [0300] VGA compatible controller: <vendor> <device>, which is the full address, vendor:device, the 4-digit class code, and the class and names.
  • Per-device form pci-dev:<slot> (e.g. pci-dev:0000:03:00.0 or pci-dev:03:00.0): the full card described under Chipset MCH, including PCIe link and IOMMU group.

Double-click a 1002:7550-style ID to open Device ID Lookup.

Healthy / typical values. On the author's PC: 0000:04:00.0 144D:A80A [0108] Non-Volatile memory controller: Samsung Electronics Co Ltd SSD 980 PRO and 0000:00:14.3 1022:790E [0601] ISA bridge: ... FCH LPC Bridge.

Where Linux gets it. /sys/bus/pci/devices/* and pci.ids.

Background - PCI address and class code. 0000:03:00.0 is domain🚌device.function. One chip can hold several functions. The GPU is 03:00.0 and its HDMI audio is 03:00.1. The class code says what kind of device it is: 0300 display, 0108 NVMe, 0200 Ethernet, 0280 other network (Wi-Fi), 0403 HD audio, 0604 PCI bridge, 0C03 USB controller.

PCI flags

pci-flag - Windows-only (Linux equivalent shown)

In plain words. On Windows, SIV shows the HAL's PCI workaround flags. On Linux the matching controls are kernel command-line options, so SRS lists the PCI, PCIe, IOMMU and ASPM options you booted with.

What you see. One line per option starting with pci, pcie, or containing iommu or aspm. Or the note "No pci=/pcie_*/iommu options on the kernel command line".

Healthy / typical values. No options at all is the normal default. On the author's PC: pcie_aspm.policy=performance (keeps links out of power saving), pci=pcie_bus_perf (sets the largest safe packet size) and iommu=pt (pass-through: the IOMMU does not remap the host's own devices, which is a little faster).

Unusual values and what they suggest. pci=noaer or pcie_aspm=off are often added to silence error floods. They hide the symptom and do not fix the link. pci=nomsi is a heavy workaround that can reduce performance.

Where Linux gets it. /proc/cmdline.

PCI HAL

pci-hal - Linux data - Needs root data

In plain words. This shows the address "windows" that the firmware gave each PCI bus: which slices of memory and I/O space each bridge passes on to the devices behind it.

What you see.

  • Memory windows - lines of the memory map naming PCI Bus, PCI ECAM, MMCONFIG or pcie, up to 3 levels deep.
  • I/O windows - the same for I/O ports, 2 levels deep, including 0cf8-0cff PCI conf1.
  • PCI buses - the count and the list of bus numbers.

Healthy / typical values. On the author's PC: root window 80000000-dfffffff below 4 GB, a big window 10000000000-1ffffffffff above 4 GB (where the GPU's 16 GB BAR lives, 1f800000000-1fc0fffffff for buses 01-02), the ECAM block e0000000-efffffff, and 21 buses.

Unusual values and what they suggest. No window above 4 GB means "Above 4G Decoding" is off, so Resizable BAR cannot work.

Where Linux gets it. /proc/iomem, /proc/ioports (srs-root cache), /sys/class/pci_bus.

PCI ID database

pci-info - Linux data

In plain words. These are facts about the file SRS uses to turn PCI ID numbers into names.

What you see.

Field Meaning
Database The file path, normally /usr/share/hwdata/pci.ids.
SIV equivalent pcidevs.txt (SIV's own file).
Version / Date When the list was built.
Records How many vendor, device and subsystem names it holds.
Load time How long loading took, and how long this lookup took.
Lookup chain V:D:S:s:RR -> V:D:S:s -> V:D:RR -> V:D -> V, the order SRS tries (see Device IDs).
Class names How many class, subclass and programming-interface names it holds.

Healthy / typical values. On the author's PC: version 2026.10.01, 42,228 names, 224 class records, loaded in about 10 ms.

Unusual values and what they suggest. A date more than a year old means new hardware will show as "Device XXXX". Update the hwdata package. "ids file not found" means hwdata is not installed.

Where Linux gets it. /usr/share/hwdata/pci.ids.

PCI MMIO

pci-mmio - Linux data - Needs root data

In plain words. PCIe devices have up to 4 KB of configuration space each. The CPU reaches it through one big memory window called ECAM (Enhanced Configuration Access Mechanism). The ACPI MCFG table tells the OS where that window is. This item shows it.

What you see.

  • MCFG table - present or absent.
  • ECAM base - its address, PCI segment and bus range (needs the srs-root cache).
  • The PCI ECAM / MMCONFIG line from the memory map.

Healthy / typical values. On the author's PC: ECAM base 0xE0000000 segment 0 buses 0-255, and e0000000-efffffff PCI ECAM 0000 [bus 00-ff]. That is 256 MB: 1 MB per bus × 256 buses.

Unusual values and what they suggest. If MCFG is absent, Linux falls back to the old port 0xCF8 method. That method only reaches the first 256 bytes, so PCIe extended capabilities (AER, ReBAR, link details) become invisible.

Where Linux gets it. /sys/firmware/acpi/tables/MCFG, /proc/iomem.

PCMCIA all

pcm-all - Not present on most PCs

In plain words. PCMCIA / CardBus were credit-card-sized expansion cards for laptops from the 1990s and 2000s. ExpressCard and USB replaced them.

What it would show. Whether /sys/class/pcmcia_socket exists, and how many CardBus/PCMCIA bridges (PCI class 0605/0607) are on the PCI bus.

What "not present" means. On the author's PC: absent and 0. That is expected on any desktop.

PCMCIA bus

pcm-bus - Not present on most PCs

In plain words. This is the same check as PCMCIA all: socket class and bridge count.

What you see. /sys/class/pcmcia_socket absent and CardBus/PCMCIA bridges 0 (PCI class 0605/0607).

PCMCIA ID database

pcm-info - Not present on most PCs

In plain words. SIV has a name list for PCMCIA cards. With no PCMCIA hardware, SRS does not load one.

What you see. Status: Not present on this system, Checked: n/a (no PCMCIA).

I/O PM1 data

pm1-area - Linux data - Needs root data

In plain words. ACPI defines a few fixed blocks of I/O ports for power management. The PM1 blocks handle sleep, wake and the power button. PM_TMR is a 3.58 MHz timer. GPE (General Purpose Events) are wake and event signals. The firmware's FADT (Fixed ACPI Description Table) says where they are. SRS shows the addresses and does not read the registers.

What you see.

  • From the FADT (srs-root cache): PM1a_EVT_BLK, PM1b_EVT_BLK, PM1a_CNT_BLK, PM1b_CNT_BLK, PM2_CNT_BLK, PM_TMR_BLK, GPE0_BLK, GPE1_BLK, each with its port address and length. Unused blocks show 0x0000 in gray.
  • The matching I/O port map lines (ACPI, PM1, PM_TMR, GPE).
  • PM profile - the firmware's "preferred power profile": 1 = Desktop, 2 = Mobile, 3 = Workstation, 4 = Enterprise server, 0 = unspecified.

Healthy / typical values. On the author's PC: PM1a_EVT_BLK 0x0800 length 4, PM1a_CNT_BLK 0x0804 length 2, PM2_CNT_BLK 0x00B4 length 1, PM_TMR_BLK 0x0808 length 4, GPE0_BLK 0x0820 length 8, the "b" blocks unused, and PM profile 1 (Desktop).

Unusual values and what they suggest. A laptop reporting profile 1, or a desktop reporting 2, can change some power defaults. That is a firmware quirk.

Where Linux gets it. /sys/firmware/acpi/tables/FACP (root), /proc/ioports, /sys/firmware/acpi/pm_profile.

PMBus

pmb-bus - Not present on most PCs

In plain words. PMBus is an SMBus-based protocol for "smart" power supplies and voltage regulators that report volts, amps and temperature. Servers have it. A few PSUs expose it over USB instead.

What you see. Status: Not present on this system, Checked: /sys/bus/i2c/devices (no PMBus devices).

What "not present" means. No kernel PMBus driver is bound. A USB-linked PSU (Corsair, NZXT) shows up under the USB items and sensor tools instead.

PnP manager

pnp - Linux data

In plain words. PnP (Plug and Play) devices here are the motherboard's built-in legacy devices that the firmware describes, such as the COM port. This item shows the resources (ports, IRQ, DMA) each one has.

What you see. For each device: <pnp name> <ID> <description> (ACPI <firmware node>), then its resource lines exactly as Linux reports them: state = active, io 0x3f8-0x3ff, irq 4, dma disabled.

Healthy / typical values. On the author's PC there is one device, 00:00 PNP0501 16550A-compatible COM Port (ACPI PNP0501:00), active at io 0x3f8-0x3ff, irq 4. Modern Linux binds most other firmware devices through ACPI directly, so the PnP list is short (see PnP manager details).

Where Linux gets it. /sys/bus/pnp/devices/*/id, .../resources, .../firmware_node.

PnP devices

pnp-dev - Linux data

In plain words. These are the same PnP devices as a one-line table. It is the PnP Dev button in the PCI Bus panel.

What you see.

Column Meaning
Device The PnP device name (00:00).
ID The PnP ID (PNP0501).
Description A built-in name, or the vendor from pnp.ids.
Driver The bound driver (serial).
Resources The active resources in one line (lines that say disabled are left out).

Healthy / typical values. 00:00 PNP0501 16550A-compatible COM Port serial io 0x3f8-0x3ff, irq 4.

Where Linux gets it. /sys/bus/pnp/devices.

PnP ID database

pnp-info - Linux data

In plain words. This item explains the PnP/ACPI ID names and lists every kind of ACPI device ID found on this PC.

What you see.

  • Database - /usr/share/hwdata/pnp.ids. SIV equivalent - pnpdevs.txt.
  • Records - how many 3-letter vendor codes the file has.
  • Built-in - SRS also knows the standard PNPxxxx, ACPIxxxx and LNXxxxx names itself.
  • IDs on this system - each distinct ACPI ID with its name.

Healthy / typical values. On the author's PC: 2557 vendor codes. Some IDs: PNP0C09 ACPI Embedded Controller, PNP0A08 PCI Express Root Bus, MSFT0101 TPM 2.0, AMDI0030 AMD GPIO Controller, ACPI0007 Processor, LNXVIDEO ACPI Video Bus.

Unusual values and what they suggest. For IDs SRS does not know by heart, the name is a guess from the first three letters of the ID. That guess comes from the old 3-letter EISA vendor list. Newer ACPI IDs use a 4-letter vendor prefix (AMDI, ASMT, RTK), so for those the guessed vendor can be wrong. Read such names as hints only.

Where Linux gets it. /usr/share/hwdata/pnp.ids, /sys/bus/acpi/devices.

Background. A PnP ID is 3 letters for the vendor plus 4 hex digits (PNP0501). ACPI also allows 4 letters plus 4 hex digits (AMDI0030). PNP and ACPI IDs are industry-standard device types.

PnP manager details

pnp-man - Linux data

In plain words. This is every device the firmware's ACPI tables describe, with its path in the ACPI "namespace", whether the firmware says it is present, and what Linux attached it to.

What you see.

Column Meaning
Device The ACPI device name (AMDI0010:00).
ACPI Path Its namespace path (\_SB_.I2CA).
_STA The firmware's status value. 0x0F = present, enabled and working. 0x00 absent = turned off or not fitted. - = no status method, so treated as present.
Description The name from the built-in list or pnp.ids.
Bound to The Linux device it became (e.g. cpu0), if any.

Last line: Total of N ACPI devices, P present (no _STA = present).

Healthy / typical values. On the author's PC: 258 ACPI devices, 229 present. The 16 ACPI0007 processor objects map to cpu0-cpu15 (in the order C000 -> cpu0, C001 -> cpu8...: the firmware lists the SMT siblings in turn). AMDI0010:00 (I2C controller A) is 0x0F. I2C B-D and I3C controllers are 0x00 absent, because the board does not wire them.

Unusual values and what they suggest. Many absent entries are normal. Boards share one firmware across models. A device you need (touchpad I2C, TPM) showing absent means it is turned off in the BIOS.

Where Linux gets it. /sys/bus/acpi/devices/*/path, status, physical_node.

COM ports

ports - Linux data

In plain words. This lists the serial (COM) ports. It is the same view as Serial COM ports.

What you see / values. See Serial COM ports.

Device properties

properties - Linux data

In plain words. These are all the udev properties of every PCI and USB device: IDs, names from the hardware database, paths, driver. It is the Properties button in the PCI Bus panel.

What you see. For each PCI device and each USB device (USB interfaces are skipped), the sysfs path in bold, then one line per property:

  • Teal lines from udev's own records: symlink, devnode, priority (symlink priority) and driver.
  • E: properties such as PCI_ID, PCI_SUBSYS_ID, PCI_CLASS, MODALIAS, ID_VENDOR_FROM_DATABASE, ID_MODEL_FROM_DATABASE, ID_PATH. USB devices add BUSNUM, DEVNUM, ID_VENDOR_ID, ID_MODEL_ID, ID_REVISION, ID_SERIAL and so on.

Values whose key contains TOKEN, KEY, SECRET, PASS, AUTH or COOKIE are shown as ********. Use properties:<name> for any single device, e.g. properties:nvme0n1 or properties:0000:03:00.0. Double-click a PCI_ID value (1022:14D8) to open Device ID Lookup.

Healthy / typical values. On the author's PC the Root Complex shows PCI_ID 1022:14D8, PCI_SUBSYS_ID 1043:8877, ID_MODEL_FROM_DATABASE Raphael/Granite Ridge Root Complex, ID_PATH pci-0000:00:00.0.

Unusual values and what they suggest. Missing ID_*_FROM_DATABASE keys mean udev's hardware database (hwdb) does not know the device. Run systemd-hwdb update after updating hwdata. Note that USB serial numbers (ID_SERIAL) appear in full. Remove them before you share a report.

Where Linux gets it. udevadm info --export-db.

Device property

property - Linux data

In plain words. This shows one udev property across every device that has it. By default it shows ID_MODEL_FROM_DATABASE (the database model name).

What you see. Property <KEY>, then one line per device: the device path and the value. At the end: N devices have <KEY>. Choose another key with property:<KEY>, e.g. property:ID_PATH or property:DRIVER. Device property keys lists all keys.

Healthy / typical values. On the author's PC 117 devices have ID_MODEL_FROM_DATABASE, e.g. .../0000:03:00.0 Navi 48 [Radeon RX 9070/9070 XT/9070 GRE]. Child entries (sound cards, network interfaces) repeat their parent's name.

Where Linux gets it. udevadm info --export-db.

PYXIS 21174

pyxis - Not present on most PCs

In plain words. The 21174 "Pyxis" was the core logic chipset of DEC Alpha workstations (about 1997). SIV can read it on Alpha Windows NT. No x86 PC has one.

What you see. Status: Not present on this system, Checked: n/a (DEC Alpha chipset).

Smart cards

scard - Not present on most PCs

In plain words. These are smart card readers: CCID (Chip Card Interface Device) USB readers for ID cards, bank cards and some security tokens.

What you see. Status: Not present on this system, Checked: pcsc_scan (no CCID reader; pcscd inactive).

What "not present" means. No reader is plugged in, and the pcscd smart-card service is not running. With a reader attached, start pcscd and run pcsc_scan. A FIDO/U2F security key is a HID device, not a smart card (see HID bus).

Serial COM ports

serial - Linux data

In plain words. This lists the real serial ports (UARTs, Universal Asynchronous Receiver-Transmitters) and every serial-type TTY driver the kernel has.

What you see.

Column Meaning
Port The Linux name (ttyS0 = COM1, ttyUSB0 = a USB adapter).
I/O The I/O port base address (0x3F8).
IRQ The interrupt line.
UART The chip type (16550A, 16950...). USB and other adapters show usb/other.
Base clock The UART's input clock. The standard is 1.8432 MHz, which gives 115200 baud at the maximum.
Device The device it belongs to (the PnP device 00:00:0.0).

Then N real ports; M unconfigured 8250 placeholders (nr_uarts) hidden. Linux makes empty ttyS1-ttyS31 slots by default, and SRS hides those. Then comes the TTY drivers table from /proc/tty/drivers: driver name, /dev prefix, major number, minor range and type. The note says per-line statistics need root.

Healthy / typical values. On the author's PC: ttyS0 0x3F8 4 16550A 1.8432 MHz 00:00:0.0, with 31 placeholders hidden. The drivers include usbserial /dev/ttyUSB 188, usbch343 /dev/ttyCH343USB 170 (a CH343 USB adapter driver), rfcomm (Bluetooth serial) and serial_8250 /dev/ttyS 4 64-95.

Unusual values and what they suggest. A port with UART unknown is not really there. Many boards have a COM header that only works with a bracket cable fitted. An IRQ of 0 means the port is polled, which is slow. A USB serial adapter appears here only while it is plugged in.

Where Linux gets it. /sys/class/tty/* (type, port, irq, uartclk, device), /proc/tty/drivers.

SI USB

si-usb - Linux data

In plain words. This lists the USB host controllers. Each controller appears as two "root hubs": one for USB 2.0 devices and one for USB 3.x devices.

What you see. Two lines per root hub:

  • usbN <PCI address> <controller name>. Software-only controllers show the platform device and "virtual host controller".
  • USB <version> root hub, <speed> Mbps, <P> ports, <D> devices attached, driver <driver>.

Healthy / typical values. On the author's PC (11 root hubs):

  • usb1/usb2 on 73:00.0 ASMedia ASM4242: USB 2.00 at 480 Mbps and USB 3.10 at 20000 Mbps (20 Gbps, the USB 3.2 Gen 2x2 / USB4 ports).
  • usb3-usb6 on the CPU's two USB 3.1 controllers (75:00.3, 75:00.4): 480 and 10000 Mbps.
  • usb7 on the CPU's USB 2.0 controller 76:00.0.
  • usb8/usb9 on the chipset controller 0b:00.0: 12 USB 2.0 ports with 13 devices, and 5 USB 3 ports at 20000 Mbps.
  • usb10/usb11 = vhci_hcd.0, the USB/IP virtual controller (USB over the network), with 0 devices.

Unusual values and what they suggest. Too many devices on one controller can run out of bandwidth or endpoints. Webcams and audio interfaces are the usual culprits. Move one to a port on a different usbN. A controller that is missing completely may be turned off in the BIOS.

Where Linux gets it. /sys/bus/usb/devices/usb* (version, speed, maxchild), with the controller found from the sysfs path.

Background - USB speeds and descriptors.

Speed Name First in
1.5 Mbps Low Speed USB 1.0 (keyboards, mice)
12 Mbps Full Speed USB 1.1
480 Mbps High Speed USB 2.0
5000 Mbps SuperSpeed USB 3.0 / 3.2 Gen 1
10000 Mbps SuperSpeed+ USB 3.1 / 3.2 Gen 2
20000 Mbps SuperSpeed+ 20 Gbps USB 3.2 Gen 2x2

A USB 3 port is really two buses in one connector. That is why each controller has a 2.0 root hub and a 3.x root hub, and why a slow device plugged into a blue port appears on the 2.0 hub. Every USB device describes itself with descriptors. The device descriptor gives the vendor ID (VID), product ID (PID), release number (bcdDevice) and class. The configuration descriptor gives the power draw. Each interface descriptor has a class, subclass and protocol, for example 03 = HID, 08 = mass storage, 0E = video. Each endpoint descriptor is one data pipe with its type and packet size. Part 2 of this reference covers the USB device lists, which show all of these.

SMBus

smb - Linux data

In plain words. SMBus (System Management Bus) and I2C (Inter-Integrated Circuit) are slow two-wire buses for small chips: RAM SPD (Serial Presence Detect) EEPROMs, temperature sensors, RGB controllers, and the graphics card's monitor (DDC) lines. This item lists every bus adapter.

What you see.

  • Controller - the PCI SMBus controller (class 0C05) with its revision and driver.
  • One line per adapter: i2c-N <adapter name> <parent device>. SMBus adapters are in bold.
  • A note: names come from sysfs only. No bus is opened or scanned.

Healthy / typical values. On the author's PC: controller 0000:00:14.0 FCH SMBus Controller rev 71 driver piix4_smbus. Adapters i2c-1/i2c-2 "SMBus PIIX4 adapter port 0/2 at 0b00" and i2c-3 "port 1 at 0b20" (the RAM slots are on port 0). i2c-0 is the Synopsys DesignWare I2C, i2c-4/5 are "AMDGPU SMU", and i2c-6 to 12 are the GPU's display (DM) and DisplayPort AUX buses.

Unusual values and what they suggest. No PIIX4 adapters means i2c_piix4 is not loaded. Then RAM SPD, temperature and OpenRGB RAM lighting will not work.

Where Linux gets it. /sys/bus/i2c/devices/i2c-*/name, /sys/bus/pci/devices (class 0C05).

SMBus devices

smb-bus - Linux data

In plain words. These are the chips on the SMBus / I2C buses that a kernel driver has claimed. SRS lists only those. It never probes for others.

What you see.

Column Meaning
Client <bus>-<address> (e.g. 1-0051 = bus 1, address 0x51), or an ACPI name.
Name The chip type.
Driver The bound driver, or (none).
Adapter The bus it is on and that bus's name.

Last line: Total of N I2C client devices (bus-addr; 0x50-0x57 = SPD5118 hub on DDR5).

Healthy / typical values. On the author's PC: 1-0051 and 1-0053, both spd5118, on i2c-1 SMBus PIIX4 adapter port 0. These are the SPD hubs of the two DDR5 sticks (their addresses tell you which slots are filled). There are also two Realtek ACPI devices on the DesignWare I2C bus with no driver.

Unusual values and what they suggest. Fewer spd5118 entries than DIMMs fitted means the spd5118 module is not loaded, or a stick's SPD hub did not answer. That is worth a reseat if the memory count is also wrong.

Where Linux gets it. /sys/bus/i2c/devices/<bus>-<addr> (name, driver).

SMBus status

smb-sts - Linux data - Needs root data

In plain words. SIV reads the SMBus controller's status registers. SRS only shows where they are, because touching them can collide with the kernel driver and with RGB or sensor programs that use the bus at the same time.

What you see. The I/O port ranges owned by piix4_smbus / smbus, and a note explaining why the registers are not read.

Healthy / typical values. On the author's PC: 0b00-0b08 and 0b20-0b28, both piix4_smbus (the FCH's two SMBus controllers).

Where Linux gets it. /proc/ioports (srs-root cache).

SMBus setup

smbus-setup - Linux data

In plain words. This shows how SRS handles SMBus: it never probes, and it trusts only what the kernel has found. It also lists every I2C driver and how many chips each one has claimed.

What you see.

  • Probing - disabled, with the reason (CoolerControl, liquidctl, OpenRGB and the kernel own the bus).
  • Data source - kernel-made clients in /sys/bus/i2c/devices/<bus>-<addr>.
  • I2C drivers - every loaded I2C driver with N clients.

Healthy / typical values. On the author's PC almost every driver has 0 clients. These are built into the kernel for other hardware. spd5118 has 2 clients (the two DDR5 sticks).

Where Linux gets it. /sys/bus/i2c/drivers/*.

System SMBus access

smbus-system - Linux data

In plain words. This shows whether programs can reach the SMBus / I2C buses from user space, and who is allowed to.

What you see.

  • i2c-dev module - loaded (/dev/i2c-* nodes exist) or not loaded.
  • One line per /dev/i2c-N: mode (permissions), uid, gid. These are checked with stat only, never opened.
  • Device nodes - the count.
  • piix4_smbus - whether the AMD/Intel PIIX4 SMBus driver is loaded.

Healthy / typical values. On the author's PC: 13 nodes, all mode 0660 uid 0 gid 963. Root and one group (the i2c group that OpenRGB-style packages create) can read and write. Everyone else cannot.

Unusual values and what they suggest. 0666 (anyone can write) lets any program send raw commands to RAM or GPU chips. That is a risk, so prefer a group. i2c-dev not loaded explains why OpenRGB or decode-dimms find nothing. Load it with modprobe i2c-dev.

Where Linux gets it. /sys/class/i2c-dev, stat() of /dev/i2c-*, /sys/module/i2c_dev, /sys/module/i2c_piix4.

Buses / Devices (part 2 of 2) (SRS Section Reference)

Back to the section index - Glossary

Part 1

Where to find these items (SRS 2.0). In the main window they are on the USB & PCI devices page (Alt+0). Its tabs are ALL Devices, PCI bus, USB bus, USB tree, HID bus and Thunderbolt; All N items lists the rest. You can also type an item's name or id into the search box (Ctrl+F). The rest of this introduction describes the classic view (Menu -> Classic View), with its Menu and panel buttons.

This is the second half (alphabetical) of the Buses / Devices group. It covers the system resource maps (memory, I/O ports, interrupts), bus address translation, Thunderbolt / USB4, every USB view (bus, tree, devices, names, owners, flags, ID database), portable (MTP/PTP) devices, and two families of items for rare hardware: XMC mezzanine cards and the HP zx1 chipset. Open any item from Menu -> Buses / Devices -> item. The panel buttons lead to the busiest ones: USB Bus opens USB bus, and its sub-buttons are Link Devices, USB Disks, HID Bus and USB Info (the last opens USB ID database); PCI Bus has the sub-buttons Properties, PnP Dev, Drives, PCI Dev, UAA Dev and ALL Dev (see part 1). Only System HAL resources and System resources need root data: without it the kernel hides the real addresses, so start the root helper once with Menu -> Run as root (srs-root). In any panel, double-clicking a device ID written as VVVV:DDDD (for example 0bda:8153) opens Device ID Lookup for that ID.
