CPU IPI Delay

ipi-delay - Linux data

In plain words. It measures how long it takes one CPU to pass a message to another CPU through the cache. Every pair of CPUs is tested, and the result is a table in nanoseconds.

What you see.

Field Meaning Why it matters
Header "CPU IPI Delay (core-to-core cache-line round trip / 2, ns)". The number is the one-way time: a full there-and-back trip divided by 2.
Rounds per pair How many there-and-back trips were timed for each pair (GUI default 20000, range 1000-1000000). More rounds give a steadier average.
From\To Row = sending CPU, column = receiving CPU. Find any pair at the crossing point.
- The diagonal (a CPU to itself). Not measured.
Numbers One-way delay in ns. Shown in green below 40 ns, normal colour from 40 to 99 ns, orange at 100 ns or more. Low = the two CPUs are close together on the chip.
Footer Board and BIOS.

Each pair is measured once, so the table is a mirror: the CPU-3 -> CPU-5 cell always equals CPU-5 -> CPU-3. If it has never been run, the item shows Status Not run yet, Run it (Menu > Tools > IPI Delay, then Run) and Command line srs-gui ipi [--cpus N] [--rounds R].

The GUI window (Menu -> IPI Delay...) has a CPUs box (test only the first N CPUs), a Rounds per pair box, a Run button (it asks first: two CPU threads busy at a time, about a second at the defaults; sysreport-search ipi asks the same, --yes starts at once), and a heat map under the text. The heat map is coloured from green (fastest) to red (slowest), scaled to the largest value.

Healthy / typical values. On the author's 7800X3D (one CCD, 8 cores, 50000 rounds):

  • Sibling pairs (CPU-0 and CPU-8, CPU-1 and CPU-9, ...): 24-25 ns. They share one core and its L1 and L2 caches.
  • All other pairs: about 28-39 ns. They meet in the shared L3 cache.
  • The table is flat apart from the sibling diagonal, because all 8 cores sit on the same CCD.

Unusual values and what they suggest.

  • A block of the table much higher than the rest (often 70-150 ns): the CPU has more than one CCD (core complex die), for example a Ryzen 9 7950X, or more than one socket or NUMA node. Pairs on different dies must go through the Infinity Fabric (or the ring/mesh between tiles) and are much slower. Games and audio work run better when their threads stay on one die.
  • One CPU slow to every other CPU: it was busy with other work during the test, or it was in a deep sleep state. Close other programs and run again.
  • Siblings no faster than other pairs: SMT may be off, or the CPU numbering is not what you expect.

Where Linux gets it. Built-in test. Two threads are pinned to the two CPUs and bounce one shared cache line (a flag in memory) back and forth with atomic loads and stores. The first third of the rounds is an untimed warm-up. Timing uses CLOCK_MONOTONIC. The result is stored in ~/.cache/srs/bench-ipi-delay.txt.

Background. "IPI" stands for Inter-Processor Interrupt, a signal one CPU sends to another. SRS keeps SIV's name, but it does not send real interrupts. It measures the core-to-core cache-line delay, which is the cost every program pays when threads on two cores share data (locks, queues, game engine job systems).

For a step-by-step reading of one real 16-CPU result (partner threads, the shared L3, what a two-CCD CPU looks like, and what the table is useful for), see the User Guide, section 9.2.2 Reading the CPU IPI Delay table - a worked example.

IPI Dump

ipi-dmp - Linux data

In plain words. In SIV this is the raw dump of the IPI measurements. In SRS it prints exactly the same table as CPU IPI Delay.

What you see. The same Rounds per pair line and From\To matrix, from the last stored run. See CPU IPI Delay for what every number means.

Where Linux gets it. ~/.cache/srs/bench-ipi-delay.txt (the last IPI run).

IPI Plots

ipi-plots - Linux data

In plain words. In SIV this shows the IPI results as graphs. In a saved report SRS prints the same table as CPU IPI Delay. The picture version is the heat map in the GUI IPI Delay window.

What you see. In a report: the same matrix as CPU IPI Delay. In the GUI: a square grid with one cell per CPU pair, green for the fastest pairs and red for the slowest. The heat map appears after a run in the open program. After a restart you see the stored table but an empty map until you press Run again.

Healthy / typical values. On the author's single-CCD 7800X3D the map is almost one colour, with a darker green diagonal line for the sibling pairs. A dual-CCD CPU shows four clear squares: two fast (inside each die) and two slow (between the dies).

Where Linux gets it. Same test as CPU IPI Delay.

Memory Latency

latency - Linux data

In plain words. It measures how long the CPU waits for one piece of data, using blocks of memory that get bigger and bigger. Small blocks fit in the fast caches. Big blocks have to come from RAM. The jumps in the result show where each cache ends.

What you see.

Column Meaning Why it matters
Block Size of the memory block tested: 4KB, 8KB, 16KB, ... doubling up to the largest size (default 256MB; 1-4096 MB in the GUI and on the command line). Each size lands in a different cache level.
Latency Average time for one load, in nanoseconds. Best of 5 passes of 2 million loads. Lower is faster.
Level L1, L2, L3 or DRAM - a rough label for where a block of that size usually lives. Helps you read the table.

The last line names the cache sizes used for the Level column, read from /sys/devices/system/cpu/cpu0/cache (for example "L1d 32KB, L2 1MB, L3 96MB"): a block is labelled with the smallest cache it fits in, and DRAM above the last level. Labels are indicative; the jumps in the Latency column are the real boundaries (compare Cache Levels, cache). If never run, the item shows Status Not run yet and Command line srs-gui latency [--max MB].

The GUI window (Menu -> Latency...) has a "Largest block (MB)" box, a Run button (it asks first: one CPU thread and that much memory, about 3 seconds at 256 MB; sysreport-search latency asks the same, --yes starts at once) and a line graph of latency against block size.

Healthy / typical values. On the author's 7800X3D (L1 data 32K, L2 1024K, L3 96 MB "3D V-Cache"), run up to 64MB:

  • 4KB-32KB: about 1-4 ns (L1). The 4KB result, 0.94 ns, is about 4-5 clock cycles at 5 GHz.
  • 64KB-1MB: about 3.0-3.3 ns (L2), roughly 14 cycles.
  • 2MB-64MB: about 8.6-11 ns (L3). 64MB still reads as L3 because the X3D's L3 is 96 MB.
  • Larger blocks (128MB, 256MB) would show the DRAM step. On a typical DDR5 system that is around 60-90 ns.

Small blocks can jump around a little (8KB was 3.74 ns in the same run). That is timing noise: the whole 4-32 KB range is still L1.

Unusual values and what they suggest.

  • The L2 to L3 step happens at a smaller block than your L2 size: something else is using the cache, or the run was disturbed.
  • DRAM latency well above about 100 ns on DDR5 (or about 80 ns on a tuned DDR4 system): loose memory timings, EXPO/XMP not enabled, or the memory controller running at a lower ratio (for example UCLK at half the memory clock on AM5).
  • L3 latency much higher than expected on a multi-die CPU: on most Ryzen chips each CCD has its own L3. A block bigger than one CCD's L3 goes to DRAM, not to the other die's cache.

Where Linux gets it. Built-in "pointer chase": a buffer is filled with links in random order, and each load needs the address from the load before. That defeats prefetching, so every step pays the full delay. Lines are 64 bytes. A 200 ms busy spin first brings the core to full clock. Stored in ~/.cache/srs/bench-latency.txt.

Background. A cache level is a small, fast memory between the core and RAM. L1 is the smallest and fastest (tens of KB per core), L2 is bigger (about 1-2 MB per core), and L3 is shared by many cores (tens of MB). Data the CPU uses often stays close. Latency (waiting time) matters most for programs that jump around in memory, such as games and databases.

Cache & Memory benchmark

cache-memory - Linux data

In plain words. How fast the RAM and each cache level (L1, L2, L3) can read, write and copy data, and how long each takes to answer one request (latency). It shows whether the memory runs as fast as it should after a BIOS, EXPO/XMP or memory-timing change, and what each cache level gives you.

What you see. A table: rows Memory (RAM), L1 cache, L2 cache, L3 cache; columns Read, Write, Copy (MB/s for the RAM, GB/s for the caches; 1 MB = 1,000,000 bytes) and Latency (ns). Below it: threads and vector code used (AVX-512, AVX2 or SSE2), how the RAM write was measured, the processor, the measured clock during the run, the base clock (measured, so a board running 105 MHz shows 105), the multiplier, the Infinity Fabric clock (AMD Ryzen 7000 desktop with the ryzen_smu driver), the memory type, speed and channels (from root data), the memory clock as a multiple of the base clock, and the cache sizes.

Value How it is measured
Read / Write / Copy One thread pinned to every chosen logical CPU, each in its own block sized to stay inside that cache level (half of its share of L1 / L2 / L3), or for the RAM a block of at least 4 x L3 (at least 256 MB, default 1 GB). Best of repeated 40-80 ms trials over the measuring time (default 1 s per value). Copy counts the bytes read plus the bytes written.
RAM Write on AMD With CLZERO (whole zeroed cache lines written to memory), one thread per core, in 4 KB turns, over 256 MB or 2.5 x L3 - what the memory itself absorbs. Ordinary streaming stores stop at the core-to-memory link's write limit; --mem-write stream shows that figure. Other CPUs use streaming stores.
Latency One thread, a random chain through every 64-byte line of a block. Caches on ordinary 4 KB pages (L1: half of L1d, L2: half of L2, L3: 8 x L2); the RAM on 2 MB pages over 8 x L3 (at least 256 MB, at most half of free RAM), so page-table walks and L3 hits do not distort it.

Healthy / typical values. Ryzen 7 7800X3D, 2 x 16 GB DDR5-6000, FCLK 2000-2133, all 16 threads: RAM about 63,700 MB/s read, 93,800 MB/s write (CLZERO), 63,600 MB/s copy, 80-82 ns; L1 about 2,300 GB/s read and 0.8 ns; L2 about 1,200 GB/s and 3.7 ns; L3 about 700 GB/s and 11-12 ns. Results vary by a few % from run to run.

Unusual values and what they suggest.

  • RAM read far below the kit's rating (DDR5-6000 dual channel: roughly 60,000+ MB/s): EXPO/XMP off, one stick in the wrong slot (single channel), or the memory controller at a lower ratio.
  • RAM latency well over 90 ns on DDR5: loose timings, or UCLK at half the memory clock.
  • Everything 10-50% low or jumping between runs: other programs are busy. Close them and run again; never run another benchmark (or a second copy of SRS) at the same time - both results are spoiled.

Where Linux gets it. Built in. The measuring engine comes unchanged from Linux System Audit (LSA) 0.2.0, the same author's project, now part of SRS. x86-64 CPUs only (it uses x86-64 vector code). The base clock is the TSC rate x 100 / the CPU's ACPI CPPC nominal frequency; the Infinity Fabric clock is read (read-only) from the ryzen_smu driver's PM table, layout 0x540104 only; the memory sticks come from the root DMI data (Tools > Collect root data). Stored in ~/.cache/srs/bench-cachemem.txt; each run is added to the Benchmark history. It asks before it starts, and only one benchmark runs at a time in SRS.

Storage benchmark

storage-bench - Linux data

In plain words. How fast the drive that holds a folder you choose can read and write: big files in one go (sequential), lots of small 4 KB pieces at once (like a busy system), and one small piece at a time (how snappy the PC feels). It works on its own temporary test file only - your files are never opened, changed or deleted.

What you see. Six rows - Sequential 1 MiB (Q8T1), 4K random (Q32T16; Q8T4 in the Light profile) and 4K random (Q1T1), each Read and Write - with Average (the whole test), Peak (the best quarter second) and IOPS (requests per second) for the 4K rows. Then the response time of single 4K reads and writes (mean, median, 95% and 99% under, slowest), the drive model and connection (NVMe, SATA, USB; never the serial number), the folder and file system, the test file size and I/O mode, and the drive temperature before and after (when the drive has a sensor). Q = requests in flight per thread, T = threads; Q x T requests are in flight at once.

Setting Choices
Folder Any folder you can write to on the drive you want to test (default: your home folder)
Test file 256 MB, 1 GB (default), 4 GB, 16 GB
Seconds per test 1-30 (default 5)
Profile Standard (4K random Q32T16 = 16 threads) or Light (Q8T4 = at most 4 threads)
Allow USB drives Off by default

Safety.

  • The test file is created new (it can never be one of your files) and is unlinked at once: it has no name while the test runs and its space is freed the moment the test ends - also after Stop, a crash or a forced kill. Nothing is ever left behind.
  • Refused: folders in RAM (tmpfs - /tmp on many systems), network and FUSE file systems, read-only media, and anything with less than twice the test size free (+0.5 GB). USB drives only when you tick Allow USB drives (some USB enclosures drop off under heavy load). Hard disks get a warning.
  • It asks before it starts, showing the drive, the folder and how much it writes.
  • Writes count only once they are on the drive (fdatasync is inside the timing).

Healthy / typical values. Samsung 980 PRO 1 TB (PCIe 4.0 x4 NVMe), btrfs, 64 MB file, 1 s per test, Light profile: sequential read about 6,500 MB/s, write about 3,200 MB/s; 4K Q8T4 read about 1,400 MB/s (350,000 IOPS); 4K Q1T1 read about 51 MB/s (median 72 us), write about 150 MB/s. A SATA SSD tops out near 550 MB/s sequential; a hard disk manages about 150-250 MB/s sequential and around 1 MB/s (100-200 IOPS) at 4K Q1T1.

Unusual values and what they suggest.

  • NVMe sequential read far below its rating: the drive sits in a slower M.2 slot or PCIe lanes are shared (see the PCI pages for the link speed and width), or it is hot and throttling (watch the temperature line).
  • Write much lower on a longer test than a short one: the drive's fast SLC write cache filled up; that is normal for consumer SSDs.
  • Small test files (256 MB) can fit in the drive's own cache and read very fast; use 1 GB or more for figures to compare.
  • "buffered I/O" in the Test file line: the file system refused direct I/O; the page cache was dropped before each read test, but results can still be a little high.

Where Linux gets it. Built in: O_DIRECT I/O with Linux native asynchronous I/O (io_submit) for real queue depths, incompressible random data; the drive is found through /proc/self/mountinfo and /sys/block (device-mapper and RAID followed to the first member); the temperature from the drive's hwmon sensor. Drive health (SMART) is on the Storage page. Stored in ~/.cache/srs/bench-storage.txt; each run is added to the Benchmark history.

OS latency benchmark

os-latency - Linux data

In plain words. How quickly the operating system answers a program: how long a basic request to the kernel takes, how fast it switches between two programs, how long it takes to start a thread or a program, how soon a sleeping program wakes up, and what a new page of memory or a small file costs. Lower is better. Steady numbers (95% and 99% close to the median) mean a smooth, responsive desktop.

What you see. One row per test with Median (typical), 95% and 99% (19 in 20 and 99 in 100 samples were this fast or faster), Worst, Best, the number of samples and how it was measured. The groups are System calls, Context switches, Starting threads and processes, Wake-up latency, Timers, Memory mapping and page faults, and File metadata. Below the table: the CPU scheduler that is running (for example scx_lavd under sched_ext, BORE or EEVDF), the preemption mode, the timer tick (CONFIG_HZ), the clock source, the timer slack, transparent huge pages, the CPUs used and the file system of the test folder. Times are in ns, µs or ms.

Group (--only word) Rows
System calls (syscall) getpid() as a real system call; clock_gettime through the vDSO and as a system call; read() of 1 byte from /dev/zero; sched_yield() (each sample is a batch of 32, divided)
Context switches (switch) Pipe ping-pong between 2 threads and between 2 processes, on the same CPU and on two cores; the figure is half a round trip
Starting threads and processes (spawn) Thread create + join; fork() + wait (with the program's RAM use, which fork cost grows with); posix_spawn of /bin/true + wait
Wake-up latency (wake) Futex wake on two cores and not pinned; condition-variable signal on two cores; from the wake call until the sleeper runs
Timers (timer) How late a 50 µs and a 1 ms sleep end; how late a periodic 1 ms tick fires, with missed ticks counted
Memory (memory) First-write page fault on a 4 KiB page and on a 2 MiB transparent huge page (skipped when THP is never); mmap and munmap of 64 KiB
File metadata (files) Create a small file (open + 100-byte write + close), stat it, delete it
Setting Choices
Samples 1,000-200,000 in the window (command line 100-1,000,000), default 20,000
Tick test 1-30 s in the window (command line 0.1-60), default 3

Safety. It asks before it starts. It only reads system settings: no root, and no scheduler, priority or timer change. At most two CPUs are busy at a time, for about 6 seconds at the defaults. CPU affinity follows the limits you set (taskset, cpusets). The file test works in its own temporary folder in ~/.cache/srs, which is removed at the end, after Stop, and (for a killed run) on the next run; a folder that holds anything not made by SRS is left alone.

Healthy / typical values. Ryzen 7 7800X3D, Linux 7.3 with scx_lavd (medians): system call 35 ns, vDSO clock read 16 ns, pipe switch 1.1 µs on one CPU and 2.0 µs between two cores, thread start 10 µs, fork 59 µs, program start 142 µs, futex wake 1.9 µs, 4 KiB page fault 0.4 µs, 2 MiB page fault 19 µs, small file create 1.8 µs (tmpfs). Sleeps and the 1 ms tick run about 50 µs late, which is Linux's default timer slack.

Unusual values and what they suggest.

  • Wake-ups, the 99% column or Worst in the hundreds of µs, or missed ticks: deep CPU power-saving states (C-states), heavy background work or a busy scheduler. Outliers like this on idle cores are real wake-up costs, not a fault in SRS.
  • Sleeps late by much more than 50 µs: a larger timer slack (some power-saving tools raise it).
  • A slow fork: a large program; the row shows its RAM use.
  • 2 MiB faults much slower than usual: the kernel had to compact memory to find a huge page; the row says how many faults really got one.

Where Linux gets it. Built in: system calls, pipes, futexes and clocks timed with clock_gettime; the scheduler from /sys/kernel/sched_ext (sched_ext ops such as scx_lavd), /proc/sys/kernel/sched_bore, the kernel config or the kernel version; preemption from uname and the kernel command line; CONFIG_HZ from /boot/config-<release> or the kernel headers' .config (not from /proc/config.gz); the clock source from /sys/devices/system/clocksource; THP from /sys/kernel/mm/transparent_hugepage. Stored in ~/.cache/srs/bench-os-latency.txt; each run is added to the Benchmark history. Only one benchmark runs at a time in SRS.

CPU compute benchmark

cpu-compute - Linux data

In plain words. How fast the processor does floating-point number crunching, the maths in 3D, video, science and AI programs. Higher is better. Every answer is checked: a wrong answer is shown as WRONG instead of a score.

What you see. One row per test with the result on 1 thread and on N threads (default all logical CPUs, one pinned thread per CPU, each with its own copy of the work), the unit, the code path used (Code) and the check. Below: the self-test, the threads and the measuring time.

Test (--tests word) What it does Unit
Matrix multiply, single / double (sgemm, dgemm) 288 x 288 matrices, register-blocked GFLOPS (2 n³ per multiply)
Peak multiply-add, single / double (fma-sp, fma-dp) 12 independent chains of multiply-adds GFLOPS (a fused multiply-add counts 2)
FFT, single / double (fft-sp, fft-dp) 4096-point complex radix-2 transform GFLOPS (5 N log2 N per transform)
N-body (nbody) gravity between 1,024 bodies, double precision GFLOPS (20 per pair)
Mandelbrot (mandelbrot) 640 x 480, up to 255 steps, double precision Mpixels/s
Ray tracer (raytrace) 320 x 240, 4 balls on a floor, shadows, 2 reflections, single precision Mpixels/s
Setting Choices
Threads 1 to all logical CPUs (default all)
Seconds per test 0.1-10 in the window (command line 0.1-60), default 0.5
Code best available (default), plain C, SSE2, AVX2 + FMA, AVX-512; a path the CPU lacks falls back to the best it has
1 thread only skip the N-thread column

How the answers are checked. Matrix multiply uses inputs whose products and sums are exact, so the result must match an integer reference exactly on every code path. Multiply-add returns every value to its start exactly. The FFT is compared with a direct transform and an energy check (Parseval). N-body is compared with a separate double-precision reference. The Mandelbrot vector code must give the same picture as plain C. The ray tracer's single-precision picture is compared with a double-precision one. Every timed repeat must give the same output as the first. A failed check shows the row as WRONG (red), the history line says WRONG and the exit code is 1.

Safety. It asks before it starts. With N threads every CPU is 100% busy and gets hot, and AVX-512 draws a lot of power: an unstable overclock or undervolt may crash the PC. 1 thread only keeps it light. It does not start while CPU Burnin or Stress runs.

Healthy / typical values. Ryzen 7 7800X3D, AVX-512, 2 threads, 0.1 s (a short test run, not a full result): SGEMM about 145 GFLOPS on 1 thread, DGEMM about 77, peak multiply-add single about 160, FFT single about 8, N-body about 29 GFLOPS, Mandelbrot about 44 Mpixels/s, ray tracer about 28 Mpixels/s; the 2-thread column is about double. Plain C SGEMM on the same CPU is about 7 GFLOPS, SSE2 about 47, AVX2 about 121.

Unusual values and what they suggest.

  • WRONG in any row: the CPU gave a wrong answer - an unstable overclock, undervolt or memory setting. Go back to stock settings and run it again.
  • The N-thread column far below threads x the 1-thread figure: thermal or power limits, or other programs are busy.
  • AVX-512 not much faster than AVX2: normal on CPUs that run AVX-512 at half width (Zen 4) or lower their clock under AVX-512 load.

Where Linux gets it. Built in: SRS's own code with Intel intrinsics, the code path chosen at run time with __builtin_cpu_supports, so a generic x86-64 package still uses AVX-512. On ARM (aarch64) only plain C runs. Stored in ~/.cache/srs/bench-compute.txt; each run is added to the Benchmark history. Only one benchmark runs at a time in SRS.

Everyday work benchmark

everyday-work - Linux data

In plain words. How fast the PC does the work it does all day long: compressing and unpacking files, sorting, checksums and hashes, searching and checking text, and running a small program in an interpreter. Higher is better. Every result is checked, so a wrong answer is reported instead of a fast number.

What you see. One row per test with the result on 1 thread and on N threads (default all logical CPUs; one pinned thread per CPU, each with its own copy of the data) and the check. Compression rows also show the ratio on text-like, record-like and random data. Below: the library versions found, the self-test, the data size and the threads.

Group (--only word) Rows Unit How each result is checked
Compression (compress) zlib -1 / -6 / -9, zstd -1 / -3 / -19, lz4, xz -1 / -6; compress and decompress MB/s of original data full round trip: length and every byte equal the original
Sorting (sort) 64-bit integers: C library qsort, radix sort; strings: qsort, multikey quicksort Mkeys/s in order, and a sum / hash of the keys shows nothing was lost or doubled
Checksums and hashes (hash) CRC32 (byte table, slicing-by-8), CRC32C (table, CPU instruction on x86-64), xxHash64, FNV-1a GB/s known-answer self-test, then every pass equals a value from the simple version
Text processing (text) substring search (memmem, Boyer-Moore-Horspool), JSON check, UTF-8 check GB/s match count, JSON token count and code point count equal what the generator wrote
Bytecode interpreter (interp) switch dispatch, threaded dispatch Mops/s prime count and hash equal a plain C reference
Setting Choices
Threads 1 to all logical CPUs (default all)
Seconds per test 0.1-10 in the window (command line 0.1-60), default 0.5
Test groups / libraries tick boxes (command line --only, --libs)
1 thread only skip the N-thread column
Data size 1024 KB of each kind per thread (command line --part-kib, 64-16384)

Libraries. The compression libraries are the system's own - libz.so.1, libzstd.so.1, liblz4.so.1, liblzma.so.5 - loaded when the test runs; SRS needs none of them to start. A missing one shows "not installed" and its rows are skipped.

Safety. It asks before it starts, with the expected time (about half a minute at the defaults; the estimate is rough). The data is generated by SRS from fixed seeds, so every run and every PC does the same work; your files are never read or written. With N threads every CPU is 100% busy; xz -6 and zstd -19 use about 100 MB of memory per thread, and fewer threads are used (with a note) when free memory is short. It does not start while CPU Burnin or Stress runs.

Healthy / typical values. Depend strongly on the CPU and the library versions; compare runs on the same PC and SRS build. Ryzen 7 7800X3D, one thread, generic package build (a short run): lz4 about 1,000 MB/s compress and 7,400 MB/s unpack; zstd -1 about 650 / 2,200 MB/s; zlib -6 about 74 / 1,800 MB/s; zstd -19 and xz -6 about 6-7 MB/s compress; radix sort about 110 Mkeys/s against 17 for qsort; CRC32C with the CPU instruction about 14 GB/s, xxHash64 about 15 GB/s, CRC32 slicing-by-8 about 3 GB/s; the interpreter about 1,250-1,500 Mops/s. Random data does not shrink (ratio about 1.0); text and records shrink about 1.8-4.8 times.

Unusual values and what they suggest.

  • A row marked as failed: a wrong result - an unstable overclock, undervolt or memory setting.
  • "not installed": the library is missing; install it (zstd, lz4, xz / liblzma packages) to get those rows.
  • N-thread figures far below threads x the 1-thread figure: memory bandwidth, thermal or power limits, or other programs are busy.

Where Linux gets it. Built in: SRS's own sorting, checksum, text and interpreter code; the compression libraries through dlopen; threads pinned with sched_setaffinity. Stored in ~/.cache/srs/bench-work.txt; each test group adds a line (work-compress, work-sort, work-hash, work-text, work-interp) to the Benchmark history. Only one benchmark runs at a time in SRS.

Network benchmark

net-bench - Linux data

In plain words. Two separate tests. On this computer (loopback, 127.0.0.1) sends data between two programs on this PC: how fast Linux and the CPU move network data, and how long a message takes to go there and back. Nothing leaves the computer and no network card is used. Internet (optional, asks separately) measures the real connection against Cloudflare's public speed test (speed.cloudflare.com): name lookup (DNS), connect and HTTPS times, and download and upload speed with 1 and N connections.

What you see.

Row How Unit
TCP, 1 stream (loopback) one connection, 128 KiB writes Mbit/s average and peak
TCP, N streams (loopback) N connections at once (default 4) Mbit/s
UDP, 1472-byte packets (loopback) one sender, one receiver; lost packets counted Mbit/s received, % lost
TCP / UDP round trip (loopback) 8-byte ping-pong (TCP_NODELAY; UDP with sequence numbers) median, best, 99% under, jitter
DNS lookup (internet) first lookup of the server name, repeated (median of 5, usually cached), one made-up name under the server's domain (not cached) ms
HTTPS request (internet) 3 new connections: TCP connect, TLS handshake, server reply (medians) ms
Connect time (internet) 10 plain TCP connects to port 443 of each host median, best, 99%, jitter, lost
Download / upload, 1 and N streams (internet) GET /__down?bytes=25000000 / POST /__up with 25 MB of random data per request, repeated until the time is up Mbit/s average and peak

Below: the connection (kind such as wired, Wi-Fi, VPN; link speed, duplex, MTU, Wi-Fi signal), the IP version used, the libcurl version and whether a proxy variable is set (only its name).

Setting Choices
Parts On this computer (default on), Internet speed test (default off; asks separately)
Streams 1-32 (default 4)
Seconds per test 1-30 in the window (command line 0.1-60), default 5; round trip tests use at most 1 s
IP version IPv4 or IPv6 (default), IPv4 only, IPv6 only
Data cap per transfer test 250 MB (command line --max-mb, 0 = no cap)

Safety and privacy.

  • The loopback test asks before it starts; the internet test asks separately (No is the default) and states the server, the hosts, the tests, the time and the data use - up to about 1000 MB with the defaults (4 x 250 MB; about 250 MB on a 100 Mbit/s line). It also says the server sees your public IP address. It never runs without that Yes. Avoid metered or mobile connections.
  • Nothing private is shown or saved: no IP address (local or public), MAC address, Wi-Fi network name (SSID), host name or proxy address. Interface names that contain a MAC address (enx..., wlx...) are shortened. Requests carry a plain srs-sysinfo user agent and no cookies; https only, certificates checked.
  • Stop ends the current test within about 0.2 s (loopback) or at libcurl's next progress check (internet); a DNS lookup in progress finishes first (bounded by the system's resolver timeout).

Healthy / typical values. Loopback on a Ryzen 7 7800X3D (Linux 7.3, 0.3 s tests): TCP about 110 Gbit/s on 1 stream and 205 Gbit/s on 2, UDP about 8 Gbit/s with 0-1% loss, TCP and UDP round trip about 7 µs. Internet results depend on your plan: a result close to the speed you pay for is healthy; Wi-Fi is often half of it or less.

Unusual values and what they suggest.

  • Loopback far below these figures: a busy CPU, power saving, or firewall / traffic-shaping rules that also apply to loopback.
  • Internet download far below your plan: Wi-Fi, other traffic in the house, a VPN, or a busy server; run it again at another time and compare with https://speed.cloudflare.com in a browser.
  • High jitter or lost connects: an overloaded router or Wi-Fi interference.
  • Speed rows say "the server did not answer 200 OK": the public endpoints changed or are rate limited (they are not a documented API); DNS and connect times still work.

Where Linux gets it. Built in: plain sockets for loopback; getaddrinfo for DNS; libcurl (loaded at run time with dlopen, optional) for HTTPS and the transfers; the default route from /proc/net/route and /proc/net/ipv6_route; the interface from /sys/class/net and Wi-Fi signal from /proc/net/wireless. Setups with only policy routing (some VPNs) are reported as "no network connection". Stored in ~/.cache/srs/bench-net.txt; each run is added to the Benchmark history. Only one benchmark runs at a time in SRS.

GPU benchmark

gpu-bench - Linux data

In plain words. How fast the graphics card (GPU) computes and moves data, measured through Vulkan, the graphics and compute interface every modern Linux GPU driver offers. It runs short pieces of work on the GPU and checks every answer: a wrong answer is shown as WRONG, never as a speed. Higher is better, except for the latency row.

What you see.

Row What it measures Unit
FP32 multiply-add single-precision (32-bit) floating-point maths, the kind games and most GPU programs use GFLOPS
FP16 multiply-add half precision (16-bit), used by AI and some game effects; "not supported" when the GPU or driver lacks it GFLOPS
FP64 multiply-add double precision (64-bit), used by science programs; most gaming GPUs do it at a small fraction of FP32 speed GFLOPS
INT32 multiply-add 32-bit whole-number maths GIOPS
Video memory read / write / copy how fast the GPU reads and writes its own memory (copy counts the bytes read plus the bytes written) GB/s
Upload / Download data moving from system memory to the GPU and back, over PCIe on a graphics card GB/s
Dispatch latency the round trip of an empty piece of GPU work: how quickly the GPU answers µs (median, best, 95% under)

Below: the device and its type (discrete GPU, integrated GPU, software renderer), the driver and its version, the Vulkan version, the device memory, the subgroup (wave / warp) size, the buffer size of the memory tests, how it was timed (GPU timestamps, else the host clock) and the Build line. GFLOPS = billions of floating-point operations per second (a fused multiply-add counts as 2); GIOPS the same for whole numbers; 1 GB = 1,000,000,000 bytes; µs = millionths of a second.

Setting Choices
GPU Default (the first discrete GPU, else the first device) or a device from the list; the list is read when you open it
Seconds per test 0.1-2 in the window (command line 0.1-10), default 1
Memory test size 0 = auto (256 MiB, less on small cards), up to 4096 MiB

Safety. It asks before it starts, naming the GPU, the time (about 15 seconds at the defaults) and that the GPU works at full load; an unstable GPU overclock or undervolt can crash the PC or the display driver under that load. The work is cut into pieces of about 25 ms of GPU time, one at a time, each waited for with a 5 s watchdog, so the desktop stays usable. A lost or stuck GPU ends the run cleanly with the results so far. Stop ends it at once. SRS never changes clocks, voltages or fans. Vulkan overlay layers (such as MangoHud) are kept out of the run.

Healthy / typical values. Not measured by SRS on a real GPU yet (only on the software renderer); as a rough guide from the makers' published figures, a current graphics card: FP32 in the tens of thousands of GFLOPS, video memory several hundred GB/s, upload and download 10-25 GB/s on PCIe 4.0 x16 (about half on PCIe 3.0), dispatch latency 5-30 µs. An integrated GPU: FP32 a few hundred to a few thousand GFLOPS, and the memory rows measure the system RAM it shares. The software renderer (lavapipe, which runs on the CPU) is far slower; it is there for testing.

Unusual values and what they suggest.

  • FP64 at 1/16 to 1/64 of FP32: normal for gaming GPUs; workstation and data-centre cards are faster.
  • Upload / download far below the card's link: the card is in a slot with fewer PCIe lanes or a lower PCIe generation, or the link has dropped to a slower speed (see the PCI items).
  • Much lower numbers than last time: heat (the GPU slows down when hot), a power-saving profile, another program using the GPU, or a driver change. Compare only results from alike SRS builds and the same driver version.
  • WRONG RESULT: the GPU computed something wrong - usually too much overclock or undervolt, too much heat or a faulty card. Run GPU Burnin to check.

Where Linux gets it. Built in: the Vulkan loader (libvulkan.so.1) is opened at run time with dlopen, so SRS does not need Vulkan to build or start; without it, or without a Vulkan driver, the window says "not available". The compute programs (shaders) are pre-compiled into SRS. Stored in ~/.cache/srs/bench-gpu.txt; each run is added to the Benchmark history. Only one benchmark runs at a time in SRS, and none runs while CPU Burnin / Stress runs.

GPU Burnin

gpu-burnin - Linux data

In plain words. A stress test for the graphics card, the GPU counterpart of CPU Burnin. It keeps the GPU fully busy with large matrix multiplications for as long as you choose and checks every result: the first multiplication is the reference and every later one must match it exactly. 0 errors = PASS. Use it to check a GPU overclock or undervolt, the cooling and the power supply. Inspired by gpu-burn (Ville Timonen); the code is SRS's own.

Back ends. The same test can run through four ways of talking to the GPU:

Back end What it is
Vulkan the graphics and compute interface every modern GPU driver on Linux offers (AMD, Intel, NVIDIA); the default
ROCm / HIP AMD's compute platform (needs ROCm installed)
CUDA NVIDIA's compute platform (needs the NVIDIA driver); "CUDA (ZLUDA)" when the CUDA library is really ZLUDA running on an AMD GPU
OpenCL the older cross-vendor compute interface; each installed OpenCL driver (ROCm, Mesa Rusticl, NVIDIA, PoCL ...) is its own entry
Auto Vulkan when it has a GPU, else the first back end that has one

All four are loaded at run time: a back end that is not installed says "not installed" with a one-line hint, and the others still work. HIP, CUDA and OpenCL use SRS's own kernel when their compiler is there (hipRTC, NVRTC, the OpenCL driver), else the vendor's matrix library (hipBLAS, cuBLAS, CLBlast).

What you see. While it runs, per GPU: the time, the errors (green 0, red otherwise), GFLOPS now and on average, multiplications per second and the matrix size, the edge, hotspot / junction and memory temperatures, power, GPU clock and fan speed with the highest values ("not available" when the card or driver does not report one). At the end: PASS / FAIL / Stopped / Ended early, errors found, multiplications, average speed, the highest temperatures, power, clock and fan, the back end, driver / runtime, matrix size and precision.

Setting Choices
Back end Auto (Vulkan), Vulkan, ROCm / HIP, CUDA, OpenCL (those not installed say so)
GPU The first GPU, All GPUs, or one from the list (read when you open it; for HIP, CUDA and OpenCL this starts that runtime)
Precision FP32 (default) or FP64
Seconds 1 to 86,400 (24 hours), default 60
Stop at °C 50-120, default 100

Safety.

  • It asks before it starts (No is the default answer), saying that the GPU draws a lot of power and gets hot, that a bad overclock or undervolt can crash the PC or the display driver, and that a weak power supply or poor cooling can make the PC shut down.
  • It ends by itself when the GPU reaches the temperature limit (hotspot / junction when the card reports one, else edge), on any driver error, when the GPU stops answering ("device lost"), or when one piece of work takes more than 2 s (each piece should take about 20 ms). Stop works at any time. The work is cut into small pieces so the desktop stays usable.
  • It never changes clocks, voltages or fans.
  • It does not start while CPU Burnin / Stress or another benchmark runs, and CPU Burnin does not start while it runs.

Healthy / typical values. 0 errors, always. Temperatures: most graphics cards slow down by themselves before their limit (AMD hotspot about 100-110 °C, NVIDIA about 83-90 °C edge); a card that sits at its limit needs better cooling or airflow. Speeds depend on the card; compare only with your own earlier runs on the same driver.

Unusual values and what they suggest.

  • Any errors: too much overclock or undervolt, too high a temperature, a weak or overloaded power supply, or a faulty card or video memory. Undo the overclock / undervolt and run again.
  • Ended early on a driver error or "device lost": the GPU crashed or was reset by the driver - usually an unstable overclock or undervolt, or the power supply.
  • GFLOPS that fall over a run while the temperature rises: the card slows down when hot.
  • "not available" sensors: the driver does not report them (NVIDIA's own driver reports no temperature to Linux's hwmon, for example), or a software renderer.

Where Linux gets it. Built in: Vulkan (libvulkan.so.1), ROCm / HIP (libamdhip64, libhiprtc, libhipblas), CUDA (libcuda.so.1, libnvrtc, libcublas) and OpenCL (libOpenCL.so.1, libclblast) are opened at run time with dlopen. The sensors come from the card's hwmon folder in /sys/bus/pci/devices/<address>/hwmon (amdgpu: all of them; i915, xe and nouveau: what they offer). Stored in ~/.cache/srs/bench-gpuburn.txt; each run is added to the Benchmark history.

GPU Compute: Vulkan vs HIP vs CUDA vs OpenCL

gpu-compare - Linux data

In plain words. The same pieces of GPU work, with the same sizes, run through every compute back end you have installed (Vulkan, ROCm / HIP, CUDA, OpenCL) on the same graphics card, and shown side by side. It answers "which way of programming this GPU is fastest here, and how much does the vendor's own library add?". Every result is checked; a wrong one is shown as an error, never as a speed.

What you see. Rows = tests, columns = back ends. The fastest in each row has a *; every other column also shows its speed as a percentage of Vulkan (above 100% = faster than Vulkan; for the launch round trip, above 100% = quicker).

Row What it measures Unit
FP32 / FP16 / FP64 matrix multiply, own kernel SRS's plain tiled matrix multiply, the same work on every back end GFLOPS
FP32 / FP16 / FP64 matrix multiply, vendor library the maker's tuned library: hipBLAS (ROCm), cuBLAS (CUDA), CLBlast (OpenCL); Vulkan has none ("not available") GFLOPS
FP32 / FP64 multiply-add chain (peak) long chains of multiply-adds: close to the card's peak GFLOPS
Video memory copy copying inside the card's memory GB/s
Upload / Download system memory to the card and back GB/s
Kernel launch round trip how long an empty piece of work takes to start and finish (lower is better) µs

Columns: "Vulkan", "ROCm / HIP", "CUDA" - or "CUDA (ZLUDA)" when the CUDA library is really ZLUDA translating CUDA calls to an AMD GPU - and one column per OpenCL driver, such as "OpenCL (ROCm)" and "OpenCL (Rusticl)" on the same card; CPU OpenCL drivers (PoCL) are marked CPU. A back end that is not installed shows "not installed" with a one-line hint. Below: each column's device and driver / runtime version, whether a vendor library was found, the sizes and the Build line.

Setting Choices
GPU the Vulkan device that names the card (Default = the first discrete GPU); the other back ends use the card at the same PCI address
Back ends Vulkan, ROCm / HIP, CUDA, OpenCL (only installed ones can be ticked)
Seconds per test 0.1-2 in the window (command line 0.1-10), default 1

Safety. It asks first (the back ends, the GPU, the time, full GPU load, the overclock / undervolt warning). HIP, CUDA and OpenCL start their runtimes only after that Yes. Work is cut into short pieces, each with a watchdog; a GPU that fails ends that column cleanly. Stop works. SRS never changes clocks, voltages or fans.

Healthy / typical values. Not measured by SRS on real hardware yet (only on the software renderer). In general the vendor libraries are much faster than a plain kernel for matrix multiply, and the own-kernel rows show how well each driver compiles the same simple code; a healthy result has every row filled in and no errors.

Unusual values and what they suggest.

  • One back end far behind the others on the same card: an old or debug runtime, or a driver that does not support that card well.
  • "not available" in the own-kernel rows of CUDA (ZLUDA): ZLUDA has no NVRTC compiler, so only the library rows run.
  • FP16 library rows "not available" on OpenCL: the driver has no cl_khr_fp16.

Where Linux gets it. Built in: all four back ends and the libraries are opened at run time with dlopen (see GPU Burnin); ZLUDA is recognised by marker strings in the CUDA library file. Stored in ~/.cache/srs/bench-gpucompare.txt; each run is added to the Benchmark history. Compare results only between alike SRS builds and the same driver and runtime versions.

SRS Pi

srs-pi - Linux data

In plain words. SRS works out pi (3.14159...) to many decimal places - from 128 thousand up to 32 million - and then checks every single digit. It is a classic CPU test: the time tells you how fast one core is at heavy number work, and a wrong digit means the computer made a mistake, which usually points to an unstable overclock, too little voltage or bad memory.

What you see.

Line Meaning Why it matters
Digits How many decimal places were worked out (after "3."). 1 million = 1,000,000. With SuperPi sizes ticked, powers of two: 1M = 1,048,576, marked "(SuperPi size 1M)". Bigger takes longer and uses more memory.
Method Chudnovsky series (fast) or Gauss-Legendre / AGM (the method SuperPi uses). Only compare runs made with the same method.
Threads 1 = single-thread score. Chudnovsky can split its work over more threads; AGM always uses one.
Time Seconds from start to the last digit (the check is not counted). Lower is faster.
Check "every digit right" when the SHA-256 checksum of all the digits matches the true digits. Anything else means a wrong result: do not trust that PC's stability.
Last 20 digits The end of the result, for a quick look.
Build Compiler and CPU code level the program was built for. Results only compare between alike builds.

If never run, the item shows Status Not run yet and the command line.

Healthy / typical values. Ryzen 7 7800X3D, package build (generic x86-64, -O2), one thread: 128 thousand digits 0.23 s, 1 million 3.1 s, 2 million 7.7 s, 4 million 17.7 s, 8 million 39.6 s. 1 million on 4 threads: 1.4 s. Gauss-Legendre is about four times slower than Chudnovsky (1 million: 13.2 s). A build made for this CPU (-march=native -O3) did 1 million in 2.1 s.

Unusual values and what they suggest.

  • Check says "wrong": the hardware made an error. Undo the last overclock or voltage change and run it again; a wrong result at stock settings points to memory (run a memory tester).
  • Much slower than usual: another program is busy, the CPU is hot and throttling, or a power-saving profile is active.
  • "Not enough memory": 32 million digits needs about 1-2 GB of free RAM (more with more threads).

Safety. It asks before it starts, with the expected time, the threads and the memory it needs. From 8 million digits, or with all threads, it warns that an unstable overclock or undervolt can crash the PC under this load, and No is the default answer. Stop (or closing the window) ends it at once. On the command line sysreport-search pi asks the same; --yes starts at once.

Where Linux gets it. Built in (no outside program): big numbers in base 10^8, multiplied with a number-theoretic transform; Newton steps for division and square roots. The true digits' SHA-256 checksums for 128K, 1M, 2M, 4M, 8M, 16M and 32M digits are built into SRS (computed once with the independent mpmath library). Stored in ~/.cache/srs/bench-pi.txt; each run is added to the Benchmark history.

Background. SuperPi (1995) made "pi to 1 million digits" a famous overclocking test. SRS Pi is SRS's own program with its own name and timings; its times are not SuperPi times. SuperPi's "1M" is 2^20 = 1,048,576 digits; SRS's 1 million is exactly 1,000,000. Tick SuperPi sizes to work out the same digit counts SuperPi does (16K = 16,384 up to 32M = 33,554,432), so at least the amount of work matches; each of these sizes has its own built-in checksum too. 1M = 1,048,576 digits took 4.2 s on one thread on the 7800X3D (a little more than 5% over 1,000,000 digits, because the multiplications step up to the next power-of-two size).

Crypto benchmark

crypto-bench - Linux data

In plain words. How fast the CPU can encrypt data (AES-128, used by disk encryption, VPNs and HTTPS) and make fingerprints of data (SHA-256, used by package checks, backups and git). Each is measured twice: with the CPU's own crypto instructions (AES-NI, SHA-NI) and in plain C without them, so you can see how much the hardware helps.

What you see. A table in MB/s (1 MB = 1,000,000 bytes) with one column for one thread and one for the chosen number of threads (default: all), and a Check line.

Row Meaning
AES-128-CTR, AES-NI AES-128 in counter mode using the AES instructions, eight blocks at a time.
AES-128-CTR, plain C The same work with lookup tables in ordinary C code.
SHA-256, SHA-NI SHA-256 using the SHA extensions.
SHA-256, plain C SHA-256 in ordinary C code.

A row says "not available on this CPU" when the CPU lacks those instructions.

Healthy / typical values. Ryzen 7 7800X3D, one thread: AES-NI about 15,000 MB/s, plain C about 180 MB/s; SHA-NI about 2,100 MB/s, plain C about 430 MB/s. With four threads the numbers grow about four times. For comparison, openssl speed on the same core: AES-128-CTR about 12,600 MB/s, SHA-256 about 2,400 MB/s.

Unusual values and what they suggest. Check not "pass": the CPU gave a wrong answer - treat it like a failed stability test. AES-NI rows missing on a modern CPU: the instructions may be switched off in the BIOS or hidden by a virtual machine.

Safety. It asks before it starts. With all threads (the default) every CPU thread is 100% busy, so it warns about unstable overclocks and No is the default answer. On the command line sysreport-search crypto asks the same; --yes starts at once.

Where Linux gets it. Built in, written from the standards FIPS 197 (AES) and FIPS 180-4 (SHA-256). Before every run the official test vectors are checked, and the hardware results are compared with the plain C results. Stored in ~/.cache/srs/bench-crypto.txt. Runs about 8 seconds at the default of 1 second per measurement.

Prime sieve

prime-sieve - Linux data

In plain words. Counts all the prime numbers up to a limit (100 million to 100 billion) and checks the count against the known answer. It is simple integer and cache work that splits well over many threads.

What you see. Limit, Threads, Time, Speed (million numbers per second), Primes found, and a Check line ("right" when the count matches the known value, for example 455,052,511 primes below 10 billion).

Healthy / typical values. Ryzen 7 7800X3D, up to 10 billion: 4.5 s on one thread, 1.15 s on four threads. The specialised primesieve program does the one-thread run in 0.75 s: SRS uses a plain, easy-to-read sieve, so compare SRS with SRS.

Safety. It asks before it starts. From 10 billion, or with all threads (the defaults), it warns about unstable overclocks and No is the default answer. Stop ends it at once. On the command line sysreport-search prime asks the same; --yes starts at once.

Where Linux gets it. Built in: a segmented sieve of Eratosthenes over the odd numbers, in 128 KB pieces that fit in the L2 cache, shared between threads. Stored in ~/.cache/srs/bench-prime.txt.

Benchmark history

bench-history - Linux data

In plain words. A list of every SRS Pi, Crypto and Prime sieve run, newest first, so you can compare before and after a change (BIOS setting, kernel, cooler).

What you see. When, Test, Settings (digits, threads, method), Result, and Build. Results in red were wrong.

Where Linux gets it. ~/.cache/srs/bench-history.tsv, a tab-separated text file (one line per run) that any spreadsheet opens. Only compare lines with the same settings and the same Build: a package built for every x86-64 CPU can be much slower than one built for this CPU.

Lookup

lookup - Linux data

In plain words. It lists the name databases SRS uses to turn ID numbers into names (PCI, USB, monitor maker and network card maker), with their dates and versions. It also shows the SRS program itself.

What you see.

Column Meaning Why it matters
Description What the file is for: PCI Device Names, USB Device Names, PNP / Monitor Names, MAC Vendor Names, SRS Program, SRS Kernel Driver.
File Specification Full path of the file, for example /usr/share/hwdata/pci.ids. Where to look if names are missing.
Current Identification "Date ... Version ... (N)". N is the number of record lines in the file. When the file has no version line, the file size in bytes is shown instead, and Date is ?. For SRS Program it is the SRS version. An old file means new hardware shows as "Unknown".
Code Page Text encoding (UTF-8).
WEB Download Location Where the newest copy of each file is published.

Under the table: "No network access: srs-gui shows the upstream URLs but never downloads." The SRS Kernel Driver row says none: SRS loads no kernel driver of its own, and root-only data comes from srs-root.

Healthy / typical values. On the author's PC: pci.ids Version 2026.10.01 (42452 records), usb.ids Version 2026.06.26 (25615), pnp.ids 63479 bytes, oui.txt 6321491 bytes. SRS Program /usr/bin/sysreport-search, V2.0.0.

Unusual values and what they suggest.

  • not found: the hwdata package is missing. Install hwdata (Arch) or hwdata / pciutils / usbutils (other distros).
  • A pci.ids or usb.ids date more than a year old with very new hardware: update the hwdata package (or run update-pciids where it exists) to get names for new devices.

Where Linux gets it. /usr/share/hwdata/pci.ids, usb.ids, pnp.ids and oui.txt, plus /proc/self/exe for the program path.

Ping

ping - Linux data

In plain words. It sends three small test packets to your router (the default gateway) and shows whether they came back and how fast. In SIV this is a Windows ping. SRS uses the Linux ping tool.

What you see.

  • Target - the IPv4 default gateway, read from the routing table.
  • The normal ping output: one line per reply with icmp_seq (packet number), ttl (time to live, how many more router hops the reply could have made) and time (round trip in ms).
  • The summary: packets sent and received, % packet loss, and rtt min/avg/max/mdev (fastest, average, slowest, and how much the times vary).
  • Error lines in red when the ping fails, No IPv4 default gateway when there is no route out, or ping not available when the tool is missing.

Healthy / typical values. On the author's wired PC, pinging a home router (for example 192.168.1.1): 3 sent, 3 received, 0% loss, average about 0.3 ms. Wired links to a router are usually below 1 ms. Wi-Fi is usually 1-10 ms.

Unusual values and what they suggest.

  • Any packet loss to your own router: a bad cable or port, weak Wi-Fi, or an overloaded router.
  • Times of tens of ms on a wired link: the router is busy, or the link fell back to a slow speed.
  • 100 % loss but the internet works: the router is set to ignore ping. That is harmless.

Where Linux gets it. /proc/net/route for the gateway, then ping -c 3 -i 0.2 -W 1 <gateway>.

Configuration Find

reg-find - Linux data

In plain words. SIV searches the Windows Registry. Linux keeps its settings in text files instead, so SRS searches the text files in /etc (system settings) and ~/.config (your own settings) for a word or pattern.

What you see.

  • With no pattern: Usage reg-find:PATTERN (regex; searches /etc and ~/.config text files).
  • With a pattern: one line per hit, path:line-number followed by the matching line.
  • At the end: N Matches, N Matches (limit 200) when it stopped at 200 hits, or No Matches for PATTERN. A broken pattern gives Match String [...] is Invalid: and the reason.

Run it from a report with -save=[reg-find:PATTERN]. Example: -save=[reg-find:HandleLidSwitch] finds where lid-close behaviour is set.

Healthy / typical values. On the author's PC, ^HandleLidSwitch gives No Matches, because the setting only appears commented out (#HandleLidSwitch=...) in /etc/systemd/logind.conf. Leave out the ^ to see commented lines too.

Unusual values and what they suggest. Fewer hits than expected: some files under /etc can only be read by root and are skipped without a message. Use sudo grep for those.

Where Linux gets it. A walk of /etc and ~/.config, up to 4 folders deep. Only regular files up to 256 KB. Files whose name contains "shadow" (password hashes) are skipped. Case is ignored.

Background. A regex (regular expression) is a search pattern. . means any character, ^ means "start of line", a|b means "a or b".

Device ID Lookup

id-lookup - Linux data

In plain words. Type a device's ID numbers and SRS tells you the maker and the device name, from the same databases Linux uses.

What you see.

  • With no ID: Usage id-lookup:VVVV:DDDD[:SSSS:ssss][:RR] or id-lookup:usb:VVVV:PPPP.
  • A list of keys, from the most exact to the least exact. Each key shows its database entry, or (no entry). A < marks the key that matched.
  • Vendor - the maker of the chip (from VVVV).
  • Subsystem - the maker of the card or board (from SSSS). Only shown for 4-part PCI IDs.
  • Stock - the plain chip name (VVVV:DDDD), as the chip maker names it.
  • Resolved - the best name found (the < row), or No Matches.
  • Errors: bad ID ... expected VVVV[:DDDD[:SSSS:ssss]][:RR] when the format is wrong, or cannot find the .ids file.

ID parts: VVVV = vendor, DDDD = device, SSSS:ssss = subsystem vendor and subsystem device (the card maker's own ID), RR = revision. All are hexadecimal. For USB: VVVV = vendor, PPPP = product.

The GUI window (Menu -> Device ID Lookup..., or Ctrl+L) adds a PCI / USB choice and a three-way mode box. Tree does a fast binary search of a sorted table. Scan reads the .ids file from top to bottom. Info asks the system device database (systemd-hwdb) instead. A footer shows the number of records and the load and lookup times.

Healthy / typical values. On the author's PC, 1002:7550:1EAE:8811:C0 (the graphics card) gives no entry for the three exact keys and matches 1002:7550 = "Navi 48 [Radeon RX 9070/9070 XT/9070 GRE]". Vendor = Advanced Micro Devices, Inc. [AMD/ATI], Subsystem = XFX Limited. usb:1d6b:0002 resolves to "2.0 root hub" by the Linux Foundation.

Unusual values and what they suggest. Only the vendor matches, or nothing at all: the device is newer than your pci.ids / usb.ids file (see Lookup), or the ID was typed wrongly. Info mode can sometimes still name it, because systemd-hwdb is updated separately.

Where Linux gets it. /usr/share/hwdata/pci.ids and usb.ids. Info mode uses systemd-hwdb.

Background. Every PCI and USB device reports a vendor ID and a device ID. These are the numbers Linux uses to choose a driver. The name is only a label from a community-kept list.

Find

find - Linux data

In plain words. It searches your newest saved system report (made by srs-sysreport) for a word or pattern and shows every matching line, grouped by section file.

What you see.

  • With no pattern: Usage find:PATTERN (regex over the newest ~/sysreports report).
  • Searching <report folder> for "PATTERN".
  • For each file with hits: == file - N Matches, then each hit as line-number: text, with the matching part highlighted.
  • N Matches in X of Y sections, or No Matches for PATTERN.
  • No report found under ~/sysreports - run srs-sysreport first when there is no report yet.

From a report (-save=[find:PATTERN]) the search is case-sensitive and shows up to 20 hits per file. The GUI window (Menu -> Find in Report..., or Ctrl+F) adds: Ignore case, Literal (search for the exact text, not a regex), Highlight Matches, Max (hits shown per file, then "... N more (raise Max)"), Report (which report folder; Browse... and Latest buttons), Next / Prev buttons and F3 / Shift+F3 to jump between hits, Colour (the highlight colour), and Lookup (opens Device ID Lookup).

Healthy / typical values. On the author's PC, find:Tctl found 1 match in sensors.txt (line 7, Tctl: +59.6°C), "1 Matches in 1 of 16 sections".

Unusual values and what they suggest. The report folder date is old: the search only looks at the newest sysreport-* folder. Run srs-sysreport again for fresh data, or pick a folder with Browse.

Where Linux gets it. The newest ~/sysreports/sysreport-* folder: every .txt and .html file except index.html.

ALL Devices

all-dev - Linux data

In plain words. Every PCI and USB device in the PC, each one turned from its ID numbers into a maker and device name. Devices the name lists do not know are marked.

What you see. One block per bus, PCI first, then USB.

  • Block header: [PCI] 54 devices, 42,228 records /usr/share/hwdata/pci.ids - how many devices were found, how many entries the name list has, and which file was used.
Column Meaning Why it matters
Slot PCI address (domain🚌device.function, e.g. 0000:03:00.0) or USB port path (e.g. 1-2.4, or usb1 for a root hub). Where the device sits.
ID The full ID: PCI vendor:device:subvendor:subdevice:revision, USB vendor:product. The numbers to search for online.
Matched The most exact part of the ID that has a name in the list, or -. Shows how well the device is known.
Vendor The chip maker, or Unknown Vendor.
Resolved The device name. Unknown Device (red) when only the vendor is known. [subsystem: ...] is added when the card maker is known but the exact card is not in the list.

At the end: N device(s) resolved only to vendor or not at all. Use all-dev:pci or all-dev:usb to show one bus only.

Healthy / typical values. On the author's PC: 54 PCI devices, all named. For example 0000:03:00.0 = Navi 48 [Radeon RX 9070/9070 XT/9070 GRE] [subsystem: XFX Limited], and the Samsung SSD 980 PRO matched on all four ID parts. 40 USB devices, with 16 known only by vendor or not at all. That is common for USB: many hubs, receivers and controllers are simply not in usb.ids.

Unusual values and what they suggest.

  • Many PCI devices "Unknown Device": your pci.ids is old (see Lookup).
  • A device you expect is missing from the list: it is switched off in the BIOS, not seated, or (for USB) not powered or not detected. Check dmesg for errors.

Where Linux gets it. PCI devices from /sys/bus/pci/devices, USB devices from /sys/bus/usb/devices, names from /usr/share/hwdata/pci.ids and usb.ids.

CPU Burnin

burnin - Linux data

In plain words. A stress test: it makes the CPUs you choose 100 % busy for a set time, watches the temperatures, and ends with Pass or Fail. Use it to check that a new build, cooler, overclock or undervolt is stable. The saved item only shows the current state and sensor readings. It never starts a run.

What you see in a report.

Field Meaning
State Running, or Idle (start it from Menu > Tools > CPU Burnin).
Worker threads How many CPUs can get a worker thread ("16 CPUs available").
Hottest CPU sensor The hottest CPU temperature right now, with chip and label (k10temp, coretemp or zenpower).
Hottest SIO sensor The hottest motherboard Super I/O sensor right now.
GPU Graphics card load %, temperature (junction if available) and core clock.
Command line srs-gui burn [--threads N | --cpus 0,2] [--seconds S] [--mode same|swap] [--limit C].
Safety note Never auto-starts; stops at the temperature limit (default 90 C) and the time cap.

What you see in the CPU Burnin window (Menu -> CPU Burnin...).

  • Settings: Burn Time (0-750, in minutes, or in hours if "Hours" is ticked; default 15 minutes), Cool Time (0-900 seconds idle between burns, default 60), Cycles (1-99 burn/cool rounds, default 1), Temperature limit °C (50-100, default 90), Same CPU (Whetstone) or Swap CPU (affinity test), an optional GPU Load command, and one tick box per CPU with Select All / Deselect All. Start asks for confirmation first.
  • Status line: Idle / Burning / Cooling / Pass / Fail / Stopped, with Elapsed and Remaining time (hh:mm:ss) and the reason text (for example "Pass - Finished").
  • A sensor table with 7 rows (CPU Load, CPU Frequency, Hottest Core Temp, Hottest SIO Sensor Temp, GPU Load, GPU Temp, GPU Frequency) and 4 columns: Current, Overall Average (since start), Rolling Average (recent values count most) and Maximum.
  • A thread table:
Column Meaning
Thread Worker number.
CPU The CPU this worker was pinned to.
On CPU The CPU it actually ran on during its last pass.
User / Kernel How busy that CPU was with program work / kernel work, in %.
Clock That CPU's current clock in MHz.
Whetstone Score of the last pass, in MWIPS.
Average / Min / Max Average, lowest and highest pass score so far.
Affinity ok, FAIL (red), or - before the first pass ends.
  • A graph of the last 10 minutes: green CPU load %, red hottest core °C, orange SIO °C, blue GPU °C, on a 0-100 scale.

Pass and Fail.

  • Fail - the hottest CPU sensor reached the temperature limit ("Fail - k10temp Tctl 90.0 C reached the 90 C limit"), or a worker ran on the wrong CPU ("Fail - a worker thread ran on the wrong CPU (affinity / APIC check)"). The run stops at once.
  • Pass - all cycles finished ("Pass - Finished"), or the overall time cap was reached.
  • Stopped - you pressed Stop or closed the window.
  • Command line srs-gui burn: exit code 0 = Pass, 1 = Fail, 130 = Stopped (Ctrl+C). It prints one status line per second and a thread table at the end. It also accepts --cool S and --cycles N.

Saved results. When a run ends (Pass, Fail or Stopped), SRS saves the window's summary - the status, the sensor table and the thread table, the same text the Copy button gives - to ~/.cache/srs/burnin-YYYYMMDD-HHMMSS.txt (date and time the run ended), and the status line says where. Each run gets its own file, so you can compare runs before and after a change, for example with diff or meld. The command line burn saves its summary the same way. SRS never deletes these files; remove old ones by hand when you no longer need them.

Affinity ok / FAIL. After every pass each worker checks two things: (1) Linux says it is running on the CPU it was pinned to (sched_getcpu), and (2) the CPU's own ID number (APIC ID, read with the CPUID instruction) matches the one /proc/cpuinfo lists for that CPU. ok means both matched every time. FAIL means the thread was found somewhere else at least once. That should never happen, so it points to a scheduler problem, a CPU that went offline, or a firmware or topology fault. In Swap mode each worker moves to the next selected CPU before every pass. That tests that moving threads between cores works.

Healthy / typical values. On the author's 7800X3D at idle: Tctl 56.0°C, nct6799 CPUTIN 30.0°C, GPU 5 % load, 29.0°C, 1725 MHz. Under a full all-core load, a 7800X3D usually settles around 80-89°C. It is designed to hold near its 89°C limit (its Tjmax), so on this chip the default 90°C cut-off never triggers: the CPU slows itself down first. If you want the Fail cut-off to act, set the limit a few degrees below your own CPU's Tjmax. A good run shows steady Whetstone scores per thread (Min close to Max), all Affinity ok, and Pass.

Unusual values and what they suggest.

  • Fail on temperature within a few minutes: cooler not seated well, pump not running, or not enough case airflow.
  • Min far below Max on some threads: the CPU is throttling (heat or power limit). Watch CPU Frequency drop at the same time.
  • A sudden reboot or freeze during the burn: the system is not stable. Undo the latest overclock, undervolt or memory change.
  • Hottest SIO sensor reading very high (80°C or more) with a cool case: usually a disconnected sensor input. SRS already ignores AUXTIN, PECI, TSI and PCH inputs. You can turn a real one back on with SIO Sensors=chip:LABEL in ~/.config/srs/SRSDEF.ini.

Where Linux gets it. Load: built-in Whetstone in one pinned thread per CPU. Sensors: /proc/stat (load), /sys/devices/system/cpu/cpuN/cpufreq/scaling_cur_freq (clock), /sys/class/hwmon (CPU and Super I/O temperatures), /sys/class/drm/cardN/device (gpu_busy_percent, pp_dpm_sclk, hwmon temperature). The GPU load command's output goes to ~/.cache/srs/gpu-load.log. Finished runs are saved to ~/.cache/srs/burnin-YYYYMMDD-HHMMSS.txt.

Background. Tctl is AMD's "control temperature". It is the value the CPU uses for fan control and throttling. A Super I/O (SIO) chip is the motherboard chip that reads fan speeds, voltages and board temperatures. A burn-in finds weak cooling and unstable settings now, at your desk, instead of in the middle of a game or a long job.

CPU Stress

cpu-stress - Linux data

In plain words. The same load engine as CPU Burnin, but with no timer. The CPUs stay 100 % busy until you press Stop (or a safety limit hits). Use it to watch temperatures and clocks for as long as you like.

What you see. In a report: exactly the same lines as CPU Burnin (State, Worker threads, sensors, GPU, Command line, Safety note). In the CPU Stress window (Menu -> CPU Stress...): the same sensor table, thread table, graph and controls as CPU Burnin, but without Burn Time, Cool Time and Cycles.

Pass and Fail. Stress has no "finished" point. It ends as Stopped when you press Stop, as Fail if the hottest CPU sensor reaches the temperature limit or an affinity check fails, or as Pass if the overall time cap (750 hours) is reached. Either way the summary is saved to ~/.cache/srs/burnin-YYYYMMDD-HHMMSS.txt, as for CPU Burnin.

Healthy / typical values. As for CPU Burnin: temperatures climb for a few minutes and then level off. Clocks stay steady.

Unusual values and what they suggest. Temperatures that keep rising after 10-15 minutes and never level off: the cooler is saturated (for example an AIO whose liquid keeps heating up). Improve airflow or the fan curve.

Where Linux gets it. The same sources as CPU Burnin.

SRS (SIV items) (SRS Section Reference)

Back to the section index - Glossary

Where to find these items (SRS 2.0). In the main window they are on the Tools page (Alt+Backspace). Its tabs are About SRS and Help; All N items lists the rest. Menu -> About SRS opens About too. You can also type an item's name or id into the search box (Ctrl+F). The rest of this introduction describes the classic view (Menu -> Classic View), with its Menu and panel buttons.

This group holds the items that describe SRS itself rather than your hardware: its version and credits, help text, settings file, command-line options, program image, threads, and a set of small "buffer" snapshots of live system data. In SIV64X (System Information Viewer, by Ray Hinchliffe, RH Software) these items describe SIV's own program, driver and internal buffers. SRS keeps the same item names so a save file lines up with SIV's, and fills each one with the nearest Linux data. Open them from Menu -> SRS (SIV items) -> item. The About and Help panels have their own button row (DNS Names, Lookup, USB Dev, About, Help), and the SRS DLLs panel has the Lookup row (DNS Names, Signature, SRS DLLs, Lookup, ID Lookup). Almost everything here works as a normal user. Only the board serial number in SGB info and the SPD cache line in Fake SPDs use data from the root helper (srs-root); start it with Menu -> Run as root.

How to read these items

  • Most items start with a title line: srs-gui - <what> on \\<host> - <OS>. On the author's PC that reads srs-gui - Help on \\MYPC - CachyOS 7.3.0-273-tkg-bore-llvm.
  • [=] is a ticked box and [_] an empty one. A few items use |X| and |_| the same way.
  • SRS is read-only. None of these items change a setting, write a register or open a device.
  • SRS is one program image. Run with no arguments it is the window (srs-gui). Run with arguments it is the command line (sysreport-search). So "this process" in the items below is whichever one made the report.

About SRS

about - Linux data

In plain words. Who made this program, which version you have, what it is running on, and which name-database files it uses.

What you see.

Field What it means Why it matters
Title line srs-gui - System Report Search V<version> <host>::<user> Quick check of version and machine.
Program One image works as the GUI (no arguments) and the CLI (with arguments). Explains why reports name sysreport-search.
Version Program version, e.g. V2.0.0. Quote this in bug reports.
Program Build File format, compiler and C runtime the program was built with. Tells a self-built copy from a packaged one.
Built Date and time the program was compiled. Shows how old your copy is.
Image Full path and size of the running program file. Shows which copy ran, if you have several.
Running on Kernel name, release, build string and machine type (from uname). The exact kernel the data came from.
Operating System Distribution name and kernel. Context for every other item.
Machine Board maker, model and BIOS version/date. Context; BIOS updates change many values.
Processor CPU brand string. Context.
PCI Device Names / USB Device Names / PnP / Monitor Names Path of each name database, then its date and version (from the file header) or the file date. Old files mean new devices show as "unknown".
Settings Path of the settings file SRSDEF.ini. Where your choices are kept.
Live data The kinds of source SRS reads. Reminds you some data needs the root helper.
Created by / Licensed under / Home page The author (Eugene Flanagin), the licence (GPL-2.0-or-later) and the GitHub page. Who made it and where to get it.
Why SRS / Credit / Disclaimer Origin, credit to SIV's author and use-at-your-own-risk note. Credit information.

Healthy / typical values. On the author's PC: V2.0.0, built with gcc 16.2.1 and glibc, image /usr/bin/sysreport-search (1.38MB), Linux 7.3.0 x86_64 on an ASUS TUF GAMING X870-PRO WIFI7 W NEO (BIOS 1805), AMD Ryzen 7 7800X3D. pci.ids version 2026.10.01, usb.ids 2026.06.26. pnp.ids has no version header, so only its file date is shown.

Unusual values and what they suggest.

  • A database line says not found: the hwdata package is missing, so device names cannot be resolved.
  • A database date that is a year or more old: update your distribution's hwdata package.

Where Linux gets it. Built-in version strings, uname(), /etc/os-release, /sys/class/dmi/id, and the header lines of /usr/share/hwdata/*.ids.

Background. The .ids files are community lists that turn numeric device IDs (like 1002:7550) into names (like an AMD Radeon card). SRS does not ship its own copy; it uses the system's.

BSB info (battery/HID sensor buffer)

bsi - Linux data

In plain words. A list of the batteries and power supplies Linux knows about, plus a count of HID (Human Interface Device: keyboards, mice, game pads) devices.

What you see. One row per entry in /sys/class/power_supply:

Column What it means Why it matters
# Row number. -
Device Name Kernel name of the supply, e.g. BAT0, AC, or a wireless controller battery. Tells you which device it is.
Type Battery, Mains, USB and so on. Mains = wall power; Battery = something that drains.
Status Charging, Discharging, Full, Not charging. Shows if the battery is being charged.
Capacity Charge left, in percent. Low values mean recharge soon.
Model Model name if the driver reports one. Identifies the battery pack.

Below the rows: act N num N (how many supplies were found) and a count of HID devices registered in /sys/bus/hid/devices. SRS only counts them; it never opens them. This panel refreshes every 2 seconds.

Healthy / typical values. A desktop often has no battery at all, or only the batteries of wireless game pads and mice. On the author's PC: one entry, a Nintendo Switch controller battery, type Battery, status Discharging; 15 HID devices. A laptop shows BAT0 (Battery) and AC or ADP1 (Mains).

Unusual values and what they suggest.

  • Capacity or Model blank: the driver does not report it. Common for game pads.
  • A laptop with no BAT0: battery not detected, or the ACPI battery driver is not loaded.
  • Not charging at less than 100% on a laptop: often a charge limit set in firmware or by a vendor tool.

Where Linux gets it. /sys/class/power_supply/*/{type,status,capacity,model_name} and the entries in /sys/bus/hid/devices.

CPU group buffer

cgb - Linux data

In plain words. Shows that all your CPUs belong to one group, and which CPUs are online.

What you see.

Column What it means Why it matters
CGN CPU group number (always 0 on Linux), with a tick box. Windows splits more than 64 CPUs into groups; Linux does not.
Num How many logical CPUs are online. Should match your thread count.
Affinity A 64-bit hex mask, one bit per online CPU. FFFF = CPUs 0-15.
Members [CPU-0 to CPU-N], the highest online CPU number. Quick range check.
Online / Possible The kernel's online list and possible list. Different lists mean some CPUs are switched off.

Healthy / typical values. On the author's 7800X3D (8 cores, 16 threads): 0 16 000000000000FFFF [CPU-0 to CPU-15] 0-15 / 0-15.

Unusual values and what they suggest.

  • Online smaller than Possible: CPUs were taken offline (for example with nosmt, maxcpus= on the kernel command line, or by writing 0 to a CPU's online file).
  • Possible much bigger than your real CPU count: firmware reports spare hot-plug slots. Harmless.

Where Linux gets it. /sys/devices/system/cpu/online, /sys/devices/system/cpu/possible and /sys/devices/system/cpu/cpuN/online.

Background. A logical CPU is one hardware thread. With SMT (Simultaneous Multi-Threading) each core runs two, so 8 cores show as 16 CPUs. An affinity mask is a bit pattern saying which CPUs a task may run on.

CSV logging

csv - Linux data

In plain words. SIV can log sensor data to a CSV (Comma-Separated Values) file. SRS has no separate CSV logger; this item tells you what to use instead.

What you see. Fixed lines: CSV logging (not separate), Save (the -save syntax), Example (srs-gui '-save=[sensors][cpu]=/tmp/log.txt'), Tabular data (columns are padded with spaces at the panel tab stops), and Environmental log (SIV's -ENVLOG / -EXCEL sensor log has no equivalent; run -save on [sensors] instead).

Healthy / typical values. Always the same text.

Where Linux gets it. Built-in text.

Background. To log sensors over time, run a -save of [sensors] on a timer (for example from a shell loop or a systemd timer) and keep each file.

CSV titles

csv-titles - Linux data

In plain words. Describes the layout of a save file, since there is no CSV header to show.

What you see.

  • File header - srs-gui - System Report Search V<version> <host> <YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS> [<items>].
  • Section header - [<item>] [<category>], e.g. [gpu] [xxb].
  • Section body - the item's own column titles, then its rows.
  • Separator - two blank lines after each section.

Healthy / typical values. Fixed text. Useful if you write a script that splits a save file into items.

Where Linux gets it. Built-in text.

Debug API

debug-api - Linux data

In plain words. Build facts and pointers for people who debug SRS.

What you see.

  • Build - compiler and runtime, same as in About.
  • Assertions - on or off (NDEBUG). Assertions are self-checks compiled into the program.
  • Item list - the command srs-gui --list prints every item.
  • Dump any item - srs-gui -save=[item]=STDOUT prints one item.
  • Process state - where to look: [stc] threads, [mutex] locks, [siv-dll] modules.

Healthy / typical values. On the author's PC: Assertions on.

Where Linux gets it. Compile-time build information.

Delta/cost settings

delta - Linux data

In plain words. SIV can turn power use into an energy cost. SRS has no such setting.

What you see. Energy cost (not used) and Nearest (live power is in PMB info and the sensor items).

Where Linux gets it. Built-in text.

DSB info (DIMM sensor buffer)

dsb - Linux data

In plain words. The temperature of each memory stick (DIMM) that has a sensor.

What you see. One row per DIMM sensor:

Column What it means Why it matters
# Row number. -
hwmon The hwmon device name, e.g. hwmon7. Lets you find the raw files.
Device The I2C (Inter-Integrated Circuit) bus and address, e.g. 1-0051 = bus 1, address 0x51. Address 0x50-0x57 maps to a slot.
Current Temperature now, in degrees C. The main value.
Maximum The "high" limit set in the sensor. Above this the stick may slow itself down.
Critical The "critical" limit. Above this is a real problem.

If no sensor is found you see no DIMM temperature sensors (spd5118 / jc42 hwmon) loaded. This panel refreshes every 2 seconds.

Healthy / typical values. On the author's two DDR5 sticks: 31.00 C and 30.50 C at idle, limits 55 C (max) and 85 C (critical). Idle 30-45 C is normal; 50-60 C under heavy load is common with no airflow over the RAM.

Unusual values and what they suggest.

  • Above 55 C at idle: poor case airflow, or a hot GPU blowing on the RAM.
  • Above 70-80 C: DDR5 starts to slow itself (it refreshes more often) and errors become more likely. Improve cooling.
  • One stick much hotter than the other: it sits closer to a heat source, or its sensor is off.
