  • No rows on DDR5: load the spd5118 driver (modprobe spd5118). DDR4 sticks with a sensor use jc42; many DDR4 sticks have none.

Where Linux gets it. /sys/class/hwmon/hwmonN/temp1_{input,max,crit} for hwmon devices named spd5118 (DDR5) or jc42 (DDR4 and older).

Background. hwmon (hardware monitoring) is the Linux system that exposes sensor chips as files. Each DDR5 stick has a small hub chip on the SMBus (System Management Bus) that holds the SPD (Serial Presence Detect: the stick's own description of its size and speeds) and a temperature sensor.

Emoji glyph test

emoji - Linux data

In plain words. Checks that your fonts can draw symbols and emoji, so the display looks right.

What you see.

  • Glyphs - a row of sample symbols (smiley, monitor, thermometer, lightning, battery, floppy disk, tick, cross, °C, µs, arrow).
  • Boxes - one ticked and one empty tick box.
  • Fonts with emoji coverage - every font that has the smiley emoji (U+1F600), from fontconfig.

Healthy / typical values. All glyphs drawn, and at least one colour emoji font in the list. The author's PC lists Noto Color Emoji, Twemoji, Segoe UI Emoji, DejaVu Sans and others.

Unusual values and what they suggest. Empty boxes or question marks instead of glyphs, or none found: install an emoji font such as Noto Color Emoji.

Where Linux gets it. fc-list :charset=1f600 family.

Fake IMCs

fak-imcs - Not present on most PCs

In plain words. In SIV this replays saved memory-controller data from Intel Xeon servers, for testing. SRS has no replay mode, so this always says "Not present".

What you see. Status (Not present on this system), Checked (what it looked for: Intel Xeon ICX IMC fixtures) and your Processor name.

Background. An IMC (Integrated Memory Controller) is the part of the CPU that talks to RAM. "ICX" is Intel's Ice Lake server family. A "fixture" is a saved data dump used to test a program without the real hardware.

Fake MCHBAR

fak-mchbar - Linux data - Needs root data

In plain words. In SIV this replays saved Intel memory-controller register dumps, for testing. SRS reads no such registers; this item tells you where memory timing data comes from instead.

What you see. Status (what the SIV feature is), srs-gui (reads no MCHBAR registers, never opens /dev/mem, uses no replay files) and Memory timings (come from the [spd] item via the srs-root cache file spd.txt, and from the kernel EDAC / amd64 drivers).

Where Linux gets it. Nothing is read. The memory timing data it points to needs the root helper (Menu -> Run as root).

Background. MCHBAR (Memory Controller Hub Base Address Register) is the address of a block of Intel memory-controller registers. Reading it needs raw physical memory access, which SRS avoids.

Fake PM tables

fak-pmts - Linux data

In plain words. SIV can replay saved AMD power-management tables. SRS has no replay; it tells you if the live table is available.

What you see.

  • Status - no replay; the live PM table is in the [amd-pmt-0] item.
  • pm_table - present if the ryzen_smu driver exposes the table, else ryzen_smu driver not loaded.
  • pm_table_version, pm_table_size - the driver's table version and size files.
  • SMU firmware - the firmware version of the SMU, e.g. 4.84.4.0 on the author's PC.

Unusual values and what they suggest. ryzen_smu driver not loaded: install and load the out-of-tree ryzen_smu module if you want PM table data. Intel PCs never have it.

Where Linux gets it. /sys/kernel/ryzen_smu_drv/{pm_table,pm_table_version,pm_table_size,version}.

Background. The SMU (System Management Unit) is a small controller inside AMD Ryzen chips that runs clocks, voltages and power limits. Its PM (power management) table is a live block of numbers: power, temperatures, clocks and limits.

Fake SPDs

fak-spds - Linux data

In plain words. SIV can replay saved memory-stick SPD dumps. SRS has no replay; it shows where the real SPD data comes from.

What you see.

  • Status - no replay; real SPD data is in the [spd] item.
  • SPD cache - path of spd.txt in the root cache, or Needs root: Menu > Run as root (srs-root).
  • One line per DIMM sensor (spd5118 or jc42), with its hwmon name and I2C address, e.g. spd5118 hwmon7 at i2c 1-0051.
  • no spd5118 / jc42 hwmon devices if none are loaded.

Healthy / typical values. On the author's PC: cache present, two spd5118 sensors at 1-0051 and 1-0053.

Unusual values and what they suggest. Needs root: run Menu -> Run as root once so the [spd] item can show memory timings.

Where Linux gets it. ~/.cache/srs/root/spd.txt (written by srs-root) and /sys/class/hwmon.

Filter

filter - Linux data

In plain words. Lists the ways you can narrow what SRS shows.

What you see.

  • Find pattern - regular expression or literal text, Ignore case, Max matches.
  • Lookup filter - PCI or USB bus; Tree, Scan or Info mode.
  • Device panels - PCI Bus, USB Bus and ALL Dev pick the bus.
  • -save filter - [item][item]... picks which items are written.
  • Column filter - none; every column is always shown.

Where Linux gets it. Built-in text.

Background. A regular expression (regex) is a search pattern. For example nvme[0-9] finds nvme0, nvme1 and so on.

Final processing

final - Linux data

In plain words. How long SRS has been running and how much CPU time it used so far.

What you see.

  • Elapsed - seconds since the process started.
  • CPU time - CPU seconds the process has used.
  • Sections - how many items SRS has.
  • On exit - what happens at close (save settings in GUI mode, free tables, close panels).

Healthy / typical values. On the author's PC, during a full [all] save: Elapsed 3.140 s, CPU time 0.160 s, 545 items. Elapsed is much larger than CPU time because most of the time is spent waiting on files and helper tools, not computing.

Unusual values and what they suggest. In a full save, Elapsed far above 10-20 s means some item waited a long time; often a slow or sleeping disk, or a network tool timing out.

Where Linux gets it. /proc/uptime, /proc/self/stat (start time) and the process CPU clock.

GPU info buffer

gpu - Linux data

In plain words. One line per graphics card: driver, PCI address, load, video memory, PCIe link and current clocks.

What you see.

Column What it means Why it matters
GPU DRM card name, e.g. card0. Matches /sys/class/drm/card0.
Driver Kernel driver, e.g. amdgpu, i915, nvidia. Wrong or missing driver = no acceleration.
PCI ID / Slot Vendor-device ID and PCI address, e.g. 1002-7550 0000:03:00.0. Identifies the exact chip.
Busy GPU load in percent. High at idle means something is rendering.
VRAM Used / Total Video memory in use and installed. Near full causes stutter in games.
Link PCIe link width and speed now, e.g. x16 32.0 GT/s PCIe. Lower than expected costs bandwidth.
Clocks (sclk / mclk) Current core clock and memory clock (the starred level). Low at idle, high under load.

Columns the driver does not provide show -. Busy, VRAM and Clocks come from amdgpu files, so on other drivers they are usually -. This panel refreshes every 2 seconds.

Healthy / typical values. On the author's Radeon RX 9070 XT: card0 amdgpu 1002-7550 0000:03:00.0 7% 1.03GB / 15.92GB x16 32.0 GT/s PCIe 664Mhz / 875Mhz on the desktop.

Unusual values and what they suggest.

  • Link x8 or x4 on an x16 card: the card is in a lower slot, or that slot shares lanes with an M.2 drive.
  • Link 2.5 GT/s at idle: normal power saving; it rises under load. If it stays low under load, check the BIOS PCIe setting.
  • Busy stuck near 100% at idle: a program is using the GPU; check with a GPU monitor.

Where Linux gets it. /sys/class/drm/cardN/device/ files: driver, vendor, device, gpu_busy_percent, mem_info_vram_used, mem_info_vram_total, current_link_speed, current_link_width, pp_dpm_sclk, pp_dpm_mclk.

Background. PCIe link width is how many lanes the card uses (x16 is full size). GT/s (gigatransfers per second) is the speed per lane: 8 = PCIe 3.0, 16 = 4.0, 32 = 5.0. sclk is the shader (core) clock and mclk the memory clock. DPM (Dynamic Power Management) levels are the clock steps the card can pick from.

Help

help - Linux data

In plain words. The built-in help: what each main-window button does, the hot-keys, and the command-line options. Also opened with F1.

What you see. Three blocks:

  • Main window buttons - OK, Copy, PCI Bus / USB Bus, ALL Dev, Lookup, Find, Data Files, About / Help, Menu, Refresh, Next / Prev, Highlight / Colour.
  • Hot-keys - Ctrl+F Find, Ctrl+L Lookup, Ctrl+D ALL Dev, F3 / Shift+F3 next / previous match, Ctrl+H highlight on/off, F5 refresh, F1 help, Esc close.
  • Command line - srs-gui, -save, id, find, devices, burn, --list, --version / -h.

A last line gives the file locations: settings in ~/.config/srs/SRSDEF.ini, root cache in ~/.cache/srs/root, reports in ~/sysreports.

Where Linux gets it. Built-in text.

Background. The PCI Bus button resolves each device by trying the most exact ID first: vendor:device:subvendor:subdevice:revision, then shorter keys, down to vendor only. That is what V:D:S:s:RR -> ... -> V means.

Highlight setup

highlight - Linux data

In plain words. Your Find highlight colour, whether highlighting is on, and the panel font.

What you see. Columns: (key), Colour, Find Description, Setting, Reported Value.

  • [F] row - the Colour Find Text as #RRGGBB and as RGB( r, g, b ).
  • Highlight Matches - tick box and on / off.
  • Panel Font - the Font Name setting.

Below: the settings file path (or SRSDEF.ini not written yet - defaults shown), and a note that SIV's CPU/GPU speed highlight colours are the coloured columns of the [cpu] and [gpu-clocks] items.

Healthy / typical values. Defaults, and the author's values: #FFFF00 (yellow, RGB( 255, 255, 0 )), on, Tahoma.

Where Linux gets it. Keys Colour Find Text, Highlight Matches and Font Name in section [SRSDEF] of SRSDEF.ini.

Hotkeys

hot-keys - Linux data

In plain words. The keyboard shortcuts of the SRS window.

What you see. A header (Profile, Hotkeys Enabled ticked) and one row per shortcut: letter code, action, key and panel accelerator (fixed). The ten shortcuts are Find (Ctrl+F), Lookup (Ctrl+L), ALL Dev (Ctrl+D), Highlight Matches (Ctrl+H), Next Match (F3), Previous Match (Shift+F3), Refresh (F5), Help (F1), Close Panel (Esc) and Copy Selection (Ctrl+C).

Where Linux gets it. Built-in list.

Background. These keys only work while an SRS window has focus. SIV's global hot-keys (which work from any program and can switch screens or LEDs) have no SRS equivalent.

SIV image (EXE)

image-exe - Linux data

In plain words. The internal layout of the SRS program file: its sections.

What you see. The program path and size, then the full readelf -S -W table: [Nr] section number, Name, Type, Address, Off (file offset), Size, ES (entry size), Flg (flags, explained in the "Key to Flags" at the end), Lk, Inf, Al (alignment). If binutils is missing you see readelf not available (binutils).

Healthy / typical values. About 28 sections. .text (the code) is the largest; on the author's 1.38 MB build it is 0x0d333c bytes (about 845 KB). .rodata holds fixed text and tables.

Where Linux gets it. readelf -S -W /proc/self/exe.

Background. Linux programs use the ELF (Executable and Linkable Format) file format. A section is one named part of the file: .text = code, .data = initial variables, .bss = zero-filled memory reserved at start, .rodata = read-only data.

SIV image (SYS driver)

image-sys - Windows-only (Linux equivalent shown)

In plain words. SIV on Windows loads its own kernel driver (SIVX64.sys). SRS needs none. Instead this lists the Linux kernel modules SRS reads data from.

What you see.

  • Status - no kernel driver; root data comes from the srs-root helper.
  • SIV equivalent - SIVX64.sys is not needed.
  • One line per module that is present: name, loaded (a loadable module) or built-in (part of the kernel), its version if it reports one, and refcnt (how many users hold it).

Modules checked: k10temp, zenpower, coretemp, amdgpu, i915, nvidia, nct6775, nct6683, nct6687, it87, asus_ec_sensors, asus_wmi_sensors, spd5118, jc42, ee1004, ryzen_smu, msr, cpuid, drivetemp, nvme, acpi_cpufreq, amd_pstate, zenergy. Only those present are listed.

Healthy / typical values. On the author's AMD PC: k10temp, amdgpu (refcnt 61), nct6775, spd5118, ee1004, ryzen_smu (version 0.1.7), msr (built-in), drivetemp, nvme, zenergy.

Unusual values and what they suggest.

  • No CPU temperature module (k10temp on AMD, coretemp on Intel): CPU temperatures will be missing.
  • No Super-I/O module (nct6775, it87 and so on): board fan speeds and voltages will be missing.
  • No drivetemp: SATA drive temperatures are not in hwmon.

Where Linux gets it. /sys/module/<name>/, version and refcnt.

Background. A kernel module is a driver that can be loaded into the running kernel. A Super-I/O chip on the motherboard (Nuvoton, ITE) reads fan speeds, voltages and board temperatures.

Image tree

image-tree - Linux data

In plain words. Which shared libraries SRS needs, and which libraries those need.

What you see. The program name and path, then a tree: each library the program needs, the file it was loaded from (or (not loaded)), and below it the libraries that one needs. A last line counts the shared objects mapped into the process.

Healthy / typical values. SRS needs very little. On the author's PC: libm.so.6 and libc.so.6, each pulling in ld-linux-x86-64.so.2; 6 shared objects mapped.

Unusual values and what they suggest. (not loaded) next to a needed library: unusual for a running program; the library may be loaded under another path.

Where Linux gets it. readelf -d (the NEEDED entries) and /proc/self/maps. SRS does not run ldd, since ldd can run the program.

Background. A shared library (.so file) is code many programs use at once, such as the C library libc.so.6. ld-linux is the loader that links them at start.

Initial processing

initial - Linux data

In plain words. The steps SRS takes when the window starts.

What you see. A numbered list: 1 read SRSDEF.ini; 2 load pci.ids and usb.ids; 3 find PCI and USB devices and resolve names; 4 find the newest report in ~/sysreports for Find; 5 build the item list for the Menu; 6 open the main window and set up the shortcut keys; 7 start refresh timers only for open live panels. A note: with arguments, the GUI is skipped and the command line runs.

Where Linux gets it. Built-in text.

Install

install - Linux data

In plain words. Where SRS is installed and whether its menu entry and folders exist.

What you see. Program image path, then a tick box for each:

  • Menu entry in ~/.local/share/applications, /usr/share/applications and /usr/local/share/applications (srs-gui.desktop). If found, the Exec line it runs.
  • Settings folder ~/.config/srs.
  • Root cache folder ~/.cache/srs/root.

Healthy / typical values. A packaged install has the /usr/share/applications entry with Exec srs-gui. On the author's PC that entry, the settings folder and the root cache folder are all ticked.

Unusual values and what they suggest.

  • No menu entry ticked: SRS will not show in your app menu; reinstall the package.
  • Root cache folder not ticked: the root helper has never run, so root-only items will say "Needs root".

Where Linux gets it. Checks those paths and reads Exec= from the .desktop file.

SIV languages

languages - Linux data

In plain words. SRS is English only, using UTF-8 text. This also shows your language settings.

What you see. UI language (English only), Encoding (UTF-8), then the values of the environment variables LANG, LC_ALL, LC_MESSAGES, LC_CTYPE and LANGUAGE (<unset> if not set).

Healthy / typical values. On the author's PC: LANG en_US.UTF-8, the LC_ values unset.

Unusual values and what they suggest. A LANG without UTF-8 (for example C or POSIX): symbols such as °C and µs may print wrongly in a terminal.

Where Linux gets it. The process environment.

Background. A locale is the set of language, number and date rules a program uses. LANG sets the default; LC_* variables override parts of it.

Lock setup

lck-setup - Linux data

In plain words. How SRS keeps its own threads from getting in each other's way. In short: it needs almost no locks.

What you see. Instance lock (none; several copies may run), Find (one worker thread, the GUI thread owns all windows), Burn-in (one thread per CPU, pinned, polls a stop flag), Hardware locks (none, because SRS does no SMBus, ISA or PCI config access).

Where Linux gets it. Built-in text.

Background. A lock or mutex (mutual exclusion) stops two threads using the same thing at the same time. SIV needs global locks because it talks to hardware buses directly; SRS leaves that to the kernel.

Maker icons

makers - Linux data

In plain words. The companies that made the PCI devices in your PC, with a count for each.

What you see. Columns: Vendor (4-digit hex PCI vendor ID), Maker (name from pci.ids, or (unknown)), PCI functions (how many PCI functions from that vendor). If pci.ids is missing: pci.ids not found.

Healthy / typical values. On the author's AMD PC: 1022 AMD (38 functions, the chipset and CPU parts), 1002 AMD/ATI (4, the graphics card and its audio), 1B21 ASMedia (7, USB and SATA controllers), 10EC Realtek (2, network), plus Samsung, ADATA and MAXIO (one each, NVMe drives).

Unusual values and what they suggest. (unknown) maker: pci.ids is too old for that device, or it is a very new or rare vendor. Update hwdata.

Where Linux gets it. The PCI devices in sysfs, names from pci.ids.

Background. A PCI function is one logical device. One physical chip can show several (a GPU usually shows a graphics function and an audio function). SIV shows maker logos here; SRS shows names.

SIV manifest

manifest - Windows-only (Linux equivalent shown)

In plain words. Windows programs carry a "manifest" describing them. The Linux equivalent is the ELF note sections, shown here.

What you see. The output of readelf -n: for each note section, Owner, Data size and Description. Typical notes:

  • .note.gnu.build-id - a unique build ID (a long hex number) for this exact build.
  • .note.gnu.property - CPU instruction-set levels the code needs and uses (x86-64-v2, v3, v4) and features (XMM, YMM, ZMM).
  • .note.ABI-tag - the oldest Linux kernel ABI the program supports.

Healthy / typical values. On the author's build: build ID XXXX..., ABI OS: Linux, ABI: 6.1.0.

Unusual values and what they suggest. If "x86 ISA needed" lists x86-64-v4 (AVX-512 level), that build only runs on CPUs with AVX-512. A copy built that way will crash with "illegal instruction" on an older CPU. Use a build made for a lower level.

Where Linux gets it. readelf -n -W /proc/self/exe.

Background. The ABI (Application Binary Interface) is the set of low-level rules a program and the kernel agree on. x86-64-v2/v3/v4 are CPU feature levels: v3 needs AVX2, v4 needs AVX-512.

Mapping cache

map-cache - Windows-only (Linux equivalent shown)

In plain words. In SIV this shows how its driver maps physical memory. SRS never maps physical memory, so it just explains that.

What you see. Status (Windows-only feature), srs-gui (no driver, /dev/mem is never opened), Nearest Linux (kernel drivers expose registers in sysfs; root-only tables come from the srs-root cache).

Background. Mapping physical memory means reading hardware registers by their raw address. It is powerful but risky; on Linux the kernel drivers do it for you.

Map/unmap test

map-unmap - Windows-only (Linux equivalent shown)

In plain words. In SIV this times its driver mapping and unmapping physical memory. SRS has nothing to time; it shows the same three lines as Mapping cache.

Menus

menus - Linux data

In plain words. The full list of every item SRS has, grouped by category.

What you see. For each category, a line [category] N items, then one line per item: [id], title, bucket and group. At the end: N items in M categories.

  • Bucket Linux (green) - real Linux data.
  • Absent - hardware most PCs do not have.
  • Windows-only - a Windows feature; the Linux equivalent is shown.
  • (stub) after an item - the item has no data function yet.

Healthy / typical values. On the author's PC the [tuning] category alone has 48 items, and the whole program has 545.

Where Linux gets it. The program's own item list (same as srs-gui --list).

Mutex info

mutex - Linux data

In plain words. File locks that SRS holds right now. Normally none.

What you see. Columns # (lock number), Class (POSIX, FLOCK, OFDLCK), Mode (ADVISORY or MANDATORY), Access (READ or WRITE), PID / Inode (process, device and file, and byte range). Then a count: N file locks held by this process (/proc/locks).

Healthy / typical values. 0 file locks held by this process on the author's PC.

Where Linux gets it. /proc/locks, filtered to this process ID.

Background. A file lock tells other programs "I am using this file". The kernel lists every lock in /proc/locks.

PMB info (power monitor buffer)

pmb - Linux data

In plain words. Every live power (watts) and current (amps) reading the kernel's sensor drivers provide.

What you see.

Column What it means Why it matters
# Row number. -
Device hwmon chip name, e.g. amdgpu, zenergy. Which part the reading belongs to.
Description Sensor label (e.g. PPT) or the raw name (power1). Which rail or limit.
Current Power in W (3 decimals) or current in A. The live value.
Characteristic cap N W if a power cap is set for that sensor. How close you are to the limit.

The panel refreshes every second.

Healthy / typical values. On the author's PC: amdgpu PPT 35.000 W cap 374 W (graphics card on the desktop). A desktop GPU idles at roughly 10-40 W; under game load it runs near the cap.

Unusual values and what they suggest.

  • GPU power near the cap at idle: something is rendering, or a monitor setup keeps memory clocks high (common with several screens or high refresh rates).
  • A cap well below the card's rated power: a power limit was lowered, by a tuning tool or the BIOS.
  • No rows: no hwmon driver reports power; CPU power on AMD needs a module such as zenergy.

Where Linux gets it. /sys/class/hwmon/*/power*_input, power*_average, curr*_input, with *_label and power*_cap.

Background. PPT (Package Power Tracking) is AMD's name for total power drawn by the chip package. A power cap is the limit the firmware holds it to.

Colour RGB debug

rgb-debug - Linux data

In plain words. The colour palette SRS uses for text, with what each colour means.

What you see. Columns Colour (internal name), Default Colour (RGB( r, g, b )), Hex and Colour Description. Rows: C_LABEL (labels, light blue 3399FF), C_VALUE (values, dark blue 0000CC), C_PURPLE (paths, IDs, commands, 9C0FB8), C_TEAL (secondary values, 009999), C_ORANGE (build and warnings, FF8800), C_GREEN (OK / enabled, 00A000), C_RED (errors / not found, E00000), C_BLACK (plain text), C_GRAY (notes, disabled, 808080), and Find Text (your Colour Find Text setting).

Where Linux gets it. Built-in palette, plus SRSDEF.ini for Find Text.

Background. Knowing the colours helps you scan a panel: red means missing or error, orange means "changed from default" or a warning, green means OK.

SDM info (storage device monitor)

sdm - Linux data

In plain words. Every whole disk the kernel sees, with its size and how much has been read and written since boot.

What you see.

Column What it means Why it matters
# Row number. -
Device Name Kernel name: nvme0n1, sda, sr0, zram0. Matches /dev/<name>.
Model Model string, or -. Identifies the drive.
Size Capacity. 0B = no media (empty card reader or USB slot).
Reads Data read since boot. Shows which drives are busy.
Writes Data written since boot. Heavy writes wear SSDs.
In flight Requests in progress right now. Stuck above 0 can mean a hung drive.
Rotational / Removable Spinning disk or solid state; fixed or removable. Affects which I/O scheduler suits it.

Partitions, loop and ram devices are skipped. Refreshes every 2 seconds.

Healthy / typical values. On the author's PC: three NVMe SSDs (Samsung 980 PRO 1 TB, ADATA S70 2 TB, PNY CS2340 500 GB), a 4 TB Seagate hard disk (rotational / fixed), USB sticks, a DVD writer and zram0 (15.23 GB compressed RAM swap). In flight 0 on all of them.

Unusual values and what they suggest.

  • In flight stays above 0 for many seconds: the drive is stuck or very slow. Check dmesg for errors.
  • A drive you know is there is missing: cable, power, or the drive has dropped off the bus.
  • USB sticks shown as rotational: normal. Many USB bridges report this by default, not because the stick spins.
  • An optical drive shows a size even with no disc: the kernel keeps the last size; ignore it.

Where Linux gets it. /sys/class/block/<dev>/{size,stat,removable,queue/rotational,device/model}.

Background. zram is a block device in RAM that stores compressed data, used as fast swap. Size and sector counts are in 512-byte sectors, which SRS converts to bytes.

Sequence setup

sequence - Linux data

In plain words. The order in which items appear in a plain -save (one with no item list). It is the same order SIV64X uses.

What you see. A numbered list: position, [id] and title. It starts 1 [overview], 2 [sgb-ini], 3 [sdm], 4 [dsb], 5 [bsi] and so on.

Healthy / typical values. About 120 items in the default save.

Where Linux gets it. The program's built-in default save list.

Background. Keeping SIV's order means you can compare an SRS save with a SIV save side by side.

SGB end

sgb-end - Linux data

In plain words. In SIV this marks the end of the system/board buffer. In SRS it is a marker line plus how long the process has been running.

What you see. SGB end (explains there is no shared buffer; SGB info reads sysfs live) and Elapsed (seconds since start).

Healthy / typical values. On the author's full save: 9.230 seconds since start at that point.

SGB info (system/board buffer)

sgb-ini - Linux data

In plain words. The motherboard, BIOS and chipset IDs, plus a few facts about the SRS process.

What you see.

Field What it means Why it matters
Maker Name / Model Name / Board Version The motherboard maker, model and revision. Find the right manual and BIOS.
Serial Number Board serial. Needs root; read from the cached dmidecode output. Else Needs root: .... Warranty and asset tracking. Keep it private.
System System maker and product name. Prebuilt PCs show a product here; self-builds show placeholders.
BIOS Vendor / Version / Date / Release The firmware maker, version, date and release number. Check if a newer BIOS exists.
Chassis Type SMBIOS chassis code (3 = desktop, 10 = notebook, and so on). What kind of case firmware reports.
MCH (00:00.0) Vendor-device ID of PCI device 00:00.0, the host bridge. Identifies the CPU / chipset family.
ACT CPUs Online CPUs (configured CPUs). Should match your thread count.
SRS Affinity Hex mask of CPUs SRS may run on. Normally all CPUs.
SRS PID Process ID of this SRS run. -
SRS Driver none. SRS uses no kernel driver.
Root cache Whether dmidecode.txt is in the root cache. If not, the serial cannot be shown.
RAW Command Path of the running program. -

Healthy / typical values. On the author's PC: ASUSTeK COMPUTER INC., TUF GAMING X870-PRO WIFI7 W NEO, Rev 1.xx, serial XXXX, System ASUS System Product Name (a placeholder, normal for a self-built PC), American Megatrends BIOS 1805 dated 09/18/2026, release 18.5, chassis type 3, MCH 1022-14d8 (AMD), ACT CPUs 16 (16), affinity 000000000000FFFF.

Unusual values and what they suggest.

  • Fields like "To Be Filled By O.E.M." or "Default string": the board maker left them blank. Harmless.
  • SRS Affinity not all ones: SRS was started with taskset or inside a restricted cgroup or container.
  • ACT CPUs smaller than the number in brackets: some CPUs are offline.

Where Linux gets it. /sys/class/dmi/id/* (SMBIOS types 0, 1, 2 and 3), PCI 0000:00:00.0 vendor and device files, sched_getaffinity(), and ~/.cache/srs/root/dmidecode.txt for the serial.

Background. SMBIOS (System Management BIOS) is a table the firmware fills with facts about the board, BIOS, memory and case. Linux copies the public fields to /sys/class/dmi/id; serial numbers are root-only.

Active SIV instances

siv-active - Linux data

In plain words. Every copy of SRS running right now.

What you see. Columns Name (process name), PID, Version (V<version> (this) for the copy making the report, - for others) and Image Filename (program path, or (not readable)). Then a count. Names come from /proc/<pid>/comm, which the kernel cuts to 15 characters, so sysreport-search shows as sysreport-searc.

Healthy / typical values. On the author's PC: the tray copy srs-gui and the sysreport-searc copy making the save; 2 instances.

Unusual values and what they suggest. Many old copies: earlier windows or tray icons did not close. They are safe to close; SRS holds no driver or hardware lock.

Where Linux gets it. /proc/*/comm and /proc/*/exe.

SIV autorun

siv-autorun - Linux data

In plain words. Whether SRS starts by itself when you log in.

What you see. Two tick-box lines: User autostart (~/.config/autostart/srs-gui.desktop) and System autostart (/etc/xdg/autostart/srs-gui.desktop), each with its Exec command if present. Then srs-gui starts at login. or how to enable it.

Healthy / typical values. Off by default. On the author's PC the user entry is on and runs /usr/bin/srs-gui --gui-tray (start in the system tray).

Where Linux gets it. The XDG autostart folders.

Background. XDG autostart is the desktop standard: any .desktop file in an autostart folder is run at login. Delete or rename the file to stop it.

SIV DLLs

siv-dll - Linux data

In plain words. The files SRS depends on: name databases, the program itself, the settings file and every shared library it has loaded. Opens with the Lookup button row.

What you see. A table with Description, File Specification (path), Current Identification (version or date), Code Page (text encoding, always UTF-8) and WEB Download Location. Rows:

  • PCI Device Names, USB Device Names, PnP / Monitor Names - the .ids files, their version and upstream URL.
  • srs-gui Program - path, version and size.
  • Settings - SRSDEF.ini and when it was last written, or not written yet.
  • Kernel driver - none.

Then "Shared objects mapped into this process": each library name, path, size and file date.

Healthy / typical values. On the author's PC: libc, libm, ld-linux and a few gconv modules (character-set converters loaded by the C library, such as CP932.so), all from /usr/lib.

Unusual values and what they suggest. A library loaded from an odd folder (your home directory, /tmp): something is setting LD_LIBRARY_PATH or LD_PRELOAD. Check your shell setup.

Where Linux gets it. /proc/self/maps, file sizes and dates, and the .ids file headers. No network check is made.

Background. On Windows a DLL (Dynamic-Link Library) is a shared code file. The Linux equivalent is a shared object (.so).

SIV driver

siv-drv - Windows-only (Linux equivalent shown)

In plain words. SIV shows its kernel driver here. SRS has no driver; it shows the root helper's cache instead, which is how SRS gets root-only data.

What you see.

  • Kernel driver - none.
  • Root helper - srs-root (Menu -> Run as root) writes a read-only cache; items never run as root.
  • Root cache - the cache folder path.
  • One line per cache file: name, size and date. Or empty - Needs root: Menu > Run as root (srs-root).

Healthy / typical values. On the author's PC the cache has about 24 files, all from the same run: dmidecode.txt, dmesg.txt, msrs.txt, pci-all.txt, spd.txt, smart-<drive>.txt, NVMe details and more. Tiny smart-*.txt files (55 bytes) belong to drives that report no SMART data, such as card readers.

Unusual values and what they suggest.

  • Cache files days or weeks old: root-only items show old data. Run the root helper again.
  • smart-* files for drives no longer attached: left over from an earlier run. Harmless.

Where Linux gets it. ~/.cache/srs/root/.

Background. SMART (Self-Monitoring, Analysis and Reporting Technology) is a drive's own health log. Reading it needs root, which is why it comes from the cache.

SIVDEF.ini

siv-ini - Linux data

In plain words. The whole SRS settings file, printed as it is.

What you see. Each [section] in bold, then each key value line. Comment lines (# or ;) show as notes. Last line: N section(s) in <path>. If the file does not exist yet: No Sections Found within the SRSDEF.ini file, Status 2 File not found. and the path.

Healthy / typical values. One [SRSDEF] section. On the author's PC: Colour Find Text FFFF00, Highlight Matches 1, Font Name Tahoma, GPU Load Command, Tray Icon 1, Close To Tray 1, Minimize To Tray 1, Start In Tray 1, Theme Dark.

Unusual values and what they suggest. "File not found" on a fresh install: normal until you change a setting in the window.

Where Linux gets it. $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/srs/SRSDEF.ini, by default ~/.config/srs/SRSDEF.ini. SIV keeps its settings in SIVDEF.ini and the Windows registry; SRS uses this file.

SIV location / window poke

siv-location - Linux data

In plain words. How SRS sizes and places its windows, and what kind of desktop session it is in.

What you see. Main window (default 1000 x 420), Panels (default 1180 x 560, cascaded on X11), Saved positions (none; SRS does not remember positions), Session (Wayland, X11 or no display (CLI)), Desktop (from XDG_CURRENT_DESKTOP, if set), GDK_SCALE (window scale factor) and Window poke (not supported on Linux).

Healthy / typical values. On the author's PC: Wayland, KDE, GDK_SCALE 1 (default).

Unusual values and what they suggest. Text far too small or large: set GDK_SCALE=2 (or 1) before starting SRS on a high-DPI screen.

Where Linux gets it. The environment variables WAYLAND_DISPLAY, DISPLAY, XDG_CURRENT_DESKTOP and GDK_SCALE.

Background. On Wayland the compositor (the desktop) decides where windows go; programs cannot place themselves. "Window poke" in SIV sends messages to another program's window; Linux has no general way to do that.

SIV qualifiers

siv-qualifiers - Linux data

In plain words. Every command-line option SRS accepts, with what it does.

What you see. A two-column table, Qualifier and Meaning:

  • -save, -save=[item][item]..., -save=[...]=file|STDOUT - write items as text.
  • id ID with --bus pci|usb and --mode tree|scan|info - look up a device ID.
  • find PATTERN with --report DIR, -i, -F, --max N, --color auto|always|never - search a report.
  • devices - resolve every local device.
  • burn - CPU burn-in test, with thread, CPU, time, mode and temperature limit options.
  • --list, --version, -h, --help.

Last line: Command Used (the program path).

Healthy / typical values. Fixed list for each version.

Where Linux gets it. Built-in list.

Background. In SIV, options are called qualifiers. Defaults are given in brackets, e.g. --bus pci and --mode tree.

SIV qualifier list

siv-quals - Linux data

In plain words. The same options as SIV qualifiers, names only, without sub-options or meanings.

What you see. -save, -save=[item][item]..., -save=[...]=file|STDOUT, id ID, find PATTERN, devices, burn, --list, --version, -h, --help.

SIV setup

siv-setup - Linux data

In plain words. The main settings SRS knows about, and whether each is set in your file.

What you see. Columns (tick), Name, Data and Meaning:

  • |X| = the key is in SRSDEF.ini, with its value in quotes. |_| = not set, showing <default ...>.
  • Keys: Colour Find Text (Find match background, RRGGBB), Highlight Matches, Font Name, and SIO Sensors (Super-I/O sensor inputs you have switched back on, e.g. nct6799:AUXTIN1,...).

Healthy / typical values. On the author's PC: the first three set ("FFFF00", "1", "Tahoma"), SIO Sensors <default none>.

Where Linux gets it. Section [SRSDEF] of SRSDEF.ini. (SIV keeps these in the Windows registry.)

Background. Super-I/O chips have spare inputs that boards often leave unconnected, so SRS hides some by default. SIO Sensors lets you show chosen ones again.

SIV sizes

siv-sizes - Linux data

In plain words. The size in bytes of SRS's main internal data structures. Mainly for developers.

What you see. Columns Structure, Bytes and Use, for: srs_item (one item), srs_out (output sink), srs_db (a loaded .ids database), srs_rec (one database record), srs_result (a Lookup result), srs_info (an Info lookup), srs_findres and srs_hit (Find results), srs_dev (one device), and the C types void *, long, size_t. Then Items (how many registered) and Page size.

Healthy / typical values. On a 64-bit PC: pointer, long and size_t are 8 bytes; page size 4096. The author's build: srs_item 64 bytes, 545 items.

Unusual values and what they suggest. Page size 16384 or 65536: normal on some ARM systems.

Where Linux gets it. Compile-time sizes and sysconf(_SC_PAGESIZE).

Background. A memory page is the unit the CPU and kernel use to manage memory, usually 4 KB on x86.

SIV driver service

siv-srv - Windows-only (Linux equivalent shown)

In plain words. In SIV this controls the Windows service that loads its driver. SRS installs no service.

What you see. Status (Windows-only), srs-gui (no driver, no service; root data via the srs-root helper), Helper start (on demand from Menu -> Run as root, with a polkit password prompt; it exits after writing the cache) and Nearest Linux (kernel modules, see SIV image (SYS driver)).

Background. polkit is the Linux service that asks for your password before a program may do something as root.

SIV usage history

siv-usage - Linux data

In plain words. Which version you have, when the program file was made, and when your settings were last saved.

What you see. Columns Version, Image Date (program file date) and Settings Last Written (SRSDEF.ini date, - if none). A note: SRS keeps no usage counter.

Healthy / typical values. On the author's PC: V2.0.0, image 2026-10-26, settings 2026-10-25.

Where Linux gets it. File modification times of the program and SRSDEF.ini.

SIV use / update

siv-use - Linux data

In plain words. Version facts and how up to date the name databases are. SRS never goes online to check for updates.

What you see. Program (version, local build, no update channel), Update check (not performed; no network access), then one line per database: name, version or date, and the upstream URL. Last line: update the .ids files with your distribution's hwdata package (or update-pciids / update-usbids).

Healthy / typical values. pci.ids a few weeks old at most on a rolling distribution. On the author's PC: pci.ids 2026.10.01, usb.ids 2026.06.26.

Unusual values and what they suggest. Databases many months old: new devices may show as unknown. Update the system's hwdata package.

Where Linux gets it. The header lines of the .ids files.

SMB end

smb-end - Linux data

In plain words. In SIV this marks the end of the SMBus buffer. In SRS it is one marker line: SRS does no SMBus access; see SMB info.

SMB info

smb-ini - Linux data

In plain words. The I2C / SMBus adapters and devices the kernel has registered, by name only.

What you see. Columns Device (sysfs name), Name (kernel's name for it) and Driver (driver bound to it, or -). Adapters are named i2c-N; devices on them are named bus-address, e.g. 1-0051. A note: SRS never opens /dev/i2c-* or probes addresses.

Healthy / typical values. On the author's AMD PC: SMBus PIIX4 adapter ports (the chipset SMBus, where the RAM sits), AMDGPU DM buses (one per display output, used to read monitor data), AMDGPU SMU, a Synopsys DesignWare adapter, and two spd5118 devices at 1-0051 and 1-0053 (the RAM sticks).

Unusual values and what they suggest.

  • No PIIX4 / i801 adapter: the chipset SMBus driver is not loaded (i2c_piix4 on AMD, i2c_i801 on Intel), so RAM sensors cannot appear.
  • RAM devices missing while the adapter is there: load spd5118 (DDR5) or ee1004 / jc42 (DDR4).

Where Linux gets it. /sys/bus/i2c/devices/*/name and the driver link.

Background. I2C and SMBus are slow two-wire buses that link small chips: RAM SPD chips, sensors, RGB controllers and the monitor's DDC (Display Data Channel) for its name and settings. Each device has a 7-bit address.

Lock states

states - Linux data

In plain words. Each thread of SRS and what it is doing right now.

What you see. Columns TID (thread ID), Thread (name), State (one letter) and Wait channel (the kernel function it sleeps in, or -).

Healthy / typical values. In a command-line save: one thread, state R (running).

Unusual values and what they suggest. A thread in state D for a long time: it is stuck waiting on a device (often a disk or USB drive).

Where Linux gets it. /proc/self/task/*/{comm,stat,wchan}.

Background. Thread states: R running, S sleeping (waiting for an event), D waiting on hardware and cannot be interrupted, T stopped, Z zombie (finished but not yet collected).

STC info (thread contexts)

stc - Linux data

In plain words. A fuller view of SRS's threads: CPU time used, which CPUs each may run on, and priority.

What you see.

Column What it means
TID Thread ID.
Name Thread name (cut to 15 characters).
State One-letter state, see Lock states.
Total CPU User + system CPU time, as minutes:seconds.
Affinity CPUs the thread may run on, e.g. 0-15.
Last CPU The CPU it last ran on, e.g. CPU-15.
Priority / Nice Kernel priority and nice value.

Then a count of threads. Refreshes every 2 seconds in the window.

Healthy / typical values. On the author's PC during a save: one thread, R, 0:00.420, 0-15, CPU-15, 16 / -4.

Unusual values and what they suggest. Nice not 0: the program was started with nice, or a tool such as a scheduler daemon or ananicy changed it.

Where Linux gets it. /proc/self/task/*/stat and status (Cpus_allowed_list).

Background. Nice runs from -20 (most favoured) to 19 (least). The kernel priority shown is 20 + nice for normal tasks.

Tune system

tune - Linux data

In plain words. A list of common kernel tuning values (sysctls), with the kernel default, your current value and a commonly used "tuned" value side by side.

What you see.

Column What it means
Value Name The sysctl name, e.g. vm.swappiness.
Default The usual kernel default, in brackets.
Current Your value now. Green = same as default; orange = changed; grey <none> = not present in this kernel.
Other A value often used by tuning guides and gaming distributions, in brackets.
Path The /proc/sys file it comes from.

The values covered: memory (vm.swappiness, vm.vfs_cache_pressure, vm.dirty_*, vm.page-cluster, vm.max_map_count, vm.compaction_proactiveness, vm.watermark_boost_factor, vm.overcommit_memory, vm.zone_reclaim_mode), kernel (nmi_watchdog, watchdog, sched_autogroup_enabled, split_lock_mitigate, numa_balancing, kptr_restrict, dmesg_restrict, perf_event_paranoid, unprivileged_bpf_disabled, printk, timer_migration), files (fs.inotify.max_user_watches, fs.file-max) and network (default_qdisc, tcp_congestion_control, rmem_max, wmem_max, netdev_max_backlog, tcp_fastopen, tcp_mtu_probing). SRS only reads; it offers no Apply button.

Healthy / typical values. There is no single "right" value. On the author's tuned gaming setup: vm.swappiness 150 (high, normal with zram swap), vm.max_map_count 2147483642 (needed by some games), net.core.default_qdisc fq, tcp_congestion_control bbr3, kernel.split_lock_mitigate 0.

Unusual values and what they suggest.

  • vm.max_map_count at 65530 and some games crash or fail to load: raise it (many distributions now set 1048576 or more).
  • vm.swappiness high without zram: the system may swap to disk too soon.
  • kernel.numa_balancing <none>: the kernel was built without NUMA balancing. Normal on single-socket kernels.
  • fs.inotify.max_user_watches at 8192 and an IDE or file sync tool says "too many watches": raise it.

Where Linux gets it. /proc/sys/<name with dots changed to slashes>.

Background. A sysctl is a kernel setting you can read and change at run time. Swappiness sets how eagerly the kernel swaps. Dirty values set how much changed data may wait in RAM before it is written to disk. qdisc (queueing discipline) and congestion control decide how network packets are sent.

Tuning

tuning - Linux data

In plain words. The current power and performance profile: CPU frequency driver, governor, boost, CPU scheduler, memory and disk scheduler settings.

What you see. Lines appear only when the source exists:

Field What it means
tuned profile / tuned mode The active profile of the tuned service, or tuned not active.
cpufreq driver The CPU frequency driver, e.g. amd-pstate-epp, intel_pstate, acpi-cpufreq.
Governor (CPU-0) The frequency policy, e.g. performance, powersave, schedutil.
EPP (CPU-0) Energy Performance Preference hint to the CPU.
amd_pstate amd-pstate mode: active, passive or guided.
Boost Turbo / boost clocks enabled or disabled.
Platform profile ACPI platform profile (laptops): balanced, performance, low-power.
sched_ext Whether an extensible CPU scheduler is loaded, and which one.
THP enabled / THP defrag Transparent huge page settings; the value in [brackets] is active.
KSM run Kernel same-page merging on (1) or off (0).
PCIe ASPM policy PCIe link power saving policy; the [bracketed] one is active.
vm.swappiness Same as in Tune system.
I/O scheduler The disk request schedulers available; the [bracketed] one is active.

Healthy / typical values. On the author's PC: tuned cachyos-gaming, amd-pstate-epp, governor and EPP performance, amd_pstate active, boost enabled, sched_ext enabled with lavd, THP [always], NVMe drives on [none] or [adios], the hard disk and USB drives on [bfq]. A plain distribution install usually shows powersave / balance_performance and madvise THP.

Unusual values and what they suggest.

  • Boost disabled: the CPU never reaches its rated top speed. Check the BIOS or a power tool.
  • acpi-cpufreq on a modern Ryzen: amd-pstate is not in use (old kernel, or disabled in BIOS / kernel command line).
  • A hard disk on none: works, but bfq or mq-deadline usually suits spinning disks better.

Where Linux gets it. /etc/tuned/active_profile, /sys/devices/system/cpu/cpu0/cpufreq/*, /sys/devices/system/cpu/amd_pstate/status, /sys/firmware/acpi/platform_profile, /sys/kernel/sched_ext/, /sys/kernel/mm/transparent_hugepage/, /sys/kernel/mm/ksm/run, /sys/module/pcie_aspm/parameters/policy, /sys/class/block/*/queue/scheduler.

Background. A governor decides how fast the CPU should run. EPP is a hint the CPU's own firmware uses to balance speed and power. Transparent huge pages use 2 MB memory pages instead of 4 KB, which can speed up large programs. ASPM (Active State Power Management) lets PCIe links sleep when idle. An I/O scheduler orders disk requests.

TZM info (thermal zone buffer)

tzm - Linux data

In plain words. The ACPI thermal zones: temperatures the firmware itself reports, with its trip points.

What you see.

Column What it means
# Row number.
Device Name (Zone) Zone type and number, e.g. acpitz (0), x86_pkg_temp (1).
Current Temperature now.
Passive Temperature at which the system starts slowing down to cool.
Critical Temperature at which the system shuts down.
Policy The kernel's thermal governor for the zone, e.g. step_wise.

Then act N num N. Refreshes every 2 seconds.

Healthy / typical values. Many desktops, including the author's, have no thermal zones at all: act 0 num 0 and a note that CPU and GPU temperatures come from hwmon. Laptops usually have several (acpitz, x86_pkg_temp, iwlwifi).

Unusual values and what they suggest.

  • Current near Passive: the system is about to throttle. Clean fans, check the cooler.
  • A zone stuck at a fixed value like 27.8 C or 0 C: a dummy zone from the firmware. Ignore it.

Where Linux gets it. /sys/class/thermal/thermal_zone*/{type,temp,policy,trip_point_*_type,trip_point_*_temp}.

Background. A thermal zone is a firmware-defined area with a sensor. A trip point is a temperature where the system acts: passive = slow down, critical = shut down.

Words

words - Linux data

In plain words. The list of interface words SRS uses. SIV uses this to check translations; SRS is English only.

What you see. Language (English (built in, no translation tables)) and a comma list of the button and label words: OK, Copy, PCI Bus, USB Bus, ALL Dev, Lookup, Find, Data Files, About, Help, Refresh, Next, Prev, Highlight, Colour, Browse..., Latest, Ignore case, Literal, Highlight Matches, Menu, Run as root, Save.

XXB internal buffers

xxb - Linux data

In plain words. An index of the "buffer" items. In SIV these are internal data buffers. In SRS each is a live reading of a Linux source.

What you see. Columns Buffer, Description and srs-gui snapshot source:

Buffer Description Source
sgb-ini System/board buffer /sys/class/dmi/id, PCI 00:00.0, process affinity
sdm Storage device monitor /sys/class/block/*/stat
dsb DIMM sensor buffer hwmon spd5118 / jc42
bsi Battery / HID sensor buffer /sys/class/power_supply, /sys/bus/hid/devices
pmb Power monitor buffer hwmon power* / curr*
tzm Thermal zone buffer /sys/class/thermal
cgb CPU group buffer /sys/devices/system/cpu/online
cpu CPU info buffer (in the CPU group) /sys/devices/system/cpu, cpufreq
gpu GPU info buffer /sys/class/drm
stc Thread contexts /proc/self/task

A note: SRS keeps no shared buffers; each item reads its source when shown.

SRS - Command-Line Reference

Back to the User Guide - Section Reference - Glossary

I wanted a Linux version of SIV (System Information Viewer) for myself, so I built one and set out to improve on it along the way. SRS is free and open source for the Linux and open-source community. (SRS is an independent project, not affiliated with SIV or its author.) SIV is the work of Ray Hinchliffe, RH Software (rh-software.com).

In plain words

SRS has four programs:

Program What it is
srs-gui The window. Given arguments, it behaves exactly like sysreport-search (except arguments starting with --g, which are window options).
sysreport-search The command line: text reports, device-ID lookup, report search, burn-in, benchmarks. Needs no desktop.
srs-root The root helper that saves root-only data to ~/.cache/srs/root.
srs-sysreport Writes a full text report folder to ~/sysreports/.

So srs-gui -save and sysreport-search -save do the same thing.

Note: sysreport-search --help lists every command, including -save, --list, burn, bench, ipi, latency, pi, crypto, prime, cachemem, storage, os-latency, compute, work, net, gpu, gpu-burn and gpu-compare.

zsh users: quote anything with square brackets: sysreport-search '-save=[cpuid]'. Without quotes zsh treats [...] as a file pattern and says "no matches found".

Quick list

sysreport-search -h | --help
sysreport-search --version
sysreport-search --list
sysreport-search -save[=FILE] [--redact]
sysreport-search '-save=[item][item]...[=FILE]' [--redact]
sysreport-search guide [ITEM] [--print]
sysreport-search id VVVV[:DDDD[:SSSS:ssss]][:RR] [--bus pci|usb] [--mode tree|scan|info]
sysreport-search find PATTERN [--report DIR] [-i] [-F] [--max N] [--color auto|always|never]
sysreport-search devices [--bus pci|usb|all]
sysreport-search burn [--threads N | --cpus 0,2,5] [--seconds S] [--mode same|swap] [--limit C] [--cool S] [--cycles N]
sysreport-search bench ac|as|dd|dw|ec|ep|lc|lp|pc|pp [--seconds S] [--yes]
sysreport-search ipi [--cpus N] [--rounds R] [--yes]
sysreport-search latency [--max MB] [--yes]
sysreport-search pi [--digits 128k|1m|..|32m|16ki|..|1mi|..|32mi|N] [--threads N] [--method chudnovsky|agm] [--save-digits FILE] [--yes]
sysreport-search crypto [--threads N] [--seconds S] [--yes]
sysreport-search prime [--limit 1e8|1e9|1e10|1e11|N] [--threads N] [--yes]
sysreport-search storage --dir FOLDER [--size MB] [--seconds S] [--profile standard|light] [--allow-usb] [--yes]
sysreport-search cachemem [--threads N] [--seconds S] [--isa avx512|avx2|sse2] [--mem-mib M] [--only mem,l1,l2,l3] [--tests read,write,copy,latency] [--mib] [--mem-write auto|clzero|stream] [--yes]
sysreport-search os-latency [--samples N] [--tick-seconds S] [--only syscall,switch,spawn,wake,timer,memory,files] [--yes]
sysreport-search compute [--threads N] [--seconds S] [--tests sgemm,dgemm,...] [--code auto|c|sse2|avx2|avx512] [--single] [--yes]
sysreport-search work [--threads N] [--seconds S] [--only compress,sort,hash,text,interp] [--libs zlib,zstd,lz4,xz] [--single] [--part-kib K] [--yes]
sysreport-search net [--local] [--internet] [--seconds S] [--streams N] [--samples N] [--max-mb MB] [-4|-6] [--server URL] [--hosts HOST[:PORT],...] [--yes] [--yes-internet]
sysreport-search gpu [--device N] [--seconds S] [--only fp32,fp16,fp64,int32,read,write,copy,upload,download,latency] [--mem-mib M] [--list] [--yes]
sysreport-search gpu-burn [--seconds N] [--backend vulkan|hip|cuda|opencl|auto] [--device N|all] [--fp32|--fp64] [--limit C] [--list] [--yes]
sysreport-search gpu-compare [--backends vulkan,hip,cuda,opencl] [--seconds S] [--device N] [--yes]

srs-gui [--gui-open=WHAT[,WHAT...]] [--gui-tray] [--gui-classic | --gui-new]
srs-gui --power-recorder
srs-root [--user NAME]
srs-sysreport

Information commands (safe, read-only)

--help, -h

Prints the usage text: every command, -save, --list, guide, the load commands and the srs-gui start options. Exit code 0.

usage: sysreport-search [-h] [--version] {id,find,devices,-save,--list,burn,bench,ipi,latency,pi,crypto,prime,cachemem,storage,os-latency,compute,work,net,gpu,gpu-burn,gpu-compare} ...

SIV-style search for the native system report (srs-sysreport).

  id VVVV[:DDDD[:SSSS:ssss]][:RR] [--bus pci|usb] [--mode tree|scan|info]
        hierarchical device-ID lookup, most specific key first
  find PATTERN [--report DIR] [-i] [-F] [--max N] [--color auto|always|never]
        regex search across a report's sections with highlighted matches
  devices [--bus pci|usb|all]
        resolve every local PCI/USB device

System information items (SIV syntax; quote the argument in zsh/fish, [..] is a glob):
  -save[=[item][item:arg]...][=FILE|STDOUT] [--redact]
        render items as text (no items = SIV's default set, [all] = every item)
        --redact masks serial numbers, UUIDs, MAC addresses (vendor prefix kept),
        boot/machine IDs and the host name, for reports you share
  --list
        every item: id, category, bucket (linux/absent/windows-only), group, title
  guide [ITEM] [--print]
        open the user guide at ITEM's section (PDF viewer, else the HTML guide);
        --print only shows the section and the command that would run

Benchmarks and stress (load the CPU, the drive, the network or the GPU; run only when you ask):
  burn [--threads N | --cpus 0,2,5] [--seconds S] [--mode same|swap] [--limit C] [--cool S] [--cycles N]
        CPU burn-in with a temperature limit (default 10 s, limit 90 C)
  bench {ac,as,dd,dw,ec,ep,lc,lp,pc,pp} [--seconds S] [--yes]
        Dhrystone / Whetstone in a SIV benchmark mode (S = 0.1..60 s per measurement);
        asks first, --yes starts at once
  ipi [--cpus N] [--rounds R] [--yes]
        core-to-core (cache-line ping-pong) latency matrix; asks first, --yes starts at once
  latency [--max MB] [--yes]
        memory latency by block size, up to MB (1..4096, default 256); asks first, --yes starts at once
  pi [--digits 128k|1m|..|32m|16ki|..|1mi|..|32mi|N] [--threads N] [--method chudnovsky|agm] [--save-digits FILE]
     [--yes]
        SRS Pi: pi to N decimal places (default 1m, 1 thread), every digit checked;
        ki / mi = SuperPi sizes (powers of two): 1mi = 1,048,576 digits, 32mi = 33,554,432;
        asks first (with the time and the memory it needs), --yes starts at once
  crypto [--threads N] [--seconds S] [--yes]
        AES-128 and SHA-256 speed, plain C and with AES-NI / SHA-NI (default all threads, 1 s);
        asks first, --yes starts at once
  cachemem [--threads N] [--seconds S] [--isa avx512|avx2|sse2] [--mem-mib M] [--only mem,l1,l2,l3]
           [--tests read,write,copy,latency] [--mib] [--mem-write auto|clzero|stream] [--yes]
        Cache & Memory benchmark: Read / Write / Copy and Latency of the RAM and L1-L3 (all threads,
        ~20 s; asks first, --yes starts at once)
  storage --dir FOLDER [--size MB] [--seconds S] [--profile standard|light] [--allow-usb] [--yes]
        read / write speed of the drive holding FOLDER, on a temporary test file (default 1024 MB,
        5 s per test); never touches existing files; asks first, --yes starts at once
  os-latency [--samples N] [--tick-seconds S] [--only syscall,switch,spawn,wake,timer,memory,files] [--yes]
        how quickly the OS answers: system calls, context switches, thread / process start, wake-ups,
        timer lateness (with the CPU scheduler in use), page faults, file create / stat / unlink
        (default 20000 samples, 3 s tick test; ~6 s on one or two CPUs; asks first, --yes starts at once)
  compute [--threads N] [--seconds S] [--tests sgemm,dgemm,fma-sp,fma-dp,fft-sp,fft-dp,nbody,mandelbrot,raytrace]
          [--code auto|c|sse2|avx2|avx512] [--single] [--yes]
        CPU Compute: matrix multiply, peak multiply-add, FFT, N-body, Mandelbrot, ray tracer in GFLOPS /
        Mpixels/s, 1 thread and N threads (default all), every answer checked; ~10 s, all threads 100%
        busy (--single: one thread); asks first, --yes starts at once
  work [--threads N] [--seconds S] [--only compress,sort,hash,text,interp] [--libs zlib,zstd,lz4,xz]
       [--single] [--part-kib K] [--yes]
        Everyday work: compression (system zlib / zstd / lz4 / xz), sorting, checksums, text processing
        and a bytecode interpreter, 1 thread and N threads (default all), every result checked;
        generated data only; asks first, --yes starts at once
  net [--local] [--internet] [--seconds S] [--streams N] [--samples N] [--max-mb MB] [-4|-6]
      [--server URL] [--hosts HOST[:PORT],...] [--yes] [--yes-internet]
        Network: loopback TCP / UDP speed and round trip (default; nothing leaves the computer);
        --internet adds DNS, connect, HTTPS, download and upload tests against speed.cloudflare.com
        (up to ~1000 MB of data). Asks first; --yes answers the loopback question, the internet test
        asks separately and only --yes-internet skips that question
  gpu [--device N] [--seconds S] [--only fp32,fp16,fp64,int32,read,write,copy,upload,download,latency]
      [--mem-mib M] [--list] [--yes]
        GPU compute (Vulkan): FP32 / FP16 / FP64 / INT32 multiply-add (GFLOPS / GIOPS), video memory
        read / write / copy and upload / download (GB/s), dispatch latency (us), every result checked;
        ~15 s at full GPU load; Vulkan is loaded at run time; asks first, --yes starts at once
  gpu-burn [--seconds N] [--backend vulkan|hip|cuda|opencl|auto] [--device N|all] [--fp32|--fp64]
           [--limit C] [--list] [--yes]
        GPU Burnin: repeated matrix multiplications at full GPU load, compute errors counted
        (0 = PASS), live temperature / power / clock; stops at the temperature limit (default
        100 C), on a driver error or a GPU that stops answering; never changes clocks, voltages
        or fans (default 60 s); asks first, --yes starts at once
  gpu-compare [--backends vulkan,hip,cuda,opencl] [--seconds S] [--device N] [--yes]
        GPU Compute comparison: the same tests (matrix multiply with the own kernel and the vendor
        library, multiply-add, copy, upload / download, launch time) through every installed back end
        on the same GPU, side by side: fastest marked, % of Vulkan; asks first, --yes starts at once
  prime [--limit 1e8|1e9|1e10|N] [--threads N] [--yes]
        count the primes up to the limit, checked against the known count (default 1e9, all threads);
        asks first, --yes starts at once

srs-gui only: --gui-open=ITEM[,ITEM|burnin|stress|bench|ipi|latency|pi|crypto|prime|cachemem|storagebench|oslatency|compute|work|netbench|gpubench|gpuburn|gpucompare|sensors|idlookup|find]
        open those panels / tools at start (also SRS_OPEN=...), --gui-tray start in the tray
        --gui-classic start in the classic SIV-style main window, --gui-new in the new one
        --gui-open=power-cost the Power & cost page; --power-recorder record its history with no window

--gui-scan-empty (not listed) is internal: the main window runs it in a child process to find the items that have nothing to show on this PC, only on Options > Check now or Check daily; it never runs the network items or Ping.

--version

sysreport-search 2.0.0 (ELF x86-64, gcc 16.2.1 20260810, glibc (system C runtime))
Inspired by SIV64X (System Information Viewer) by Ray Hinchliffe, RH Software (rh-software.com),
built to improve on it; free for the Linux and open-source community.
Independent project, not affiliated with SIV or its author. GPL-2.0-or-later.
Home page: https://github.com/eugenesflanagin-spec/srs-sysinfo

The part in brackets describes how your copy was built.

--list

Lists every item SRS knows (558 lines), one per line:

about                tuning    linux         siv      About SRS
acpi-buses           hardware  linux         machine  ACPI PCI root buses
acpi-ipf             hardware  absent        machine  ACPI IPF (Intel Platform Framework) methods
Column Meaning
1 Item id - use it in -save=[id] and --gui-open=id
2 Category (SIV's: hardware, tuning, ...)
3 Bucket: linux (real Linux data), absent (hardware most PCs lack), windows-only
4 Group (the Menu group: cpu, machine, sensors, storage, network, os, gpu, bus, tools, siv)
5 Title

What each item shows: Section Reference.

-save - text reports (SIV syntax)

Form What it does
-save SIV's default set of items, to the screen.
-save=FILE Default items, to FILE.
-save=[id1][id2] Chosen items, to the screen.
-save=[id1][id2]=FILE Chosen items, to FILE.
-save=[all] Every item (about 52,000 lines and 12 seconds on the author's PC).
-save=...=STDOUT The file name STDOUT means the screen.
  • -SAVE works too (case does not matter), as in SIV.
  • Some items take an argument after a colon, the same as the panel buttons: [processor:4] (CPU-4), [cache:2], [volumes:/], [ntfs:/].
  • An unknown id prints No such item for that item (exit code still 0).
  • --redact (anywhere on the command line) masks identifiers for reports you share: serial numbers (board, system, chassis, DIMM, disk, NVMe, USB, monitor), UUIDs (file systems, partitions, the system UUID, the root file system in the kernel command line), MAC addresses (the vendor half is kept: 04:7c:16:XX:XX:XX), WWNs, the GPU and Thunderbolt unique IDs, the boot and machine IDs, and the host name. Letters and digits become X and the length is kept, so columns stay aligned; the header says (identifiers redacted). Published constants such as GPT partition-type GUIDs are left as they are. Without --redact the report is complete, as in SIV. IP addresses and Wi-Fi network names are not masked.
  • Saving never starts the burner or a benchmark. Benchmark items print their last stored result.
  • Root-only values come from ~/.cache/srs/root (run srs-root first). Run as root (sudo sysreport-search -save) it uses the invoking user's cache, or collects one first.

Examples (all verified):

sysreport-search -save | less
sysreport-search '-save=[cpuid][cache]=cpu.txt'
srs-gui '-save=[sensors]'
sysreport-search '-save=[all]=full-report.txt'
sysreport-search '-save=[all]=for-forum.txt' --redact

Output starts with a header and then each item:

srs-gui - System Report Search V2.0.0 MYPC 2026-10-25 08:28:53  [[cpuid][cache]]

[cpuid]  [hardware]
...

guide - open the user guide at an item

sysreport-search guide [ITEM] [--print]

Opens this guide at ITEM's section (no ITEM: the start). With Okular, Evince or Papers as the default PDF viewer the PDF opens at the section; with any other viewer the HTML copy of the guide (/usr/share/doc/srs-sysinfo/html/SRS-User-Guide.html) opens in the web browser at the section. --print only prints the section and the command that would run:

$ sysreport-search guide sensors --print
Item     sensors
Section  sections-sensors--sensor-status
Command  'okular' '/usr/share/doc/srs-sysinfo/SRS-User-Guide.pdf#sections-sensors--sensor-status'

Exit code 0, 1 when the guide is not installed, 2 for an unknown item. In srs-gui the same is the Guide button on every panel, F1 and the panel's right-click menu.

id - device-ID lookup

Turns PCI or USB numbers into names, using hwdata's pci.ids / usb.ids (or systemd-hwdb).

Argument / option Meaning Default
VVVV Vendor ID (4 hex digits) required
:DDDD Device ID
:SSSS:ssss Subsystem vendor and subsystem device (the card maker's IDs)
:RR Revision (2 hex digits)
--bus pci|usb Which list pci
--mode tree|scan|info tree: load the sorted list once, binary search (fast). scan: read the file line by line. info: ask systemd-hwdb, the system's device database. tree

Options can be written --bus usb or --bus=usb.

$ sysreport-search id 1002:7550
  < 1002:7550                Navi 48 [Radeon RX 9070/9070 XT/9070 GRE]
    1002                     Advanced Micro Devices, Inc. [AMD/ATI]
Vendor     Advanced Micro Devices, Inc. [AMD/ATI]
Stock      Navi 48 [Radeon RX 9070/9070 XT/9070 GRE]
Resolved   Navi 48 [Radeon RX 9070/9070 XT/9070 GRE]
tree mode: 42,228 records loaded in 9.4 ms, lookup 0.002 ms
  • Each key tried is listed, most specific first; < marks the one that matched. (no entry) means that exact key is not in the list.
  • Vendor - the maker. Subsystem - the card maker, when a subsystem ID is given and known (e.g. 1002:7550:1EAE:7550:C0 -> XFX Limited). Stock - the chip's plain name. Resolved - the most specific name found.
$ sysreport-search id 046d:c52b --bus usb
  < 046D:C52B                Unifying Receiver
    046D                     Logitech, Inc.
...
$ sysreport-search id 1002:7550 --mode info
Query      pci:v00001002d00007550
Vendor     Advanced Micro Devices, Inc. [AMD/ATI]
Resolved   Navi 48 [Radeon RX 9070/9070 XT/9070 GRE]
info mode (systemd-hwdb) in 5.00 ms

To find the IDs of your own devices: sysreport-search devices, or lspci -nn / lsusb.

devices - every PCI and USB device, named

Option Meaning Default
--bus pci|usb|all Which buses all 
$ sysreport-search devices --bus usb
[USB] 40 devices, 23,964 records (/usr/share/hwdata/usb.ids)
Slot           ID                         Matched              Vendor                       Resolved
1-2.4          0BDA:5411                  0BDA:5411            Realtek Semiconductor Corp.  RTS5411 Hub
1-2.4.5        0BDA:1100                  0BDA                 Realtek Semiconductor Corp.  Unknown Device
  • Slot - where it is plugged in (PCI address, or USB bus-port path).
  • ID - its full ID. Matched - the most specific key found in the list (0BDA alone means only the vendor is known). Resolved - the name, or "Unknown Device" when the list does not have it yet (update the hwdata package).

find - search a full system report

Searches every section file (*.txt, lshw.html) of a folder made by srs-sysreport.

Argument / option Meaning Default
PATTERN A regular expression (Python-style), unless -F required
--report DIR Which report folder the newest in ~/sysreports
-i, --ignore-case Ignore upper/lower case off
-F, --fixed Literal text, not a regular expression off
--max N Show at most N matches per section 20
--color auto|always|never Highlight matches (auto = only on a terminal) auto 
$ sysreport-search find 'RX 9070' --max 3 --color never
Searching /home/user/sysreports/sysreport-20261017-050453 for "RX 9070"

== devices.txt - 1 Match
     30: 0000:03:00.0   1002:7550:1EAE:8811:C0     1002:7550            Advanced Micro Devices, Inc. Navi 48 ...

== inxi.txt - 3 Matches
     59:   Device-1: Advanced Micro Devices [AMD/ATI] Navi 48 [Radeon RX 9070/9070
...
7 Matches in 4 of 16 sections

Numbers on the left are line numbers in that section file. When a section has more matches than --max, a line says ... N more (raise --max).

Load and benchmark commands (make the CPU busy)

burn starts at once: it is the burn-in itself, and you choose its threads, time and temperature limit on the command line. Every benchmark asks first - bench, ipi, latency, pi, crypto, prime and the ones below - on the terminal (stderr): what it runs, about how long, how many CPU threads it keeps busy and (SRS Pi) how much memory it needs, then Start now? [y/N]. Only y starts it. --yes (or -y) starts it without the question, for scripts. Without a terminal and without --yes it does not start and exits with 2. --help (-h) prints the command's usage and exits 0; an unknown option or a missing value exits 2 - neither starts anything. The windows ask the same question. Close other heavy programs first. Press Ctrl+C to stop. Never run them on a PC you are not allowed to load.

$ sysreport-search crypto --threads 1
It checks the official AES and SHA-256 test vectors, then measures AES-128 encryption and SHA-256
speed with the CPU's crypto instructions and in plain C, 1.0 s per measurement: about 8 seconds.
Each test runs on one CPU thread (light load).

Close other programs for accurate results.
Start now? [y/N] n
crypto: not started

burn - CPU Burnin from the command line

Option Meaning Default
--threads N Use logical CPUs 0..N-1 all
--cpus 0,2,5 Use exactly these logical CPUs all
--seconds S Burn time per cycle, 1 to 2,700,000 seconds 10
--mode same|swap same: each worker stays on its CPU and runs Whetstone. swap: workers move between CPUs (affinity test). same
--limit C Stop if the hottest CPU sensor reaches C degrees Celsius 90
--cool S Rest between cycles, seconds 0
--cycles N Number of burn + cool cycles 1

Output: a start line, then one line per second (example values):

    12s  load 100.0%  Tctl 78.5 C  CPUTIN 33.0 C  CPU 5050 MHz  GPU 3% 28.0 C  Burning

(elapsed, CPU load, hottest core sensor, hottest motherboard sensor, CPU clock, GPU load and temperature, state), then a table per worker (Thread, CPU, Passes, MWIPS last / average / min / max, Affinity ok or FAIL), the maxima and the final status. The last line names the file the summary was saved to (Summary saved to /home/you/.cache/srs/burnin-YYYYMMDD-HHMMSS.txt, one file per run; the same layout as srs-gui's Burnin window).

Exit codes: 0 = Pass, 1 = Fail (affinity error or temperature limit), 130 = stopped (Ctrl+C), 2 = bad option or nothing to run.

An unknown option prints the usage line and exits 2 without starting anything:

$ sysreport-search burn --nope
usage: sysreport-search [-h] [--version] {id,find,devices} ...
sysreport-search: error: burn [--threads N | --cpus 0,2,5] [--seconds S] [--mode same|swap] [--limit C] [--cool S] [--cycles N]

bench - Dhrystone and Whetstone

sysreport-search bench MODE [--seconds S] [--yes]
Mode What runs
ac All CPUs concurrently: Dhrystone then Whetstone on every logical CPU at once
as All CPUs sequentially, one logical CPU at a time
dd Per core: both SMT threads run Dhrystone, then both run Whetstone
dw Per core: one thread Dhrystone while its sibling runs Whetstone, then swap
ec / ep Efficiency cores concurrently / one at a time (Intel hybrid CPUs; Linux lists the E-cores in /sys/devices/cpu_atom/cpus)
lc / lp Logical (SMT sibling) threads concurrently / one at a time
pc / pp Performance (physical) cores, one thread per core, concurrently / one at a time (E-cores left out)

--seconds S is the time per measurement, 0.1 to 60 (default 1). Asks first (the mode, the time and how many CPU threads are busy; the modes that load many threads at once also warn about unstable overclocks); --yes starts at once. The result is stored and shown in the window and in -save reports. Results: DMIPS (Dhrystone) and MWIPS (Whetstone), per CPU and in total; see tools.md. Exit code 0 when it ran, 1 when there is nothing to run in that mode on this CPU (for example ec without efficiency cores; then there is no question either), 2 for a bad mode or option, or when it was not started.

ipi - core-to-core delay

sysreport-search ipi [--cpus N] [--rounds R] [--yes]

--cpus N tests CPUs 0..N-1 (default all), --rounds R round trips per pair (default 20,000). Two CPU threads are busy at a time, for about a second at the defaults. Asks first; --yes starts at once. Prints a matrix of nanoseconds, one row and column per CPU. See tools.md.

latency - memory latency by block size

sysreport-search latency [--max MB] [--yes]

--max MB is the largest block, 1 to 4096 MB (default 256; the window too). It uses that much memory and one CPU thread, for about 3 seconds at the default. Asks first; --yes starts at once. Prints block size, nanoseconds per read and the cache level. See tools.md.

pi - SRS Pi: pi to many digits, every digit checked

sysreport-search pi [--digits 128k|1m|..|32m|16ki|..|1mi|..|32mi|N] [--threads N] [--method chudnovsky|agm] [--save-digits FILE] [--yes]

--digits is the number of decimal places (default 1m = 1,000,000; k = thousand, m = million; ki = 1,024 and mi = 1,048,576 for the SuperPi sizes 16ki ... 32mi; 100 to 32mi). The listed sizes are checked digit for digit with built-in SHA-256 checksums; other sizes only have their first 100 digits checked. --threads N (default 1) splits the Chudnovsky series over N threads; --method agm uses Gauss-Legendre (always one thread). --save-digits FILE writes the digits (without "3.") to FILE. Asks first, with the time, the threads and the memory it needs (up to about 1.6 GB for 32mi digits); from 8 million digits, or with all threads, it also warns about unstable overclocks. --yes starts at once. Exit code 0 when every checked digit is right, 1 when a digit is wrong or memory ran out, 2 for a bad option or when it was not started. See tools.md.

crypto - AES-128 and SHA-256 speed

sysreport-search crypto [--threads N] [--seconds S] [--yes]

Measures AES-128-CTR and SHA-256 in MB/s on one thread and on N threads (default all), with AES-NI / SHA-NI when the CPU has them and in plain C. --seconds S per measurement, 0.1 to 60 (default 1), about 8 measurements in all. Asks first (with all threads it warns that every CPU thread is 100% busy); --yes starts at once. The FIPS test vectors are checked first; exit code 1 if they fail, 2 for a bad option or when it was not started. See tools.md.

prime - count the primes up to a limit

sysreport-search prime [--limit 1e8|1e9|1e10|1e11|N] [--threads N] [--yes]

Counts the primes up to --limit (default 1e9; 100 to 1e11) on N threads (default all) and checks the count for the powers of ten 1e7 to 1e11. Asks first (from 1e10, or with all threads, it also warns about unstable overclocks); --yes starts at once. Exit code 1 when the count is wrong, 2 for a bad option or when it was not started. See tools.md.

cachemem - Cache & Memory benchmark

sysreport-search cachemem [--threads N] [--seconds S] [--isa avx512|avx2|sse2] [--mem-mib M]
                          [--only mem,l1,l2,l3] [--tests read,write,copy,latency] [--mib]
                          [--mem-write auto|clzero|stream] [--yes]

Read / Write / Copy (MB/s, caches in GB/s) and Latency (ns) of the RAM and the L1, L2 and L3 caches. It loads every CPU thread and the memory bus for about 20 seconds and asks first; --yes (-y) starts at once (scripts). Without a terminal and without --yes it does not start (exit code 2).

Option Meaning
--threads N Threads for the bandwidth tests (default all logical CPUs)
--seconds S Measuring time per value, 0.1-60 (default 1)
--isa Force the vector code (default: the best the CPU has)
--mem-mib M RAM block in MiB, all threads together (default 1024, at least 4 x L3)
--only / --tests Run only some rows / columns, e.g. --only l1 --tests read
--mib Binary units (MiB/s, GiB/s)
--mem-write RAM write method: auto (CLZERO on AMD CPUs that have it), clzero, stream

x86-64 only. Exit code 0 when it ran, 1 if memory could not be allocated, 2 for a bad option or no confirmation. See tools.md.

storage - drive read / write speed

sysreport-search storage --dir FOLDER [--size MB] [--seconds S] [--profile standard|light] [--allow-usb] [--yes]

Tests the drive that holds FOLDER on a new temporary test file (--size, 16-65536 MB, default 1024) that is unlinked at once and gone when the test ends - existing files are never touched. Six tests of --seconds S each (0.5-60, default 5): sequential 1 MiB Q8T1, 4K random Q32T16 (--profile light: Q8T4) and 4K random Q1T1, read and write; average, peak, IOPS and 4K Q1T1 response times. Refuses RAM (tmpfs), network and FUSE folders and too little free space; USB drives only with --allow-usb. Asks first; --yes starts at once. Exit code 0 when it ran, 1 when it was stopped or hit an I/O error, 2 when it did not start (the message says why). See tools.md.

os-latency - how quickly the OS answers

sysreport-search os-latency [--samples N] [--tick-seconds S]
                            [--only syscall,switch,spawn,wake,timer,memory,files] [--yes]

Times many single samples of system calls, pipe context switches (threads and processes, same CPU and two cores), thread create, fork and posix_spawn, futex and condition-variable wake-ups, sleep overshoot and a periodic 1 ms tick, page faults (4 KiB and 2 MiB), mmap / munmap, and small-file create / stat / unlink. Each row shows the median, 95%, 99%, worst and best. The CPU scheduler in use (sched_ext such as scx_lavd, BORE, EEVDF), the preemption mode, the timer tick, the clock source and the timer slack are shown with the result. It keeps one or two CPUs busy for about 6 seconds at the defaults and asks first; --yes (-y) starts at once. Without a terminal and without --yes it does not start (exit code 2).

Option Meaning
--samples N Samples for the fast tests, 100-1,000,000 (default 20,000); the slow tests use a tenth to a fortieth
--tick-seconds S How long the 1 ms tick is watched, 0.1-60 (default 3)
--only Run only some groups, e.g. --only syscall,switch

Nothing on the system is changed. The file test uses a temporary folder in ~/.cache/srs that is always removed. Exit code 0 when it ran, 1 when it was stopped, 2 when it did not start (bad option, not confirmed, not available). Example:

$ sysreport-search os-latency --only syscall,timer --yes

See tools.md.

compute - CPU Compute (floating-point work)

sysreport-search compute [--threads N] [--seconds S]
                         [--tests sgemm,dgemm,fma-sp,fma-dp,fft-sp,fft-dp,nbody,mandelbrot,raytrace]
                         [--code auto|c|sse2|avx2|avx512] [--single] [--yes]

Matrix multiply (SGEMM / DGEMM), peak multiply-add, FFT, N-body, Mandelbrot and a small ray tracer, in GFLOPS or Mpixels/s, on 1 thread and on N threads, with the best vector code the CPU has. Every answer is checked; a wrong one is shown as WRONG. With N threads every CPU is 100% busy (AVX-512 where the CPU has it), so it asks first; --yes (-y) starts at once. Without a terminal and without --yes it does not start (exit code 2). An unstable overclock or undervolt can crash the PC under this load; --single keeps it light.

Option Meaning
--threads N Threads for the right-hand column (default 0 = all logical CPUs)
--seconds S Measuring time per test and column, 0.1-60 (default 0.5)
--tests Run only some tests, e.g. --tests dgemm,mandelbrot
--code Force a code path (a path the CPU lacks falls back to the best it has)
--single Only the 1-thread column (light load, half the time)

Exit code 0 when every check passed, 1 when a check failed (WRONG) or it was stopped, 2 when it did not start (bad option, not confirmed, CPU Burnin running). Example:

$ sysreport-search compute --single --tests sgemm,nbody --yes

See tools.md.

work - Everyday work

sysreport-search work [--threads N] [--seconds S] [--only compress,sort,hash,text,interp]
                      [--libs zlib,zstd,lz4,xz] [--single] [--part-kib K] [--yes]
