Compression and decompression with the system's zlib, zstd, lz4 and xz libraries (MB/s and ratio), sorting (Mkeys/s), checksums and hashes (GB/s), text processing (GB/s) and a bytecode interpreter (Mops/s), on 1 thread and on N threads; every result is checked. The data is generated by SRS (your files are never read or written). It keeps every CPU busy and asks first with the expected time; --yes (-y) starts at once. Without a terminal and without --yes it does not start (exit code 2). A library that is not installed shows "not installed" and its rows are skipped.

Option Meaning
--threads N Threads for the right-hand column (default 0 = all logical CPUs)
--seconds S Measuring time per test and column, 0.1-60 (default 0.5)
--only Test groups, e.g. --only compress,hash
--libs Compression libraries, e.g. --libs zstd,lz4
--single Only the 1-thread column
--part-kib K Size of each generated data part per thread, 64-16384 KiB (default 1024)

Exit code 0 when every check passed, 1 when a check failed or it was stopped, 2 when it did not start (bad option, not confirmed, CPU Burnin running, not enough memory). Each test group adds a line (work-compress ... work-interp) to the history. Example:

$ sysreport-search work --only compress --libs zstd,lz4 --single --yes

See tools.md.

net - Network benchmark

sysreport-search net [--local] [--internet] [--seconds S] [--streams N] [--samples N] [--max-mb MB]
                     [-4|-6] [--server URL] [--hosts HOST[:PORT],...] [--yes] [--yes-internet]

Without options: the loopback test only - TCP throughput with 1 and N streams, UDP throughput and loss, TCP and UDP round trip time between two programs on this PC (127.0.0.1). Nothing leaves the computer. It asks first; --yes (-y) starts the loopback test at once.

--internet adds DNS, connect, HTTPS, download and upload tests against https://speed.cloudflare.com. Before it starts it prints the server, the hosts, the tests, the time and the data use (up to about 4 x --max-mb, 1000 MB with the defaults) and says the server sees your public IP address. It asks its own question, which --yes does not answer: type y at the prompt, or pass --yes-internet (scripts). Without a terminal and without --yes-internet the internet test does not start (exit code 2). --internet alone runs only the internet part; --local --internet runs both.

Option Meaning
--local The loopback test (the default when neither --local nor --internet is given)
--internet The internet tests (asks separately)
--seconds S Seconds per throughput test, 0.1-60 (default 5); round trip tests use at most 1 s
--streams N Connections for the "N streams" tests, 1-32 (default 4)
--samples N TCP connects per host for the connect-time test, 1-100 (default 10)
--max-mb MB Each transfer test stops after this many MB (default 250, 0 = no cap)
-4 / -6 IPv4 only / IPv6 only
--server URL Another speed test server with the same /__down and /__up paths (https only)
--hosts H,H Extra hosts for the connect-time test (host or host:port)
--yes Start the loopback test without asking
--yes-internet Start the internet test without asking

Without libcurl the DNS and connect tests still run and the HTTPS and speed rows say "not available". No IP address, MAC address, network name or host name is printed or saved. Exit code 0 when it ran, 1 when it was stopped or a test failed, 2 when it did not start (bad option, not confirmed, no network connection for the internet test). Examples:

$ sysreport-search net --yes                      # loopback only
$ sysreport-search net --internet --seconds 3 --max-mb 50   # asks; at most about 200 MB

See tools.md.

gpu - GPU benchmark (Vulkan)

sysreport-search gpu [--device N] [--seconds S] [--only fp32,fp16,fp64,int32,read,write,copy,upload,download,latency]
                     [--mem-mib M] [--list] [--yes]

Measures the graphics card through Vulkan: FP32, FP16, FP64 and INT32 multiply-add (GFLOPS / GIOPS), video memory read, write and copy, upload and download (GB/s, 1 GB = 10^9 bytes) and the round trip of an empty dispatch (µs). Every result is checked; a wrong one is printed as WRONG RESULT. The Vulkan loader is opened at run time: without it, or without a Vulkan driver, the command says so and exits with 2. It asks first (the GPU, the time, full GPU load, and that an unstable overclock or undervolt can crash the PC); --yes (-y) starts at once. Without a terminal and without --yes it does not start (exit code 2).

Option Meaning
--device N The Vulkan device to test, numbered as --list shows them (default: the first discrete GPU, else the first device)
--seconds S GPU time per test, 0.1-10 (default 1)
--only LIST Run only these tests (comma-separated): fp32, fp16, fp64, int32, read, write, copy, upload, download, latency
--mem-mib M Buffer size of the memory and transfer tests in MiB, 1-4096 (default: 256, less on small cards)
--list List the Vulkan devices (number, name, type, video memory, driver) and exit; nothing runs on a GPU
--yes Start without asking

Exit code 0 when every test ran and was right, 1 when it was stopped, a result was wrong or the GPU failed during the run, 2 when it did not start (bad option, not confirmed, no Vulkan, no such device, CPU Burnin running). Examples:

$ sysreport-search gpu --list
$ sysreport-search gpu --only fp32,read,upload --seconds 0.5

See tools.md.

gpu-burn - GPU Burnin

sysreport-search gpu-burn [--seconds N] [--backend vulkan|hip|cuda|opencl|auto] [--device N|all]
                          [--fp32|--fp64] [--limit C] [--list] [--yes]

Keeps the GPU fully busy with large matrix multiplications and counts every result that differs from the first one (0 = PASS). On a terminal a live line shows the time, GFLOPS, the error count, edge and hotspot temperature, power and clock; the full result follows at the end. It asks first (the GPU, the back end, the time, high power and heat, the overclock / undervolt warning, the temperature limit); --yes (-y) starts at once; without a terminal and without --yes it does not start (exit code 2). Before you say yes it starts no HIP, CUDA or OpenCL runtime. It ends by itself at the temperature limit, on a driver error, when the GPU stops answering or when a piece of work takes more than 2 s; Ctrl+C stops it. It never changes clocks, voltages or fans.

Option Meaning
--seconds N How long, 1-86400 (default 60)
--backend B vulkan, hip (ROCm), cuda, opencl or auto (default: Vulkan when it has a GPU, else the first back end that has one)
--device N The device number in that back end's list (see --list), or all (default: the first)
--fp32 / --fp64 Precision of the multiplications (default FP32)
--limit C Stop at this GPU temperature in °C, 50-120 (default 100; hotspot / junction when the card reports it, else edge). --limit-c is the same
--list List the devices of each installed back end (or only --backend's) and exit. This starts each runtime but runs no work
--yes Start without asking

Exit code 0 = PASS, 1 = FAIL (errors found), stopped, or ended early by a safety rule, 2 = not started (bad option, not confirmed, back end not installed, no device, CPU Burnin running). Examples:

$ sysreport-search gpu-burn --list
$ sysreport-search gpu-burn --seconds 600 --limit 95
$ sysreport-search gpu-burn --backend hip --fp64 --seconds 120

See tools.md.

gpu-compare - GPU Compute: Vulkan vs HIP vs CUDA vs OpenCL

sysreport-search gpu-compare [--backends vulkan,hip,cuda,opencl] [--seconds S] [--device N] [--yes]

Runs the same tests (matrix multiply FP32 / FP16 / FP64 with SRS's own kernel and with the vendor library - hipBLAS, cuBLAS, CLBlast -, FP32 / FP64 multiply-add chain, video memory copy, upload, download, kernel launch round trip) through every chosen back end that is installed, on the same GPU, and prints one table: * = fastest in the row, (N%) = that column compared with Vulkan. CUDA that is really ZLUDA is labelled "CUDA (ZLUDA)"; every OpenCL driver is its own column; a back end that is not installed shows "not installed" and a hint. It asks first; --yes (-y) starts at once; without a terminal and without --yes it does not start (exit code 2). HIP, CUDA and OpenCL start their runtimes only after that. Ctrl+C stops it.

Option Meaning
--backends L Comma-separated: vulkan, hip, cuda, opencl (default: every installed one). --backend B is the same
--seconds S GPU time per test, 0.1-10 (default 1)
--device N The Vulkan device that fixes "the GPU" (numbers from gpu --list); the others use the card at the same PCI address (default: the first discrete GPU)
--yes Start without asking

Exit code 0 when it ran and every result was right, 1 when it was stopped, a result was wrong or a GPU failed, 2 when it did not start (bad option, not confirmed, none of the chosen back ends installed). Example:

$ sysreport-search gpu-compare --backends vulkan,hip --seconds 0.5

See tools.md.

Every cachemem, storage, os-latency, compute, work, net, gpu, gpu-burn, gpu-compare, pi, crypto and prime run is added to ~/.cache/srs/bench-history.tsv.

srs-gui window options

Option What it does
(none) Open the main window (the window with the sidebar, or the classic one when Options -> Start in classic view is on).
--gui-open=WHAT[,WHAT...] Also open these panels or tools at start. In the main window an item opens on its page (for example sensors on the Sensors page); in the classic view it opens as its own panel.
--gui-tray Start hidden in the system tray (used by the autostart entry).
--gui-classic Start in the classic view: SIV's main window with its button row, every item in its own panel (as in SRS 1.1).
--gui-new Start in the main window with the sidebar, even when Start in classic view is on.
--power-recorder Record Power & cost history with no window, following the page's Recording setting (Off / For a set time / Always). Used by the optional systemd user service that Power & cost -> Setup -> Keep recording when SRS is closed writes. Only one process records at a time (a lock file beside the database); stop it with Ctrl+C or SIGTERM.
any other argument Run as the command line (srs-gui -save = sysreport-search -save).

WHAT can be any item id from --list (e.g. sensors, processors, pci-bus, processor:4), or one of these tool names:

Name Opens
burnin CPU Burnin
stress CPU Stress
bench Benchmark
ipi IPI Delay
latency Latency
pi SRS Pi
crypto Crypto benchmark
prime Prime Sieve
cachemem Cache & Memory
storagebench Storage benchmark (storage alone is the Storage page's item)
oslatency OS Latency
compute CPU Compute
work Everyday Work
netbench Network benchmark (network alone is the Network page's item)
gpubench GPU Benchmark
gpuburn GPU Burnin
gpucompare GPU Compute: Vulkan vs HIP vs CUDA vs OpenCL
idlookup Device ID Lookup
find Find
menu Pops up the Menu
power-cost Shows the Power & cost page (the item power is the expert Power status tab on Sensors)

Opening a tool never starts it. Example: srs-gui --gui-open=sensors,burnin. The environment variable SRS_OPEN=sensors,burnin does the same.

The menu entries use: --gui-open=burnin,stress (SRS CPU Burnin & Stress), --gui-open=bench,ipi,latency (SRS Benchmark), and the jump-list actions sensors, processors, burnin, stress, bench, cachemem, storagebench, oslatency, compute, work, netbench, gpubench, gpuburn, gpucompare, pi, idlookup, find, and Classic View (--gui-classic).

srs-root

pkexec srs-root            # or: sudo srs-root
sudo srs-root --user NAME  # collect for another user (used by the boot unit)

Collects root-only data into ~/.cache/srs/root/ of the user who started it (via PKEXEC_UID or the current user), then gives the files to that user. It prints one line per step:

srs-root: dmidecode
srs-root: decode-dimms
srs-root: smart
srs-root: acpi-tables
srs-root: lspci
srs-root: msrs
srs-root: done -> /home/you/.cache/srs/root
  • It has no --help; any argument other than --user NAME is ignored.
  • --user NAME works only as root; exit code 2 if not root or the user does not exist.
  • Set SRS_SMART_USB=1 to include USB-attached disks in the SMART collection.
  • Tools that are not installed are skipped.

Boot unit: srs-root@NAME.service runs srs-root --user NAME once per boot (Nice 19, idle I/O). sudo systemctl enable --now srs-root@$USER.service / disable.

srs-sysreport

srs-sysreport

No options. Writes ~/sysreports/sysreport-YYYYMMDD-HHMMSS/ (one file per tool plus index.html), asks once for your password (pkexec) for the root sections, opens index.html in your browser and prints:

Report written to: /home/you/sysreports/sysreport-20261017-050453
Search it with: sysreport-search find PATTERN   (or: sysreport-search id VVVV:DDDD)

Exit codes (sysreport-search)

Code Meaning
0 Success; find found matches; burn passed
1 find found no matches; lookup or benchmark failed; burn failed
2 Usage error (missing or unknown argument, bad value); find found no report folder; burn had nothing to run; a benchmark was not started (answered No, or no terminal and no --yes)
130 burn stopped with Ctrl+C

Environment variables

Variable Effect
SRS_SMART_USB=1 srs-root: include USB disks in SMART
SRS_KWH_COST, SRS_CURRENCY Price per kWh and currency symbol for the kWh Cost item (default $ 0.15)
SRS_OPEN Same as --gui-open=
SRS_POWER_DB, SRS_POWER_INI Power & cost: use another history database / settings file instead of ~/.local/share/srs/power.db and ~/.config/srs/power.ini (for tests)
SRS_DATA_DIR Folder holding power-zip-rates.tsv for the offline US ZIP price lookup (default: next to the program, then /usr/share/srs-sysinfo)
SRS_DOC_DIR Folder holding SRS-User-Guide.pdf / html/ for guide, F1 and the Guide button (default /usr/share/doc/srs-sysinfo)
SRS_VULKAN_LIB GPU benchmarks: open this file instead of libvulkan.so.1 (a name that does not exist = "not installed"; for tests)
SRS_HIP_LIB, SRS_CUDA_LIB, SRS_OPENCL_LIB GPU Burnin and the GPU Compute comparison: open this file instead of the ROCm / HIP, CUDA or OpenCL library (a name that does not exist = "not installed"; for tests)
SRS_GPU_SOFTWARE_ONLY=1 GPU benchmarks: refuse every Vulkan device that is not a software renderer such as lavapipe (for tests)
SUDO_USER, PKEXEC_UID Used to find whose root-data cache to use when run as root

SRS Glossary

Back to the User Guide - Section Reference

Plain-English meanings of the technical words used in the SRS documents, A to Z. After each definition, "See" lists the Section Reference pages that use the word most.

SRS is a Linux system information viewer inspired by SIV64X (System Information Viewer) by Ray Hinchliffe, RH Software; it is an independent project, not affiliated with SIV or its author.

A

  • ABI (Application Binary Interface) - the low-level rules a program and the kernel (or libraries) agree on so compiled code can work together. See: srs-items.
  • ACPI (Advanced Configuration and Power Interface) - Advanced Configuration and Power Interface; the firmware tables and code that describe the board's devices, power states and interrupts to the operating system. See: buses-1, buses-2, linux-os, machine, sensors.
  • ACPI namespace - The tree of named objects in the ACPI tables, e.g. \_SB_.PCI0.SBRG.EC0_, which is the firmware's own map of the board's devices. See: buses-1, machine.
  • AER (Advanced Error Reporting) - A PCI Express feature that counts and reports link errors (correctable and uncorrectable) to the kernel. See: buses-1, graphics.
  • AES (Advanced Encryption Standard), AES-NI - the standard way to encrypt data (disk encryption, VPN, HTTPS). AES-NI are CPU instructions that do one AES round in hardware, many times faster than plain code. See: tools.
  • Affinity mask - a bit pattern, one bit per CPU, saying which CPUs a task may run on. FFFF = CPUs 0-15. See: processors, srs-items.
  • AGM (arithmetic-geometric mean), Gauss-Legendre - a way to compute pi that doubles the number of correct digits at every step; the method SuperPi uses. See: tools.
  • AIO - All-In-One liquid cooler: a sealed pump, radiator and fans in one unit. See: tools.
  • AIO (all-in-one) cooler - A sealed liquid cooler with pump, radiator and fans in one kit. See: sensors.
  • ALSA (Advanced Linux Sound Architecture) - The kernel's sound driver layer. It talks to the sound chips and gives each card numbered devices such as hw:1,0. See: graphics.
  • amd_pstate - the Linux driver that controls clock speed on AMD Zen 2 and newer CPUs using CPPC; modes are active, guided and passive. See: processors.
  • AML - ACPI Machine Language; the bytecode in the DSDT and SSDTs that the operating system runs to control devices. See: machine.
  • APIC - Advanced Programmable Interrupt Controller; each CPU thread has one, and its APIC ID is the hardware's own number for that thread. See: machine, processors.
  • APIC ID - the ID number each logical CPU reports about itself through the CPUID instruction. CPU Burnin uses it to check that a thread really runs where it was pinned. See: tools.
  • ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) - how an IPv4 machine finds the MAC (hardware) address that belongs to an IP address on the local network. See: network.
  • ASLR (Address Space Layout Randomization) - loading programs and libraries at random memory addresses each run, to make attacks harder. See: linux-os.
  • ASPM (Active State Power Management) - lets a PCIe link drop into a low-power state when idle. See: machine, srs-items.
  • Associativity (ways) - how many places in a cache a given piece of memory may be stored; more ways means fewer collisions. See: processors.
  • Asynchronous I/O (AIO) - handing the kernel several read or write requests at once and collecting the answers later; how the storage benchmark keeps Q requests in flight. See: tools.
  • ATA - AT Attachment: the command set used by SATA (and older IDE/PATA) hard disks and SSDs. See: storage.
  • At the wall - what the PC draws from the socket, including the power supply's own losses; what the electricity meter counts and you pay for. See: User Guide 6.11.
  • AUR (Arch User Repository) - community build recipes for Arch-based systems. Packages built from it show as "foreign" in pacman. See: linux-os.
  • Autosuspend - the USB core's habit of putting an idle device to sleep after a set number of seconds; -1 turns it off. See: buses-2.
  • AUXTIN - Auxiliary temperature inputs on a Nuvoton Super I/O chip. The board maker decides which are wired; unwired ones float and show fake values. See: sensors.
  • Available Spare - NVMe health field: the percentage of spare flash blocks an SSD has left (starts at 100%). See: storage.
  • AVX / AVX2 / AVX-512 - Advanced Vector Extensions; instruction sets that work on many numbers at once (256 or 512 bits wide: 8 or 16 single-precision numbers per instruction). AVX-512 draws a lot of power under full load. See: processors, tools.

B

  • Back end (GPU) - the way a program talks to the GPU for computing: Vulkan, ROCm / HIP, CUDA or OpenCL. GPU Burnin and the GPU Compute comparison can use each one. See: tools.
  • BAR (Base Address Register) - a register in a PCI device that asks for a window of memory or I/O address space; the firmware or kernel assigns its start address at boot. See: buses-1, buses-2, graphics.
  • BBR - a TCP congestion-control algorithm that measures bandwidth and delay instead of waiting for packet loss. See: network.
  • bcdDevice / bcdUSB - fields in a USB device descriptor: the device's own release number, and the USB version it claims to follow. See: buses-2.
  • bfq - Budget Fair Queueing: a Linux I/O scheduler that suits spinning disks and slow USB devices. See: storage.
  • Binary MOF - a compressed description of a vendor's WMI classes, stored in the firmware. See: machine.
  • Binary splitting - computing a long series by splitting it in halves again and again and joining the halves with big multiplications, so the work stays fast and can be shared between threads. See: tools.
  • Bind mount - Attaching a folder of an existing filesystem at a second place in the folder tree. See: storage.
  • BMC (Baseboard Management Controller) - A small separate computer on server boards that monitors sensors and allows remote management through IPMI. See: sensors.
  • BogoMIPS - a rough number from a busy loop the kernel times at boot; not a real speed benchmark. See: processors.
  • BOINC - Berkeley Open Infrastructure for Network Computing, a volunteer computing client. See: tools.
  • Boost (CPB / Turbo Boost) - running above the base clock when power and temperature allow; CPB (Core Performance Boost) is AMD's name, Turbo Boost is Intel's. See: processors.
  • BootOrder - the UEFI variable listing the boot entries (Boot####) in the order the firmware tries them. See: machine.
  • BORE (Burst-Oriented Response Enhancer) - a change to Linux's EEVDF CPU scheduler that favours tasks which run in short bursts (typically interactive programs), shipped in some gaming kernels. See: tools.
  • Boyer-Moore-Horspool - a fast way to find a word in a text by skipping ahead using the last letter of the word. See: tools.
  • Bridge (USB bridge) - The chip in a USB enclosure, stick or card reader that converts USB to SATA, NVMe or flash commands. See: buses-1, storage.
  • BSSID - the radio (MAC) address of one Wi-Fi access point; one network name (SSID) can have several. See: network.
  • btrfs - A Linux copy-on-write filesystem with checksums, subvolumes, snapshots, compression and built-in multi-disk support. See: storage.
  • BTU/h (British thermal units per hour) - a unit of heat flow: 1 W is about 3.412 BTU/h. All the power a PC uses ends up as heat in the room. See: User Guide 6.11.
  • Built-in driver - a driver compiled into the kernel file itself. It is always present and never appears in /proc/modules. See: linux-os.
  • Bulk-Only Transport (BOT) - the older, simpler USB mass-storage protocol (interface 08/06/50); slower than UAS. See: buses-2.

C

  • Carbon intensity - grams of CO2 released per kWh of electricity on a grid, on average over a year. See: User Guide 6.11.
  • Compute error (GPU) - a GPU result that differs from the right one. GPU Burnin counts them: any error means the card is not stable as set up (overclock, undervolt, heat, power) or faulty. See: tools.
  • C-state - an idle power level of a CPU core; C0 is running, deeper states (C1, C2, C3) save more power but take longer to wake. See: processors.
  • Cache - small fast memory on the CPU that keeps copies of recently used RAM; L1 is smallest and fastest, L3 largest and shared. See: processors.
  • Cache level (L1, L2, L3) - small, fast memories between the core and RAM. L1 is the smallest and fastest; L3 is the largest and is shared by many cores. See: tools.
  • Capability (Linux) - one split-off piece of root's power, such as CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE. It is the Linux counterpart of a Windows privilege. See: linux-os.
  • CardBus / PCMCIA - Old credit-card-sized laptop expansion cards, replaced by ExpressCard and USB. See: buses-1.
  • CCD - Core Complex Die, one chiplet of CPU cores on a Ryzen processor. Each CCD usually has its own L3 cache. See: processors, sensors, tools.
  • CCID (Chip Card Interface Device) - The standard USB class for smart card readers. See: buses-1.
  • CEM (Card Electromechanical) - The PCI Express standard for normal plug-in cards; board_info type : cem means a regular desktop graphics card. See: graphics.
  • Charmap - a glibc file that defines a character set; used when building locales. See: linux-os.
  • CHS - Cylinder-Head-Sector: the old way of addressing disk blocks, replaced by LBA. SRS shows the legacy 255-head, 63-sector translation. See: storage.
  • Chudnovsky series - a formula for pi that gives about 14 more digits for every term; the fastest way known to compute many digits. See: tools.
  • Class code - The PCI number that says what kind of device it is, e.g. 0300 display, 0108 NVMe, 0604 PCI bridge. See: buses-1.
  • Clock source - the hardware timer Linux uses to keep time (tsc, hpet, acpi_pm). See: processors.
  • Clocksource - the hardware counter the kernel reads to keep time (TSC, HPET, ACPI PM timer). See: linux-os.
  • Cluster - The smallest unit of space a FAT, exFAT or NTFS filesystem hands out to a file. See: storage.
  • CLZERO - an AMD instruction that writes a whole zeroed 64-byte cache line straight to memory; the Cache & Memory benchmark uses it to measure how fast the RAM itself can take writes. See: tools.
  • CMOS - the battery-backed clock chip and its small memory on the motherboard; the name comes from the chip technology. See: machine.
  • Code page - an old table that maps byte values to characters (e.g. 437, 1252). UTF-8 has replaced code pages on Linux. See: linux-os.
  • Code point - Unicode's number for one character, written like U+0041. See: linux-os.
  • COM port - A serial port. COM1 is traditionally at I/O 0x3F8, IRQ 4 (ttyS0 on Linux). See: buses-1.
  • Commit charge - the total memory programs have reserved; it can exceed RAM when swap exists. See: machine.
  • Compression ratio - how much smaller data became: 2.5 means the packed data is 2.5 times smaller than the original. See: tools.
  • Compute unit (CU) - A block of shader cores inside the GPU. RDNA GPUs pair two CUs into a WGP. See: graphics.
  • Congestion control - the method TCP uses to guess how fast it can send without overloading the path. See: network, srs-items.
  • Context switch - the kernel stopping one task on a CPU and starting another; the OS Latency benchmark times it with two threads or programs passing a byte back and forth through a pipe. See: tools.
  • Core dump - a snapshot of a crashed program's memory, saved for debugging. See: linux-os.
  • CPPC - Collaborative Processor Performance Control; an ACPI standard where the CPU offers a smooth scale of performance levels and the OS sets a target range. See: processors.
  • CPU affinity - a rule that ties a thread to one or more chosen CPUs, so the scheduler does not move it elsewhere. See: tools.
  • cpufreq - the Linux subsystem that sets CPU clock speed, made of a driver (talks to hardware) and a governor (picks the speed). See: processors.
  • CPUID - an x86 instruction that returns facts about the CPU (vendor, family, features, caches) in four registers, organised by leaf number. See: processors.
  • cpuidle - the Linux subsystem that puts idle CPUs into C-states. See: processors.
  • CRB - Command Response Buffer; the memory-based interface used by firmware TPMs. See: machine.
  • CRC32, CRC32C - checksums that detect damaged data (CRC32 in ZIP and Ethernet, CRC32C in storage and networks); many CPUs have an instruction for CRC32C. See: tools.
  • Critical Warning - NVMe health field: a bit field that is 0x00 when the drive sees no serious problem. See: storage.
  • CRTC - The part of the display engine that reads one picture from memory and sends it to one or more outputs. VRR is switched on per CRTC. See: graphics.
  • CSM (Compatibility Support Module) - Compatibility Support Module; the UEFI option that emulates a legacy BIOS for old operating systems and cards. See: linux-os, machine.
  • CSMI - Common Storage Management Interface: a Windows driver interface some RAID controllers offer for status queries. See: storage.
  • CSV (comma-separated values) - A plain-text table format, one line per row, columns split by commas; opens in any spreadsheet. See: sensors, srs-items.
  • CTA-861 - An EDID extension block with TV and HDMI data: extra video modes, audio formats and HDR information. See: graphics.
  • CUDA - NVIDIA's GPU computing platform, used by most AI programs; needs the NVIDIA driver. With ZLUDA, CUDA programs can run on AMD cards. See: tools.
  • Curve Optimizer - an AMD Ryzen BIOS setting that lowers (or raises) the voltage curve of each core. Too negative a value makes a core unstable or slow. See: tools.

D

  • DC power (inside the PC) - the power after the power supply, used by the parts; always less than the power at the wall. See: User Guide 6.11.
  • Device lost - the GPU stopped answering and its driver reset it; SRS ends a GPU test cleanly when it happens. See: tools.
  • D-states - device power states: D0 fully on, D3hot off but powered, D3cold power removed. See: machine.
  • D0 / D3hot / D3cold - PCI power states. D0 is fully on; D3hot and D3cold are sleep states (D3cold removes power completely). See: graphics.
  • DAD (Duplicate Address Detection) - a check that no other device already uses an address before the PC starts using it. See: network.
  • Data Units - NVMe counters of data read and written; one unit is 1,000 x 512 bytes (512,000 bytes). See: storage.
  • dBm - signal power on a logarithmic scale; for Wi-Fi, -30 is excellent and -80 is barely usable. See: network.
  • dconf - the binary settings database used by GNOME and GTK apps. See: linux-os.
  • DDC (Display Data Channel) - The I2C wires in a video cable that carry the monitor's EDID and DDC/CI commands such as brightness. See: graphics, srs-items.
  • Default gateway - the router your PC sends traffic to when the destination is not on the local network. See: tools.
  • Descriptor (USB) - a small data table a USB device sends when plugged in, describing its IDs, class, interfaces and endpoints. See: buses-2.
  • .desktop file - a small text file that describes an app (name, icon, command, file types it opens). See: linux-os.
  • dev_t - The major:minor number pair the kernel uses to find a device file in /dev. See: buses-1.
  • Device descriptor - The USB record that gives a device's vendor ID, product ID, release number and class. See: buses-1.
  • Device-mapper (dm) - The Linux kernel layer that maps virtual block devices onto real ones; used by LVM and dm-crypt. See: storage.
  • DGEMM, SGEMM - double- and single-precision general matrix multiply: the standard way to measure floating-point speed, counted as 2 x n³ operations for n x n matrices. See: tools.
  • DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol) - the way a router hands out IP addresses, gateway and DNS settings to devices automatically. See: network.
  • DHCP lease - an IP address the router lends to a device for a set time; the device renews it before it runs out. See: network.
  • Dhrystone - a classic integer (whole-number) CPU benchmark. Its score is given in DMIPS. See: tools.
  • DIMM - Dual In-line Memory Module; a desktop memory stick (SODIMM is the laptop size). See: machine, srs-items.
  • Dirty flag - A filesystem marker meaning it was not closed cleanly and should be checked. See: storage.
  • Dirty pages - file data changed in RAM but not yet written to disk. See: linux-os.
  • Discard - The Linux name for TRIM. See: storage.
  • DisplayID - A newer monitor description format, often added as an EDID extension for high resolutions and refresh rates. See: graphics.
  • DKMS (Dynamic Kernel Module Support) - a system that rebuilds out-of-tree kernel modules automatically for each new kernel. See: linux-os.
  • DLL (Dynamic-Link Library) - a Windows shared code file; the Linux equivalent is a shared object (.so). See: linux-os, srs-items.
  • dm-crypt - Linux disk encryption built on device-mapper (usually set up with LUKS). See: storage.
  • DMA (Direct Memory Access) - A device reading or writing memory by itself, without the CPU copying the data. See: buses-1, buses-2, machine.
  • DMI (Desktop Management Interface) - Desktop Management Interface; another name for the SMBIOS inventory, shown by Linux in /sys/class/dmi/id. See: linux-os, machine, sensors.
  • DMIPS - Dhrystone MIPS: Dhrystone loops per second divided by 1757, the speed of a DEC VAX 11/780. See: tools.
  • DNS (Domain Name System) - the service that turns names like example.com into IP addresses. See: network.
  • DNS cache - a local store of recent DNS answers so repeated lookups are instant. See: network.
  • DNS lookup - turning a name like speed.cloudflare.com into an address; the first lookup asks the network, a repeat usually comes from a cache. See: tools.
  • DPM (dynamic power management) - The GPU's list of clock and voltage steps; the firmware switches between them many times a second. See: graphics, srs-items.
  • DPMS (Display Power Management Signaling) - The monitor's power state: On, Standby, Suspend or Off. See: graphics.
  • DRAM - Dynamic RAM, the main system memory. It is much slower to reach than the caches. See: tools.
  • drivetemp - A Linux kernel module that reports SATA drive temperatures through hwmon without root. See: storage.
  • DRM (Direct Rendering Manager) - The kernel subsystem for GPUs. It creates /dev/dri/cardN and /dev/dri/renderDN and the folders in /sys/class/drm. See: graphics.
  • DSDT - Differentiated System Description Table; the main ACPI table holding the board's AML code. See: machine.
  • DSDT / SSDT - The main and the extra ACPI code tables; they contain the firmware's methods, including WMI code. See: sensors.
  • dup - A btrfs profile that keeps two copies of a block on the same disk. See: storage.
  • Duplex - whether both ends of a link can send at once (full) or must take turns (half). See: network.
  • Duty (duty cycle) - The share of time a PWM signal is on; 100% means full power to the fan. See: sensors.
  • DXVK - A translation layer that turns Direct3D 8/9/10/11 calls into Vulkan, used by Wine and Proton. See: graphics.

E

  • E-core - Efficiency core, a small, low-power core on hybrid CPUs such as Intel 12th generation and newer. See: tools.
  • E820 - the firmware memory map that lists which physical address ranges are RAM or reserved. See: machine.
  • e820 map - the memory map the PC firmware hands to the operating system at boot, marking RAM, reserved and ACPI ranges. See: buses-2.
  • EBDA - Extended BIOS Data Area; a small legacy-BIOS data block just below 640 KB. See: machine.
  • EC (Embedded Controller) - A small microcontroller on the motherboard that handles power buttons, battery, fans and some sensors (ACPI ID PNP0C09). See: buses-1.
  • ECAM (Enhanced Configuration Access Mechanism) - The memory window through which the CPU reads each PCIe device's 4 KB configuration space. See: buses-1, buses-2.
  • ECC - Error-Correcting Code memory; detects and fixes single-bit memory errors. See: machine.
  • ECDT - The ACPI Embedded Controller Boot Resources Table, an optional early description of the EC. See: buses-1.
  • EDAC - Error Detection And Correction; the Linux subsystem that reports ECC memory errors. See: machine.
  • EDID (Extended Display Identification Data) - A 128-byte block (plus extensions) stored in the monitor that describes its maker, model, size and supported modes. See: graphics.
  • EEVDF (Earliest Eligible Virtual Deadline First) - the standard Linux CPU scheduler since Linux 6.6 (it replaced CFS). See: tools.
  • EGL - The interface that connects OpenGL and OpenGL ES to windows on Wayland or X11. See: graphics.
  • ELD (EDID-Like Data) - The audio part of a monitor's EDID, passed to the HDMI/DisplayPort sound driver. See: graphics.
  • ELF (Executable and Linkable Format) - the file format of Linux programs and shared libraries. See: srs-items.
  • Embedded controller (EC) - a small microcontroller on the board for keyboard, battery, fans and buttons (mainly on laptops). See: machine.
  • Endpoint (USB) - a one-way data pipe inside a USB interface; its type is Control, Interrupt, Bulk or Isochronous. See: buses-1, buses-2.
  • EPP (Energy Performance Preference) - Energy Performance Preference; a hint to the CPU about how much to favour speed over power saving. See: linux-os, processors, srs-items.
  • ESP (EFI System Partition) - EFI System Partition: the FAT partition the UEFI firmware loads bootloaders from. See: linux-os, storage.
  • ESRT - EFI System Resource Table; lists the firmware parts that can be updated with UEFI capsules. See: machine.
  • exFAT - Extended FAT: a simple filesystem for flash media that allows files over 4 GiB. See: storage.
  • EXPO - AMD Extended Profiles for Overclocking; faster memory settings stored in the SPD. See: machine.
  • EXPO / XMP - memory profiles (AMD EXPO, Intel XMP) stored on the RAM sticks, which set the rated speed and timings in one step. See: tools.

F

  • FADT (Fixed ACPI Description Table) - Fixed ACPI Description Table (signature FACP); points to the other key tables and lists fixed power-management hardware. See: buses-1, machine.
  • Family / Model / Stepping - numbers from CPUID that identify a CPU's generation, design and silicon revision. See: processors.
  • Fan curve - A list of temperature:duty points the fan controller follows, with straight lines between them. See: sensors.
  • FAT - File Allocation Table: a simple filesystem family (FAT12, FAT16, FAT32) used on USB sticks and EFI partitions. See: storage.
  • FCH (Fusion Controller Hub) - AMD's built-in southbridge logic: SMBus, LPC, GPIO, power management. See: buses-1.
  • fclk / socclk / dcefclk - GPU clocks for the internal data fabric, the chip's support logic, and the display engine. See: graphics.
  • FCLK / UCLK / MCLK - on AMD: Infinity Fabric clock, memory controller clock and memory clock. See: machine.
  • FFT (Fast Fourier Transform) - a fast way to split a signal into its frequencies; used in audio, images and science. Counted as 5 N log2 N operations for N points. See: tools.
  • File descriptor - a small number a process uses for each open file, pipe, socket or device; the Linux version of a Windows handle. See: linux-os.
  • File lock - a marker a program sets so others know it is using a file; listed in /proc/locks. See: srs-items.
  • firewalld zone - a named set of firewall rules; each network interface belongs to one zone. See: network.
  • FireWire (IEEE 1394) - An older high-speed bus used for camcorders and pro audio. See: buses-1.
  • Fixture - a saved data dump used to test a program without the real hardware. See: srs-items.
  • Floating input - A sensor pin with nothing connected. Its voltage drifts with leakage and noise, so the reading is meaningless. See: sensors.
  • fontconfig - the Linux library that finds fonts and picks one for each character. See: linux-os.
  • FP16 / FP32 / FP64 - numbers with a decimal point stored in 16, 32 or 64 bits: half, single and double precision. Games mostly use FP32; most gaming GPUs are much slower at FP64. See: tools.
  • FPDT - Firmware Performance Data Table; records how long the firmware took to boot. See: machine.
  • FPGA (Field-Programmable Gate Array) - a chip whose logic circuits are loaded from a configuration file, so its function can be changed after manufacture. See: buses-2.
  • FQDN (fully qualified domain name) - a host name plus its domain, such as pc.example.lan. See: network.
  • FSR (FidelityFX Super Resolution) - AMD's upscaling technique: render at a lower resolution, then scale up and sharpen. See: graphics.
  • fTPM - firmware TPM; a TPM implemented inside the CPU's security processor instead of a separate chip. See: machine.
  • Function (PCI) - One logical device inside a PCI chip. A GPU's audio part is function 1 (03:00.1). See: buses-1.
  • Futex - "fast user-space mutex": the Linux building block that lets a waiting thread sleep and be woken by another; the OS Latency benchmark times the wake-up. See: tools.

G

  • gamescope - Valve's small game compositor; it can upscale games with FSR (gamescope -F fsr). See: graphics.
  • Gateway - the router that forwards your packets to other networks, usually your home router. See: network.
  • GBM (Generic Buffer Management) - A library compositors use to get GPU memory buffers for the screen. See: graphics.
  • GC (graphics core) - The 3D and compute engine of an AMD GPU. Its version gives the gfx target name (GC 12.0.1 = gfx1201). See: graphics.
  • GEMM (matrix multiplication) - multiplying two big tables of numbers (general matrix multiply); the core of AI and many science programs, and a hard, steady load for a GPU. See: tools.
  • GFLOPS - billions of floating-point (decimal-point) operations per second. See: tools.
  • GIOPS - billions of whole-number (integer) operations per second. See: tools.
  • GLVND - The vendor-neutral OpenGL dispatch library that lets several OpenGL drivers be installed side by side. See: graphics.
  • Governor (CPU) - the cpufreq policy that decides which speed to ask for (performance, powersave, schedutil). See: linux-os, processors, srs-items.
  • GPE (General Purpose Event) - General Purpose Event; an ACPI event bit used for wake-up and hot-plug signals. See: buses-1, machine.
  • GPIO (General Purpose Input/Output) - Simple on/off signal pins that chips use for LEDs, buttons, resets and enables. See: buses-1.
  • GPT - GUID Partition Table: the modern partition table format, with type GUIDs, PARTUUIDs and names for each partition. See: storage.
  • GSI - Global System Interrupt; the interrupt number space used by I/O APICs. See: machine.
  • GStreamer - The main Linux media framework; plugins handle file formats, codecs and audio/video effects. See: graphics.
  • GT/s (gigatransfers per second) - Gigatransfers per second: the per-lane speed of a PCIe link (8.0 = PCIe 3.0, 16.0 = PCIe 4.0, 32.0 = PCIe 5.0). See: buses-1, buses-2, srs-items, storage.
  • GTT (graphics translation table) - System RAM that the GPU is allowed to map and use, much slower for the GPU than VRAM. See: graphics.
  • GUID - Globally Unique Identifier; a 128-bit ID, used for WMI interfaces and UEFI variable vendors. See: machine.

H

  • H:C:T:L - Host:Channel:Target:LUN, the address of a device in the Linux SCSI layer. See: storage.
  • HAL (Hardware Abstraction Layer) - the lowest layer of Windows that hides hardware differences; SIV uses the name for its resource-map pages. See: buses-2.
  • HD Audio (High Definition Audio) - The Intel standard used by almost all PC sound chips and by GPU HDMI audio: a controller plus one or more codecs. See: graphics.
  • HDD - Hard disk drive: storage on spinning magnetic platters. See: storage.
  • Heap - the memory a program requests while it runs (malloc). See: linux-os.
  • HECI - Host Embedded Controller Interface; the link between the OS and the Intel Management Engine (MEI on Linux). See: machine.
  • HID (Human Interface Device) - The device class and protocol for keyboards, mice, game pads, RGB controllers and security keys. See: buses-1, buses-2, machine, srs-items.
  • hidraw - A Linux device node (/dev/hidrawN) that gives programs raw access to a HID device. See: buses-1.
  • HIP - AMD's CUDA-like programming language for GPU computing, part of ROCm. See: graphics.
  • Holder - A Linux block device built on top of another one (for example an encrypted volume on a partition). See: storage.
  • Host bridge - The PCI device that connects the CPU to the PCI bus (class 0600). See: buses-1.
  • Hotspot temperature - the hottest point measured on a GPU chip; AMD calls it junction temperature. Usually 10-20 °C above the edge temperature. See: tools.
  • HPA - Host Protected Area: a part of an ATA disk hidden from the operating system, which makes the disk look smaller. See: storage.
  • HPET (High Precision Event Timer) - High Precision Event Timer; a hardware timer described by its own ACPI table. See: buses-2, machine.
  • Hub (USB) - a device that turns one USB port into several. See: buses-2.
  • hwdata - The package that ships the pci.ids, usb.ids and pnp.ids name lists. See: buses-1.
  • hwdb - udev's hardware database, which adds properties such as vendor and model names to devices. See: buses-1.
  • hwmon - The kernel's standard sensor interface. Each driver makes a folder of files such as temp1_input and fan1_input. See: graphics, linux-os, machine, processors, sensors, srs-items, storage.
  • Hybrid CPU - a CPU that mixes two kinds of cores (P-cores and E-cores). See: tools.

I

  • I/O APIC - the interrupt controller that collects legacy interrupt lines and routes them to CPUs; "IR-" in front means the IOMMU remaps them. See: buses-2.
  • I/O port - An address in the separate 64K x86 I/O space, used by legacy devices (keyboard controller, RTC, COM ports, SMBus). See: buses-1, buses-2.
  • I/O scheduler - The kernel part that decides the order in which waiting read/write requests go to a drive. See: srs-items, storage.
  • I2C (Inter-Integrated Circuit) - A slow two-wire bus that chips use to talk to each other. Monitors use it for DDC. See: buses-1, graphics, srs-items.
  • I2C / SMBus - slow two-wire buses for small chips such as sensors and memory SPD hubs; SMBus is the PC variant. See: machine.
  • ICD (installable client driver) - A small file that tells the Vulkan or OpenCL loader where a driver library is. See: graphics.
  • ICMP (Internet Control Message Protocol) - the protocol that carries ping and network error messages. See: network.
  • iconv - the glibc library for converting text between character sets. See: linux-os.
  • IMC (Integrated Memory Controller) - the part of the CPU that talks to RAM. See: srs-items.
  • IMSM - Intel Matrix Storage Manager: the RAID metadata format used by Intel RST and VROC, supported by Linux mdadm. See: storage.
  • Infinity Fabric - AMD's internal link between the CCDs, the I/O die and the memory controller. See: tools.
  • initramfs - a small early-boot file system that loads drivers needed to mount the real root disk. See: linux-os.
  • Inode - A filesystem's record for one file or folder. See: storage.
  • Interface (USB) - One function of a USB device, with its own class and driver. One device can have several. See: buses-1.
  • IOMMU (input-output memory management unit) - Input-Output Memory Management Unit; controls which memory each device can reach, needed for passing devices to virtual machines. See: buses-1, buses-2, graphics, machine, processors.
  • IOMMU group - The smallest set of devices the IOMMU can isolate from each other. It matters for passing a device to a virtual machine. See: buses-1.
  • IOPS - input/output operations per second: how many separate read or write requests a drive answers each second. See: tools.
  • IP block - A reusable hardware building block inside an AMD chip (graphics core, video engine, memory controller...), each with its own version. See: graphics.
  • IPI - Inter-Processor Interrupt, a signal from one CPU to another. SRS's IPI Delay measures the core-to-core cache-line delay instead. See: tools.
  • IPMI (Intelligent Platform Management Interface) - A standard for talking to a server's BMC: sensors, event log, remote power control. See: sensors.
  • IrDA - Infrared data transfer on old laptops and phones. Linux removed support in kernel 4.17. See: buses-1.
  • IRQ (Interrupt Request) - A signal a device uses to get the CPU's attention. Also the number of that interrupt line. See: buses-1, buses-2, graphics.
  • ISA (Industry Standard Architecture) - The original PC expansion bus. Its job now lives on in LPC. See: buses-1.
  • isohybrid - A CD/DVD image (ISO 9660) built so it can also boot when written straight to a USB stick. See: storage.
  • Itanium (IA-64) - Intel and HP's 64-bit server processor family, unrelated to x86-64, discontinued in 2021. See: buses-2.
  • IVRS - I/O Virtualization Reporting Structure; the ACPI table describing AMD's IOMMU (Intel uses DMAR). See: machine.

J

  • JEDEC - the standards body for memory; the JEDEC speed is a stick's standard base speed. See: machine.
  • Jitter - how much a time (round trip, connect) changes from one try to the next. See: tools.
  • Joule (J) - a unit of energy: 3,600 J = 1 Wh. Linux energy counters count microjoules (millionths of a joule). See: User Guide 6.11.
  • Junction temperature - the hottest point measured on a graphics chip, usually higher than its "edge" temperature. See: tools.

K

  • k10temp - the Linux driver that reads AMD CPU temperature sensors (Tctl, Tccd). See: processors.
  • Kernel (GPU) - a small program that runs on the GPU, many copies at once (not the Linux kernel). See: tools.
  • Kernel module - a loadable piece of the kernel, usually a driver; the Linux counterpart of a Windows driver. See: linux-os, srs-items.
  • KMS (kernel mode setting) - The part of DRM that sets screen resolutions and refresh rates. See: graphics.
  • KSM (Kernel Same-page Merging) - the kernel finds identical memory pages and keeps only one copy. See: srs-items.
  • KVM - Kernel-based Virtual Machine; Linux's built-in hypervisor, available through /dev/kvm. See: processors.
  • kWh (kilowatt-hour) - 1000 watts used for one hour; the unit electricity is billed in. See: sensors.
  • kW (kilowatt) - 1,000 watts. See: User Guide 6.11.

L

  • LACT - A Linux tool for AMD GPU overclocking, undervolting and fan control. See: graphics.
  • LAN (local area network) - the devices in your home or office connected to the same router or switch. See: network.
  • Lane (PCIe) - One pair of signal wires in each direction. A link has 1, 2, 4, 8 or 16 lanes. See: buses-1.
  • Latency - waiting time: how long it takes for a request (a memory load, a ping) to be answered. See: tools.
  • Lavapipe - Mesa's software Vulkan driver, which runs on the CPU; SRS's GPU tests use it so that they never touch a real graphics card. See: tools.
  • LBA - Logical Block Addressing: numbering a disk's blocks from 0 upwards, the way all modern drives are addressed. See: storage.
  • LDN (Logical Device Number) - The number of one function block (serial port, hardware monitor ...) inside a Super I/O chip. See: sensors.
  • Leaf (CPUID) - the question number given to the CPUID instruction; some leaves have several sub-leaves. See: processors.
  • LFC (low framerate compensation) - A VRR trick that shows frames twice when the frame rate falls below the monitor's VRR minimum. See: graphics.
  • Link width (PCIe) - The number of lanes a PCIe link is using (x1, x4, x8, x16). See: buses-1.
  • Link-local address - an address that only works on the local cable or Wi-Fi (fe80:: for IPv6, 169.254. for IPv4), made automatically. See: network.
  • llvmpipe - Mesa's software renderer. It draws on the CPU and is only a fallback. See: graphics.
  • lm-sensors - The standard Linux sensor package; its config files (/etc/sensors3.conf, /etc/sensors.d) rename, scale or hide readings. See: sensors.
  • Load average - the average number of tasks running or waiting for a CPU over 1, 5 and 15 minutes. See: linux-os.
  • Locale - a bundle of language and regional rules: language, date and number format, sorting, currency. See: linux-os, srs-items.
  • Locally administered MAC - a MAC address made up by software rather than assigned by the hardware maker. See: network.
  • Logical CPU - one hardware thread as Linux sees it. With SMT, each physical core shows up as two logical CPUs. See: srs-items, tools.
  • Loopback (127.0.0.1) - the computer's connection to itself; data never reaches a network card. See: tools.
  • LPC (Low Pin Count) - A slim bus from the chipset to the Super I/O chip, TPM, serial port and BIOS flash. See: buses-1.
  • LPM (Link Power Management) - USB power saving that puts the link into low-power states between transfers; some devices need it disabled. See: buses-2.
  • LSM (Linux Security Module) - a pluggable security layer in the kernel, such as Yama, Landlock, AppArmor or SELinux. See: linux-os.
  • LUN - Logical Unit Number: one device behind one SCSI address, such as one slot of a card reader. See: storage.
  • LVM - Logical Volume Manager: Linux tool for flexible volumes spread over one or more disks. See: storage.

M

  • MAC address (Media Access Control) - the 6-byte hardware address of a network adapter. See: network.
  • MADT - Multiple APIC Description Table (signature APIC); lists the CPU threads and interrupt controllers. See: machine.
  • Mandelbrot set - a famous fractal; drawing it is a simple, repeatable floating-point test. Measured in Mpixels/s. See: tools.
  • MangoHud - A Linux in-game overlay that shows frame rate, temperatures, clocks and more, and can limit the frame rate. See: graphics.
  • Masquerade - NAT (network address translation): many devices share one address on the way out. See: network.
  • Mbit/s - million bits per second; 8 bits = 1 byte, so 100 Mbit/s is 12.5 MB/s. Internet plans are sold in Mbit/s. See: tools.
  • MBR - Master Boot Record: the old partition table format (shown as dos), with four primary partitions and one-byte type codes. See: storage.
  • MCA (Micro Channel Architecture) - IBM's PS/2 expansion bus from 1987. See: buses-1.
  • MCE (Machine Check Exception) - the CPU reporting a hardware error it detected, for example in cache or memory. See: buses-2.
  • MCFG - The ACPI table that gives the ECAM base address. See: buses-1.
  • MCH (Memory Controller Hub) - The old Intel "northbridge" chip that held the memory controller. AMD CPUs have no MCH. See: buses-1.
  • MCHBAR (Memory Controller Hub Base Address Register) - the address of a block of Intel memory-controller registers. See: srs-items.
  • mclk - The GPU's memory clock. GDDR6 moves 16 bits per clock per pin, so 1258 MHz is about 20 Gbps. See: graphics.
  • mclk / sclk - a GPU's memory clock and shader (core) clock. See: srs-items.
  • MCS (Modulation and Coding Scheme) - the Wi-Fi encoding step; higher is faster but needs a cleaner signal. See: network.
  • md - The Linux software RAID driver, managed with mdadm. See: storage.
  • mDNS (multicast DNS) - lets devices announce names and services on the LAN without a DNS server. See: network.
  • Mesa - The open-source graphics driver collection on Linux, including RADV (Vulkan) and radeonsi (OpenGL) for AMD. See: graphics.
  • Metric - a route's priority number; when two routes match, the lower metric wins. See: network.
  • MFT - Master File Table: the NTFS index that holds a record for every file. See: storage.
  • Microcode - a small firmware patch for the processor, loaded by the BIOS or the OS at boot to fix bugs and security issues. See: processors.
  • MIDI sequencer (ALSA) - The kernel service that routes MIDI events between programs, synths and MIDI hardware. See: graphics.
  • MIME type (Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions type) - a standard name for a kind of file, such as image/png. See: linux-os.
  • MIO (Memory and I/O controller) - the main chip of HP's zx1 chipset, linking Itanium 2 processors to memory and I/O. See: buses-2.
  • MMIO (Memory-Mapped I/O) - device registers placed in the physical memory address space so the CPU reaches them with normal reads and writes. See: buses-1, buses-2.
  • Modalias - A device's driver-matching ID string, e.g. pci:v00001022d000014D8.... Linux uses it to load the right driver. See: buses-1.
  • Module (kernel) - A driver file loaded into the kernel at run time. "Built-in" means it is compiled into the kernel. See: buses-1.
  • Mount point - The folder where a filesystem is attached to the folder tree. See: storage.
  • MRH (Memory Repeater Hub) - An Intel 820/840-era chip that let RDRAM boards use SDRAM. See: buses-1.
  • MSI (message signaled interrupts) - A way for PCI devices to send interrupts as memory writes instead of dedicated wires. See: graphics.
  • MSI / MSI-X (Message Signalled Interrupts) - PCI Express interrupts sent as a memory write instead of a wire; each device or queue gets its own vector. See: buses-2, machine.
  • MSR - Model Specific Register; an internal CPU control or counter register read with RDMSR, root only on Linux. See: processors.
  • MT/s - mega-transfers per second; the memory data rate, twice the memory clock for DDR. See: machine.
  • MTP (Media Transfer Protocol) - the protocol phones and media players use to share files over USB without exposing a raw disk. See: buses-2.
  • MTU (Maximum Transmission Unit) - the largest packet a link carries, normally 1500 bytes on Ethernet. See: network.
  • Multicast - one-to-many traffic: devices join a group address and receive what is sent to it. See: network.
  • Multikey quicksort - a way of sorting text that compares one letter position at a time. See: tools.
  • Multipath - Reaching one drive over more than one route; Linux combines the routes into one disk. See: storage.
  • Mutex (mutual exclusion) - a lock that stops two threads using the same thing at the same time. See: srs-items.
  • MWIPS - Million Whetstone Instructions Per Second, the score of the Whetstone benchmark. See: tools.

N

  • N-body simulation - working out the gravity between every pair of a group of bodies (stars, planets); a classic floating-point workload. See: tools.
  • Namespace - A slice of an NVMe SSD presented as one disk; consumer SSDs have one. See: storage.
  • NDP (Neighbor Discovery Protocol) - the IPv6 version of ARP. See: network.
  • NetBIOS browsing - the old Windows way of listing computers on a LAN through an elected master browser. See: network.
  • Netlink - the socket type tools like ip use to talk to the Linux kernel. See: network.
  • Nice - a process's politeness value (-20 to 19); higher nice means it gives way to other processes. See: linux-os, srs-items.
  • NMI (Non-Maskable Interrupt) - an interrupt the CPU cannot ignore, used for watchdogs, profiling and serious hardware errors. See: buses-2.
  • Normalised value - A SMART attribute's score on the maker's scale (often starting at 100 or 200), which goes down as things get worse. See: storage.
  • NPU (Neural Processing Unit) - An AI accelerator such as AMD XDNA in Ryzen AI laptops. See: buses-1.
  • NQN - NVMe Qualified Name: a unique name an NVMe subsystem reports about itself. See: storage.
  • NSS (Name Service Switch) - glibc's list that decides where names are looked up and in what order. See: network.
  • NTFS - New Technology File System: the main Windows filesystem; Linux reads and writes it with the ntfs3 driver. See: storage.
  • NTP (Network Time Protocol) - the protocol that keeps the clock in sync with time servers over the network. See: linux-os.
  • NTT (number-theoretic transform) - a relative of the FFT that works with whole numbers modulo a prime, used to multiply numbers with millions of digits quickly and exactly. See: tools.
  • NUMA - Non-Uniform Memory Access; a design where memory is attached to particular CPUs, so "far" memory is slower. See: machine, processors, tools.
  • NUMA node - A group of CPUs and memory that are close to each other. Desktops have one node, which Linux shows as -1 for PCI devices. See: buses-1, graphics, storage.
  • NVMe - Non-Volatile Memory Express: the protocol fast SSDs use over PCIe. See: storage.
  • NVMe Composite - An NVMe drive's own summary temperature, used for its thermal throttling. See: sensors.
  • NX / XD - No-Execute (AMD) / Execute Disable (Intel); marks memory as data-only so it cannot be run as code. See: processors.

O

  • O_DIRECT - opening a file so reads and writes go straight to the drive, past Linux's page cache in RAM; benchmarks use it so they measure the drive, not the RAM. See: tools.
  • OpenCL - An open standard for running general computing tasks on GPUs and other processors. See: graphics.
  • OpenGL - The older cross-platform 3D graphics interface; still used by many programs and older games. See: graphics.
  • Option ROM - firmware stored on a PCI card (listed as the ROM BAR), for example a graphics card's video BIOS. See: buses-2, machine.
  • OUI (Organizationally Unique Identifier) - the first three bytes of a MAC address, identifying the maker. See: network.
  • Overcommit - the kernel promising programs more memory than it really has, betting they will not all use it at once. See: linux-os.
  • OverDrive - AMD's name for user clock, voltage and power tuning. On Linux it appears as pp_od_clk_voltage. See: graphics.

P

  • P-core - Performance core, a big, fast core on a hybrid CPU. See: tools.
  • Page fault - what happens the first time a program touches a page of memory the kernel has not set up yet: the kernel stops the program for a moment and supplies the page. See: tools.
  • PLATYPUS - a 2020 attack that used CPU energy readings to learn secrets (CVE-2020-8694/8695, CVE-2020-12912); since Linux 5.10 the powercap RAPL counters are root-only because of it. See: User Guide 6.11.
  • P-state - a performance state: a running speed and voltage level of the CPU. See: processors.
  • PAC (proxy auto-config) - a script that picks which proxy to use for each address. See: network.
  • Page - the unit the CPU and kernel use to manage memory, usually 4 KB on x86. See: srs-items.
  • Page cache - spare RAM the kernel uses to hold recently read or written file data. See: linux-os.
  • PARTUUID - The unique ID of a partition, stored in the partition table (not in the filesystem). See: storage.
  • PCH (Platform Controller Hub) - Intel's chipset; PCH temperature inputs on a Super I/O read 0 on AMD boards. See: sensors.
  • PCI address - a device's location written as domain🚌device.function, for example 0000:03:00.0. See: buses-1, buses-2.
  • PCI bridge (PtP) - a PCI-to-PCI bridge; each slot, M.2 socket or chipset port is one and creates a new bus number. See: machine.
  • PCI function - one logical PCI device; one chip can show several (for example graphics and audio). See: srs-items.
  • PCI ID - the vendor, device, subsystem and revision numbers a PCI device reports. Linux uses them to pick a driver. See: tools.
  • PCI ID database - The pci.ids file that turns vendor and device numbers into names. See: buses-1.
  • PCIe (PCI Express) - The serial point-to-point version of PCI used for graphics cards, NVMe drives and most onboard devices. See: buses-1, storage.
  • PCIe link speed and width - Speed is the transfer rate per lane (2.5, 5, 8, 16, 32 GT/s = PCIe 1 to 5); width is the number of lanes (x1 to x16). See: graphics.
  • PCIe link width - the number of PCI Express lanes in use (x1, x4, x8, x16); bandwidth scales with it. See: buses-2, srs-items.
  • PCIe switch - A chip with one upstream port and several downstream ports that share one link between devices. See: buses-1.
  • PCM (pulse-code modulation) - Plain digital audio. An ALSA PCM device is one playback or recording stream. See: graphics.
  • PCR - Platform Configuration Register; a TPM register holding a hash of what ran during boot. See: machine.
  • PECI / SB-TSI - Side channels that let the Super I/O read the CPU temperature (PECI on Intel, SB-TSI on AMD). See: sensors.
  • Percentage Used - NVMe health field: the drive's estimate of how much of its rated write life is used. See: storage.
  • PipeWire - The modern Linux sound (and video) server. It mixes programs together and routes them to outputs. See: graphics.
  • PM profile - The firmware's preferred power profile: 1 Desktop, 2 Mobile, 3 Workstation, 4 Enterprise server. See: buses-1.
  • PM table - the power-management table the AMD SMU keeps, with live powers, clocks, voltages and temperatures. See: processors, srs-items.
  • PM1 block - The ACPI I/O registers for sleep, wake and the power button. See: buses-1.
  • PM_TMR - The ACPI power-management timer, which runs at 3.58 MHz. See: buses-1.
  • PMBus - An SMBus-based protocol for smart power supplies and voltage regulators. See: buses-1.
  • PnP (Plug and Play) - The firmware's description of built-in legacy devices, with IDs like PNP0501. See: buses-1.
  • PnP ID - A 3-letter vendor code plus 4 hex digits (PNP0501), or with ACPI a 4-letter code plus 4 hex digits (AMDI0030). See: buses-1, buses-2, graphics.
  • Pointer chase - a memory test where each load needs the address from the previous load, so prefetching cannot hide the delay. See: tools.
  • polkit - the Linux service that decides which desktop users may perform admin actions, and whether a password is needed. See: linux-os, srs-items.
  • Port - a number (0-65535) that picks which program on a machine receives a packet. See: network.
  • Port path - the chain of USB port numbers from the root hub to a device, for example 2.3.4. See: buses-2.
  • Power cap - the power limit firmware holds a chip to. See: srs-items.
  • PPI - Physical Presence Interface; how the operating system asks the firmware to clear or enable the TPM at the next boot. See: machine.
  • PPT (Package Power Tracking) - AMD's measured power for a CPU or GPU package, and the limit applied to it. See: graphics, sensors, srs-items.
  • Preemption - how quickly the kernel can interrupt a running task to run another; full gives the lowest latency. See: linux-os.
  • Preferred core (prefcore) - a per-core ranking from the CPU telling the scheduler which cores boost best. See: processors.
  • Prefetchable - A BAR whose memory can be read ahead and cached safely, such as graphics memory. See: buses-1.
  • Prefix length - the "/24" or "/64" after an address: how many leading bits are the network part. See: network.
  • Proton - Valve's version of Wine, built into Steam, that runs Windows games on Linux. See: graphics.
  • Proxy - a middle server that makes web requests on your behalf. See: network.
  • PSP (Platform Security Processor) - A small security processor inside AMD chips (the MP0 block); it loads and checks other firmware. See: graphics, machine.
  • PSS (Proportional Set Size) - a process's RAM use with shared pages split fairly among the processes sharing them. See: linux-os.
  • PSU efficiency (80 PLUS, Cybenetics) - the share of the wall power that reaches the parts; 90 % means 10 % turns into heat in the power supply. 80 PLUS and Cybenetics certify it at set loads. See: User Guide 6.11.
  • PTP (Picture Transfer Protocol) - the older camera file-transfer protocol that MTP is built on; uses USB class 06 (Still Image). See: buses-2.
  • PWM (pulse-width modulation) - A way to control fan speed by switching power on and off quickly; the duty cycle sets the speed. See: graphics, sensors.

Q

  • qdisc (queueing discipline) - the kernel's waiting line for outgoing packets, such as fq or fq_codel. See: network, srs-items.
  • QST (Quiet System Technology) - Intel fan control built into the management engine of some 2007-2010 desktop boards. See: sensors.
  • Queue depth (Q), threads (T) - Q = how many requests one thread keeps waiting at the drive at once, T = how many threads do so; "Q32T16" keeps 512 requests in flight. See: tools.
  • Quirk (USB) - a kernel workaround flag for a device that does not follow the USB standard exactly. See: buses-2.

R

  • radeonsi - Mesa's OpenGL driver for AMD GPUs. See: graphics.
  • Radix sort - sorting numbers by their digits (or bytes) instead of comparing them with each other. See: tools.
  • RADV - Mesa's Vulkan driver for AMD GPUs. See: graphics.
  • RAID - Redundant Array of Independent Disks: joining disks for speed (raid0), safety (raid1 mirrors) or both. See: storage.
  • Rank - a set of memory chips on a stick that is accessed together; sticks are single- or dual-rank. See: machine.
  • RAPL (Running Average Power Limit) - A CPU feature that counts energy used; Linux exposes it under /sys/class/powercap, named intel-rapl even on AMD. See: processors, sensors.
  • Raw value - A SMART attribute's actual counter (sectors, hours, degrees); its format is up to the maker. See: storage.
  • Ray tracing - drawing a picture by following rays of light from the eye into a scene, with shadows and reflections. See: tools.
  • Regex - regular expression, a text search pattern (for example ^ = start of line, . = any character). See: tools.
  • Regular expression (regex) - a search pattern, e.g. nvme[0-9] matches nvme0, nvme1 and so on. See: srs-items.
  • Report descriptor - The HID record that tells the PC which buttons, axes and LEDs a device has. See: buses-1.
  • Resizable BAR - A PCIe feature that lets the CPU see all of the GPU's VRAM at once instead of through a 256 MB window. AMD calls it Smart Access Memory. See: buses-1, buses-2, graphics, machine.
  • Revision ID - The PCI number that tells chip steppings or versions apart. See: buses-1.
  • rfkill - the Linux kernel's on/off switch for radios (Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, mobile data); soft = software, hard = physical switch. See: network.
  • ROCm - AMD's open GPU computing platform (HIP, OpenCL, libraries) for Linux. See: graphics.
  • Root complex - The part of the CPU where PCIe starts. On AMD it is the device at 00:00.0. See: buses-1.
  • Root hub - The virtual hub that stands for a USB host controller's ports. Each USB 3 controller has a 2.0 root hub and a 3.x root hub. See: buses-1, buses-2.
  • Round trip (compression) - compress, then decompress, then compare with the original; it must be identical. See: tools.
  • Round trip time - the time for a message to go to the other end and come back. See: tools.
  • RPC - Remote Procedure Call, a way for one program to send commands to another over a network connection. See: tools.
  • RPM (revolutions per minute) - Fan or pump speed. See: sensors.
  • RSS (Resident Set Size) - the RAM a process is really using right now. See: linux-os.
  • RTC (real-time clock) - the battery-backed clock on the motherboard that keeps time while the PC is off. See: linux-os, machine.
  • Runtime PM - Kernel power management that lets an idle device sleep while the system is running. See: graphics.

S

  • SAE (Simultaneous Authentication of Equals) - the WPA3 password handshake, safer than WPA2's. See: network.
  • Samba - the Linux implementation of Windows file and printer sharing (SMB). See: network.
  • SATA - Serial ATA: the cable and protocol for most 2.5-inch and 3.5-inch drives. See: storage.
  • sched_ext - a Linux feature that lets a CPU scheduler be loaded as a BPF program while the system runs. See: linux-os, srs-items.
  • SCI - System Control Interrupt; ACPI's shared interrupt line, usually IRQ 9. See: machine.
  • sclk - The GPU's shader (core) clock. See: graphics.
  • SCSI - Small Computer System Interface: a command set Linux uses for SATA, USB and SAS storage. See: storage.
  • SCT - SMART Command Transport: an ATA channel for extra data such as temperature history and error recovery limits. See: storage.
  • SDMA (system DMA) - The GPU's copy engines, which move data between memory areas without using the 3D engine. See: graphics.
  • Section (ELF) - one named part of a program file: .text code, .data variables, .rodata fixed data, .bss zeroed memory. See: srs-items.
  • Secure Boot - a UEFI feature that only starts boot loaders and kernels signed with trusted keys. See: linux-os, machine.
  • Session (busy session) - in Power & cost, a stretch of heavy use (a game, a render) found from the CPU and graphics load; its energy is the whole PC's while it lasted. See: User Guide 6.11.
  • Setup Mode - UEFI Secure Boot state with no Platform Key installed, in which keys can be changed freely. See: machine.
  • SEV - Secure Encrypted Virtualization; AMD server feature that encrypts virtual machine memory. See: processors.
  • SHA-256, SHA-NI - SHA-256 makes a 256-bit "fingerprint" of data (package checks, backups, git); SHA-NI are CPU instructions that speed it up. See: tools.
  • Shared library - a .so code file many programs use at once, such as libc.so.6. See: srs-items.
  • Sieve of Eratosthenes - finding prime numbers by crossing out the multiples of each prime; what remains are the primes. See: tools.
  • Sink / source - In a sound server, a sink is where sound goes (speakers, HDMI); a source is where sound comes from (microphone, line in). See: graphics.
  • SLAAC (stateless address autoconfiguration) - the way an IPv6 device builds its own address from the router's advertisements. See: network.
  • Slab - the kernel's allocator for its own small objects; "reclaimable" slab is cache it can drop. See: linux-os.
  • SLAT - Second Level Address Translation (Intel EPT, AMD RVI/NPT); hardware help that makes virtual machine memory fast. See: processors.
  • Slicing-by-8 - a way of computing CRC checksums 8 bytes at a time with lookup tables. See: tools.
  • SMART (Self-Monitoring, Analysis and Reporting Technology) - Self-Monitoring, Analysis and Reporting Technology: the health log a drive keeps about itself. See: srs-items, storage.
  • SMB (Server Message Block) - the Windows file-sharing protocol. See: network.
  • SMBIOS (System Management BIOS) - System Management BIOS; the firmware inventory of board, BIOS, CPU socket and memory slots. See: buses-1, machine, srs-items.
  • SMBus (System Management Bus) - an I2C-based bus on the motherboard that links RAM SPD chips and sensors. See: buses-1, srs-items.
  • SMN (System Management Network) - AMD's internal register network for the Data Fabric and memory controllers. SRS never touches it. See: buses-1, machine, processors.
  • SMT - Simultaneous Multi-Threading (Intel: Hyper-Threading); one physical core runs two threads, shown as two CPUs. See: processors, srs-items, tools.
  • SMT sibling - the other logical CPU that shares the same physical core. See: tools.
  • SMU (System Management Unit) - System Management Unit; a small processor inside a Ryzen CPU that controls boost, voltage and power limits. See: graphics, processors, srs-items.
  • Socket - a program's handle for one network conversation or local channel. See: network.
  • soname - the version number in a shared library's file name (the 6 in libc.so.6); it changes only when compatibility breaks. See: linux-os.
  • SPD (Serial Presence Detect) - Serial Presence Detect; the data on each memory stick describing its size, speeds, timings and profiles. See: buses-1, machine, srs-items.
  • spd5118 - the SPD hub chip on DDR5 sticks, and its Linux driver; it also provides a temperature sensor. See: machine.
  • Speculative execution - the CPU guessing ahead to run faster; flaws in it (Spectre, Meltdown) can leak data and are closed by mitigations. See: processors.
  • SPIR-V - the compiled form of a Vulkan compute or graphics program (shader); SRS ships its GPU shaders pre-compiled as SPIR-V. See: tools.
  • SQLite - a small database kept in one file; SRS keeps the Power & cost history in one. See: User Guide 6.11.
  • srs-root - the SRS root helper, started from Menu > Run as root; it saves root-only data (such as real resource addresses) for SRS to read. See: buses-2, srs-items.
  • SSD - Solid-state drive: storage on flash memory, with no moving parts. See: storage.
  • SSDT - Secondary System Description Table; extra ACPI code tables, often one per firmware module. See: machine.
  • SSID (Service Set Identifier) - a Wi-Fi network's name. See: network.
  • _STA - the ACPI status value of a device; SRS shows it as hex plus letters P (present), E (enabled), S (shown), F (functioning). See: machine.
  • Standing charge - what an electricity supplier charges per day whatever you use. See: User Guide 6.11.
  • statvfs - The system call that returns a mounted filesystem's size, free space and block size. See: storage.
  • Stratum (NTP) - how many steps a time server is from a reference clock; stratum 1 is directly attached to one. See: linux-os.
  • Subsystem ID - The second PCI ID pair, which names the board or card maker and their product built around a chip. See: buses-1.
  • Subvolume - A btrfs folder tree that can be mounted on its own, like a partition inside the filesystem. See: storage.
  • Super I/O - A motherboard chip that reads fans, voltages and board temperatures and drives fan headers (Nuvoton NCT, ITE IT87 ...). See: buses-1, sensors, tools.
  • Super-I/O - a motherboard chip (Nuvoton, ITE and others) that reads fan speeds, voltages and board temperatures. See: srs-items.
  • SuperSpeed / SuperSpeed+ - USB 3 speeds: 5 Gbps (SuperSpeed, USB 3.2 Gen 1) and 10 or 20 Gbps (SuperSpeed+, Gen 2 and Gen 2x2). See: buses-2.
  • SVI - Serial VID Interface; the link a CPU uses to ask the board's voltage regulator for a voltage and read it back. See: processors.
  • SVM / AMD-V - AMD's hardware virtualization feature (Secure Virtual Machine). See: processors.
  • Swap - disk space or compressed RAM used when real RAM is full; the Linux version of the Windows paging file. See: linux-os, machine, storage.
  • Swappiness - a kernel setting for how eagerly memory is moved to swap. See: srs-items.
  • sysctl - a kernel setting you can read and change at run time, under /proc/sys. See: srs-items.
  • sysfs - The /sys folder tree where the kernel shows devices and their settings as small text files. See: buses-1, graphics, storage.
  • System call - a request from a program to the operating system kernel (open a file, read the clock, start a thread); the cost of crossing from the program into the kernel and back. See: tools.
  • systemd target - a named group of systemd units that the system boots into, similar to a Windows boot mode. See: linux-os.
  • systemd unit - a systemd configuration object (service, socket, timer...); a service unit is the Linux version of a Windows service. See: linux-os.

T

  • Taint flag - a kernel record of an unusual condition since boot (unsigned module, hardware error, warning); it clears only on reboot. See: linux-os.
  • TBW - Terabytes written: the amount of data an SSD maker rates the drive to survive. See: storage.
  • TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) - the reliable, ordered connection protocol used by the web, SSH and most apps. See: network.
  • TCP states - the stages a TCP connection goes through, such as Listen, Established, Close Wait and Time Wait. See: network.
  • Tctl - AMD's control temperature, the CPU temperature value used for fan control and throttling. See: sensors, tools.
  • Tctl / Tccd - AMD temperatures: Tctl is the control value used for fans and limits (may include an offset), Tccd is each core die. See: processors.
  • Thermal zone - A firmware-defined temperature area with trip points (passive, active, hot, critical); common on laptops. See: sensors, srs-items.
  • Thermistor - A resistor whose value changes with temperature; most board temperature probes are thermistors. See: sensors.
  • THP (Transparent Huge Pages) - grouping memory into 2 MB pages automatically so the CPU spends less time on address lookups. See: linux-os, srs-items.
  • Thread state - a one-letter code: R running, S sleeping, D waiting on hardware, T stopped, Z zombie. See: srs-items.
  • Threaded dispatch - an interpreter technique where each instruction jumps straight to the next one's code instead of going back through one big switch. See: tools.
  • Threshold - The SMART failure line for an attribute; a normalised value at or below it means the attribute has failed. See: storage.
  • Throttling - the CPU lowering its clock to stay under a temperature or power limit. See: tools.
  • Thunderbolt - Intel's high-speed port that carries PCI Express, DisplayPort and USB over one cable; USB4 is based on it. See: buses-2.
  • Tiered price - an electricity price that changes after so many kWh a month. See: User Guide 6.11.
  • Time-of-use price - an electricity price that depends on the hour and the day. See: User Guide 6.11.
  • Timer slack - how much later than asked Linux may wake a sleeping thread, so that wake-ups can be grouped to save power; 50 µs by default. See: tools.
  • Tjmax - the highest temperature a CPU allows before it throttles itself. See: tools.
  • TLB shootdown - an interrupt one CPU sends others to make them forget cached address translations after memory mappings change. See: buses-2.
  • TLS handshake - setting up the encrypted connection that https uses, before any data flows. See: tools.
  • TPM - Trusted Platform Module; a security device that stores keys and measures the boot process. See: machine.
  • Transparent huge pages (THP) - Linux handing out memory in 2 MiB pages instead of 4 KiB ones when it can, so the CPU needs fewer page-table look-ups. See: tools.
  • TRIM - A command that tells an SSD which blocks no longer hold data, so it can erase them ahead of time. See: storage.
